explanation.summary: AF management in HFrEF stacks several constraints: (1) most class I antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone) are contraindicated due to CAST trial mortality signal in structural heart disease; (2) sotalol has negative inotropy and is contraindicated in reduced LVEF; (3) amiodarone is the only oral AAD with adequate safety profile in HFrEF but carries thyroid/hepatic/pulmonary toxicity; (4) digoxin has rate-control role but no mortality benefit and possible neutral-to-harmful long-term effect; (5) catheter ablation has level I evidence (CASTLE-AF) for reduced mortality and HF hospitalisation in HFrEF + AF and is now CSANZ/ESC Class IIa recommendation. Workflow: optimise GDMT, ensure anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc + apixaban first-line), exclude LV thrombus on echo, refer for catheter ablation if symptomatic and recurrent.
key_points: Class IC AADs (flecainide, propafenone) contraindicated in structural HD
Sotalol contraindicated in HFrEF
Amiodarone usable but with multi-organ toxicity profile
CASTLE-AF: ablation reduces mortality + HF hospitalisation in HFrEF + AF
Confirm no LV thrombus on echo before cardioversion or ablation
explanation.pearls: When considering rhythm control in HFrEF + AF in 2026 practice, always ask if catheter ablation is available - the evidence base now favours ablation over amiodarone for symptomatic patients on optimised GDMT.

options.rationale: Digoxin is a reasonable adjunct for rate control in HFrEF + AF when beta-blocker alone is insufficient, but the AFFIRM-AF and CASTLE-AF era has shifted preference toward rhythm control in HFrEF + AF given mortality and HF hospitalisation benefits. Source: ESC/CSANZ AF Guidelines.

MULTI-STEP LADDER CONSTRAINT: in HFrEF + AF, catheter ablation has demonstrated reduced all-cause mortality and HF hospitalisation (CASTLE-AF 2018) and is now Class IIa recommendation in CSANZ + ESC guidelines for symptomatic HFrEF + AF. Patient is on optimised GDMT, has no contraindication, LV thrombus excluded, anticoagulation in place. AAD options are constrained in HFrEF: amiodarone is the only oral AAD with adequate safety profile (flecainide and sotalol contraindicated in HFrEF), but amiodarone carries thyroid, hepatic, pulmonary toxicity and is reserved when ablation is not feasible. Ablation offers the strongest evidence base for prognostic and symptomatic benefit. Source: CSANZ HF Position; ESC AF Guidelines; CASTLE-AF.
Flecainide is CONTRAINDICATED in structural heart disease including HFrEF (CAST trial: increased mortality). Source: AMH; ESC AF Guidelines.
Sotalol has class III antiarrhythmic effects with negative inotropy and is contraindicated in HFrEF + reduced LVEF. Source: AMH.
Maximum recommended bisoprolol dose is 10 mg daily; 15 mg is off-label and adds bradycardia risk without proven benefit over alternative rate or rhythm control. Source: AMH.

explanation.summary: QT prolongation from additive drug interaction is a recurring exam scenario. The TIME-OF-ONSET maps each new drug to the QT change: citalopram has been stable for years and is not the trigger; the addition of azithromycin (macrolide class effect on K+ delayed-rectifier currents) followed by ondansetron (5HT3 antagonists block IKr potassium current) produces additive QT prolongation that pushes a previously controlled QTc into a high-torsades risk range. Management priorities: telemetry, electrolyte correction (Mg first, target >0.9; K target 4.5+), discontinue the most recent QT-prolonging drugs (rarely all of them - choose alternatives), monitor for torsades. CredibleMeds QTdrugs.org maintains an up-to-date list. Risk factors that compound: female sex, older age, baseline cardiac disease, renal impairment, electrolyte abnormality.
key_points: Always check QTc when adding ANY drug to a patient on QT-prolonging therapy
Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) prolong QT
Ondansetron prolongs QT (dose-dependent above 16 mg)
IV magnesium is first-line torsades prophylaxis and treatment
Replace K+ to >4.5 and Mg to >0.9 in any QT prolongation scenario
explanation.pearls: When prescribing for any patient already on a QT-prolonging drug, look up CredibleMeds.org or use eTG to verify additive risk. Doxycycline is the safer macrolide-alternative for CAP when QT is a concern.

options.rationale: Citalopram at 40 mg has been stable for 6 years with prior QTc 440 ms - it has not changed. The TIME-OF-ONSET points to the new drugs as additive contributors. Stopping citalopram alone misses the bigger discontinuation. Source: AMH.

Three QT-prolonging drugs in additive combination: citalopram (FDA black-box at >40 mg), azithromycin (class effect of macrolides), ondansetron (5HT3 antagonists). The TIME-OF-ONSET maps the QT escalation precisely to addition of azithromycin then ondansetron in the past 4 days. QTc 580 ms is a high torsades risk. Management: admit to telemetry, replace IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min as torsades prophylaxis (target Mg 0.9+), stop both new QT-prolongers (switch macrolide to doxycycline; replace ondansetron with metoclopramide which has lower QT signal); continue citalopram (long-term, no acute change). Re-check ECG 24 hours after offending drugs ceased. Source: AMH; eTG Cardiovascular; CredibleMeds QTdrugs.org.
K is 4.1 (within normal). Hypokalaemia is not the issue here. Source: eTG.
Troponin is negative; presentation is presyncope without typical ischaemic symptoms. QT prolongation in this context is drug-induced. Source: eTG.
QTc 580 ms is a high torsades risk and must be treated as a medical emergency until the offending drugs are stopped and Mg restored. Discharge is unsafe. Source: eTG.

explanation.summary: Three drug classes cause gingival hyperplasia in Australian practice: phenytoin, ciclosporin, and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine). Phenytoin is the only one that ALSO causes the cerebellar triad and hirsutism. The discriminator is the combination, not any single feature. Modern practice has shifted to levetiracetam, lamotrigine and valproate for generalised epilepsy, but phenytoin remains in use for status epilepticus and in patients stable on long-standing therapy.
key_points: Gingival hyperplasia: phenytoin > ciclosporin > CCBs
Hirsutism + gingival hyperplasia = phenytoin or ciclosporin
Add cerebellar signs = phenytoin
GGT rise reflects enzyme induction, not hepatotoxicity
Consider switching to levetiracetam if cosmetic burden is significant
explanation.pearls: Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics in the therapeutic range; a small dose increase can tip into toxicity. Free phenytoin level is more useful than total in hypoalbuminaemia or pregnancy.

options.rationale: The classic quartet of gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, cerebellar signs (nystagmus, ataxia, intention tremor), and raised GGT is pathognomonic for chronic phenytoin therapy, mediated by altered fibroblast collagen turnover, androgenic effects, dose-dependent cerebellar toxicity, and hepatic enzyme induction. Coarsening of facial features is also recognised.
Causes gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism but not cerebellar signs or nystagmus; would also expect hypertension and renal impairment. (Source: AMH).
Calcium-channel blockers cause gingival hyperplasia but do not cause hirsutism or cerebellar ataxia. (Source: AMH).
Causes tremor, weight gain, hair LOSS (alopecia) not hirsutism, and hepatotoxicity; does not cause gingival hyperplasia. (Source: AMH).
Causes cognitive slowing, paraesthesiae, weight loss and renal stones; no gingival hyperplasia or hirsutism. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) is driven by inhaled organic antigens (avian proteins, mould, isocyanates) producing a non-IgE immune reaction in alveoli and bronchioles. The chronic form looks like restrictive ILD; the discriminator is exposure history. Mid-upper-lobe predominance and centrilobular nodules differ from IPF (basal, reticular, honeycomb) and sarcoid (lymphadenopathy). Antigen avoidance is the central management step - even before steroids - because continued exposure causes irreversible fibrosis.
key_points: Bird-fancier's lung is the prototypical chronic HP exposure
Mid-upper-lobe centrilobular nodules + ground glass = HP pattern
Restrictive PFTs with low DLCO and exercise desaturation
Antigen avoidance is mandatory and primary therapy
Precipitating IgG (against pigeon serum) supports but does not exclude
explanation.pearls: Always ask explicitly about birds, hot tubs, mould exposure, and farming - patients rarely volunteer these on standard history. The Central Coast and Hunter regions have an active pigeon-racing culture, making this a regionally relevant differential.

sources.label: TSANZ Interstitial Lung Disease Position Statement

options.rationale: IPF is basal-predominant with honeycombing and reticulation, age >60 with insidious onset, and would show a UIP pattern on CT - not mid-upper-lobe ground glass with centrilobular nodules. Source: TSANZ/Lung Foundation Australia IPF guidelines.

The pigeon loft, easily lost in a long social history, is the exposure that makes the diagnosis. Avian antigens (bird droppings, feathers, bloom proteins) drive a type III/IV hypersensitivity reaction producing centrilobular nodularity and ground-glass with mid-upper-lobe predominance - exactly the imaging described. Restrictive PFTs with reduced DLCO, fine crackles without clubbing in a non-smoker fit. Source: TSANZ Interstitial Lung Disease Position Statement; Cormier 2016.
source_refs: TSANZ Interstitial Lung Disease Position Statement

options.rationale: Brief brake-pad exposure 40 years ago is below threshold for asbestos disease, and asbestos causes pleural plaques or asbestosis with basal reticulation - not centrilobular nodularity. Source: ATS/ERS Asbestos guidelines.

Sarcoidosis would typically show bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with upper-lobe interstitial change and is age 20-40 in most Australian cohorts; ACE level and Ca often abnormal. The imaging here lacks lymphadenopathy and ANA/ENA are non-discriminating. Source: TSANZ Sarcoidosis Guidelines.

COP usually has patchy peripheral or peribronchovascular consolidation rather than centrilobular nodularity, and responds rapidly to steroids - the discriminator is the imaging pattern + occupational/animal history. Source: eTG Respiratory.

explanation.summary: AIH is a T-cell-mediated attack on hepatocytes producing a hepatocellular injury pattern (ALT/AST elevation), polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia (IgG specifically), and characteristic autoantibodies. Type 1 (ANA + ASMA positive, anti-LKM-1 negative) accounts for ~75 percent of cases and presents in young adults, often with associated autoimmunity (thyroid, vitiligo, T1DM). The IAIHG simplified score combines autoantibody titre, IgG level, biopsy histology and exclusion of viral hepatitis. Treatment is prednisolone +/- azathioprine; biopsy is recommended before commencing to grade activity and exclude overlap syndromes.
key_points: Type 1 AIH = ANA + ASMA (anti-LKM-1 negative); type 2 = anti-LKM-1 or anti-LC1
Hepatocellular pattern + raised IgG + ANA/ASMA in a young woman = AIH until proven otherwise
Personal or family history of other autoimmune disease supports
Biopsy: interface hepatitis + plasma cell infiltrate confirms
Treatment: prednisolone 30-60 mg, taper, add azathioprine; long-term remission >80%
explanation.pearls: Beware overlap syndromes (AIH-PBC, AIH-PSC) - if ALP is disproportionately high or AMA is positive, image the biliary tree and consider MRCP.

options.rationale: PBC is cholestatic (ALP-dominant, raised GGT, elevated IgM) with positive AMA in 95 percent. Here ALT/AST dominate, GGT is only mildly elevated, IgG (not IgM) is high, and AMA is negative. Source: eTG Gastrointestinal.

The pattern fits AIH type 1: young woman, hepatocellular injury (ALT > ALP), markedly elevated IgG, ANA homogeneous + ASMA positive (the type 1 serology), AMA and anti-LKM-1 negative. The associated autoimmunity (vitiligo, family T1DM) supports. International AIH Group simplified criteria score >=7 (definite). Source: eTG Gastrointestinal; AASLD AIH Practice Guidance.
AIH type 2 has anti-LKM-1 or anti-LC1 antibodies (negative here) and typically presents in childhood/adolescence. ASMA-positive AIH is type 1. Source: AASLD.

PSC is cholestatic with bile-duct strictures on imaging; ALP > ALT; pANCA positive in 65 percent. Pattern here is hepatocellular and ANCA was not even part of the differential. Source: eTG Gastrointestinal.
Wilson is excluded by normal caeruloplasmin and presents with mixed neurological/psychiatric features and Kayser-Fleischer rings. AIH-like ANA + ASMA in Wilson is rare. Source: eTG Gastrointestinal.

explanation.summary: The discriminating cue is the timing of the macrolide course relative to symptom onset. Atorvastatin is metabolised by CYP3A4; clarithromycin is one of the strongest CYP3A4 inhibitors in clinical use. Co-administration produces dose-dependent rises in atorvastatin exposure and significantly increases rhabdomyolysis risk, with symptoms typically appearing within 5-14 days of macrolide initiation. Management: stop atorvastatin, IV crystalloid to maintain urine output >100 mL/h, monitor K and renal function, repeat CK trend. Restart a non-CYP3A4 statin (rosuvastatin, pravastatin) only once CK and renal function normalise.
key_points: Clarithromycin and erythromycin are strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Atorvastatin, simvastatin, lovastatin are CYP3A4 substrates
Rosuvastatin and pravastatin are NOT CYP3A4 dependent
Statin-macrolide interaction is the single most common drug-induced rhabdomyolysis in AU primary care
Always pause CYP3A4-substrate statins for the duration of macrolide therapy
explanation.pearls: Helicobacter eradication regimens almost always include clarithromycin; flag statin-substrate switching at the time of prescribing.

options.rationale: TSH is normal at 2.4, excluding overt hypothyroid myopathy. Source: eTG Endocrinology.

Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor and atorvastatin is a CYP3A4 substrate; co-administration causes a several-fold rise in plasma statin and risk of rhabdomyolysis. The TIME-OF-ONSET is the discriminator: symptoms started during/after the macrolide course on an otherwise unchanged statin regimen of >2 years. Eradication therapy is a recognised trigger. Australian Medicines Handbook and eTG both list this interaction. Source: AMH 2024; eTG Cardiovascular.

Anti-HMGCR necrotising myopathy is a recognised but uncommon statin-triggered syndrome; it tends to persist after statin cessation and has a longer subacute onset. Time-of-onset linkage to clarithromycin makes the interaction explanation more likely first. Source: ACR myopathy guidance.
Exertional rhabdo would have a clear inciting episode in the days before symptom onset; the patient denies this and bilateral proximal distribution is unusual. Source: eTG Renal.

ACE inhibitors do not cause primary rhabdomyolysis; the CK 38 400 represents true muscle injury, not a creatinine artefact, and the AKI is secondary to myoglobin nephrotoxicity. Source: KDIGO AKI guidance.

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal sits on a ladder: withhold (INR 4.5-10 stable, no risk factors) → oral vitamin K1 1-2 mg (INR 4.5-10 with bleeding risk factors OR INR >10 stable) → IV vitamin K1 5-10 mg + PCC (major or life-threatening bleeding). This patient is at INR 7.4 without active bleeding but has multiple amplifiers of bleeding risk (recent fall with extracranial haematoma, age, dementia, AKI affecting drug clearance and platelet function). That moves him from 'withhold alone' to 'low-dose vitamin K1', without justifying full PCC reversal. AKI also matters for any LMWH bridging decision: enoxaparin needs dose reduction at CrCl <30 mL/min. Long-term, anticoagulation will be reassessed after acute illness resolves; falls themselves are not an absolute contraindication if HAS-BLED-adjusted benefit favours continuation.
key_points: INR 4.5-10, no bleeding, no risk factors: withhold alone
INR 4.5-10, no bleeding, but bleeding risk factors: add oral vitamin K1 1-2 mg
INR >10 or any major bleed: IV vitamin K1 5-10 mg + Prothrombinex-VF
Renal impairment: enoxaparin at CrCl <30 mL/min needs dose reduction or switch to UFH
AKI also impairs warfarin metabolism and platelet function - lower threshold for reversal
explanation.pearls: Antibiotics that potentiate warfarin: ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, macrolides, azoles. Anticipate INR rise and pre-emptively reduce warfarin dose.

options.rationale: Withholding alone is appropriate for INR 4.5-10 in a stable patient without bleeding; this patient has multiple bleeding risk factors (recent fall with extracranial haematoma, AKI raising drug-handling unpredictability, age, dementia) that push the threshold for active reversal. Source: BSH Anticoagulation Guidelines; eTG Cardiovascular.

INR 4.5-10 without bleeding but with elevated bleeding risk (recent head trauma + extracranial haematoma + AKI + age) is reversed with low-dose oral vitamin K1 1-2 mg, plus warfarin withhold and INR recheck at 12-24 hours. IV vitamin K reserved for major bleeding (not present here despite negative CT). PCC is for major bleeding. Continued AF anticoagulation is reassessed after the acute illness; not stopped permanently. Source: eTG Cardiovascular; AHA AF Guidelines; ANZSBT/NBA Massive Transfusion / Warfarin reversal flowchart.

Prothrombinex-VF (Australian 3-factor PCC) plus IV vitamin K1 is for major or life-threatening bleeding, not for non-bleeding over-anticoagulation. CT brain is clear; haematoma is extracranial and not active. This is over-reversal and risks rebound thrombosis. Source: ANZSBT.

Enoxaparin at 1 mg/kg BD is contraindicated at this creatinine clearance (estimated <30 mL/min): use renally-dose-reduced enoxaparin (1 mg/kg daily) or UFH if bridging needed - and bridging itself is rarely indicated for AF cessation of <1 week. The over-anticoagulation should be reversed first, not switched. Source: AMH; AHA AF Guidelines.

Continuing supratherapeutic warfarin in a patient with AKI, recent head trauma and infection is unsafe; INR will likely climb further as antibiotics displace warfarin from protein binding and inhibit gut vitamin K synthesis. Source: eTG Cardiovascular.

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 bundle comprises lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics where possible, broad-spectrum antibiotic, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and vasopressor for persistent hypotension. Australian empirical therapy for serious urosepsis is gentamicin plus amoxicillin in the absence of beta-lactam allergy or ESBL risk. Lactate above 4 mmol/L is a key trigger for aggressive resuscitation. ICU escalation is required for septic shock not responding to initial fluid.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotic, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor
Empirical urosepsis: gentamicin plus amoxicillin in Australia
Balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg over the first hour
Lactate above 4 indicates need for aggressive resuscitation
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose by lean body weight is the Australian standard for severe gram-negative sepsis; redose at 24 hours guided by levels.

options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 bundle: blood cultures, broad spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, lactate and ICU escalation; gentamicin plus amoxicillin covers community-onset urosepsis in Australian practice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Ceftriaxone 1 g underdoses serious sepsis; metronidazole not required for urosepsis; 1 L over 4 hours is insufficient for septic shock; ward disposition undertreats severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Hypertonic saline is not first line in septic shock resuscitation; balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg precedes vasopressor; pip-taz is acceptable but balanced fluid is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Oral or narrow gram-positive cefalexin underdoses urosepsis and oral route is inappropriate in shock; deferring escalation breaches hour-1 standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Ciprofloxacin monotherapy is not first-line for severe urosepsis in Australia given fluoroquinolone resistance; bolus over 2 hours is too slow for septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 recommends noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor for septic shock not responding to 30 mL/kg crystalloid. The MAP target is at least 65 mmHg. Vasopressin 0.03 units/min may be added to noradrenaline if MAP cannot be maintained or to reduce noradrenaline dose. Adrenaline is third line. Dopamine is no longer recommended due to arrhythmia risk and worse outcomes.
key_points: Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor in septic shock
Target MAP at least 65 mmHg
Vasopressin is added second line at 0.03 units/min
Avoid dopamine in septic shock
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 200 mg per day IV is recommended in septic shock requiring ongoing vasopressor support; consider when noradrenaline is above 0.25 micrograms/kg/min.

options.rationale: Dopamine is no longer recommended due to greater arrhythmia risk and worse outcomes compared with noradrenaline in septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor for septic shock with MAP below 65 after adequate fluid resuscitation per Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Vasopressin is added when noradrenaline cannot maintain MAP, not as first-line monotherapy; pure vasopressin can cause coronary and digit ischaemia at higher doses. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
After 30 mL/kg with hyperdynamic LV and variable IVC, further large volume risks pulmonary oedema; vasopressor support is appropriate. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Adrenaline is reserved for shock not responding to noradrenaline plus vasopressin and can worsen lactate due to beta-mediated metabolic effects. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency presenting with hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia in a patient with known or unrecognised adrenal insufficiency. Immediate management is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours, isotonic crystalloid resuscitation and glucose for hypoglycaemia. Cortisol level can be sent but treatment should not wait. Sick-day rules require patients to double oral hydrocortisone for febrile illness and use IM emergency hydrocortisone for vomiting.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus is first step in adrenal crisis
Isotonic saline resuscitation, not dextrose alone
Treat glucose with IV dextrose if symptomatic
Sick-day rules: double oral dose for fever, IM if vomiting
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity that fludrocortisone is not needed acutely; restart fludrocortisone when oral intake resumes.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is unreliable in vomiting and shock; IV route is mandatory; ED short stay underestimates severity. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Dexamethasone has minimal mineralocorticoid activity and is less appropriate; oral glucose in shock is unreliable; hydrocortisone is preferred. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis requires immediate hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, isotonic crystalloid resuscitation, and glucose for hypoglycaemia; this is the standard ESA and Endocrine Society approach. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has no acute glucocorticoid effect; awaiting cortisol delays life-saving treatment; hydrocortisone is given empirically. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Methylprednisolone is acceptable but hydrocortisone is preferred for mineralocorticoid effect; pure dextrose without sodium worsens hyponatraemia; vasopressor before steroid is wrong order. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

explanation.summary: Hypotension after removal of a catecholamine secreting tumour reflects sudden loss of catecholamine drive against persisting alpha blockade and a vasodilated vascular bed. Fluid resuscitation comes first, with vasopressors added if the response is inadequate.
key_points: Anticipate hypotension in the first 24 to 48 hours after resection.
Higher than usual vasopressor doses are often required because the receptors are blocked.
Monitor for rebound hypoglycaemia as beta mediated insulin suppression is released.
explanation.context: A catecholamine secreting tumour maintains chronic vasoconstriction, which shrinks the plasma volume over months, and preoperative alpha blockade is deliberately combined with salt and fluid loading to refill that space before surgery. Clamping the venous drainage removes the vasoconstrictor drive in a single step, and phenoxybenzamine, being an irreversible antagonist, does not wear off with it. The result is a predictable, treatable hypotension rather than a surprise. The mirror image of the same physiology explains postoperative hypoglycaemia: with beta adrenergic suppression of insulin release gone, insulin secretion rebounds and the glucose falls.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Removing the tumour withdraws the catecholamine drive while irreversible alpha blockade persists, unmasking a vasodilated and relatively underfilled circulation. Volume is the first response, with vasopressors reserved for a poor reply to fluid. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Noradrenaline is added where hypotension persists after adequate volume replacement, and higher doses are often needed because the receptors are blocked. It is the second step, not the first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Return to theatre is warranted where the abdomen is distended or tender, the haemoglobin is falling or the response to fluid is transient. None of those features is present. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Hydrocortisone cover is needed after bilateral adrenalectomy, or where the contralateral gland is suppressed, since those patients become steroid dependent. A unilateral procedure leaves a functioning gland. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Metaraminol serves as a temporising measure for transient hypotension under anaesthesia. Relying on a short-acting vasoconstrictor leaves the underlying volume deficit uncorrected. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal osteoporosis with fragility fracture qualifies for pharmacotherapy regardless of T-score. Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) is first-line in the absence of significant GI disease or eGFR below 35. Denosumab is second-line and requires careful long-term planning due to rebound vertebral fracture on discontinuation. Adequate vitamin D and calcium intake are prerequisites and ongoing during therapy. Bone turnover markers and DEXA support monitoring of response.
key_points: Oral bisphosphonate is first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis after fragility fracture
Denosumab requires careful discontinuation planning due to vertebral fracture rebound
Teriparatide is reserved for severe disease
Maintain calcium 1000 to 1300 mg/day and vitamin D 25(OH)D above 50 nmol/L
explanation.pearls: Atypical femur fractures and osteonecrosis of jaw are rare bisphosphonate adverse effects; consider drug holiday after 5 years of oral bisphosphonate in low-risk patients.

options.rationale: Strontium ranelate has been withdrawn from many markets and is not first-line due to cardiovascular safety concerns; not recommended in current AU practice. (Source: AMH: Bone disorders)

Denosumab is second line after bisphosphonate failure or intolerance, primarily because of the rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation, requiring careful long-term planning. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guidelines)
Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis with very low T-score, multiple vertebral fractures or bisphosphonate failure; not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guidelines)

Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip fractures and is reserved for women without vasomotor symptoms or VTE risk; not first-line after hip-relevant DEXA decline. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guidelines)
Oral bisphosphonate is first-line therapy for postmenopausal osteoporosis after fragility fracture with eGFR above 35; alendronate is PBS-funded and effective. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (less than 10 percent BSA detachment), SJS/TEN overlap (10 to 30 percent) and TEN (greater than 30 percent) are dermatological emergencies. Immediate management is cessation of the culprit drug and transfer to a burns or specialised dermatology unit. Supportive care includes fluid balance, wound care, ocular surface protection, nutrition and infection surveillance. The role of systemic therapies (ciclosporin, IVIG, etanercept, steroids) is debated; SCORTEN at 24 to 72 hours predicts mortality.
key_points: SJS/TEN: cease culprit drug immediately and transfer to burns/dermatology unit
Supportive care is the foundation; specific immunomodulatory therapy is debated
Allopurinol, lamotrigine, sulfonamides, anti-epileptics are common triggers
HLA-B*5801 testing reduces allopurinol risk in high-risk populations
explanation.pearls: SCORTEN parameters: age over 40, malignancy, HR over 120, BSA over 10 percent, urea over 10, glucose over 14, bicarbonate under 20; each adds 1 to predicted mortality.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.rationale: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are managed by immediate cessation of the culprit drug and transfer to a burns or specialised dermatology unit; supportive care with fluid balance, wound care, infection control and ocular care is the cornerstone. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug is dangerous; systemic steroids in SJS/TEN have unclear benefit; cessation and supportive care are the priority. (Source: ASCIA: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.rationale: Ciclosporin has emerging evidence in TEN but is not first-line; specialised burns or dermatology unit transfer takes priority over ward-level care. (Source: ASCIA: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.rationale: IVIG is controversial in SJS/TEN with conflicting evidence; transfer to specialised unit is the priority intervention. (Source: ASCIA: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics in SJS/TEN without infection signs increase nosocomial resistance; biopsy can be done but should not delay cessation and transfer. (Source: ASCIA: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

explanation.summary: Following a first unprovoked PE, anticoagulation should generally continue beyond 3 to 6 months if bleeding risk is acceptable. The AMPLIFY-EXT and EINSTEIN-CHOICE trials demonstrated that reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) effectively reduce recurrent VTE without significantly increasing major bleeding compared with full-dose. Bleeding risk should be reviewed annually. Provoked VTE with a transient major risk factor typically requires only 3 months of anticoagulation.
key_points: Unprovoked PE: extended anticoagulation beyond 6 months if bleeding risk acceptable
Reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily preferred for extended phase
Annual review of bleeding risk and goals of care
Aspirin alone is much less effective than reduced-dose DOAC
explanation.pearls: Provoked VTE with transient major risk factor (surgery, trauma, immobility) typically warrants only 3 months of anticoagulation; cancer-associated VTE requires DOAC or LMWH for 6 months minimum.

options.rationale: Off-treatment D-dimer informs risk but is not sufficient alone for cessation in unprovoked PE; extended anticoagulation is generally preferred when bleeding risk is low. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines)

After 6 months for unprovoked PE with low bleeding risk, extended therapy with reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily reduces recurrent VTE without significantly increasing major bleeding (AMPLIFY-EXT data); annual review balances ongoing benefit. (Source: THANZ VTE Guidelines)
DOACs are preferred over warfarin for VTE in absence of antiphospholipid syndrome or other contraindication; warfarin offers no advantage and adds monitoring burden. (Source: THANZ VTE Guidelines)
Aspirin reduces recurrent VTE by only about 30 percent compared with around 80 percent for low-dose DOAC; not preferred when DOAC is tolerated. (Source: THANZ VTE Guidelines)

Recurrent VTE risk after unprovoked event is 10 percent at 1 year and 30 percent at 5 years after stopping anticoagulation; extended therapy is generally indicated when bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: THANZ VTE Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria diagnose infective endocarditis as definite, possible or rejected. Major criteria include typical organism in 2 separate blood cultures and evidence of endocardial involvement on echocardiography (vegetation, abscess, new valve regurgitation). Minor criteria include predisposing valve disease, fever above 38, vascular phenomena (Janeway, emboli) and immunological phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis). Two majors, or one major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors satisfy definite endocarditis. Targeted antimicrobial therapy is selected by organism and valve type.
key_points: Two majors satisfy definite endocarditis
Native valve viridans strep: benzylpenicillin 4 weeks plus gentamicin 2 weeks
Surgical indications: heart failure, abscess, large mobile vegetation, persistent bacteraemia
TOE indicated if TTE non-diagnostic or for prosthetic valves
explanation.pearls: Surgery within 7 days is indicated for heart failure from valve dysfunction, perivalvular abscess, or persistent bacteraemia despite 5 to 7 days of appropriate antibiotic.

options.rationale: This patient meets definite criteria with 2 major (typical organism with 2 sets of blood cultures positive plus vegetation on echo) and multiple minor criteria; treatment is targeted not empirical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
The criteria fulfilled exceed possible; TOE may further define vegetation but should not delay treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Two major Duke criteria (typical organism in 2 cultures plus vegetation with regurgitation) confirm definite endocarditis; targeted treatment for viridans strep native valve endocarditis is benzylpenicillin 4 weeks with gentamicin for the first 2 weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Rejected requires firm alternate diagnosis or resolution within 4 days of antibiotic; this patient has classic endocarditis features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin plus quinolone is incorrect empirical cover for native-valve streptococcal endocarditis; species is already identified as viridans group streptococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis based on respiratory distress, hypotension, ipsilateral hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation and distended neck veins. Immediate decompression is required without waiting for imaging. Australian and ATLS guidance increasingly favours finger thoracostomy at the safe triangle (5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line) over the traditional 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular needle decompression because of high failure rates with needles in adults. Definitive intercostal catheter follows immediately. Positive pressure ventilation before decompression is dangerous.
key_points: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; treat before imaging
Finger thoracostomy at 5th ICS mid-axillary is preferred over needle at 2nd ICS
Avoid positive pressure ventilation before decompression
ICC follows immediately after decompression
explanation.pearls: If using needle decompression as first step, a longer 14G cannula (at least 8 cm) is recommended because the standard short cannula fails to reach the pleural space in over half of adults.

options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; awaiting imaging or starting NIV worsens the tension and delays life-saving decompression. (Source: ANZCOR Guidelines)
Volume and vasopressor without decompression do not address the obstructive shock; decompression is the only effective treatment. (Source: ATLS Australia)
Positive pressure ventilation in tension pneumothorax worsens the tension and can precipitate cardiac arrest; decompression is required before intubation. (Source: ATLS Australia)

Immediate finger thoracostomy in the safe triangle (5th ICS mid-axillary) followed by ICC is the current preferred technique for tension pneumothorax due to reliability in adults with chest wall thickness; needle decompression at 2nd ICS mid-clavicular is an alternative with higher failure rate. (Source: ATLS Australia)
Nebulisers and steroids treat COPD exacerbation not tension pneumothorax; do not address the obstructive physiology. (Source: ANZCOR Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the commonest secondary cause of hypertension and is often missed because hypokalaemia is present in only about a third of cases. Screening with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio is indicated for resistant hypertension, hypertension with hypokalaemia, hypertension with adrenal incidentaloma, hypertension under 40 and hypertension with first-degree family history of aldosteronism or early stroke. Hypokalaemia should be corrected and interfering medications swapped before testing. Confirmatory testing (saline suppression or fludrocortisone suppression) follows a positive ARR; adrenal vein sampling guides surgical decision-making.
key_points: ARR is the screening test for primary aldosteronism
Correct hypokalaemia and use non-interfering antihypertensives before sampling
Confirmatory testing follows positive ARR
Adrenal vein sampling guides surgical decisions
explanation.pearls: Verapamil and doxazosin do not interfere significantly with ARR and are the preferred bridging antihypertensives during workup.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.rationale: DST screens for Cushing's, not aldosteronism; ARR is the appropriate first test for this clinical picture. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.rationale: Metanephrines test for phaeochromocytoma; clinical picture is aldosteronism with hypokalaemia; ARR is the appropriate screen. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.rationale: Renovascular disease is a differential but ARR screen for aldosteronism comes first given hypokalaemia; spironolactone confounds ARR if started before sampling. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.rationale: Late-night salivary cortisol screens for Cushing's; no Cushingoid features present and hypokalaemia with resistant hypertension is more characteristic of aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.rationale: ARR is the screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism in resistant hypertension; medications that affect the RAAS (ACEi, ARB, beta blocker, diuretic) should be stopped where possible and replaced with non-interfering agents like verapamil or doxazosin before sampling, and hypokalaemia corrected. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, crystalloid 30 mL/kg over 3 hours if hypotensive or lactate above 4, and add vasopressors if MAP remains below 65 despite fluid. Hydrocortisone 200 mg daily is added in fluid-refractory shock. Source control identifies the focus and removes infected hardware or pus. Reassess perfusion using lactate clearance, capillary refill and dynamic markers.
key_points: Cultures before antibiotics; antibiotics within 1 hour
Crystalloid 30 mL/kg over 3 hours for hypotension or lactate above 4
Vasopressors if MAP below 65 after fluids
Hydrocortisone in fluid-refractory shock
explanation.pearls: Empirical antibiotic for urosepsis in Australia is piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 hours, or ceftriaxone 2 g if community-acquired without risk factors for resistant organisms.

options.rationale: Initial fluid resuscitation precedes vasopressors in sepsis; vasopressors are added if hypotension persists after 30 mL/kg crystalloid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Septic shock with lactate above 4 requires IV antibiotics and resuscitation; oral therapy is not appropriate for an unstable patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Sepsis hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, take cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour, crystalloid 30 mL/kg over 3 hours, vasopressors if MAP below 65 after fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Activated protein C was withdrawn from the market after PROWESS-SHOCK showed no benefit; it is not part of current sepsis management. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Hydrocortisone 200 mg per day is added in fluid-refractory and vasopressor-dependent septic shock, not as first-line ahead of antibiotics. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency suggested by pain out of proportion to skin findings, dusky discolouration, bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia over the lesion, rapid spread and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, Cr, glucose) supports the diagnosis; score 8 or above indicates high risk but should never delay surgical consultation. Management is urgent surgical debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics (carbapenem, vancomycin, clindamycin for anti-toxin effect), source control and intensive care.
key_points: Necrotising fasciitis features: pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus
LRINEC 8 or above is high risk but not required for surgery
Urgent debridement is the principal intervention
Empirical antibiotics: carbapenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin
explanation.pearls: Mortality in necrotising fasciitis approaches 30 to 50 percent and rises with each hour of delay to surgical debridement; never delay surgery for imaging.

options.rationale: Pain disproportionate to skin findings, bullae, crepitus and systemic features suggest necrotising fasciitis; cellulitis monotherapy delays critical surgical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency, not a candidate for ultrasound and outpatient oral antibiotics; rapid spread without prompt surgery is fatal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive at most and never substitutes for source control; urgent surgical debridement is the definitive treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Necrotising fasciitis features (pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, hypotension, LRINEC 8) mandate urgent surgical debridement plus empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for anti-toxin effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
MRI delays definitive surgery in suspected necrotising fasciitis; clinical diagnosis with prompt surgery and antibiotics is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Latent TB infection screening with an interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON Gold Plus or T-SPOT.TB) is standard before TNF inhibitor or organ transplant. Tuberculin skin testing is an alternative where IGRA is unavailable. Confirmed latent TB is treated with isoniazid for 9 months plus pyridoxine, isoniazid plus rifapentine weekly for 3 months (3HP), or rifampicin alone for 4 months. Biologic therapy is deferred until at least 4 weeks of treatment. Active disease must be excluded before treatment of latent infection.
key_points: IGRA preferred before TNF inhibitor or transplant
Treat latent TB with isoniazid 9 months plus pyridoxine, or 3HP, or rifampicin 4 months
Defer biologic by 4 weeks after starting LTBI treatment
Always exclude active TB before treating latent infection
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine 25 mg daily is added with isoniazid in patients at risk of neuropathy (diabetes, alcohol use, pregnancy, HIV, malnutrition) to prevent peripheral neuropathy.

options.rationale: Positive interferon gamma release assay before TNF inhibitor warrants treatment for latent TB; missed treatment carries up to 10 percent reactivation risk on biologic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Confirmed positive QuantiFERON does not require repeat for confirmation; biologic should not be started without treating latent TB. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Pyrazinamide plus ethambutol is part of treatment for active TB, not latent infection; latent TB is treated with isoniazid, rifampicin or short-course combinations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Standard latent TB regimens are 6 to 9 months of isoniazid or 4 months of rifampicin; 24-month therapy is not a current standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Positive QuantiFERON before TNF inhibitor mandates latent TB treatment; isoniazid 9 months (or rifampicin 4 months) is first line; pyridoxine prevents neuropathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Australian PBS criteria for antiresorptive therapy include prior minimal trauma fracture, T-score -2.5 or below, or high fracture risk by FRAX. First-line is oral alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly, alongside calcium and vitamin D. Intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg annually is an alternative when oral therapy is poorly tolerated. Denosumab is second line; teriparatide is reserved for severe disease. Drug holiday is considered at 5 years for bisphosphonates; denosumab cannot be stopped without follow-on therapy due to rebound vertebral fracture risk.
key_points: Prior minimal-trauma fracture or T-score below -2.5 meets PBS criteria
Oral alendronate or risedronate first line; IV zoledronate alternative
Denosumab second line; never stop without follow-on therapy
Bisphosphonate drug holiday considered at 5 years
explanation.pearls: Denosumab cessation without follow-on bisphosphonate causes multiple vertebral fracture rebound within 9 to 18 months due to rapid loss of antiresorptive effect.

options.rationale: Prior low-trauma fracture and T-score below -2.5 meet PBS criteria for oral bisphosphonate; alendronate weekly is first line; review at 5 years considers drug holiday. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)
Denosumab is second line where bisphosphonate is poorly tolerated or contraindicated; ceasing calcium is unsafe and risks hypocalcaemia with denosumab. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)
HRT is not first-line for established osteoporosis in a 68-year-old; absolute thromboembolism risk exceeds vasomotor benefit at this age. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)
Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple vertebral fractures or failure of bisphosphonate, not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

Raloxifene is reserved for vertebral fracture prevention in women intolerant of bisphosphonates; it does not reduce hip fracture risk and is not first line here. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Indications for early surgery in active infective endocarditis include heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate antibiotics, perivalvular extension, abscess, fistula), and prevention of embolism (mobile vegetations greater than 10 mm with prior embolism or larger than 15 mm). Heart failure due to severe valvular regurgitation is the most common class I indication and typically requires surgery within 24 to 48 hours. Antibiotics are continued throughout the perioperative period and adjusted based on intra-operative cultures.
key_points: Heart failure from valve dysfunction is class I urgent surgical indication
Uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia) also class I
Vegetations greater than 10 to 15 mm with embolic risk warrant surgery
Antibiotics continue around surgery
explanation.pearls: MSSA native valve endocarditis is treated with flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours for 4 to 6 weeks; vancomycin is reserved for MRSA or severe penicillin allergy.

options.rationale: Heart failure from severe acute aortic regurgitation in infective endocarditis is a class I indication for urgent surgery; delay risks decompensation and death. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

New heart failure from severe valvular regurgitation in active endocarditis is a class I indication for urgent surgery within 24 to 48 hours; ongoing antibiotics continue around surgery. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

Routine gentamicin in MSSA native valve endocarditis is no longer recommended due to nephrotoxicity without survival benefit; surgery is indicated here irrespective. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

MSSA is best treated with flucloxacillin; vancomycin is inferior in MSSA. Embolic risk does not generally delay urgent surgery for haemodynamic indications. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)
Medical therapy temporises but does not address acute severe AR; delay for 1 week risks fatal decompensation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Cushing's syndrome screening uses first-line tests that capture loss of diurnal cortisol rhythm or feedback suppression: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol below 50 nmol/L excludes), late-night salivary cortisol (low at night in normal), and 24-hour urinary free cortisol. Two abnormal first-line tests confirm hypercortisolism. Subsequent ACTH measurement classifies as ACTH-dependent (pituitary adenoma or ectopic) vs ACTH-independent (adrenal). Localisation by MRI pituitary or adrenal CT follows.
key_points: Screen with 1 mg DST, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24-hour UFC
Two abnormal first-line tests confirm hypercortisolism
ACTH classifies dependent vs independent
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation
explanation.pearls: False positives on 1 mg DST occur with oestrogen (raised CBG), depression, alcohol use, obesity and pregnancy; consider these before pursuing further testing.

options.rationale: Random cortisol does not screen for Cushing's because of pulsatility; loss of diurnal variation is the key abnormality, requiring late-night cortisol or 1 mg DST. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)
Imaging is not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome; biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism precedes localisation imaging. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)

Endocrine Society guidance recommends two abnormal first-line tests from 1 mg overnight DST, late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol to confirm Cushing's syndrome before localisation. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)
Insulin tolerance test assesses adrenal insufficiency, not Cushing's; it is not a Cushing's screen. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)

High-dose dexamethasone suppression (8 mg) is used to differentiate Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH after confirmation; it is not first-line screening. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)

explanation.summary: Unprovoked proximal DVT or PE carries approximately 10 percent annual recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation. Australian guidance recommends extended-phase anticoagulation beyond 3 to 6 months in patients without high bleeding risk. Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (AMPLIFY-EXT) and rivaroxaban 10 mg daily (EINSTEIN-CHOICE) are non-inferior to full dose with lower bleeding. Provoked VTE with a transient risk factor stops at 3 months. Cancer-associated VTE continues while cancer is active. Bleeding risk is reviewed annually.
key_points: Unprovoked proximal VTE: extended anticoagulation beyond 6 months
Apixaban 2.5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily extended phase
Provoked VTE (transient): stop at 3 months
Cancer-associated VTE: continue while cancer active
explanation.pearls: AMPLIFY-EXT showed extended apixaban 2.5 mg BD reduced recurrence by 80 percent compared with placebo with bleeding rates similar to placebo.

options.rationale: Aspirin offers some VTE prevention after stopping anticoagulation but is inferior to extended DOAC at standard or reduced dose for unprovoked VTE. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)

Full-dose extended therapy is appropriate but the AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily as the standard extended-phase dose, with similar efficacy and lower bleeding. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)
Higher-intensity warfarin is associated with more bleeding without efficacy benefit; DOACs are preferred in non-cancer non-valvular VTE. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)

Unprovoked proximal DVT carries 10 percent annual recurrence risk; extended-phase apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (AMPLIFY-EXT) is non-inferior to full dose with reduced bleeding and is the Australian standard. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)
Routine thrombophilia screening rarely changes management; IVC filters are for contraindication to anticoagulation, not first-line VTE prevention. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection requires immediate reduction of aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt) to limit propagation. First-line is intravenous beta blockade (labetalol or esmolol) targeting systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate below 60 per minute within 20 minutes. Vasodilators (sodium nitroprusside or GTN) are added after beta blockade if BP target not met. Pain control (IV opioid) reduces sympathetic drive. Uncomplicated type B is managed medically; type A and complicated type B require surgical or endovascular intervention.
key_points: Target SBP 100 to 120 mmHg and HR below 60 within 20 minutes
Beta blockade first; vasodilator second to avoid reflex tachycardia
Type A and complicated type B require surgery
Uncomplicated type B managed medically in ICU
explanation.pearls: Labetalol IV bolus 20 mg every 10 minutes (max 300 mg) or infusion at 0.5 to 2 mg/min is the Australian first-line agent; esmolol is an alternative when shorter half-life is preferred.

options.rationale: Vasodilator-only therapy causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic wall shear stress; a beta-blocker must be started first or alongside to control heart rate. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

Acute aortic dissection requires admission to a critical care setting with continuous IV antihypertensive therapy, not single-bolus management and discharge. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically first; TEVAR is for complicated dissection (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, rapid expansion). (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

Furosemide does not address aortic wall shear; pain management is adjunctive; primary therapy is beta blockade plus vasodilator to lower systolic BP and dP/dt. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

Acute type B dissection requires immediate IV beta-blockade with systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate below 60 to reduce aortic wall shear stress and dP/dt; labetalol is the standard first agent in Australia. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

explanation.summary: HFrEF guideline-directed medical therapy comprises four pillars with additive prognostic benefit: ACEi/ARB (switch to sacubitril/valsartan when tolerated), beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol), MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) and SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin). Each is up-titrated to target or maximum tolerated dose. SGLT2 inhibitors benefit HFrEF regardless of diabetes status, with risk reduction of 25 to 30 percent for HF hospitalisation and CV death. Ivabradine is added when sinus rhythm with HR 70 or above persists despite optimal beta-blocker.
key_points: Four pillars: ARNI/ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i
SGLT2 inhibitor benefit independent of diabetes
ARNI requires 36-hour washout from ACEi
Ivabradine for sinus rate 70+ despite optimal beta-blocker
explanation.pearls: Sacubitril/valsartan reduces NT-proBNP within 4 weeks; transient hypotension is the commonest reason for dose reduction during titration.

options.rationale: Up-titration of ACEi is reasonable but the bigger gain is adding the fourth pillar SGLT2 inhibitor, which reduces hospitalisation and mortality in HFrEF irrespective of diabetes status. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)
MRA discontinuation in stable HFrEF removes a mortality-reducing pillar; SGLT2i is added in addition, not in place of, MRA. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)

Ivabradine is added when sinus rhythm with HR 70 or above persists despite maximum tolerated beta-blocker; HR 68 with first-line GDMT incomplete does not warrant ivabradine yet. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)
Digoxin is reserved for symptom control after the four pillars are optimised or when AF coexists; it has no mortality benefit. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)

Australian guidance for symptomatic HFrEF on ACEi recommends switching to sacubitril/valsartan (after washout) and adding SGLT2 inhibitor; the four pillars (ARNI/ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) provide additive prognostic benefit. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Septic shock is defined by sepsis plus persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor to maintain MAP 65 or above AND serum lactate over 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4, vasopressor (noradrenaline first-line) if MAP under 65 despite fluid. Source control as soon as feasible. Stress-dose hydrocortisone 200 mg per day is added in fluid- and vasopressor-refractory shock. Critical care input is required.
key_points: Septic shock: vasopressor + lactate over 2 despite fluid
Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor
Lactate, cultures, antibiotics within first hour
Hydrocortisone for refractory shock on rising vasopressor
explanation.pearls: Peripheral noradrenaline can be safely commenced through a large bore (16G or larger) antecubital cannula for up to 24 hours while central access is arranged; do not delay vasopressor waiting for central line.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: De-escalation occurs after clinical improvement and culture results; immediate priority in septic shock is haemodynamic stabilisation, not antibiotic switching. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Persistent MAP under 65 after 30 mL/kg crystalloid defines fluid-refractory septic shock; ongoing fluid risks pulmonary oedema without improving perfusion, and vasopressor is the next step. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Septic shock unresponsive to 30 mL/kg fluid resuscitation requires vasopressor (noradrenaline first-line) to target MAP 65 or above and parallel critical care consultation; further fluid alone risks pulmonary oedema without restoring perfusion. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Stress-dose hydrocortisone is added in septic shock requiring noradrenaline at moderate dose; it is not first-line ahead of vasopressor. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Source control is important but septic shock unresponsive to fluid demands immediate vasopressor; catheter alone does not restore perfusion. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is guided by the CHA2DS2-VA score in Australia (replacing CHA2DS2-VASc, sex no longer a modifier). Score 1 or higher: anticoagulation indicated. DOACs are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF. Choice in CKD: apixaban is preferred in CKD stages 3 to 4 due to lowest renal clearance (27 percent); dabigatran is contraindicated when eGFR is under 30 and used cautiously 30 to 50; rivaroxaban dose-reduced to 15 mg daily for eGFR 15 to 49. Apixaban dose reduces to 2.5 mg twice daily only if 2 of 3 criteria met: age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 or above. Warfarin remains preferred for mechanical valves and significant mitral stenosis.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA score (sex removed) guides anticoagulation
Apixaban preferred in CKD stage 3 to 4
Dabigatran contraindicated eGFR under 30
Apixaban dose reduction: 2 of 3 of age 80+, weight 60 or less, creatinine 133+
explanation.pearls: Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban; for dabigatran, idarucizumab reverses fully within 5 minutes for emergency procedures or major bleeding.

options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is acceptable in CKD stage 3 at reduced dose but apixaban has lower renal dependence and lower major bleed risk in this population. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)
DOACs are permitted across CKD stages 1 to 4 with dose adjustment; apixaban is preferred in CKD stage 3 to 4 because of lowest renal clearance. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)
Dabigatran is 80 percent renally cleared and is contraindicated when eGFR is under 30 and used cautiously between 30 and 50; apixaban remains preferred in CKD. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

Apixaban has the lowest renal clearance of the DOACs and is preferred in CKD stage 3b; dose reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily only when 2 of 3 criteria met (age 80+, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above). (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)
Aspirin monotherapy is not effective stroke prevention in AF and is not recommended; anticoagulation is indicated based on CHA2DS2-VA. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 mmol/L or above, or any level with ECG changes) requires staged emergency management. Step 1: cardiac membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes (effect within 3 minutes, lasts 30 to 60 minutes; repeat if ECG changes persist). Step 2: intracellular shift with IV insulin 10 units plus 50 mL 50 percent dextrose (effect 15 to 30 minutes); add nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg as adjunct shifter. Step 3: potassium removal via resin (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, patiromer) or dialysis. Step 4: stop ACE inhibitor, MRA, trimethoprim and other contributing drugs. Underlying acidosis correction with bicarbonate is reserved for metabolic acidosis with pH below 7.2.
key_points: Calcium gluconate stabilises membrane within 3 minutes
Insulin/dextrose and salbutamol shift potassium intracellularly
Resins and dialysis remove potassium
Stop ACEi, MRA, trimethoprim and other contributors
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim blocks the epithelial sodium channel similarly to amiloride, causing hyperkalaemia especially when combined with ACEi or MRA; check potassium within 7 days of starting if on these medications.

options.rationale: Resin therapy has slow onset (hours) and is inadequate as the sole acute intervention; calcium plus insulin/dextrose are required for ECG changes. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)
QRS widening on ECG indicates membrane instability and calcium gluconate is the immediate priority; insulin acts via slower potassium redistribution. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

Hyperkalaemia with QRS widening is a cardiac emergency; calcium gluconate stabilises the membrane within minutes, followed by insulin/dextrose and salbutamol for intracellular shift, then potassium removal (resin or dialysis) and discontinuation of contributing drugs. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

Dialysis is definitive treatment for hyperkalaemia but takes hours to arrange; immediate calcium and shifters must be given in the interim to protect the myocardium. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

Loop diuretic effectiveness depends on functional nephrons; in advanced CKD with anuria or oliguria, response is limited and calcium stabilisation is needed first. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

explanation.summary: A large minority of catecholamine secreting tumours are hereditary, and young age at presentation raises that likelihood. Germline testing is offered after resection, with lifelong annual biochemical surveillance and cascade testing of relatives if a variant is found.
key_points: Offer germline testing to all patients, and particularly under 50, with bilateral or extra-adrenal tumours.
Annual plasma or urinary metanephrines continue lifelong after resection.
A confirmed variant directs screening for associated tumours and testing of first degree relatives.
explanation.context: The genetics of these tumours reshaped how they are followed. Susceptibility genes cluster into a pseudohypoxic group, including the succinate dehydrogenase subunits and von Hippel-Lindau, and a kinase signalling group, including RET in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 and NF1. The group a patient belongs to predicts whether disease is likely to be bilateral, extra-adrenal or malignant, and which other tumours to look for, such as medullary thyroid carcinoma or renal cell carcinoma. That is why the question after surgery is not only whether the tumour has gone, but what its presence says about the rest of this patient's life and about their family.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Up to 40% of these tumours are driven by a germline mutation, and young age raises that probability further, so testing is offered regardless of family history. The result guides lifelong surveillance and cascade testing of relatives. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Serial computed tomography has a place where imaging surveillance is specifically indicated, such as a known syndrome with a high risk of recurrence. Annual computed tomography as routine follow up carries a radiation burden that biochemistry avoids. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Discharge from follow up is never appropriate after this tumour: recurrence and metachronous disease can appear years later, so annual biochemical surveillance continues for life. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Symptom-triggered testing suits a patient in whom no tumour was ever confirmed. After a resected tumour, recurrence is often biochemically apparent before symptoms return. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

options.rationale: Screening relatives follows once a pathogenic germline variant is identified and relatives are found to carry it. Screening relatives before the genetics are known tests the wrong people. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma guidance

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke reperfusion is governed by time window and contraindications. IV thrombolysis (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg) is offered within 4.5 hours of onset. DOAC use within 48 hours contraindicates thrombolysis unless DOAC level is undetectable or reversed. Mechanical thrombectomy is offered for proven large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1, basilar) within 6 hours of onset, extending to 24 hours with favourable perfusion imaging (DAWN, DEFUSE-3 criteria). DOAC use does not contraindicate thrombectomy. BP target before thrombolysis is under 185/110 and during the first 24 hours under 180/105.
key_points: DOAC within 48 hours contraindicates thrombolysis
DOAC does NOT contraindicate mechanical thrombectomy
Thrombectomy window 6 hours, up to 24 hours with imaging
BP target under 185/110 pre-thrombolysis
explanation.pearls: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus is non-inferior to alteplase for stroke thrombolysis with simpler administration; Australian centres are increasingly switching to tenecteplase as first-line.

options.rationale: Apixaban use within 48 hours is a contraindication to IV thrombolysis regardless of last dose timing; thrombectomy alone is preferred when thrombolysis is contraindicated. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

Heparin has no role in acute ischaemic stroke reperfusion and increases haemorrhagic transformation risk; mechanical thrombectomy is the indicated reperfusion strategy. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

Routine pre-thrombolysis DOAC reversal with andexanet is not recommended due to rebound thrombosis risk; mechanical thrombectomy is the preferred reperfusion strategy. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

Mechanical thrombectomy time window extends to 6 hours from onset and up to 24 hours with perfusion imaging selection; this patient at 2.5 hours qualifies; aspirin alone forfeits proven reperfusion benefit. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

DOAC within 48 hours is a contraindication to thrombolysis but does not preclude mechanical thrombectomy, which is the standard of care for proximal MCA occlusion within 6 hours (and up to 24 hours with imaging selection). (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis is defined as occurring within 12 months of valve surgery and is typically caused by staphylococcal organisms (Staph epidermidis, Staph aureus) acquired perioperatively. Empirical therapy is intravenous vancomycin plus gentamicin plus oral rifampicin pending blood culture results. Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites are drawn before antibiotics. Transthoracic echocardiogram is the initial imaging; transoesophageal echocardiogram is more sensitive for prosthetic vegetations and paravalvular abscess. Cardiothoracic surgical review is mandatory for prosthetic valve endocarditis to assess surgical indications including heart failure, persistent bacteraemia, large vegetations and paravalvular complications.
key_points: Early PVE under 12 months: empirical vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin
Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
TOE more sensitive than TTE for prosthetic vegetations
Cardiothoracic surgical review mandatory
explanation.pearls: Surgical indications in PVE include heart failure, paravalvular extension or abscess, persistent bacteraemia after 5 to 7 days appropriate antibiotics, fungal infection and embolic events with persistent vegetation above 10 mm.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective endocarditis

options.rationale: Native valve regimens do not cover the staphylococcal pathogens prevalent in early prosthetic valve endocarditis; vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (under 12 months from surgery) is most often Staphylococcus epidermidis or aureus; vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin is the empirical regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Streptococcus viridans is uncommon in early prosthetic valve endocarditis; staphylococcal coverage with vancomycin plus aminoglycoside plus rifampicin is the empirical standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin monotherapy is inadequate for prosthetic valve endocarditis; combination therapy with aminoglycoside synergy and rifampicin biofilm penetration is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Empirical therapy starts immediately after blood cultures drawn; deferring antibiotics in confirmed endocarditis risks valve destruction, embolic phenomena and septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis is fever, loin pain and lower urinary tract symptoms with evidence of urinary infection. The most common pathogen is E. coli, followed by Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus and Staph saprophyticus. Empirical oral therapy in non-pregnant, haemodynamically stable patients tolerating oral intake is cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days, or amoxicillin-clavulanate. Intravenous therapy (gentamicin plus ampicillin or ceftriaxone) is reserved for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, urological abnormality or failure of oral therapy. Review at 48 hours to confirm clinical improvement and switch to culture-directed therapy.
key_points: Oral cefalexin 500 mg QID for 10 days non-severe pyelonephritis
IV ceftriaxone or gentamicin plus ampicillin for severe or vomiting
Nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim short course only for cystitis
MSU before antibiotics; review at 48 hours
explanation.pearls: An ultrasound or CT kidneys is indicated for pyelonephritis failing to improve within 72 hours, recurrent episodes or any features of obstruction such as oliffuse such as oliguria or worsening loin pain with antibiotic therapy.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Three-day trimethoprim is for uncomplicated cystitis; pyelonephritis requires longer course and an agent with better renal tissue penetration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal tissue concentrations and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis; it is reserved for lower tract infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Intravenous therapy is reserved for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, urological abnormality or failure of oral therapy; oral cefalexin is appropriate here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Acute pyelonephritis in a haemodynamically stable patient tolerating oral intake is treated with oral cefalexin for 10 days with 48-hour clinical review; uropathogen susceptibility is usually adequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Empirical antibiotics are started immediately after MSU collection in confirmed pyelonephritis to limit renal damage and sepsis progression; sensitivity guides any subsequent narrowing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate reintroduction in chronically starved patients triggers intracellular shifts of potassium, magnesium and phosphate, precipitating cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure, seizures and Wernicke encephalopathy. High-risk criteria include BMI under 16, weight loss over 15 percent in three months, little nutrition for over 10 days, low potassium, phosphate or magnesium pre-feeding. Management is parenteral thiamine 200 to 300 mg before any glucose, proactive electrolyte replacement, slow caloric initiation at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day with stepwise increase over 4 to 7 days, and daily biochemistry monitoring.
key_points: Thiamine 200 to 300 mg IV before carbohydrate refeeding
Start nutrition at 10 kcal/kg/day in high-risk patients
Replace potassium, magnesium and phosphate proactively
Daily electrolytes until stable for at least one week
explanation.pearls: Pabrinex (B and C vitamins) intravenous two pairs three times daily for 5 days is the Australian first-line for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy and prophylaxis prior to refeeding in chronic alcohol misuse.

sources.label: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

options.rationale: High refeeding risk requires thiamine before carbohydrates, proactive electrolyte replacement, slow 10 kcal/kg/day caloric initiation and daily monitoring to prevent cardiac and neurological complications. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

options.rationale: Standard caloric load triggers refeeding syndrome in high-risk patients; calories must start at 10 kcal/kg/day with proactive electrolyte and thiamine replacement first. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

options.rationale: High-carbohydrate intravenous dextrose without thiamine precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and refeeding hypophosphataemia; enteral or oral is preferred with parallel electrolyte support. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults
