options.rationale: Full-rate feeding in high refeeding risk overwhelms intracellular shifts and precipitates cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure and seizures; rate must start at 10 kcal/kg/day. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

options.rationale: Extending starvation worsens nutritional deficits without addressing refeeding risk; the correct approach is cautious early nutrition with electrolyte and thiamine support. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome screening uses three recommended first-line tests, any of which can be chosen depending on patient circumstances: late-night salivary cortisol (collected at home, very sensitive for loss of diurnal nadir), 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol under 50 nmol/L at 08:00 the morning after a 23:00 dose excludes), and 24-hour urinary free cortisol (above three times upper limit of normal is diagnostic). Two abnormal screens are usually required before confirming hypercortisolism. ACTH measurement and dynamic testing (high-dose dexamethasone suppression, CRH stimulation, inferior petrosal sinus sampling) come after confirmed hypercortisolism to localise the source.
key_points: Three first-line screens: salivary cortisol, 1 mg DST, 24-hour UFC
Two abnormal screens needed to confirm hypercortisolism
ACTH differentiates pituitary, ectopic and adrenal sources after confirmation
Pituitary imaging only after ACTH-dependent confirmed
explanation.pearls: Cyclical Cushing syndrome causes intermittent biochemistry; repeat screening is often required over weeks and a single normal late-night salivary cortisol does not exclude when clinical suspicion is high.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.rationale: Random cortisol reflects pulsatile secretion and does not detect loss of diurnal rhythm or cortisol excess; it is not a recommended screening test for Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.rationale: ACTH measurement differentiates ACTH-dependent from independent causes but only after hypercortisolism is confirmed; it is not a first-line screen for hypercortisolism. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.rationale: Late-night salivary cortisol detects loss of diurnal nadir characteristic of Cushing syndrome and is one of three recommended first-line screening tests with high sensitivity and specificity. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.rationale: Pituitary MRI is reserved for confirmed ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism; pre-biochemistry imaging detects incidentalomas in 10 percent of normal people and misleads workup. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.rationale: Insulin tolerance test assesses ACTH reserve for adrenal insufficiency; it is not used to screen for Cushing syndrome and carries hypoglycaemia risk. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the most common secondary cause of hypertension, present in 5 to 10 percent of all hypertensive patients and up to 20 percent of resistant hypertension. Screening uses morning aldosterone to renin ratio after switching to non-interfering antihypertensives (verapamil, hydralazine, doxazosin, prazosin). Positive ARR requires confirmation by one of four dynamic tests (saline suppression, oral salt loading, fludrocortisone suppression, captopril challenge) before subtyping. CT adrenals plus adrenal vein sampling for lateralisation are performed after biochemical confirmation in surgical candidates under 35 with unilateral adenoma on CT or in any patient considering adrenalectomy.
key_points: Confirm ARR with saline or salt loading suppression before imaging
Spironolactone or eplerenone for bilateral or non-surgical disease
Adrenal vein sampling for lateralisation before adrenalectomy
Switch to non-interfering antihypertensives before ARR screen
explanation.pearls: Adrenal vein sampling for primary aldosteronism is operator-dependent and requires cortisol-corrected aldosterone ratios above 4 between sides to confirm lateralisation; centres with low procedural volume should refer.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.rationale: CT is performed after biochemical confirmation; incidentalomas occur in 4 to 8 percent of adults and CT cannot distinguish functioning aldosterone-producing adenoma from non-functioning incidentaloma. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.rationale: AVS is reserved for confirmed primary aldosteronism in surgical candidates after biochemical confirmation; performing it before confirmation risks unnecessary invasive testing. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.rationale: Empirical mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism without confirmation misses the opportunity for curative unilateral adrenalectomy in lateralised disease and risks side effects. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.rationale: A clearly positive ARR with biochemical features warrants confirmatory testing rather than repeat screening; delays diagnosis and risks ongoing cardiovascular damage. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.rationale: Confirmatory dynamic testing such as saline suppression, oral salt loading, fludrocortisone suppression or captopril challenge is performed after positive ARR before imaging or adrenal vein sampling. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

explanation.summary: Apixaban and rivaroxaban are direct factor Xa inhibitors. In major bleeding (intracranial, retroperitoneal, severe gastrointestinal or any with haemodynamic compromise) the specific reversal agent is andexanet alfa (recombinant decoy factor Xa) given as a bolus and infusion. Where andexanet is unavailable, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate at 25 to 50 units/kg is the recommended alternative based on observational and limited randomised evidence. Activated charcoal 50 g is given if the last dose was within 2 hours. Tranexamic acid may be added for mucosal bleeding. Dabigatran reversal is specifically idarucizumab. Warfarin is reversed with intravenous vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC.
key_points: Apixaban or rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa, then 4F-PCC if unavailable
Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g as two 2.5 g boluses
Warfarin: vitamin K 10 mg IV plus 4F-PCC 25 to 50 units/kg
Charcoal only if DOAC dose within 2 hours
explanation.pearls: Apixaban-specific calibrated anti-Xa activity assay can quantify drug effect when available; standard APTT and INR are insensitive to therapeutic apixaban concentrations.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.rationale: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor); it has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban or rivaroxaban. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is the specific factor Xa inhibitor reversal agent but where unavailable, 4-factor PCC 25 to 50 units/kg is the recommended option for apixaban or rivaroxaban major bleeding. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.rationale: Vitamin K and FFP reverse warfarin not DOACs; vitamin K has no role in factor Xa inhibitor reversal and FFP volume causes harm without correcting coagulopathy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.rationale: Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin and partially reverses LMWH; it has no role in DOAC reversal and is not indicated in apixaban bleeding. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.rationale: Charcoal is reserved for DOAC ingestion within two hours of dose and is adjunctive only; with last dose four hours ago and ICH, primary therapy is haemostatic reversal. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

explanation.summary: Sepsis with septic shock requires the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle: measure lactate (remeasure if elevated), obtain blood cultures before antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics), administer broad-spectrum empiric IV antibiotics, give 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 or higher, and start vasopressors if MAP stays below 65 after fluid. Likely urinary source here (nursing home, suprapubic tenderness, prior prostatic surgery) justifies empirically piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin in line with eTG. Antibiotic timing is the single largest modifiable mortality factor.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors if needed
Each hour of antibiotic delay raises septic shock mortality 7-8 percent
30 mL/kg crystalloid not 1 L
Cultures before antibiotics but never delay antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Lactate over 4 mmol/L on presentation has an associated in-hospital mortality around 27 percent for sepsis even when blood pressure normalises after fluid; serial lactate trend at 2 hours is a stronger prognostic indicator than the initial value.

options.rationale: Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics, but antibiotics must not wait for results; in septic shock each hour of delay increases mortality 7-8 percent. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; ANZICS)

The hour-1 bundle for septic shock includes lactate measurement, blood and other cultures before antibiotics (without delaying antibiotics), empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 or higher, and lactate re-check. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; eTG Antibiotic)
Vasopressors are second-line after fluid resuscitation; peripheral noradrenaline is acceptable when refractory but not as initial intervention. (Source: Surviving Sepsis)
A 1 L challenge is inadequate; ANZICS and Surviving Sepsis recommend 30 mL/kg within 3 hours. Antibiotics must not be deferred until BP normalises. (Source: ANZICS)
Source control imaging is important but must not delay early antibiotics; bedside catheterisation can occur alongside but does not replace empiric therapy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Suspected infective endocarditis warrants empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics after three sets of blood cultures from separate venepunctures. In a native valve IE with intravenous drug use, S. aureus is the dominant pathogen; empiric flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is first-line per Australian guidelines. Vancomycin replaces flucloxacillin if MRSA suspected (recent hospitalisation, known colonisation, severe penicillin allergy). Duke criteria are applied for diagnostic categorisation. Echocardiography (TTE then TOE if non-diagnostic) is essential and surgical referral is needed for valve perforation, heart failure, persistent bacteraemia, or large vegetations.
key_points: IVDU plus new murmur plus fevers = S. aureus dominant pathogen
Empiric: IV flucloxacillin plus gentamicin
Vancomycin if MRSA risk or penicillin allergy
Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Tricuspid valve IE in intravenous drug users frequently presents with septic pulmonary emboli and bilateral cavitating lung infiltrates rather than left-sided heart failure; CT chest should be considered when there is hypoxia even with a normal initial CXR.

options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin alone is inadequate for an intravenous drug user where S. aureus is most likely (over 60 percent of right-sided IE); broader gram-positive coverage including flucloxacillin or vancomycin is required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)
Oral antibiotics are not appropriate for empiric IE coverage; intravenous is mandatory. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

For native valve IE in an intravenous drug user, eTG recommends empiric IV flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly plus gentamicin (single daily dosing per renal function) to cover S. aureus and streptococcal species pending culture results; vancomycin substitutes if penicillin-allergic or MRSA likely. (Source: eTG Antibiotic; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
Ceftriaxone alone misses MSSA at usual doses and does not provide adequate cover for the most likely organism. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)
Vancomycin monotherapy is reserved for confirmed MRSA or penicillin allergy; gram-negative cover via gentamicin enhances activity against streptococci and provides synergy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy classically presenting with ascending symmetrical weakness, areflexia, and CSF albuminocytological dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count). Most cases follow a triggering infection (Campylobacter jejuni is the commonest). FVC less than 20 mL/kg, bulbar weakness, or rapid progression triggers ICU admission. First-line therapies are IVIG 2 g/kg total over 5 days or therapeutic plasma exchange; both are equally efficacious. Corticosteroids are not effective. Treatment is most beneficial within 4 weeks of onset and when patients are unable to walk independently.
key_points: Ascending weakness + areflexia + CSF protein high with normal WCC = GBS
IVIG and plasma exchange are equal first-line
Corticosteroids are NOT effective
Monitor FVC, bulbar function and autonomic status for ICU triggers
explanation.pearls: A 20-30 percent fall in forced vital capacity over 24 hours, or absolute FVC below 20 mL/kg, are objective triggers for ICU admission and elective intubation in Guillain-Barre syndrome; do not wait for desaturation.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in Guillain-Barre syndrome; large meta-analyses show no improvement and possible harm. (Source: Cochrane)
Oral corticosteroids are not effective in GBS; do not use. (Source: Cochrane)

Plasma exchange is an alternative first-line therapy with similar efficacy to IVIG but is logistically more demanding and less commonly available outside tertiary neurology centres; IVIG is the preferred Australian first-line in most settings. (Source: NBA; BMJ Best Practice)

IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (total 2 g/kg) is the Australian first-line treatment for GBS within 4 weeks of symptom onset, particularly when patients are non-ambulant or worsening. Plasma exchange is an equivalent alternative when available. (Source: NBA; BMJ Best Practice)
Pyridostigmine is for myasthenia gravis; GBS is a neuromuscular junction-independent demyelinating polyneuropathy. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia from ongoing menstrual loss with oral iron failure and a time-limited surgical window is a clear indication for parenteral iron in Australia. Ferric carboxymaltose is the preferred IV iron preparation (single infusion up to 1000 mg over 15 minutes, repeat at 1 week if larger replacement needed). Common adverse effects include hypophosphataemia, infusion-site reactions, and transient skin pigmentation. PBS-subsidised for documented iron deficiency where oral iron has failed or is contraindicated. Address ongoing source (menorrhagia management) in parallel.
key_points: IV iron when oral fails, not tolerated, or rapid repletion needed
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg as single infusion is Australian preferred
Treat the source: tranexamic acid, hormonal management, surgical option
Recheck Hb and ferritin 4-8 weeks after infusion
explanation.pearls: Severe symptomatic hypophosphataemia (phosphate below 0.32 mmol/L) occurs in around 1-3 percent of patients receiving ferric carboxymaltose with bone pain, fatigue and proximal weakness, typically peaking at 2 weeks - check phosphate if symptoms appear at follow-up.

options.rationale: Oral iron intolerance and ongoing menstrual loss limit oral repletion success; continuing oral iron is unlikely to achieve correction before scheduled surgery. (Source: BloodSafe; eTG)
Polymaltose is sometimes better tolerated but still requires months to correct severe iron deficiency anaemia with ongoing losses; not suitable for the 6-week timeframe. (Source: AMH)

Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia (typically Hb below 70 or acute decompensation); not indicated for stable Hb 88 with time for IV iron correction. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)
ESAs are not first-line in iron deficiency anaemia; they require adequate iron stores to be effective and are reserved for chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy-related anaemia. (Source: AMH)

Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg single infusion is appropriate when oral iron is ineffective, not tolerated, or where rapid repletion is required (within 8 weeks); reticulocyte response begins within 5-7 days and Hb rises 20-30 g/L by 4 weeks. (Source: AMH; NBA; BloodSafe)

explanation.summary: Giant cell arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis of older adults presenting with new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms. Permanent visual loss occurs in 15-30 percent of untreated cases. Australian Rheumatology Association guidelines specify pulsed IV methylprednisolone for visual involvement, oral prednisolone 40-60 mg daily for non-visual disease, with temporal artery biopsy within 7-14 days retaining sensitivity. Adjunctive low-dose aspirin reduces cerebrovascular events. Long-term tocilizumab is steroid-sparing for relapsing GCA. PMR co-occurs in 40-50 percent.
key_points: Visual symptoms - IV methylpred pulses; non-visual - oral prednisolone 40-60 mg
Biopsy within 7-14 days of starting steroids remains diagnostic
ESR and CRP not specific; clinical diagnosis takes priority
Aspirin adjunct; tocilizumab steroid-sparing
explanation.pearls: Bilateral temporal artery biopsy increases yield by 5-10 percent over unilateral but a single 1-2 cm specimen is usually sufficient; skip lesions limit shorter biopsies, so insist on at least 1 cm of artery in the sample.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement
BMJ Best Practice: Giant Cell Arteritis

options.rationale: Visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax) in suspected giant cell arteritis mandate immediate high-dose IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days to prevent permanent vision loss; temporal artery biopsy within 7-14 days remains positive despite steroids. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

options.rationale: Delaying steroids until biopsy risks permanent vision loss within hours to days; biopsy positivity remains adequate for 7-14 days after starting steroids. (Source: ARA)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

options.rationale: 40 mg oral prednisolone is appropriate for non-visual GCA, but visual symptoms warrant IV pulses for the first 3 days. (Source: ARA)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

options.rationale: Aspirin is adjunctive; alone it does not address the inflammatory mechanism and risk of permanent visual loss is unaddressed. (Source: ARA)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

options.rationale: Temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) has high specificity in expert hands but biopsy remains gold standard in Australia; do not delay treatment for either investigation. (Source: ARA)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

explanation.summary: Acute adrenal crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock unresponsive to fluid alone. Mortality is around 1 in 200 per patient-year despite known diagnosis and stress-dose education. Management is immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, followed by 200 mg/24h infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours, plus IV saline and dextrose. Investigate precipitant (infection commonest), continue stress doses until oral tolerated, then halve daily until baseline. All patients with adrenal insufficiency should have a Medic Alert bracelet and emergency hydrocortisone for self-injection.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: hypotension + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia
Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, do not wait for cortisol result
Saline 1 L stat, dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Investigate precipitant (infection most common)
explanation.pearls: Patients with adrenal insufficiency on long-term hydrocortisone must double or triple their daily dose during acute illness or fever above 38 degrees, and switch to IM hydrocortisone 100 mg self-injection for any vomiting episode lasting more than 1 hour - failure to do so is the commonest precipitant of crisis.

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis; treatment must not await laboratory confirmation; mortality rises sharply with each hour of delay. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat (then 50 mg 6-hourly or 200 mg/24h infusion), 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 1 hour, and dextrose for hypoglycaemia are the cornerstones of adrenal crisis management. Hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and modest mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: ESA; AMH)
Oral prednisolone is unreliable when the patient is vomiting and has potentially impaired gut absorption; IV access is mandatory. (Source: ESA)
Dexamethasone is acceptable if hydrocortisone unavailable, but lacks mineralocorticoid activity needed for hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia in primary adrenal crisis. (Source: ESA)
Vasopressors are second-line if hypotension persists after steroid replacement and fluid resuscitation; replacing the missing hormone treats the cause. (Source: ESA)

explanation.summary: Migraine prophylaxis is considered for 4 or more attacks per month or significant disability. First-line agents in Australia include propranolol (avoid in asthma, bradycardia), candesartan (good pregnancy profile), topiramate (teratogenic - oral cleft risk), amitriptyline, and sodium valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential). Newer CGRP-monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) are PBS-restricted to refractory cases with failed 3 prior preventives. Treatment is reviewed at 3 months. Acute attacks treated with triptans or NSAIDs.
key_points: Migraine prevention if 4 or more per month or disabling
First-line AU: propranolol, candesartan, topiramate, amitriptyline
Valproate banned in women of childbearing age (PPP TGA)
Topiramate teratogenic; counsel pre-conception
explanation.pearls: Candesartan 16 mg daily has emerging evidence as a first-line migraine preventive with the best pregnancy compatibility (taper before conception), suiting women planning pregnancy who cannot tolerate propranolol; effect onset is 6-8 weeks.

options.rationale: Propranolol is contraindicated by recurrent symptomatic bradycardia and risk in asthma; restart is not appropriate. (Source: AMH)
Amitriptyline is reasonable for migraine plus tension-type headache, but topiramate has stronger evidence as monotherapy; both require pregnancy planning discussion. (Source: AMH)

Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential because of teratogenicity (neural tube defects 1-2 percent and developmental delay) and requires the Pregnancy Prevention Program; not appropriate when pregnancy is planned. (Source: AMH; TGA)

Topiramate is first-line preventive for migraine with aura, evidence-based for 50 percent or more reduction in frequency; teratogenicity (oral cleft, low birth weight) requires effective contraception and discontinuation 4-6 weeks before planned conception. (Source: AMH; eTG Neurology)
Verapamil is for cluster headache prophylaxis, not migraine; not indicated here. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (K above 6.0 mmol/L) with ECG changes is a medical emergency. Management has three phases: membrane stabilisation (IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2-5 min, immediate effect, lasts 30-60 min, repeat if ECG changes persist), potassium shift (insulin plus dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic), and elimination (loop diuretic, dialysis if oligoanuric or refractory). Identify and reverse the trigger: ACE inhibitors, MR antagonists, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, beta-blockers, renal failure, tumour lysis. In this patient, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the likely added precipitant.
key_points: K above 6.0 with ECG changes = emergency
Membrane stabilisation FIRST: IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL
Then K-shift: insulin plus dextrose, salbutamol
Identify trigger (trimethoprim, ACEi, K-sparing diuretic, AKI)
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim blocks the renal epithelial sodium channel similar to amiloride and can raise serum K by 1-2 mmol/L within days of starting in CKD patients on ACEi or spironolactone - always check K within 7-10 days of any new trimethoprim prescription in CKD.

options.rationale: Insulin and dextrose are appropriate but second after membrane stabilisation; insulin lowers K by 0.5-1.2 mmol/L over 30 minutes, acts within 15 minutes. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)
Salbutamol shifts K but acts more slowly and unreliably than insulin; appropriate as additional shift therapy after membrane stabilisation. (Source: AMH)
Bicarbonate is reserved for severe metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia and is not the first-line membrane stabiliser. (Source: KHA-CARI)

With ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS, loss of P waves) and K above 6.0 mmol/L, immediate IV calcium stabilises the myocardial membrane within 1-3 minutes (lasts 30-60 minutes), buying time for K-shifting and elimination therapies. (Source: KHA-CARI; ANZCOR)
Polystyrene sulfonate has slow onset (hours), questionable efficacy, and risk of bowel necrosis; not for acute severe hyperkalaemia. (Source: AMH; TGA Safety Alert)

explanation.summary: AU practice treats COPD exacerbation with three Anthonisen criteria with amoxicillin first-line for 5 days plus prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days. Doxycycline is an alternative when penicillin is not tolerated. Amoxicillin clavulanate or fluoroquinolones are reserved for failed first-line therapy, severe exacerbation requiring hospitalisation, or risk factors for resistance. Oxygen target in established COPD is SpO2 88 to 92 percent to avoid worsening hypercapnia.
key_points: Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS 5 days plus prednisolone 50 mg 5 days
Doxycycline alternative for penicillin allergy
SpO2 target 88 to 92 percent in COPD
Reserve clavulanate or fluoroquinolone for failure
explanation.pearls: Eosinophil count over 0.3 x10^9/L during exacerbation predicts steroid responsiveness and a lower threshold to use systemic corticosteroids.

options.rationale: Three Anthonisen criteria (dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) support antibiotic use even in the absence of fever. (Source: Lung Foundation COPD-X)
Azithromycin is reserved for penicillin-allergic patients due to AU macrolide resistance patterns in Streptococcus pneumoniae. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
Clavulanate is reserved for failed first-line therapy or risk factors for resistance; routine first-line is amoxicillin alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
Moxifloxacin is reserved for failed first-line therapy or specific resistance; routine use is discouraged due to QT and tendinopathy risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

AU first-line for moderate exacerbation is amoxicillin for 5 days plus prednisolone 5 days; the combination reduces treatment failure and hospital readmission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Occupational HIV postexposure prophylaxis is recommended for high-risk exposures including deep injury from a hollow bore needle in a source with detectable HIV. The AU first-line regimen is tenofovir disoproxil plus emtricitabine plus dolutegravir for 28 days. PEP should commence within 72 hours and ideally within 2 hours of exposure. Baseline HIV, hepatitis B and C, and pregnancy testing are arranged with repeat HIV testing at 6 weeks and 3 months. Source resistance can guide regimen changes during the 28 day course.
key_points: Start PEP within 72 hours of high-risk exposure
First-line: tenofovir DF plus emtricitabine plus dolutegravir for 28 days
Follow-up HIV testing at 6 weeks and 3 months
Hepatitis B booster if antibody under 10 IU/L
explanation.pearls: Bictegravir based fixed dose regimens are increasingly used in AU PEP due to single tablet dosing and excellent tolerability; dolutegravir plus tenofovir emtricitabine remains widely available first-line.

options.rationale: AU PEP guidance recommends a 3 drug regimen of TDF/FTC plus dolutegravir for 28 days starting within 72 hours of high-risk exposure. (Source: ASHM PEP Guidelines)
PEP is initiated immediately for high-risk exposure and not delayed for further source testing when initial viral load is detectable. (Source: ASHM)
Zidovudine has been superseded by tenofovir-based regimens in current AU PEP guidance due to tolerability and efficacy. (Source: ASHM)
Use of antiretroviral therapy in a source with detectable high viral load does not eliminate transmission risk; PEP remains indicated. (Source: ASHM)
Resistance testing should not delay PEP initiation; modification can be made if resistance is later identified. (Source: ASHM)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is defined by severe BP elevation with acute end-organ damage including encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, acute coronary syndrome, AKI, or papilloedema. Controlled BP reduction targets a 20 to 25 percent fall in MAP in the first hour, then 160/100 over several hours, with normalisation over 24 to 48 hours. Agents used in pulmonary oedema include IV glyceryl trinitrate; in aortic dissection, esmolol then sodium nitroprusside or labetalol; in eclampsia, hydralazine or labetalol. Ischaemic stroke has its own permissive hypertension targets.
key_points: MAP reduction 20-25 percent in first hour
Normalisation over 24-48 hours not minutes
GTN for pulmonary oedema; esmolol then SNP for dissection
Aim 160/100 over the next several hours
explanation.pearls: In acute ischaemic stroke, do not lower BP unless above 220/120 (or above 185/110 if thrombolysis planned), as cerebral autoregulation is impaired and over-reduction worsens infarction.

options.rationale: Hypertensive pulmonary oedema with troponin rise mandates immediate BP reduction; waiting for troponin trend delays critical therapy. (Source: NHF)
Rapid normalisation in hypertensive emergency risks watershed cerebral infarction and acute kidney injury; controlled stepwise reduction is recommended. (Source: NHF)
Over-reduction to systolic under 100 risks watershed ischaemia; goal is staged reduction not normalisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
Oral therapy is too slow and unpredictable in true hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage; IV titratable agents are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage other than ischaemic stroke is treated with controlled MAP reduction of 20 to 25 percent in the first hour to balance perfusion and tissue protection. (Source: NHF Hypertension; Therapeutic Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The hour-1 bundle for sepsis and septic shock comprises measure lactate and remeasure if elevated, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4, and noradrenaline for MAP under 65 mmHg despite fluid resuscitation. Source control is sought as soon as feasible. Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV is added for refractory septic shock requiring escalating vasopressor support.
key_points: 30 mL/kg crystalloid in first hour for hypotension or lactate over 4
Blood cultures before antibiotics where possible
Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor for MAP under 65
Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV daily for refractory septic shock
explanation.pearls: Beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside is appropriate empirical cover in adult Australian community pyelonephritis with septic shock when local E. coli ESBL rates are above 10 percent.

options.rationale: 10 mL/kg is below the 30 mL/kg hour-1 target and antibiotic escalation should be considered immediately with rapid clinical deterioration. (Source: SSC)

The hour-1 bundle for septic shock includes 30 mL/kg crystalloid, lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and vasopressors for refractory hypotension. (Source: SSC Guidelines; CEC NSW Sepsis)
Hour-1 interventions begin where the patient is recognised; ICU transfer must not delay fluid, antibiotics, or vasopressors. (Source: CEC NSW Sepsis)
Steroids in septic shock are reserved for refractory shock on adequate vasopressor support not as first-line therapy. (Source: SSC)
Concurrent fluid resuscitation should occur with vasopressor commencement; vasopressor alone without fluid does not address hypovolaemia. (Source: SSC)

explanation.summary: Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia is classified by urine chloride into saline responsive (low urine chloride from vomiting or post-diuretic state) and saline unresponsive (high urine chloride from current diuretic use, hyperaldosteronism, or Bartter and Gitelman syndromes). Surreptitious diuretic use produces a confusing biochemical picture mimicking primary hyperaldosteronism; the clue is variable urine chloride that falls when diuretics are stopped. Definitive workup includes urine diuretic screen, plasma renin, and aldosterone with aldosterone renin ratio.
key_points: Low urine chloride: vomiting or post-diuretic effect
High urine chloride: current diuretic, hyperaldosteronism, Bartter/Gitelman
Hyperaldosteronism workup with ARR after diuretic cessation
Replace potassium and magnesium together
explanation.pearls: Urine diuretic screen for thiazide and loop diuretics is a reliable test for surreptitious diuretic use and should be considered when biochemistry mimics primary hyperaldosteronism.

options.rationale: Primary hyperaldosteronism is possible and is being investigated but the urinary chloride rise during current diuretic use is most directly explained by diuretic effect. (Source: KHA-CARI)
Loop and thiazide diuretics produce urinary chloride and potassium loss with secondary metabolic alkalosis; urine chloride may be elevated during active use. (Source: KHA-CARI)
Vomiting produces low urine chloride below 20 mmol/L; this patient has urine chloride of 32 mmol/L during diuretic use. (Source: KHA-CARI)
Bartter syndrome usually presents earlier in life and is associated with normal blood pressure; this presentation is acquired and hypertensive. (Source: KHA-CARI)
The pH of 7.52 indicates alkalosis not acidosis; the elevated PaCO2 is respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis. (Source: KHA-CARI)

explanation.summary: ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement is induced with rituximab plus high dose glucocorticoid or cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoid. Rituximab is at least as effective as cyclophosphamide and is preferred for relapsing disease, women of reproductive age, and patients at high infection risk. Plasma exchange is reserved for severe pulmonary haemorrhage or rapidly progressive AKI. Maintenance is typically rituximab or azathioprine with a steroid taper; PJP prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is recommended during prolonged immunosuppression.
key_points: Rituximab plus glucocorticoid first-line induction
Cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoid alternative induction
Plasma exchange for severe pulmonary haemorrhage
PJP prophylaxis during prolonged immunosuppression
explanation.pearls: PEXIVAS trial supports a reduced dose glucocorticoid regimen with similar efficacy and lower serious infection risk; AU practice is moving away from the historical high-dose taper.

options.rationale: Azathioprine is a maintenance agent; it is not effective for induction in AAV which requires rituximab or cyclophosphamide. (Source: KDIGO)
Plasma exchange is an adjunct in selected severe disease and does not replace immunosuppressive induction. (Source: KDIGO)
Steroid monotherapy is inadequate induction; B cell depletion or cyclophosphamide is required to reduce flare and end stage kidney disease. (Source: KHA-CARI)

Rituximab plus high dose glucocorticoid is at least equivalent to cyclophosphamide for induction in ANCA-associated vasculitis including renal disease and is increasingly preferred in AU. (Source: KHA-CARI; KDIGO Glomerular Disease)
Mycophenolate is less effective than rituximab or cyclophosphamide for AAV induction and is not first-line in PR3 disease. (Source: KDIGO)

explanation.summary: Chronic hyponatraemia is corrected slowly at 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first 6 hours and under 10 mmol/L over 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Severely symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or coma is treated with bolus 3 percent saline 150 mL until symptoms resolve. Cessation of offending agents (thiazide, SSRI) and management of underlying SIADH with fluid restriction follow. Serum sodium is checked every 2 to 4 hours during active correction.
key_points: Chronic: under 10 mmol/L per 24 hours, 4 to 6 in first 6 hours
Severely symptomatic: 150 mL 3 percent saline boluses
Cease thiazide and SSRI; rule out adrenal and thyroid causes
Overcorrection risks osmotic demyelination
explanation.pearls: If sodium has risen over 8 mmol/L in 24 hours during correction, dextrose 5 percent at 6 mL/kg over 2 hours or DDAVP 2 to 4 micrograms IV can re-lower sodium to prevent osmotic demyelination.

options.rationale: Chronic hyponatraemia with mild neurology is corrected at a controlled rate of 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first 6 hours and under 10 mmol/L per day to prevent osmotic demyelination. (Source: KHA-CARI; Therapeutic Guidelines)
Fluid restriction alone is insufficient in a symptomatic patient and the offending medications should be ceased. (Source: KHA-CARI)
Continuous 1 to 2 mmol/L per hour rise overshoots the safe 24 hour limit and risks osmotic demyelination. (Source: KHA-CARI)
Rapid full correction risks osmotic demyelination; cautious rate-limited correction is the standard. (Source: KHA-CARI)
Active correction is required in symptomatic hyponatraemia; observation alone does not address the cerebral oedema risk. (Source: KHA-CARI)

explanation.summary: Preoperative preparation for phaeochromocytoma uses alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin for at least 10 to 14 days before surgery. Beta blockade is introduced only after alpha blockade is established if reflex tachycardia or arrhythmia occurs. Liberal sodium intake and adequate hydration in the days before surgery prevent post-resection hypotension. Calcium channel blockers can be used as adjuncts. Genetic counselling is considered for SDHB and other heritable syndromes especially in younger patients or extra-adrenal disease.
key_points: Alpha blockade first then beta if needed
10 to 14 days minimum alpha blockade preop
Liberal salt and hydration to prevent post-op hypotension
Genetic counselling for younger or extra-adrenal disease
explanation.pearls: Persistent post-resection hypotension may require IV crystalloid plus noradrenaline due to abrupt loss of catecholamine drive; preoperative volume expansion reduces this risk.

options.rationale: Alpha blockade is established before any beta blocker introduction in phaeochromocytoma to prevent unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis. (Source: AU Endocrine Society; Therapeutic Guidelines)
Calcium channel blockers are second-line adjunct after established alpha blockade; not first-line preoperative preparation. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)
Adequate alpha blockade for at least 10 to 14 days reduces intraoperative haemodynamic instability and morbidity. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)
Labetalol provides predominantly beta blockade and is not recommended as first-line for preoperative phaeochromocytoma preparation. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)
Unopposed alpha stimulation after beta blockade can precipitate hypertensive crisis in phaeochromocytoma. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

explanation.summary: Discrimination of ectopic ACTH from pituitary Cushing disease relies on the high dose dexamethasone suppression test, CRH stimulation, ACTH magnitude, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling when imaging is inconclusive. Ectopic ACTH typically does not suppress on high dose dexamethasone, presents with marked hypokalaemia from cortisol mineralocorticoid effect, and progresses rapidly. Pituitary Cushing usually suppresses by over 50 percent on high dose dexamethasone, has a more indolent course, and is amenable to transsphenoidal surgery. Small cell lung cancer and bronchial carcinoid are common ectopic sources. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is the gold standard discriminator when biochemistry and imaging conflict.
key_points: Ectopic ACTH: no suppression on 8 mg dexamethasone, severe hypokalaemia, rapid onset
Pituitary Cushing: over 50 percent suppression on 8 mg dexamethasone
MRI misses up to 40 percent of pituitary microadenomas
IPSS is the gold standard when discrimination is unclear
explanation.pearls: Ketoconazole, metyrapone, and osilodrostat are used to control cortisol while definitive treatment is planned; etomidate infusion is the rapid parenteral option for severe Cushing crisis.

options.rationale: Up to 40 percent of pituitary Cushing adenomas are below MRI resolution; absent MRI lesion does not exclude pituitary disease. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)
Hyperpigmentation is seen in any ACTH-dependent state including severe pituitary Cushing disease and is not specifically discriminating. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)
Magnitude of urine cortisol elevation overlaps between aetiologies and is not a discriminating test. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

Failure to suppress on 8 mg dexamethasone, severe hypokalaemia from cortisol-mediated mineralocorticoid effect, and rapid onset are typical of ectopic ACTH rather than pituitary disease. (Source: AU Endocrine Society Cushing; KDIGO)
Higher ACTH levels typically favour ectopic ACTH; pituitary Cushing more often produces moderate ACTH elevation. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

explanation.summary: Non-contrast low-dose CT KUB is the first-line investigation for adult suspected ureteric calculus, providing high sensitivity and specificity, stone characterisation, and assessment of complications. Ultrasound is the preferred first investigation in pregnancy and children to reduce radiation. Indications for urgent urology referral include obstructed infected system, single functioning kidney, bilateral obstruction, refractory pain or vomiting, and acute kidney injury. Stones less than 5 mm typically pass spontaneously.
key_points: CT KUB is first-line imaging in adults
Ultrasound preferred in pregnancy and paediatrics
Urology if obstructed-infected, AKI, solitary kidney, or refractory symptoms
Stones under 5 mm usually pass spontaneously
explanation.pearls: Low-dose CT KUB protocols deliver effective dose around 2 mSv compared with 8 to 10 mSv for standard CT, which has driven its adoption as first-line over IVU in the past decade.

options.rationale: Plain KUB misses about 30 percent of stones and underestimates obstruction; CT KUB has replaced it for first-line workup. (Source: USANZ; RANZCR)
MR urogram has limited stone visualisation, restricted availability, and high cost; CT KUB is first-line. (Source: USANZ)
IVU is largely superseded by CT KUB for stones because of higher contrast dose and lower sensitivity. (Source: USANZ)
Ultrasound is useful in pregnancy and children but has lower sensitivity for ureteric stones in adults. (Source: USANZ)
Non-contrast low-dose CT KUB is the first-line imaging in adults with suspected ureteric calculus with sensitivity over 95 percent. (Source: USANZ; RANZCR)

explanation.summary: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterised by brief electric shock pains in the trigeminal distribution triggered by light touch or chewing. Carbamazepine is the first-line evidence-based agent with response rates around 70 percent. Oxcarbazepine is an alternative with fewer drug interactions. Baclofen and lamotrigine are add-on options. Surgical options including microvascular decompression are reserved for medication failure or intolerance. Patients of Han Chinese, Thai, and other South Asian descent require HLA-B*1502 testing before carbamazepine due to risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
key_points: Carbamazepine first-line with 70 percent response
Monitor sodium and LFTs during titration
HLA-B*1502 testing in at-risk ancestry
Surgery reserved for medication failure
explanation.pearls: Carbamazepine response in trigeminal neuralgia is so reliable that lack of response within four weeks at adequate dose should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis or MRI for secondary causes such as a vascular loop or demyelination.

options.rationale: Gabapentin is a second-line agent in trigeminal neuralgia; carbamazepine has the best evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Amitriptyline is used for other neuropathic pain but is not first-line for trigeminal neuralgia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Carbamazepine is the first-line evidence-based agent for trigeminal neuralgia with sodium and LFT monitoring during titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Simple analgesics are ineffective in trigeminal neuralgia which is neuropathic; sodium channel blockers are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Surgery is reserved for medication failure or intolerance; pharmacotherapy is first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is diagnosed by the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre eliciting torsional upbeat nystagmus that latency, fatigues, and resolves. The Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre achieves resolution in about 80 percent after one treatment and over 90 percent after two. Vestibular suppressants prolong recovery and are not first-line. MRI is reserved for atypical features such as central nystagmus, focal neurological signs, hearing loss, or persistent symptoms. Recurrence is common and patients should be taught self-treatment.
key_points: Dix-Hallpike confirms posterior canal BPPV
Epley achieves about 80 percent single-treatment resolution
Vestibular suppressants prolong recovery
MRI for atypical features or persistent symptoms
explanation.pearls: Posterior canal BPPV nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike has a 5 to 20 second latency, lasts under 60 seconds, and fatigues with repetition; absence of these features should prompt evaluation for central causes.

options.rationale: MRI is reserved for atypical features, neurological signs, or hearing loss; this is classic posterior canal BPPV. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)
Vestibular suppressants are not curative in BPPV and prolong recovery; particle repositioning is first-line. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)
Specialist vestibular testing is reserved for atypical or refractory cases; bedside Dix-Hallpike with Epley is first-line. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)
Dix-Hallpike confirms posterior canal BPPV and Epley repositioning is the first-line therapeutic manoeuvre with about 80 percent single-treatment success. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)
Vestibular rehabilitation alone is slower than particle repositioning; Epley is the proven first-line treatment. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)

explanation.summary: Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots, most commonly from a central disc protrusion. Red flag features include saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction with post-void residual over 500 mL, sexual dysfunction, and bilateral leg weakness. Whole lumbosacral spine MRI within hours confirms the diagnosis and surgical decompression within 48 hours of symptom onset preserves the best functional outcome. Delayed diagnosis risks permanent bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction.
key_points: Saddle anaesthesia and retention with PVR over 500 mL are red flags
Urgent MRI within hours
Decompression ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset
Plain films and outpatient pathways are inappropriate
explanation.pearls: Bladder PVR over 500 mL with saddle anaesthesia carries a positive predictive value of about 50 percent for cauda equina on MRI, which is why the imaging threshold is low when both features coexist.

options.rationale: Plain films do not show neural compression; MRI is required for suspected cauda equina syndrome. (Source: RACS; Therapeutic Guidelines)
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when cord or cauda equina compression is suspected before imaging. (Source: RACS)
CT has lower soft tissue and neural resolution than MRI and 48 hour delay risks irreversible deficit. (Source: RACS)
Nerve conduction studies do not show structural compression and a two-week delay risks permanent loss. (Source: RACS)
Whole lumbosacral spine MRI within hours is the standard investigation for suspected cauda equina syndrome to confirm compression and guide urgent surgery. (Source: RACS)

explanation.summary: Optic neuritis presents with subacute monocular vision loss, pain on eye movement, dyschromatopsia, and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is normal in retrobulbar optic neuritis. MRI brain and orbits with contrast confirms inflammation and stratifies multiple sclerosis risk: T2 white matter lesions raise 10-year MS risk to over 70 percent. Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days speeds recovery but does not improve final acuity. Oral prednisolone at conventional doses worsens outcomes and should be avoided as monotherapy.
key_points: Subacute monocular vision loss with eye movement pain
RAPD plus dyschromatopsia with normal fundoscopy
MRI brain and orbits with contrast
Avoid oral prednisolone monotherapy
explanation.pearls: Among patients with optic neuritis and at least one T2 brain lesion on baseline MRI, the 10-year cumulative risk of multiple sclerosis is around 72 percent versus 25 percent with a normal MRI, which underpins the urgency of imaging for prognostic and treatment decisions.

options.rationale: Outpatient fields delay assessment of demyelinating risk; urgent MRI brain and orbits is the priority. (Source: MSWA; Therapeutic Guidelines)
CT brain has low yield for demyelination; MRI brain and orbits is the standard investigation. (Source: MSWA)
MRI brain and orbits with contrast is the recommended investigation to confirm optic neuritis and assess demyelinating disease risk. (Source: MSWA)
Delayed review risks missing demyelinating disease that benefits from early disease-modifying therapy. (Source: MSWA)
Oral prednisolone monotherapy at conventional doses worsens outcomes in optic neuritis; high-dose IV methylprednisolone is used when treatment is indicated. (Source: MSWA)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic facial nerve palsy is the most common cause of acute lower motor neuron facial weakness. Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days started within 72 hours of onset improves recovery rates and is the only intervention with reliable benefit. Antivirals add no clear benefit in classic Bell palsy without vesicles but should be added if Ramsay Hunt syndrome is suspected. Eye care with lubricant drops, ointment, and taping during sleep is essential to prevent exposure keratitis. Improvement typically begins by three weeks and most patients recover by six months.
key_points: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days within 72 hours
Antivirals not routinely added in classic Bell palsy
Add antivirals if Ramsay Hunt vesicles present
Eye care critical to prevent exposure keratitis
explanation.pearls: Adding aciclovir to prednisolone does not improve House-Brackmann grade I or II recovery at 9 months in classic Bell palsy without vesicles, which is why monotherapy with prednisolone is preferred in Australian practice.

options.rationale: Topical aciclovir is not effective in Bell palsy; oral prednisolone is the proven intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)
Antiviral monotherapy without corticosteroid does not improve recovery rates in Bell palsy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)
IV pulse steroid is not standard for Bell palsy; oral prednisolone within 72 hours is the proven intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)
Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days started within 72 hours improves recovery rates in Bell palsy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)
Adding antiviral to prednisolone does not improve outcomes in classic Bell palsy without vesicles. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe asthma not controlled on triple inhaled therapy is eligible for biologic therapy. Choice depends on phenotype: omalizumab requires perennial allergen sensitisation, mepolizumab and benralizumab require elevated eosinophil counts, and dupilumab targets type 2 inflammation including asthma with nasal polyps or atopic dermatitis. Tezepelumab is approved for severe asthma irrespective of phenotype. The Australian Severe Asthma Toolkit and PBS criteria define eligibility. Switching between biologics is reasonable if response is inadequate after four to six months.
key_points: Omalizumab requires perennial allergen sensitisation
Mepolizumab, benralizumab for eosinophilic phenotype
Dupilumab for type 2 asthma plus nasal polyps
Tezepelumab is phenotype-independent
explanation.pearls: Dupilumab reduces nasal polyp size and improves asthma exacerbations by around 50 percent in patients with both conditions and is the only biologic with dual PBS indication for adult asthma plus chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps.

options.rationale: Omalizumab requires documented sensitisation to a perennial aeroallergen, which is absent in this patient. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)
Mepolizumab is reasonable but does not address her nasal polyps as effectively as dupilumab in this phenotype. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)
Reslizumab is IV monthly and reserved when subcutaneous options are unsuitable; not first preference here. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)
Benralizumab is an option for eosinophilic asthma but does not target the type 2 polyp pathway as broadly as dupilumab. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)
Dupilumab targets IL-4 and IL-13 and treats type 2 asthma with nasal polyps as a combined indication on Australian PBS criteria. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)

explanation.summary: Up to 50 percent of patients with giant cell arteritis have polymyalgia rheumatica features and 15 to 20 percent of PMR patients develop GCA. Red flags for GCA overlap include new bitemporal headache, jaw claudication, transient or persistent monocular vision loss, scalp tenderness, and constitutional symptoms. Suspected GCA mandates immediate oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily, or IV pulse for established visual loss, with temporal artery biopsy within 14 days. Methotrexate and tocilizumab are steroid-sparing options. Untreated GCA risks irreversible blindness.
key_points: Jaw claudication and amaurosis are red flags for GCA
Start oral prednisolone immediately, do not delay for biopsy
Biopsy within 14 days of steroid initiation
IV pulse for persistent or progressing visual loss
explanation.pearls: Temporal artery biopsy sensitivity falls from about 80 to 60 percent if delayed beyond 14 days of steroid treatment, which is why the biopsy window is tight even though steroids start immediately.

options.rationale: The cranial features and jaw claudication indicate GCA overlap requiring high dose prednisolone, not PMR dose. (Source: ARA; Therapeutic Guidelines)
NSAIDs do not treat GCA and biopsy must not delay steroid initiation when visual symptoms are present. (Source: ARA)
Visual symptoms and jaw claudication mandate immediate high dose prednisolone with biopsy within 14 days for confirmation. (Source: ARA; Therapeutic Guidelines)
Delay risks permanent visual loss; steroids start before specialist review when GCA is suspected. (Source: ARA)
IV pulse is reserved for confirmed or progressing visual loss; transient amaurosis without current deficit is treated with high dose oral prednisolone. (Source: ARA)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis empiric therapy is stratified by valve type and risk. For native valve endocarditis benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is standard; vancomycin replaces benzylpenicillin and flucloxacillin in severe penicillin allergy or suspected MRSA. For prosthetic valve endocarditis later than 12 months post-surgery the staphylococcal risk plus biofilm formation justifies vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within 12 months) is dominated by nosocomial pathogens and uses the same regimen but with consideration of fungi. Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites and transoesophageal echo confirm the diagnosis. Surgical referral is indicated for prosthetic involvement, large vegetations, embolic events, heart failure, or perivalvular abscess.
key_points: Three blood culture sets over time before antibiotics where possible
Native valve empiric: benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin
Prosthetic valve empiric: vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin
TOE outperforms TTE for prosthetic valves and complications
Surgical referral for prosthesis, HF, abscess, large vegetation, persistent bacteraemia
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin is added for its biofilm penetration on prosthetic material, but never given alone for staphylococci because of rapid resistance emergence.

options.rationale: Penicillin and gentamicin alone do not cover staphylococcal species (including methicillin-resistant strains) that are common in prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This regimen covers native valve endocarditis but does not address methicillin-resistant staphylococci or coagulase-negative staphylococci common on prostheses. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Late prosthetic valve endocarditis requires empiric vancomycin (MRSA and coagulase-negative staphylococci), gentamicin (synergy), and rifampicin (biofilm penetration) until pathogen is known. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not adequately cover staphylococci including MRSA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Oral monotherapy is inappropriate for prosthetic valve endocarditis; intravenous combination is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle integrates measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin rapid administration of 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at or above 4 mmol/L, and start vasopressors during or after fluid resuscitation if MAP remains below 65 mmHg. For community-acquired pyelonephritis with sepsis, Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend ampicillin plus gentamicin (with renal function adjusted dosing). Source control (urological intervention for obstructive uropathy, surgical debridement, drainage) is sought as soon as possible after stabilisation.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >= 4
Vasopressor if MAP under 65 mmHg after fluid
Source control as early as feasible after resuscitation
Ampicillin plus gentamicin is first-line for pyelonephritis sepsis
explanation.pearls: Single-dose gentamicin 5 to 7 mg/kg followed by re-dosing only after a 24-hour level minimises nephrotoxicity while achieving high peak-MIC ratios in the first 24 hours of sepsis.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.rationale: The sepsis hour-1 bundle prioritises lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L; this regimen targets pyelonephritis-related sepsis per Australian guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.rationale: Imaging is important for source control but must not delay the hour-1 antibiotic and fluid bundle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.rationale: Waiting hours for susceptibilities is unsafe and contravenes the hour-1 bundle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.rationale: Vasopressor is used when MAP remains under 65 mmHg after 30 mL/kg crystalloid; fluid resuscitation is the initial response unless contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.rationale: Dextrose is not a resuscitation fluid; balanced crystalloid (Hartmann or Plasmalyte) is preferred for septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency where rapid spreading subcutaneous and fascial necrosis develops faster than overlying skin changes can keep up. The hallmark is pain out of proportion to examination, systemic toxicity, and rapidly evolving signs (oedema, bullae, crepitus, skin necrosis, anaesthesia over the affected area). The LRINEC score uses CRP, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose to risk stratify: score 6 or more is intermediate to high risk, 8 or more confirms high risk. Definitive treatment is urgent surgical debridement; empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics include a carbapenem (or piperacillin-tazobactam), vancomycin or linezolid, plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. Repeated debridement at 24 to 48 hours is the norm.
key_points: Pain out of proportion to skin findings is the key early clue
LRINEC score 6 or more raises suspicion; 8 or more confirms it
Surgical debridement within hours saves life
Empiric antibiotics: meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin
Repeated debridement and ICU support are usually needed
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added specifically to inhibit streptococcal exotoxin and panton-valentine leukocidin production, distinct from its antibacterial effect.

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not cover the spectrum of necrotising soft tissue infection and would dangerously delay surgical debridement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Imaging should never delay surgical exploration in suspected necrotising fasciitis; clinical features and LRINEC score are sufficient to act. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Delaying debridement beyond hours in necrotising fasciitis substantially increases mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Pain out of proportion to skin findings, systemic toxicity, and an LRINEC score of 8 or more (his is 11) demand emergency surgical exploration with empiric broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Flucloxacillin alone does not cover gram-negatives or anaerobes and is insufficient for necrotising fasciitis; surgery is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Osteoporosis treatment in Australia is structured by PBS criteria: minimal trauma vertebral or hip fracture, age 70 or above with T score -2.5 or lower, or prolonged corticosteroid therapy. First line is oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) or intravenous zoledronic acid annually; denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously 6-monthly is an alternative, especially in renal impairment. An incident fracture or further bone density loss while on antiresorptive therapy indicates treatment failure and consideration of anabolic therapy. Teriparatide is approved for 18 months and is followed by an antiresorptive agent (denosumab or bisphosphonate) to preserve gains. Compliance, calcium and vitamin D status, and secondary causes must be reviewed.
key_points: Minimal trauma fracture despite bisphosphonate equals treatment failure
Teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneous daily for 18 months follows
An antiresorptive agent must follow teriparatide to preserve gains
Adherence and secondary causes must be reviewed
Denosumab is an alternative escalation in renal impairment
explanation.pearls: Teriparatide is contraindicated when there is a previous skeletal radiotherapy, hypercalcaemia, Paget disease, or open epiphyses; specialist review is required for PBS authority.

sources.label: Healthy Bones Australia: Clinical practice guideline

options.rationale: Minimal trauma vertebral fracture on alendronate represents treatment failure and demands escalation. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)

An incident minimal trauma vertebral fracture despite oral bisphosphonate is an indication for anabolic therapy with teriparatide; PBS subsidy applies under specialist authority. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)
Calcitriol is reserved for renal osteodystrophy; it does not address established bisphosphonate failure. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)
Switching between oral bisphosphonates does not address treatment failure; a different drug class is required. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)
Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip or non-vertebral fracture and is not appropriate as escalation after vertebral fracture on a bisphosphonate. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion classically presents with a mononucleosis-like illness 2 to 4 weeks after high-risk exposure: fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, rash, oral or genital ulcers, with lymphopenia, raised transaminases, and atypical lymphocytes. Diagnostically, HIV RNA viral load detects virus 1 to 2 weeks post-exposure; p24 antigen detected by 4th generation tests becomes positive about 2 weeks post-exposure; antibodies seroconvert at 3 to 6 weeks. A combination of HIV RNA PCR and 4th generation Ag/Ab test maximises sensitivity in the window. Confirmed acute infection requires immediate referral to an s100-prescribing HIV physician for early initiation of antiretroviral therapy, contact tracing, and counselling.
key_points: Acute HIV mimics infectious mononucleosis at 2 to 4 weeks post-exposure
HIV RNA PCR turns positive within 1 to 2 weeks
4th generation Ag/Ab adds p24 antigen detection at ~2 weeks
Antibody-only tests are unreliable in the window period
Immediate referral and rapid ART start are recommended
explanation.pearls: Same-day ART initiation in acute HIV reduces transmission and progression, and is the standard of care at Australian sexual health centres; the rapid test result is no longer required before starting therapy in suspected acute disease.

options.rationale: 3rd generation tests detect antibodies only and have a 3 to 6 week window; they may be negative in seroconversion. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)
Point-of-care antibody-only tests perform worst in the seroconversion window and may miss acute infection. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)
Western blot is a confirmatory antibody test and is also negative during seroconversion windows. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)
Imaging does not detect HIV infection; acute infection is confirmed by HIV RNA and serology. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)

In suspected acute seroconversion (less than 28 days), HIV RNA PCR detects virus before antibody seroconversion; the 4th generation Ag/Ab test adds p24 antigen detection. Both establish the diagnosis confidently. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome workup starts with confirmation of hypercortisolism using one of three first-line tests: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression (failure to suppress below 50 nmol/L), late-night salivary cortisol (elevated), or 24-hour urinary free cortisol (raised above reference range). Two abnormal tests from different categories are required before proceeding. Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, ACTH is measured. Suppressed ACTH indicates adrenal cause (proceed to adrenal CT or MRI). Normal or raised ACTH indicates ACTH-dependent disease, evaluated next with high-dose dexamethasone suppression, MRI pituitary, then inferior petrosal sinus sampling if non-diagnostic. Treatment is directed at the source: transsphenoidal surgery for pituitary adenoma, adrenalectomy for adrenal source, or treatment of ectopic source.
key_points: First-line: 1 mg overnight DST, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24h UFC
Two abnormal screens of different types confirm hypercortisolism
ACTH then distinguishes ACTH-dependent from independent
MRI pituitary and IPSS localise ACTH-dependent disease
Adrenal imaging follows confirmed ACTH-independent disease
explanation.pearls: Late-night salivary cortisol has the highest sensitivity in the most common form (early ACTH-dependent disease) because the earliest defect is loss of the circadian nadir at midnight.

options.rationale: Random cortisol levels are too variable and do not establish or exclude Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)
Imaging without biochemical confirmation risks discovering incidentalomas and missing pituitary or ectopic sources. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)

Any one of these three tests is acceptable as a first-line screen; confirmation requires two abnormal screening tests of different types before further localisation. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)
ACTH localises but does not establish hypercortisolism; it follows confirmed Cushing syndrome rather than precedes it. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)
IPSS is reserved for distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH after confirmed ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)

explanation.summary: Miller Fisher syndrome is the classic variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome characterised by the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, often preceded by Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis or upper respiratory infection. Anti-GQ1b antibodies are positive in over 85 percent of cases. CSF typically shows raised protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation). Treatment is IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or plasma exchange; corticosteroids are not effective and may worsen outcome. Respiratory monitoring with serial forced vital capacity is mandatory because of risk of progression to bulbar weakness and respiratory failure requiring intubation.
key_points: Triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia is diagnostic
Anti-GQ1b antibodies are positive in over 85 percent of cases
CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation
IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days or plasma exchange
Steroids are not effective and not recommended
explanation.pearls: A vital capacity below 20 mL/kg or rapidly falling on serial measurement is a stronger indicator of imminent respiratory failure in GBS than oxygen saturation, which falls late.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.rationale: MRI may be done but the clinical triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia is diagnostic for Miller Fisher syndrome and demands immediate treatment. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.rationale: Anti-GQ1b is supportive but treatment should not await serology when the clinical picture is diagnostic. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not effective in Guillain-Barre or Miller Fisher and may worsen outcomes. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.rationale: Miller Fisher syndrome is a Guillain-Barre variant treated with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days with cardio-respiratory monitoring because of risk of bulbar and respiratory weakness progression. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.rationale: Areflexia and ataxia are not features of myasthenia gravis; Tensilon test is not relevant here and is no longer routinely used. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

explanation.summary: Pre-biologic TB screening in Australia uses an interferon-gamma release assay (typically QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus) in BCG-vaccinated patients because TST has poor specificity after BCG. CXR is performed concurrently to exclude active disease before commencing latent TB therapy. If positive, isoniazid for nine months (or rifampicin 4 months or 3HP regimen via specialist clinic) is offered with monthly LFT monitoring. Untreated latent TB carries a markedly elevated reactivation risk on TNF-alpha inhibitors.
key_points: IGRA preferred over TST in BCG-vaccinated patients per NTAC
Always pair IGRA with CXR before treating latent TB
TNF-alpha inhibitors increase reactivation risk substantially
Standard latent TB therapy: isoniazid 9 months or rifampicin 4 months
explanation.pearls: Use QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus, not Mantoux, in any patient born in a high-incidence country who received BCG; if positive and CXR clear, give isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months with pyridoxine 25 mg daily and monthly LFTs.

options.rationale: TST is influenced by prior BCG vaccination; in a BCG-vaccinated patient, an interferon-gamma release assay is preferred because it is unaffected by BCG. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)

IGRA (e.g. QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus) is the preferred screen in BCG-vaccinated individuals before TNF-alpha inhibitors and is paired with CXR to evaluate for active disease before treatment of latent infection. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)
Sputum AFB is for suspected active TB with respiratory symptoms; it is not the screening test for latent TB in an asymptomatic patient. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)
HRCT does not identify latent infection; latent TB is by definition asymptomatic and radiographically silent and requires immunological detection. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)
IgE and eosinophils have no role in TB screening; they relate to allergic and parasitic disease. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)

explanation.summary: Levodopa combined with carbidopa is the most effective symptomatic therapy for Parkinson's disease and is the preferred first-line agent in older patients (over 70) where dopamine agonists carry higher risks of impulse control disorders, hallucinations and falls. Dose is titrated slowly to motor response; the goal in early disease is the lowest effective dose. Long-term motor complications such as dyskinesia and wearing-off are managed with adjuncts including COMT inhibitors and MAO-B inhibitors. Multidisciplinary care, falls prevention and bone health complete the management plan.
key_points: Levodopa first-line in patients aged over 70
Dopamine agonists more often first-line in younger patients with mild disease
Avoid anticholinergics in older adults
Multidisciplinary input - physiotherapy, OT, speech pathology - improves outcomes
explanation.pearls: In a 72-year-old with postural instability and falls, choose Sinemet 100/25 mg three times daily titrated to motor response rather than pramipexole, since the absolute risk of falls and impulse control disorder on agonist therapy outweighs the modest motor-complication advantage.

sources.label: Movement Disorder Society Evidence-Based Medicine Review Update 2018

options.rationale: Dopamine agonists are associated with higher rates of impulse-control disorders, hallucinations, ankle oedema and sleep attacks in older adults; levodopa is preferred over agonists as first-line in patients over 70. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

Levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor is the most effective symptomatic therapy and is preferred first-line in patients over 70 because of greater motor benefit, fewer neuropsychiatric complications than agonists, and lower fall risk on titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

Anticholinergics in older adults precipitate confusion, urinary retention and cognitive decline; they are not used first-line in patients over 70 with Parkinson's disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

Amantadine has modest motor benefit and is mainly used for dyskinesia later in the disease; its renal clearance and CNS side-effect profile make it unattractive first-line in a 72-year-old with CKD. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

MAO-B inhibitors have modest symptomatic effect and may be appropriate in early mild disease in younger patients, but in this patient with established motor disability and postural instability, levodopa offers superior symptom control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)
