explanation.summary: Australian guidance and PBS criteria require methotrexate as the anchor first-line DMARD for newly diagnosed seropositive RA. Initial dose is 10 mg weekly titrated to 15-25 mg weekly over 4-8 weeks, with folic acid 5 mg weekly (taken on a different day) to reduce mucosal and hepatic side effects. Bridging low-dose prednisolone (e.g. 10-15 mg daily tapered over 8-12 weeks) controls inflammation while methotrexate reaches therapeutic effect. Biologic and targeted synthetic DMARDs require documented failure of conventional therapy.
key_points: Methotrexate is first-line in seropositive RA
Titrate to 15-25 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg weekly on a separate day
Bridging prednisolone for 8-12 weeks accelerates symptom control
Biologics require failure of two conventional DMARDs per PBS
explanation.pearls: In seropositive RA with CRP over 20 mg/L, start methotrexate at 10 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg on a different day, escalate by 2.5-5 mg every 2-4 weeks to 15-25 mg, and bridge with prednisolone 15 mg daily tapered over 12 weeks.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association methotrexate patient information

options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine is a relatively weak DMARD reserved for milder disease or as a combination partner; in established seropositive RA with high CRP, methotrexate is preferred first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

JAK inhibitors are reserved for failure of methotrexate or other conventional synthetic DMARDs under PBS criteria; they are not Australian first-line therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

Methotrexate is the anchor first-line DMARD for seropositive RA with elevated CRP, titrated to 15-25 mg weekly with folic acid; low-dose corticosteroid bridges disease control while methotrexate takes effect over 6-12 weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

NSAIDs do not modify disease progression in RA and indefinite use risks cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and renal harm; DMARD therapy must be initiated promptly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

Biologic DMARDs require PBS criteria of inadequate response to at least two conventional synthetic DMARDs (including methotrexate at therapeutic dose) for at least three months; not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

explanation.summary: The combination of tearing interscapular pain, inter-arm BP differential greater than 20 mmHg, a widened mediastinum and a known bicuspid aortic valve makes acute aortic dissection the leading diagnosis. CT aortogram is the most rapidly available high-sensitivity confirmatory test in Australian emergency departments. While imaging is being arranged, target heart rate around 60 using IV beta-blocker (esmolol or metoprolol), then add nitroprusside or GTN to achieve systolic BP 100-120 mmHg, and call the cardiothoracic team for type A dissection.
key_points: Inter-arm BP gap >20 mmHg plus tearing pain is dissection until proven otherwise
CT aortogram is first-line in Australian EDs
Rate control to HR around 60 precedes BP reduction to avoid reflex tachycardia
Type A: emergency surgery; Type B uncomplicated: medical management
explanation.pearls: If the inter-arm systolic gap exceeds 20 mmHg, order CT aortogram and prepare IV esmolol 500 mcg/kg load then 50-200 mcg/kg/min infusion in parallel rather than sending a D-dimer or arranging TTE.

sources.label: ESC Guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of aortic diseases 2014

options.rationale: Inter-arm BP differential exceeding 20 mmHg, tearing interscapular pain, widened mediastinum and bicuspid aortic valve make acute aortic dissection the leading diagnosis; CT aortogram is the most sensitive and rapidly available confirmatory test in Australian EDs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)

TTE has limited sensitivity for ascending aortic dissection and cannot adequately visualise the descending aorta; it complements but does not replace cross-sectional imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)

ECG shows no ST elevation and the dominant differential is dissection; angiography could delay diagnosis and cardiac catheterisation in undiagnosed dissection is hazardous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)
Stress testing in a patient with suspected dissection is absolutely contraindicated and would not be feasible in this acute presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)
Suspected acute aortic dissection requires same-hour imaging; deferring to outpatient TOE risks rupture and death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)

explanation.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria allow MS diagnosis after a single clinical attack if dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) are demonstrated. DIS requires lesions in at least 2 of 4 typical CNS locations: periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial, or spinal cord. DIT can be met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI, by a new lesion on a later MRI, or by CSF-specific oligoclonal bands together with DIS. Exclusion of mimics (NMOSD, MOGAD, sarcoid, vasculitis) is essential.
key_points: DIS = lesions in 2 of 4 typical CNS locations
DIT = simultaneous enhancing + non-enhancing lesions, OR new lesion on follow-up, OR CSF OCBs + DIS
Always check AQP4 and MOG antibodies to exclude NMOSD and MOGAD before MS label
Early DMT after diagnosis reduces long-term disability
explanation.pearls: If a single MRI in a CIS patient shows lesions in two or more typical locations and at least one enhancing plus one non-enhancing lesion, the 2017 McDonald criteria are satisfied; refer for AQP4/MOG and discuss disease-modifying therapy.

sources.label: MS Australia Clinical Guidelines for Diagnosis 2021

options.rationale: The 2017 McDonald criteria allow MS diagnosis after a single clinical attack if dissemination in space and time are demonstrated by MRI or CSF; a second clinical attack is not mandatory. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

Dissemination in time can be met by the simultaneous presence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI, or by CSF-specific oligoclonal bands plus DIS; repeat imaging is not required. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

Once DIS and DIT are met by MRI, CSF is not required for the 2017 criteria; CSF supports diagnosis when DIT cannot be demonstrated by MRI alone. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

NMOSD must be considered and AQP4 testing performed to exclude it, but once excluded and DIS and DIT are met clinically and on MRI, MS can be diagnosed under the 2017 criteria without mandatory CSF. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

DIS is met by lesions in at least 2 of 4 typical locations (this patient has periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord involvement); DIT is met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same scan. Mimics including NMOSD and MOGAD must be excluded; MS can then be diagnosed and DMT discussed. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is associated with severe neuroleptic sensitivity (occurring in up to half of patients exposed) which can present as worsening parkinsonism, autonomic instability and NMS-like syndromes. First-line management of delirium superimposed on DLB is to identify and treat reversible causes (infection, dehydration, pain, urinary retention) and use non-pharmacological strategies. If a sedating agent is required for refractory severe distress, low-dose quetiapine (12.5-25 mg) is preferred, but it is not first-line.
key_points: DLB has high neuroleptic sensitivity, especially to typicals and risperidone
Treat reversible delirium triggers first; non-pharmacological measures next
Quetiapine 12.5-25 mg is the least bad choice if pharmacotherapy is unavoidable
Cholinesterase inhibitors can reduce visual hallucinations and behavioural symptoms
explanation.pearls: When DLB patients become agitated with delirium, fix the UTI, hydrate, analgesia and orient first; if pharmacotherapy is unavoidable, use quetiapine 12.5-25 mg orally rather than haloperidol or risperidone, which can precipitate severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics including haloperidol carry up to 50% risk of severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions in DLB, including worsening parkinsonism, autonomic instability and NMS-like syndrome; absolutely avoided. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.rationale: Risperidone has D2 affinity comparable to typical antipsychotics in this context and is associated with severe sensitivity in DLB; it should be avoided. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.rationale: Olanzapine has been associated with severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions in DLB and is not recommended; if an antipsychotic is unavoidable, quetiapine at very low dose is preferred. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.rationale: DLB carries high neuroleptic sensitivity risk; the first response to delirium is to address triggers and use non-pharmacological measures, with low-dose quetiapine reserved for severe distress that cannot be otherwise managed. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.rationale: Long-acting benzodiazepines precipitate prolonged sedation, falls and paradoxical worsening of delirium in older adults; if benzodiazepine is unavoidable, short-acting low-dose lorazepam is preferred. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

explanation.summary: After a first unprovoked VTE, current Australian guidance recommends extended (indefinite) anticoagulation with periodic bleeding-risk review unless bleeding risk becomes prohibitive. Reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) or reduced-dose rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) after the initial 6-month treatment period maintain efficacy versus full dose with lower bleeding risk. Aspirin is inferior to anticoagulation for recurrence prevention. Provoked VTE with a fully reversible trigger is typically anticoagulated for 3 months only.
key_points: First unprovoked VTE: extended anticoagulation with annual review
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily after initial 6 months retains efficacy with less bleeding
Aspirin reduces recurrence less than anticoagulation
Provoked VTE with reversible trigger: 3 months and stop
explanation.pearls: Step apixaban down from 5 mg twice daily to 2.5 mg twice daily at six months in extended therapy for unprovoked VTE; review HAS-BLED score and bleeding history annually to balance ongoing benefit and risk.

options.rationale: First unprovoked PE carries a recurrence risk around 30% over five years off anticoagulation; stopping at three months is appropriate for provoked VTE with reversible trigger only. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)

Stopping at twelve months after an unprovoked event still leaves the patient with substantial annual recurrence risk; current guidance favours indefinite anticoagulation with periodic review unless bleeding risk increases. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)

Australian and international guidance recommend extended anticoagulation after first unprovoked VTE; apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily after the initial treatment period maintains efficacy with reduced bleeding versus full dose. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)
Aspirin reduces recurrence by around 30% versus 80% with anticoagulant therapy after unprovoked VTE; it is not equivalent to extended DOAC therapy. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)
Warfarin and DOACs both have long-term efficacy data; switching to warfarin in a patient stable on apixaban adds INR monitoring burden without clinical benefit. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)

explanation.summary: Sudden rise in peak and plateau pressures with hypotension, hypoxia, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins and absent unilateral breath sounds in a ventilated patient defines tension pneumothorax. Immediate decompression is the priority and is now recommended at the 4th or 5th intercostal space anterior or mid-axillary line in adults (preferred over the historical 2nd ICS midclavicular site) because of more reliable pleural entry through thinner chest wall. Needle decompression is a temporising measure; definitive intercostal catheter insertion follows. CXR confirmation is post-decompression.
key_points: Tension pneumothorax in ventilated ARDS is the prototype of acute rise in peak/plateau pressure plus shock
Decompress at the 4th-5th ICS anterior or mid-axillary in adults (ATLS update)
Do not delay decompression for CXR confirmation
Definitive ICC follows immediately
explanation.pearls: If peak airway pressure rises more than 10 cm H2O over baseline within minutes alongside hypotension and unilateral absent breath sounds, decompress at the 4th-5th ICS mid-axillary rather than 2nd ICS midclavicular - the lateral approach has higher first-pass success in adults with thick anterior chest walls.

options.rationale: Clinical signs match tension pneumothorax superimposed on positive-pressure ventilation; immediate decompression at the safer 4th-5th ICS anterior or mid-axillary site (preferred over 2nd ICS midclavicular in ventilated adults due to chest-wall thickness) restores cardiac output, with definitive ICC to follow. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)

Brief disconnection may transiently improve haemodynamics by reducing intrathoracic pressure but delays decompression and is not the definitive next step; the clinical picture mandates immediate thoracostomy. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment must not be delayed for imaging; CXR confirmation post-decompression is acceptable. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)
Vasopressor escalation cannot overcome obstructive shock from tension pneumothorax; without decompression the patient will arrest. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)

Increasing PEEP and recruitment manoeuvres worsen tension pneumothorax by adding gas to the pleural space and dropping venous return further; this risks immediate cardiac arrest. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)

explanation.summary: Modified Duke criteria require positive blood cultures with typical organisms plus evidence of endocardial involvement. Streptococcus gallolyticus is a typical organism. TTE has limited sensitivity for prosthetic valve endocarditis (around 50%) so TOE is the test of choice when pretest probability is high. S. gallolyticus bacteraemia warrants colonoscopy because of its association with colorectal neoplasia. Empirical therapy in prosthetic valve endocarditis is broader than native valve and includes vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin pending sensitivities.
key_points: TTE sensitivity for prosthetic valve endocarditis is around 50%
TOE is first-line imaging when pretest probability is high
S. gallolyticus is a typical Duke organism and warrants colonoscopy
Empirical prosthetic valve cover includes vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin
explanation.pearls: When prosthetic valve endocarditis is clinically likely and TTE is non-diagnostic, proceed straight to TOE within 24 to 48 hours and arrange colonoscopy if blood cultures grow S. gallolyticus rather than chasing CT or PET first.

options.rationale: TTE has low sensitivity for prosthetic valve endocarditis and abscess; TOE is the test of choice when there is high pretest probability with negative or non-diagnostic TTE in a prosthetic valve patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

Cardiac CT has a role as an adjunct, particularly for prosthetic valves and pseudoaneurysm assessment, but TOE remains the first-line imaging after non-diagnostic TTE in suspected prosthetic endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

Cardiac MRI is not first-line in suspected endocarditis; its role is limited compared with TOE for vegetation and abscess detection on prosthetic valves. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

Repeat TTE adds limited yield over the initial TTE in a prosthetic valve case and delays diagnosis; TOE is significantly more sensitive and is the appropriate next step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

FDG-PET is an adjunct supporting major Duke criteria in prosthetic valve endocarditis after at least three months, not the first imaging step in this acute presentation with persistent bacteraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

explanation.summary: The Endocrine Society recommends one of three first-line screening tests for Cushing's syndrome: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol (two collections), or late-night salivary cortisol (two samples). Two abnormal first-line tests are required before further workup. Imaging is performed only after biochemical confirmation to avoid being misled by incidentalomas. Following confirmation, ACTH level dichotomises ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) causes.
key_points: Three first-line screens: 1 mg DST, 24h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol
Two abnormal screens before further workup
Imaging only after biochemical confirmation
ACTH level dichotomises dependent versus independent disease
explanation.pearls: When a patient presents with new hypertension, central weight gain and wide violaceous striae, screen with overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression (cortisol <50 nmol/L next morning excludes Cushing's) and confirm with a second first-line test before imaging.

options.rationale: Random cortisol has too much diurnal and stress variability to be used as a screening test for Cushing's syndrome and is not recommended at initial workup. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

The 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is one of three recommended first-line screens (alongside 24-hour urinary free cortisol and late-night salivary cortisol) with high sensitivity for endogenous Cushing's. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

Pituitary MRI is performed only after biochemical confirmation of ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome; pituitary incidentalomas are common and imaging without biochemistry misleads. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

Petrosal sinus sampling is reserved for distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH sources after biochemical confirmation and ACTH-dependence, not as a screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

Adrenal imaging is performed after biochemical confirmation; up to 5% of adults have incidentalomas, so imaging without biochemistry leads to overdiagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

explanation.summary: In septic shock with MAP below 65 mmHg despite an initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor. It can be commenced via a reliable peripheral large-bore line for short durations until central venous access is obtained. Vasopressin may be added when escalating noradrenaline doses are required. Beyond the initial bolus, further fluid is guided by dynamic measures rather than empiric repeat boluses to avoid pulmonary oedema.
key_points: Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor in septic shock
Target MAP is 65 mmHg
Vasopressor may be initiated peripherally while central access is sought
Dopamine has worse outcomes than noradrenaline
explanation.pearls: If MAP remains under 65 mmHg after the initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid in septic shock, commence noradrenaline via a reliable large-bore peripheral line while obtaining central access rather than giving further empirical fluid boluses.

options.rationale: Dopamine has worse outcomes including more arrhythmias than noradrenaline in septic shock and is not recommended as first-line vasopressor. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Beyond the initial 30 mL/kg, further fluid in vasopressor-resistant septic shock risks pulmonary oedema; vasopressor initiation is preferred to maintain MAP. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Surviving Sepsis recommends commencing noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor after initial fluid resuscitation when MAP remains below 65 mmHg, including via reliable peripheral access while central access is obtained. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Bolus metaraminol may temporise during set-up but is not a substitute for noradrenaline infusion in established fluid-refractory septic shock requiring sustained perfusion support. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Albumin may be used as an adjunct in patients receiving large-volume crystalloid resuscitation, but withholding vasopressor in fluid-refractory septic shock delays haemodynamic stabilisation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia is divided into PTH-dependent (elevated or non-suppressed PTH) and PTH-independent (suppressed PTH) causes. PTH-dependent causes are primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, separated by the 24-hour urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (less than 0.01 in FHH). PTH-independent causes include malignancy (PTH-rP, lytic lesions, calcitriol-secreting lymphoma), granulomatous disease, vitamin D or A toxicity, milk-alkali syndrome and immobility. Confirmation of primary hyperparathyroidism warrants imaging only when surgery is contemplated.
key_points: Elevated calcium with non-suppressed PTH = PTH-dependent
FHH separated by calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio <0.01
Malignancy and granulomatous causes suppress PTH
Imaging only when surgery is contemplated
explanation.pearls: When hypercalcaemia presents with PTH above mid-normal and calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio above 0.01, diagnose primary hyperparathyroidism without imaging first, then refer for parathyroid scintigraphy or 4D-CT only when surgical management is indicated.

options.rationale: Vitamin D toxicity suppresses PTH and is more commonly associated with elevated rather than low-normal phosphate; her PTH is elevated, ruling this out. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)
FHH typically shows a urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01; this patient's ratio of 0.018 excludes FHH on biochemistry. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)
Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia typically suppresses PTH; her PTH is elevated, which excludes humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)

Elevated calcium with non-suppressed PTH is the diagnostic pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism; the urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio above 0.01 excludes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)
Granulomatous hypercalcaemia produces a PTH-suppressed pattern; her elevated PTH and absence of granulomatous features make this implausible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection requires urgent operative source control and broad-spectrum antibiotic cover with anti-toxin clindamycin. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, Cr, glucose) above 6 raises and above 8 strongly raises suspicion, but no score replaces clinical assessment. Pain disproportionate to skin findings, rapid progression, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus and systemic toxicity are red flags. Mortality rises sharply with each hour of surgical delay beyond 12 hours of presentation.
key_points: Necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis; do not delay surgery for imaging
LRINEC over 6 raises and over 8 strongly raises suspicion
Empirical cover includes broad-spectrum antibiotic plus clindamycin for toxin suppression
Mortality rises with each hour of operative delay beyond 12 hours
explanation.pearls: When LRINEC is 8 or higher with pain disproportionate to erythema and haemorrhagic bullae, call surgery within minutes and start meropenem plus clindamycin rather than waiting for MRI or persisting with simple cellulitis cover.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is at most an adjunct after surgical debridement and broad antibiotic therapy in selected centres; it does not replace urgent operative source control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.rationale: Simple cellulitis cover does not address gas-forming organisms or polymicrobial fascial infection, and reassessment delay in suspected necrotising fasciitis costs lives; surgery within 12 hours of presentation reduces mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.rationale: Imaging delays definitive surgical exploration; necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis and surgery should not be delayed for MRI when the clinical and LRINEC suspicion is high. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.rationale: IVIG is an adjunct in confirmed streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, not a substitute for source control or appropriate antibiotic combination; delay in surgery is the dominant predictor of mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.rationale: LRINEC of 9 plus pain disproportionate to erythema, haemorrhagic bullae, rapid progression and sepsis strongly suggests necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical exploration is the only intervention that reduces mortality, with broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents 2 to 4 weeks after exposure with a mononucleosis-like illness. Fourth-generation antigen and antibody combination assays narrow but do not eliminate the diagnostic window because p24 antigenaemia can be missed in very early disease. HIV RNA NAAT detects viraemia within around 10 days of exposure and is the recommended test when acute infection is suspected and the fourth-generation result is negative. Early identification matters for prompt initiation of antiretroviral therapy and contact tracing.
key_points: Acute HIV mimics mononucleosis 2 to 4 weeks post-exposure
4th-gen Ag/Ab narrows but does not eliminate the diagnostic window
HIV RNA NAAT detects viraemia from around 10 days post-exposure
Early diagnosis enables immediate ART and contact tracing
explanation.pearls: When a sexually exposed patient presents within four weeks of risk with a mononucleosis-like illness and negative 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab, order HIV RNA NAAT immediately rather than waiting three months to repeat antibody testing.

sources.label: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.rationale: Fourth-generation Ag/Ab assays can be negative during early viraemia before p24 antigenaemia rises; HIV RNA NAAT detects infection within around 10 days of exposure and is the test of choice when acute seroconversion is suspected and Ag/Ab is negative. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.rationale: A three-month repeat alone misses the acute seroconversion window now and delays diagnosis of likely current acute HIV infection in this high-risk symptomatic presentation. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.rationale: Western blot is a confirmatory antibody test and is also negative in early seroconversion before antibody develops; HIV RNA NAAT is the appropriate sensitive test in this window. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.rationale: Empirical antiretroviral therapy without diagnostic confirmation is not standard of care; HIV RNA NAAT provides diagnostic confirmation rapidly to guide treatment initiation. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.rationale: CD4 count drops transiently in acute HIV but is non-specific and is used to stage established infection rather than diagnose acute infection in the eclipse-window phase. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

explanation.summary: Life-threatening bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban is reversed with andexanet alfa where available; the high-dose regimen (800 mg bolus and 8 mg per minute infusion) applies when the apixaban dose was more than 5 mg or taken less than 8 hours before the event. Where andexanet alfa is unavailable, 4-factor PCC at 50 units per kilogram is the accepted alternative. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only. FFP, vitamin K and platelet transfusion are not appropriate substitutes for specific reversal in DOAC-associated bleeding.
key_points: Andexanet alfa specifically reverses factor Xa inhibitor activity
High-dose andexanet for apixaban over 5 mg or last dose under 8 hours ago
Idarucizumab is for dabigatran, not apixaban
4-factor PCC 50 units per kilogram is the alternative when andexanet unavailable
explanation.pearls: For apixaban-associated intracranial haemorrhage with last dose under eight hours ago, give andexanet alfa high-dose (800 mg bolus then 8 mg per minute infusion) rather than reaching for FFP, vitamin K or idarucizumab which provide no factor Xa inhibitor reversal.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.rationale: PCC is a reasonable option where andexanet alfa is unavailable, but where andexanet alfa is accessible it is the specific direct reversal agent for apixaban with stronger evidence for haemostatic efficacy in intracranial haemorrhage. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors and is recommended for life-threatening or intracranial bleeding when last dose was within hours; the high-dose regimen applies to apixaban over 5 mg or last dose under eight hours ago. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.rationale: FFP does not reverse direct factor Xa inhibitors and risks volume overload without providing meaningful haemostatic benefit in DOAC-associated bleeding. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.rationale: Vitamin K does not reverse direct factor Xa inhibitors and platelet transfusion has no role unless the platelet count is critically low; neither addresses the underlying anticoagulant effect. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.rationale: Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran, not apixaban; using it would have no reversal effect on factor Xa inhibitor activity. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma requires careful preoperative medical preparation to prevent intraoperative haemodynamic catastrophe. Non-selective alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) or selective alpha-blockade (doxazosin or prazosin) is started 10 to 14 days preoperatively and titrated to mild orthostatic hypotension. Beta-blockade is added only after adequate alpha-blockade because beta-blockade alone unmasks unopposed alpha-vasoconstriction. Salt and fluid loading expand the contracted intravascular volume in the days before surgery. Calcium channel blockers are useful adjuncts when blood pressure remains elevated.
key_points: Alpha-blockade always precedes beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma
Phenoxybenzamine titrated to mild orthostasis for 10 to 14 days
Beta-blockade alone risks hypertensive crisis through unopposed alpha
Salt and fluid loading expand the contracted intravascular volume
explanation.pearls: When a confirmed phaeochromocytoma patient is scheduled for adrenalectomy in three weeks, start phenoxybenzamine and titrate to mild postural drop over 10 to 14 days before adding any beta-blocker, regardless of how prominent the tachycardia or anxiety symptoms appear at baseline.

options.rationale: Calcium channel and renin-angiotensin blockers are adjuncts only; they do not provide adequate intraoperative haemodynamic protection without alpha-blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

Initiating beta-blockade before adequate alpha-blockade in phaeochromocytoma can precipitate severe hypertensive crisis through unopposed alpha vasoconstriction; this sequence is contraindicated. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

Unopposed alpha-receptor stimulation after beta-blockade alone precipitates hypertensive crisis in phaeochromocytoma; non-selective alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine for 10 to 14 days, titrated to mild orthostasis, must precede any beta-blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

Unprepared phaeochromocytoma surgery carries unacceptable risk of intraoperative hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia and death; 10 to 14 days of alpha-blockade is standard preparation. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

Labetalol has a beta-blocking effect that exceeds its alpha-blocking effect and is not recommended as monotherapy preparation for phaeochromocytoma surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

explanation.summary: Septic shock has a time-dependent mortality and the international hour-1 bundle is operationalised in Australia through Therapeutic Guidelines. Within the first hour clinicians should obtain lactate, draw blood cultures (without delaying antibiotics), administer broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting likely source, and resuscitate hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol per L with 30 mL per kg of crystalloid. Vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line) are added if MAP remains under 65 mmHg after fluids. Source identification and source control follow as resuscitation proceeds.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors if MAP <65 after fluids
Initial crystalloid 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate >4
Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor
Source control is parallel to, not before, resuscitation
explanation.pearls: Lactate above 4 mmol/L or MAP below 65 mmHg defines the threshold for full hour-1 resuscitation including 30 mL/kg crystalloid and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

options.rationale: Imaging should not delay antibiotics in septic shock; the source is suggested by recent dental abscess, and antibiotics plus fluids are the priority within the hour-1 bundle. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Noradrenaline can be commenced peripherally short-term while access is upgraded; delaying antibiotics for central access worsens outcome. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

The hour-1 bundle requires lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL per kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and vasopressors if MAP remains under 65 mmHg. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Two sets from separate sites is ideal but should not delay antibiotics in septic shock; the goal is administration within the hour. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Hydrocortisone is added when shock is refractory to adequate fluid and vasopressor therapy, not before fluids and antibiotics. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infections classically present with pain out of proportion to visible changes, systemic toxicity, and rapidly evolving skin findings (bullae, anaesthesia, crepitus). The LRINEC score combines CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose to support recognition; a score of 6 or more is suspicious and 8 or more is high risk, although clinical judgement overrides the score. AU first-line empirical therapy is broad-spectrum cover with meropenem (or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin for toxin suppression and vancomycin if MRSA risk; urgent surgical debridement is the definitive intervention.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity + LRINEC >=6 = act on suspicion
Empirical: meropenem (or pip-taz) + clindamycin + vancomycin (MRSA risk)
Urgent surgical debridement is the definitive therapy
Imaging must not delay theatre when clinical suspicion is high
explanation.pearls: LRINEC score above 6 with pain out of proportion warrants urgent surgical exploration plus meropenem + clindamycin in Australian sepsis pathways.

options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and an LRINEC of 9 indicate possible necrotising soft tissue infection; oral therapy and outpatient review is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
IV flucloxacillin alone does not cover the polymicrobial mix typical of necrotising fasciitis; delaying surgery to await imaging worsens outcome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

An LRINEC score of 6 or more (here 9) combined with pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and central anaesthesia is highly suggestive of necrotising fasciitis; AU practice mandates urgent surgical exploration with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (meropenem) plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
MRI may have a role in stable patients but should not delay surgical exploration when clinical features and LRINEC strongly suggest necrotising fasciitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Single agent vancomycin under-covers anaerobes and gram negatives that contribute to type I necrotising fasciitis; broad cover plus clindamycin is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated UTI in non-pregnant women is diagnosed clinically supported by urine dipstick; routine urine culture is not required unless symptoms recur or fail to respond. AU first-line treatment is trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days; both have favourable resistance and ecological profiles. Pyelonephritis (fever, flank pain, vomiting) requires broader spectrum cover and longer duration. Recurrent UTI (more than 2 in 6 months) warrants behavioural advice, self-start regimens or post-coital prophylaxis depending on triggers.
key_points: Trimethoprim 300 mg for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 5 days is first-line
Urine MCS not routinely required for uncomplicated cystitis
Pyelonephritis needs broader spectrum cover and longer course
Quinolones and broad-spectrum agents are not first-line in Australia
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic first-line for uncomplicated UTI: trimethoprim 300 mg for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 5 days.

options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved due to resistance and tendinopathy risk; they are not first-line for uncomplicated UTI in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Amoxicillin clavulanate is broader than necessary and has higher community resistance than the recommended first-line agents. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

AU first-line therapy for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women is trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days; both are narrow-spectrum and have low resistance rates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Cefalexin is a second-line agent due to higher resistance and ecological impact; it is not the AU first-line option. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Fosfomycin is an alternative for resistant organisms; phenazopyridine is not available on PBS in Australia and is not recommended routinely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Oral oseltamivir is the AU first-line antiviral for influenza, most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Indications include severe or progressive illness, hospital admission, and high-risk groups: age over 65, chronic cardiac, respiratory, renal, hepatic, neurological, or metabolic disease, immunosuppression, pregnancy and postpartum, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults, and morbid obesity. Vaccinated status does not preclude treatment in confirmed infection. Antibiotics are reserved for documented bacterial co-infection (otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia).
key_points: Oseltamivir 75 mg BD for 5 days is the AU first-line antiviral
Start within 48 hours of symptom onset for maximal benefit
High-risk groups include age >65, chronic disease, pregnancy, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults
Vaccination does not preclude treatment
explanation.pearls: Oseltamivir 75 mg BD for 5 days within 48 hours of symptom onset is the AU standard for influenza in older or comorbid adults.

options.rationale: Symptomatic management alone misses an opportunity to shorten symptom duration and reduce complication risk in a high-risk older adult with comorbidities. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AU Influenza Treatment Guidance)
Antibiotics are reserved for documented or strongly suspected bacterial pneumonia, not routine influenza without focal signs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Inhaled zanamivir is contraindicated in patients with chronic respiratory disease and is less practical for elderly patients; oral oseltamivir is preferred. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines)

Oral oseltamivir within 48 hours of symptom onset shortens illness and reduces complications in high-risk groups (age over 65, comorbidities); 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is the AU standard dose. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Baloxavir is not currently first-line in Australia and access is limited; oseltamivir remains the AU standard. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically affects tall thin young men and is graded radiologically by size (apex to cupola or chest wall at hilum), with 2 cm a common threshold. AU and BTS guidance support initial needle aspiration over routine large-bore chest drainage for primary spontaneous pneumothorax above 2 cm in stable patients; small-bore intercostal drains are second-line if aspiration fails. Large-bore drains are not first-line. Tension pneumothorax requires immediate needle decompression followed by intercostal drainage. Recurrence prompts surgical bullectomy plus pleurodesis.
key_points: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax above 2 cm in stable patient: needle aspiration first
Small-bore intercostal drain follows failed aspiration
Tension pneumothorax = immediate needle decompression then drainage
Positive pressure ventilation is contraindicated until pneumothorax drained
explanation.pearls: Stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax >2 cm in size is managed first with needle aspiration; small-bore drain follows if residual size remains >2 cm.

options.rationale: Large-bore intercostal catheters are not first-line for primary spontaneous pneumothorax in stable patients; smaller-bore approaches or aspiration are preferred. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)
A 3 cm pneumothorax exceeds the AU threshold for conservative management at home; intervention is required as outpatient. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)
Needle thoracostomy is reserved for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise; he is stable. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)
Positive pressure ventilation worsens pneumothorax and is contraindicated; it does not accelerate sealing of the visceral pleural defect. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)

AU and BTS guidance for primary spontaneous pneumothorax with size above 2 cm in a stable patient is initial needle aspiration with a small-bore catheter; if aspiration fails (residual size above 2 cm) a small-bore intercostal drain is inserted. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory failure due to neuromuscular weakness and is precipitated by missed medication, infection, surgery, or new drugs that block neuromuscular transmission. A forced vital capacity below 15 mL/kg, weak cough, bulbar weakness, and rising PaCO2 are indications for intubation; do not rely on SpO2 because hypoxia is a late sign. Once airway is secured, definitive therapy is intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, with corticosteroids commenced under ventilatory cover because of the steroid dip. Pyridostigmine is usually withheld in crisis to avoid cholinergic crisis confusion and reinstated as bulbar function returns.
key_points: Intubate when FVC is below 15 mL/kg or bulbar weakness compromises the airway
Do not rely on SpO2; rising PaCO2 marks the failure
Definitive treatment is IVIG or plasma exchange
Withhold pyridostigmine during crisis to avoid cholinergic crisis overlap
explanation.pearls: The 20-30-40 rule flags impending failure: vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, inspiratory force less negative than -30, or expiratory force below 40 cmH2O. Falling FVC trumps SpO2 every time.

options.rationale: High-dose steroid alone risks a transient worsening of weakness and does not address the imminent respiratory failure; airway control must come first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Excess pyridostigmine causes a cholinergic crisis with the same neuromuscular picture; in established myasthenic crisis cholinesterase inhibitors are typically withheld until immunotherapy takes effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Non-invasive ventilation may be considered in early bulbar-sparing crisis but is unsafe when bulbar weakness, weak cough and a falling FVC compromise secretion clearance and airway protection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Forced vital capacity at 14 mL/kg with rising PaCO2, bulbar weakness, and weak cough is myasthenic crisis; immediate intubation is required, succinylcholine and non-depolarising relaxants are avoided or carefully dose-adjusted, and definitive treatment is IVIG or plasma exchange. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Edrophonium testing is no longer used in established myasthenia because of cardiac risk and adds no information when the diagnosis is already confirmed; the priority is airway control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Acute exacerbations of bronchiectasis are defined by an increase in sputum volume or purulence, worsening breathlessness, fever, or constitutional symptoms. Out-patient management is appropriate in the absence of sepsis, hypoxia, or treatment failure. Targeted oral antibiotics for 14 days are selected on the basis of the most recent sputum culture and known colonising organisms; in non-Pseudomonas patients with prior Haemophilus, amoxicillin-clavulanate provides reliable cover. Maintenance azithromycin reduces exacerbation frequency but does not treat an acute event. A fresh sputum culture is taken before treatment to refine therapy if symptoms do not resolve.
key_points: Bronchiectasis exacerbations are treated for 14 days, not 5 to 7 days
Antibiotic choice is guided by previous sputum culture
Maintenance azithromycin reduces exacerbation rate but does not cover acute infection
IV therapy is reserved for sepsis, hypoxia or treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Always send a sputum culture before starting empirical antibiotics in bronchiectasis to capture a possible new Pseudomonas isolate that changes both the agent and the duration.

options.rationale: Most non-Pseudomonas exacerbations of bronchiectasis are managed as out-patients with oral antibiotics for 14 days; intravenous therapy is reserved for systemic toxicity, hypoxia, or treatment failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
A 5 day course is insufficient for a bronchiectasis exacerbation; standard duration is 14 days to address the infected bronchial pool. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Maintenance azithromycin is for prevention and does not provide adequate cover for an acute exacerbation; an additional 14 day course of targeted antibiotic is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Inhaled tobramycin is used for chronic Pseudomonas suppression, not for an acute Haemophilus exacerbation; an oral agent with Haemophilus cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Australian guidance recommends a 14 day oral course directed at recent sputum isolates for a bronchiectasis exacerbation without sepsis; amoxicillin-clavulanate covers Haemophilus influenzae including beta-lactamase producers and concurrent sputum culture refines therapy if treatment fails. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection is asymptomatic Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection without radiological or microbiological evidence of active disease. QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus and other interferon-gamma release assays are unaffected by BCG vaccination. Once active disease is excluded by a normal chest X-ray and clinical assessment, Australian guidance recommends isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months with pyridoxine to prevent neuropathy, with monthly liver function tests to detect drug-induced hepatitis. Alternative shorter regimens include 4 months of rifampicin or 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine. Treatment reduces the lifetime risk of progression to active tuberculosis by about 70 percent.
key_points: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus is not affected by BCG vaccination
Latent TB is treated with isoniazid 9 months plus pyridoxine in AU first-line
Active disease must be excluded by CXR and symptoms before treating latent
Monthly LFT monitoring captures isoniazid hepatitis early
explanation.pearls: Add pyridoxine 25 mg with every isoniazid course to prevent peripheral neuropathy, especially in pregnant women, diabetics, and people with HIV.

sources.label: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.rationale: Interferon-gamma release assays such as QuantiFERON are not affected by BCG vaccination; a positive result reflects Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and warrants management. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.rationale: RIPE is treatment for active tuberculosis; the patient is asymptomatic with a normal chest X-ray, consistent with latent infection that does not require multi-drug therapy. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.rationale: Australian guidance treats latent TB with isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months plus pyridoxine to prevent peripheral neuropathy, with monthly LFTs to detect hepatitis; this regimen reduces lifetime progression to active TB by approximately 70 percent. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.rationale: Repeating an already positive interferon-gamma release assay does not add information and delays treatment that prevents progression to active tuberculosis. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.rationale: Invasive sampling is reserved for patients with clinical, radiological, or microbiological features of active tuberculosis; this patient has none. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

explanation.summary: Initial pharmacotherapy in idiopathic Parkinson disease balances symptomatic benefit against the long-term risk of motor complications. Levodopa is the most effective symptomatic agent, has the lowest short-term adverse effect burden, and is preferred in patients over 65 or those with significant functional impairment. Dopamine agonists are favoured in younger patients to defer motor fluctuations but carry impulse control disorder, somnolence, and oedema risks that limit their use in older patients. MAO-B inhibitors provide modest symptomatic benefit. Amantadine is used for dyskinesia later in disease. Levodopa-sparing strategies are no longer recommended in older patients with functional impairment.
key_points: Levodopa is first-line in older patients with functional impairment
Dopamine agonists carry impulse control disorder risk and are avoided in the elderly
MAO-B inhibitors give only modest symptomatic benefit as monotherapy
Withholding effective therapy compromises function without preventing motor complications
explanation.pearls: In a Parkinson patient over 65 whose symptoms threaten function, start levodopa at the lowest effective dose. Reserve dopamine agonists for younger patients with intact impulse control.

options.rationale: In a 68-year-old whose symptoms are interfering with work, levodopa provides the most reliable symptomatic benefit with the lowest short-term adverse effect burden; concerns about long-term motor complications do not justify delaying treatment that preserves function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Dopamine agonists are preferred in younger patients to defer motor complications; in a 68-year-old they carry significant risk of impulse control disorders, somnolence, and oedema with limited additional benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

MAO-B inhibitor monotherapy provides only modest symptomatic benefit; with established functional impairment and a UPDRS of 22, deferring more effective therapy is not appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Amantadine has weak symptomatic effect in early Parkinson disease and is typically reserved for treating later-stage dyskinesia rather than first-line motor symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Exercise is an important adjunct in Parkinson disease but does not substitute for symptomatic therapy in a patient whose tremor is interfering with paid work. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Light criteria classify a pleural effusion as exudative if any one of the following is met: pleural-to-serum protein ratio above 0.5, pleural-to-serum LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH exceeding two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Exudates require investigation for cause, with malignancy, parapneumonic effusion, tuberculosis, and connective tissue disease leading the differential. In a smoker with unintentional weight loss and a unilateral exudate, malignancy is the leading concern and contrast CT chest with pleural review for image-guided pleural biopsy is appropriate. Cytology of a single tap is positive in only 60 percent of malignant effusions, so repeat sampling and biopsy may be required.
key_points: Light criteria identify exudate when any one ratio threshold is breached
Smoker with weight loss and unilateral exudate is malignancy until proven otherwise
Cytology sensitivity is around 60 percent on a single tap
Pleural biopsy is often needed to secure the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: An exudate by Light criteria in a smoker with weight loss escalates to contrast CT and respiratory review; do not rely on a single negative cytology.

options.rationale: A pleural to serum protein ratio of 0.56 and LDH ratio of 1.40 meet Light criteria for an exudate; transudate is not consistent with these values and cardiac failure is unlikely to cause weight loss. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)
Pleural protein is high at 38 g/L; transudates have protein below 25 g/L and a ratio below 0.5; hypoalbuminaemia is not the mechanism here. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)
The exudate criteria are unequivocally met by both protein and LDH ratios; repeat tap is not required to confirm exudate status. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)
Chylothorax presents with milky fluid and elevated triglycerides; a straw-coloured fluid with these biochemistry values does not fit chylothorax. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)

Light criteria classify an effusion as exudate if pleural-to-serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, pleural-to-serum LDH ratio exceeds 0.6, or pleural LDH exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH; the ratios here are 0.56 and 1.40, mandating workup for an exudative cause including malignancy. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection management focuses on reducing aortic wall shear stress, which is proportional to the rate of rise of pressure and to heart rate. First-line intravenous beta blockade with esmolol or labetalol is titrated to a heart rate below 60 bpm before adding a vasodilator such as sodium nitroprusside to achieve a systolic pressure of 100 to 120 mmHg. Vasodilator monotherapy is contraindicated because reflex tachycardia accelerates dissection propagation. Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and requires emergency surgery. Uncomplicated type B dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian is managed medically; complicated type B with malperfusion or rupture requires TEVAR or surgery.
key_points: Reduce heart rate to below 60 before adding a vasodilator
Target systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg in acute dissection
Vasodilator monotherapy increases shear stress and is contraindicated
Uncomplicated type B dissection is initially medical, not surgical
explanation.pearls: Esmolol's short half-life allows rapid titration in dissection; achieve heart rate below 60 before reaching for nitroprusside or nicardipine.

sources.label: Heart Foundation Australia: Acute Aortic Syndromes

options.rationale: Nitrate monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic shear stress; rate control with a beta blocker must precede or accompany vasodilator therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Calcium channel blockers without rate control likewise trigger reflex tachycardia and worsen shear stress; rate control through beta blockade is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
Thrombolysis in aortic dissection is catastrophic; the ECG and imaging exclude infarction and confirm dissection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

In acute aortic dissection initial therapy is intravenous beta blockade to a heart rate below 60 to reduce aortic shear stress, with a vasodilator such as sodium nitroprusside added if systolic pressure remains above 120 mmHg; the goal is to reduce both pulse pressure and absolute pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Uncomplicated type B dissection without malperfusion or rupture is initially managed medically; surgery or thoracic endovascular aortic repair is reserved for complicated disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Pyelonephritis requiring admission is treated with intravenous antibiotics targeting Enterobacteriaceae and enterococci. Australian guidance recommends intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin as first-line empirical therapy, with gentamicin dose adjusted for renal function and levels monitored if therapy continues beyond 48 hours. Switch to oral therapy is guided by clinical improvement, ability to tolerate oral intake, and urine culture sensitivities, with a total duration of 10 to 14 days. Nitrofurantoin and oral trimethoprim do not achieve renal parenchymal concentrations and are reserved for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. Imaging is considered for treatment failure, recurrent infection, or suspected obstruction.
key_points: Australian first-line empirical pyelonephritis cover is IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin or ampicillin
Nitrofurantoin is reserved for cystitis as renal parenchymal levels are inadequate
Oral switch is guided by clinical improvement and culture sensitivities
Total course is 10 to 14 days
explanation.pearls: Always send a urine culture before starting empirical pyelonephritis cover; the culture refines the second 7 to 10 days of therapy and detects resistance early.

options.rationale: Australian guidance for pyelonephritis requiring admission is IV gentamicin plus IV amoxicillin or ampicillin, with gentamicin dose adjusted for renal function and serum levels monitored; this covers the common Enterobacteriaceae and enterococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral monotherapy is appropriate for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection only; this patient meets pyelonephritis criteria with systemic features and cannot tolerate oral fluids. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Vancomycin is not part of empirical pyelonephritis cover in the absence of MRSA risk factors; Gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae are the dominant pathogens. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Anaerobic and fungal cover is not required for uncomplicated pyelonephritis; the pathogens are Gram-negative aerobes and enterococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Nitrofurantoin achieves adequate concentration in the bladder but not in renal parenchyma and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: McDonald 2017 criteria allow diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis after a single clinical event when dissemination in space and time are demonstrated by imaging or by positive cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands. Acute optic neuritis is treated with pulse intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days, which speeds recovery but does not change long-term outcome. Disease-modifying therapy is initiated as soon as diagnosis is confirmed because early therapy reduces long-term disability; high-efficacy options including ocrelizumab and natalizumab are increasingly used first-line in patients with active disease. Pregnancy planning, comorbidities, and JC virus serology guide drug selection.
key_points: McDonald 2017 allows diagnosis from a single attack when DIS and DIT are met
Positive CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for DIT under McDonald 2017
Pulse methylprednisolone treats acute relapses; DMT modifies disease course
Early initiation of high-efficacy DMT improves long-term outcomes
explanation.pearls: Oligoclonal bands in CSF that are not present in serum substitute for dissemination in time under McDonald 2017, allowing diagnosis from a single relapse.

options.rationale: Current evidence and McDonald 2017 criteria support diagnosis of multiple sclerosis after a single clinical event when imaging and CSF satisfy dissemination in space and time; deferring disease-modifying therapy loses prevention years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Intravenous immunoglobulin is not a first-line disease-modifying therapy in multiple sclerosis and is reserved for selected indications such as pregnancy planning; established DMT classes are preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Long-term oral corticosteroids do not modify multiple sclerosis disease course and cause cumulative adverse effects; pulse intravenous methylprednisolone is used for acute relapses only. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Whole brain irradiation has no role in multiple sclerosis and would cause profound neurotoxicity; immunomodulatory disease-modifying therapy is the standard of care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

McDonald 2017 allows multiple sclerosis diagnosis when dissemination in space (multiple typical regions) and time (gadolinium-enhancing plus non-enhancing lesions, or positive CSF oligoclonal bands) are met; treatment is pulse intravenous methylprednisolone for the acute optic neuritis and prompt initiation of disease-modifying therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Adult anaphylaxis is treated with 0.5 mg intramuscular adrenaline from a 1:1000 ampoule injected into the anterolateral mid-thigh. The dose is repeated every 5 minutes if response is inadequate, with concurrent supine positioning, high-flow oxygen, intravenous crystalloid for hypotension, and salbutamol or nebulised adrenaline as adjuncts. Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases under monitoring.
key_points: Adult IM adrenaline dose is 0.5 mg of 1:1000
Anterolateral thigh, not deltoid or subcutaneous
Repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement
IV adrenaline only for refractory anaphylaxis under monitoring
explanation.pearls: ASCIA adult anaphylaxis: 0.5 mg of 1:1000 adrenaline IM into anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if needed; IV reserved for refractory cases.

options.rationale: ASCIA recommends 0.5 mg IM adrenaline from a 1:1000 ampoule into the anterolateral mid-thigh for adults with anaphylaxis featuring airway or circulatory involvement, repeated every 5 minutes if response is inadequate. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Intravenous adrenaline in anaphylaxis is reserved for refractory cases or arrest under intensive monitoring; first-line in spontaneously breathing adults is intramuscular dosing because of the lower arrhythmia risk. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts and do not treat the airway and cardiovascular components of anaphylaxis; delaying adrenaline to give them increases mortality. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Nebulised adrenaline targets upper airway oedema as adjunct only; systemic anaphylaxis with hypotension requires intramuscular adrenaline as the immediate primary intervention. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

Subcutaneous adrenaline has slow and unpredictable absorption due to peripheral vasoconstriction; intramuscular delivery into the thigh is the correct route. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Modified Duke criteria diagnose definite IE when two major, or one major and three minor, or five minor clinical criteria are met. Major criteria include typical organisms in two blood cultures from separate sites and evidence of endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, new partial dehiscence, or new regurgitant murmur). Pathological diagnosis requires tissue from surgery or autopsy. A negative TTE does not reject IE; TOE is required in prosthetic valves and high-risk cases.
key_points: Definite IE: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor
Typical organism in 2 separate cultures = major
New regurgitant murmur or vegetation = major
Negative TTE never rejects IE in prosthetic valves; TOE mandatory
explanation.pearls: Two separate cultures of viridans strep plus a new regurgitant murmur in a prosthetic valve patient = two Duke major criteria = definite IE without needing echo confirmation.

options.rationale: Pathological Duke criteria require tissue or vegetation specimens with histological or microbiological proof; without surgery these are not available, and definite IE must be reached via clinical criteria. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

Possible IE applies when one major and one minor, or three minor criteria, are met; this patient already has two major criteria once typical organism in two cultures is combined with the new regurgitant murmur evidence. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

Two separate cultures of viridans streptococci constitute one major criterion, and a new regurgitant murmur in a prosthetic valve patient constitutes the second major (evidence of endocardial involvement); two major criteria satisfy definite IE. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

A non-diagnostic TTE does not reject IE; in prosthetic valves TOE is required and patients with persistent bacteraemia and typical organisms remain in possible or definite categories. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

One major plus three minor would meet definite IE, or two major; the question stem documents one major (organism) and the new murmur (a second major), so the categorisation rests on two major criteria rather than the minor mix. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener) classically presents with granulomatous involvement of the upper airway (chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting, saddle nose, hearing loss), lower airway (cavitating or non-cavitating nodules), and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with red cell casts and proteinuria. Cytoplasmic ANCA targeting PR3 is the typical pattern. Microscopic polyangiitis is more often pauci-immune renal disease with MPO-ANCA. EGPA features asthma, eosinophilia, and neuropathy.
key_points: GPA: upper airway destruction + pulmonary nodules + RPGN
GPA typically c-ANCA targeting PR3
MPA typically p-ANCA targeting MPO; pauci-immune renal
EGPA: asthma + eosinophilia + neuropathy; often MPO-ANCA
explanation.pearls: Pattern recognition for GPA: saddle nose + sensorineural or conductive hearing loss + cavitating or non-cavitating lung nodules + RPGN with red cell casts = c-ANCA/PR3.

sources.label: EULAR/ERA-EDTA recommendations for the management of ANCA-associated vasculitis

options.rationale: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture) causes pulmonary-renal syndrome but is not associated with sinonasal or otological involvement and typically lacks the granulomatous upper airway disease seen here. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

Upper respiratory tract granulomatous involvement (sinusitis, saddle nose, hearing loss) with renal and pulmonary disease is classic for granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which most commonly shows cytoplasmic ANCA staining with PR3 specificity. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

EGPA (Churg-Strauss) typically features asthma, blood eosinophilia, and migratory pulmonary infiltrates with peripheral neuropathy; upper airway destructive disease is not its signature. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)
Drug-induced ANCA vasculitis is typically MPO-ANCA, and the granulomatous upper airway picture is not characteristic of these atypical patterns. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis typically presents with palpable purpura, peripheral neuropathy, and low complement, often with hepatitis C; the destructive upper airway picture is not characteristic. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis sit on a spectrum defined by epidermal detachment: SJS under 10 percent BSA, overlap 10 to 30, TEN over 30. Carbamazepine is a major culprit and may have HLA-B*15:02 association in some populations. Immediate steps are to cease the culprit drug, transfer to a burns unit, and provide multidisciplinary supportive care including fluids, eye care, urinary, and pain. Mortality rises sharply with later cessation of the culprit drug.
key_points: SJS under 10 percent BSA; overlap 10 to 30; TEN over 30
Cease culprit drug immediately and transfer to burns unit
Carbamazepine is a high-risk culprit
Systemic steroids are not first line; supportive care primary
explanation.pearls: SJS/TEN: cease culprit drug (often allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulfa, NSAID) and transfer to burns unit; SCORTEN within 24 h predicts mortality.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists position on SJS/TEN

options.rationale: SJS/TEN is a dermatological emergency; the culprit drug must be ceased and patients should be transferred to a burns unit for fluid balance, wound care, ophthalmology, urology and pain support, especially with epidermal detachment over 10 percent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)
The culprit drug must be stopped immediately; continuing it risks progression to TEN with much higher mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)
SSSS occurs predominantly in children and lacks mucosal involvement; mucosal involvement with a drug exposure makes SJS/TEN the working diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)

Systemic corticosteroids have mixed evidence in SJS/TEN and are not first-line; burns-unit-level supportive care, often with ciclosporin or IVIG depending on local protocol, is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)

Erythema multiforme is target lesions on extremities without significant epidermal detachment; Nikolsky positivity and 12 percent BSA detachment are SJS-TEN overlap and require urgent escalation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)

explanation.summary: The 2-level Wells score for DVT stratifies into likely (2 or more) or unlikely (1 or less). DVT-likely patients proceed to proximal compression ultrasound. DVT-unlikely patients have a D-dimer; positive D-dimer triggers ultrasound. Therapeutic anticoagulation is started pending ultrasound when delay is expected and bleeding risk is acceptable. Confirmed proximal DVT is treated with anticoagulation for at least 3 months, with extended duration if unprovoked or cancer-associated.
key_points: Wells 2+ goes to ultrasound directly
Wells under 2 uses D-dimer first
Cancer or active malignancy scores 1
Empirical anticoagulation if delay to scan and acceptable bleeding risk
explanation.pearls: DVT pathway: calculate 2-level Wells - likely (2+) goes to direct USS, unlikely uses D-dimer; high pre-test probability invalidates D-dimer.

options.rationale: D-dimer is unreliable as a standalone test; the recommended pathway uses risk stratification first then D-dimer or ultrasound depending on probability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

IVC filters are reserved for confirmed VTE with anticoagulation contraindication or breakthrough VTE on anticoagulation; they are not used presumptively. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

A patient with multiple risk factors and clinical signs of DVT must not be discharged without proceeding through the diagnostic pathway; missed DVT carries PE risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

With recent immobility, active cancer history, calf swelling over 3 cm, pitting oedema, and tenderness, Wells score is high; the pathway is direct compression ultrasound rather than D-dimer because high pre-test probability undermines D-dimer specificity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

Calf swelling with tenderness in a high-risk patient is DVT until proven otherwise; antibiotics for presumed cellulitis without erythema typical of infection delays appropriate investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

explanation.summary: Australian hypertension diagnosis requires confirmation of sustained elevation, typically by ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring before commencing treatment, except in severely elevated readings or when end-organ damage is present. Diagnostic thresholds: clinic over 140/90, ABPM daytime average over 135/85, HBPM 7-day average over 135/85. Treatment decisions also account for absolute cardiovascular risk and target lower BP thresholds in higher-risk groups.
key_points: Confirm with ABPM or HBPM before treating
ABPM/HBPM threshold 135/85; clinic 140/90
Absolute CV risk drives treatment decisions
Treat immediately if severely elevated or end-organ damage
explanation.pearls: NHF Australia: confirm hypertension with ABPM (daytime average over 135/85) or 7-day HBPM averages over 135/85 before treating; clinic 140/90 alone is insufficient unless severe or end-organ damage.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.rationale: NHF guidance recommends out-of-office confirmation by ABPM or HBPM before commencing pharmacotherapy in most cases to exclude white-coat effect, unless severely elevated or evidence of end-organ damage. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.rationale: Persistent elevated clinic readings require timely confirmation; deferring assessment 12 months risks ongoing exposure to elevated pressures if true hypertension. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.rationale: OSA assessment is appropriate when there are specific signs or refractory hypertension; it is not the first step in confirming a hypertension diagnosis. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.rationale: Secondary hypertension work-up is indicated in resistant, severe, or early-onset disease or with suggestive features; it is not first-line for moderate sustained hypertension. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.rationale: NHF Australia recommends ABPM or HBPM to confirm hypertension before pharmacotherapy in most patients; the diagnostic threshold is daytime average over 135/85 (ABPM/HBPM), which corresponds to clinic over 140/90. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

explanation.summary: Light's criteria classify a pleural effusion as exudative if any one of the following is positive: pleural protein to serum protein ratio over 0.5, pleural LDH to serum LDH ratio over 0.6, or pleural LDH greater than two thirds of upper limit of normal serum LDH. Exudates require workup for causes including malignancy, infection, pulmonary embolism, and connective tissue disease.
