Pleural fluid cytology, microbiology, and imaging guide further evaluation; thoracoscopy may be needed when cytology is non-diagnostic.
key_points: ANY one positive criterion = exudate
Protein ratio over 0.5 alone is sufficient
Exudates: malignancy, infection, PE, connective tissue disease
Cytology, microbiology, thoracoscopy as needed for cause
explanation.pearls: Light's criteria: ANY one of pleural/serum protein over 0.5, pleural/serum LDH over 0.6, or pleural LDH greater than two thirds ULN serum LDH defines exudate.

options.rationale: Light's criteria require only ONE positive criterion to label exudate; the pleural protein to serum protein ratio above 0.5 already meets criteria, making this an exudate. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)
Clinical impression cannot override Light's biochemical criteria; pleural protein to serum protein ratio of 0.56 categorically meets exudate criteria. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

Pleural LDH above two thirds of ULN serum is just one of three criteria; this case meets the protein ratio criterion regardless of whether the LDH criteria is met. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

Light's criteria use ANY one of three positive results to label exudate; the protein ratio criterion is met (0.56 over 0.5), making this an exudate irrespective of the LDH ratio. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

Light's criteria: ANY one of pleural protein/serum protein over 0.5, pleural LDH/serum LDH over 0.6, or pleural LDH over two thirds of ULN serum LDH defines exudate; protein ratio 38/68 = 0.56 meets criteria. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines individualise HbA1c targets in older adults with type 2 diabetes by frailty, life expectancy, hypoglycaemia risk and patient preference. Healthy older adults target around 7 percent (53 mmol/mol); frail elderly with multiple comorbidities target 7.5 to 8.5 percent (58 to 69 mmol/mol); end-of-life targets focus on symptom avoidance. Sulfonylureas and insulin are the highest hypoglycaemia risk drugs in this group; metformin (if eGFR appropriate) is preferred for ongoing therapy. Deintensify treatment after hypoglycaemia or falls.
key_points: Healthy older adults: HbA1c ~7 percent.
Frail elderly: HbA1c 7.5-8.5 percent.
End-of-life: symptom-focused.
Sulfonylurea + insulin = highest hypoglycaemia risk; cease first.
explanation.pearls: Document and act on every symptomatic hypoglycaemic episode in elderly diabetes patients; one severe hypoglycaemic event doubles 5-year mortality risk and is a stronger indicator than any HbA1c value.

sources.label: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults
RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia and a fall already document inappropriate over-treatment; treatment de-escalation should not wait for further monitoring data before action. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

options.rationale: Tight HbA1c targets in frail elderly increase mortality and disability from hypoglycaemia without microvascular benefit at this life-expectancy and disease duration; deintensification is recommended. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

options.rationale: Metformin is not the cause of hypoglycaemia and is well tolerated; ceasing it leaves the gliclazide and insulin (the drivers of hypoglycaemia) untouched and worsens overall regimen. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors have cardiorenal benefit but bring increased fall risk through volume depletion and increased risk of urinary infection and DKA in frail elderly; first priority is to remove the agent driving hypoglycaemia. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

options.rationale: Frail elderly with limited life expectancy, hypoglycaemia and falls have a relaxed HbA1c target of 7.5 to 8.5 percent (58 to 69 mmol/mol); ceasing the sulfonylurea (highest hypoglycaemia risk drug) and reducing basal insulin is the recommended deintensification. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.5 mmol/L or any value with ECG changes) is a medical emergency. The sequence is: cardiac monitoring, IV calcium (10 percent gluconate 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes or 10 percent chloride 10 mL via central line) to stabilise the myocardium, then potassium-shifting therapy with insulin-dextrose (10 units actrapid plus 50 mL 50 percent dextrose), nebulised salbutamol 10 mg, and consideration of sodium bicarbonate if metabolic acidosis. Definitive removal is haemodialysis or correction of cause (cease ACE inhibitor and spironolactone, treat hypovolaemia). Calcium binds to cardiac sodium channels within minutes but does not lower the potassium.
key_points: Calcium first if ECG changes (stabilises myocardium).
Then insulin-dextrose + salbutamol (shifts K intracellularly).
Definitive: dialysis, cease offending drugs.
Repeat ECG and potassium after each intervention.
explanation.pearls: Effect of calcium gluconate lasts only 30 to 60 minutes; repeat if QRS does not narrow within 5 to 10 minutes, and document the potassium and ECG before and after each treatment step to track response.

options.rationale: Hyperkalaemic ECG changes with QRS widening require immediate myocardial membrane stabilisation; IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes acts within minutes and is given before any potassium-shifting therapy. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

Haemodialysis is the definitive treatment but takes time to mobilise; immediate temporising treatment (calcium then insulin-dextrose) cannot be deferred while waiting for vascular access and dialysis circuit setup. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is slow (hours) and not first-line for life-threatening hyperkalaemia; it does not stabilise the myocardium and risks bowel necrosis in unwell patients. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

Insulin-dextrose shifts potassium into cells over 30 to 60 minutes but does not stabilise the myocardium; calcium must be given first when ECG changes are present. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

Nebulised salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly but takes 30 minutes to act and is not enough in a haemodynamically unstable patient with QRS broadening; cardiac stabilisation comes first. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

explanation.summary: Sacubitril-valsartan (ARNI) reduces cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisation compared with enalapril in HFrEF (PARADIGM-HF) and is recommended in place of ACE inhibitor or ARB in patients who remain symptomatic on GDMT. Initiation requires 36-hour washout from the ACE inhibitor (no washout needed if previous ARB). Start dose depends on baseline therapy and BP: 49/51 mg BD for patients on therapeutic ACE inhibitor or ARB with stable BP; 24/26 mg BD for those on low-dose ACE/ARB, low BP (under 110 systolic), or renal impairment. Target 97/103 mg BD if tolerated, doubling every 2 to 4 weeks.
key_points: 36-hour washout from ACE inhibitor before ARNI.
No washout needed switching from ARB.
Start 49/51 mg BD if therapeutic ACE/ARB and BP stable.
Target 97/103 mg BD, doubling every 2-4 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Angioedema risk persists for Black or African heritage patients on ARNI (slightly higher than other populations); monitor K and creatinine 1 to 2 weeks after each titration step.

sources.label: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.rationale: Concurrent ACE inhibitor and ARNI use is absolutely contraindicated owing to angioedema risk; a full washout, not overlap, is required. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.rationale: An intermediate ARB switch is unnecessary and delays therapy; direct ACE inhibitor to ARNI switch with 36-hour washout is the standard pathway. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.rationale: Co-administration of ACE inhibitor and ARNI within 36 hours causes life-threatening angioedema; a 36-hour washout is mandatory before the first ARNI dose. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.rationale: Beta-blockers should be continued without interruption (cessation causes rebound and decompensation); only the ACE inhibitor needs washout before ARNI. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.rationale: Standard switch from ACE inhibitor to ARNI requires a 36-hour washout to avoid angioedema; in patients on a therapeutic ACE inhibitor dose with stable BP and renal function, start at the intermediate sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg BD with doubling every 2 to 4 weeks. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

explanation.summary: Antibiotics in COPD exacerbation are indicated when Anthonisen criteria are met (any 2 of 3, especially purulence, or all 3): increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence. Australian first-line is amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days; doxycycline 100 mg daily for 5 days if penicillin allergy. Patients with severe exacerbations, hospital admission, recent antibiotics, or Pseudomonas-risk need broader cover (amoxicillin-clavulanate or ciprofloxacin if Pseudomonas confirmed). Systemic corticosteroid prednisolone 30 to 50 mg for 5 days shortens recovery and reduces relapse. Short-acting bronchodilator and oxygen titrated to SpO2 88 to 92 percent if hypoxic.
key_points: Anthonisen 2+ (esp. purulence) = antibiotics.
First-line amoxicillin 500 mg TDS x 5 days (AU).
Prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days shortens recovery.
Target SpO2 88-92 percent to avoid CO2 retention.
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic-resistant Pseudomonas should be considered in patients with frequent prior courses, recent hospitalisation, severe FEV1 (under 30 percent), or known prior colonisation; ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD covers it but watch QT and tendinopathy.

options.rationale: Anthonisen 3 of 3 (dyspnoea, volume, purulence) is the threshold at which oral antibiotics reduce treatment failure; withholding antibiotics in this group is associated with worse outcomes. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)
Roflumilast (a PDE-4 inhibitor) is a chronic add-on for severe COPD with frequent exacerbations and chronic bronchitis, not an acute exacerbation treatment. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

She is haemodynamically stable, SpO2 only marginally reduced, and not in respiratory failure; inpatient IV therapy is reserved for severe exacerbation with inability to maintain oxygenation, severe acidosis, altered mental state, or social factors. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

Single-inhaler triple therapy is a maintenance step-up for frequent exacerbators and would not address the acute exacerbation; the acute event needs steroid plus antibiotic now. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

She meets all 3 Anthonisen criteria (increased dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) and antibiotics are indicated; Australian first-line is amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days plus systemic corticosteroid prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

explanation.summary: New Graves disease in non-pregnant adults is treated with carbimazole 15 to 45 mg daily (titrated to TFTs) plus a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol 20 to 40 mg TDS) for symptom relief. Treat for 12 to 18 months to allow remission; 50 percent relapse and may then require definitive treatment with radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy. Monitor TFTs every 4 to 6 weeks initially, then every 3 months. Counsel about agranulocytosis (sore throat or fever; stop drug and check FBC). PTU is preferred in first trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm; methimazole is teratogenic in T1.
key_points: First-line: carbimazole + non-selective beta-blocker.
Treat 12-18 months; 50 percent relapse.
PTU in T1 pregnancy and thyroid storm.
Counsel agranulocytosis warning - sore throat = FBC.
explanation.pearls: Active orbitopathy is a relative contraindication to radioactive iodine without corticosteroid cover (40 mg prednisolone before and tapering over 6 weeks); thyroidectomy is preferred in severe orbitopathy planning.

options.rationale: Beta-blocker alone controls only adrenergic symptoms and does not reduce thyroid hormone synthesis; a thionamide is required to address the underlying biochemical hyperthyroidism. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

Radioactive iodine can transiently worsen Graves orbitopathy and is generally not first-line in active orbitopathy without preceding euthyroidism on thionamide and corticosteroid cover. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

Australian first-line for new Graves disease in a non-pregnant adult is a thionamide (carbimazole 15 to 45 mg daily based on severity) plus a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol 20 to 40 mg TDS) for sympathetic symptom control until TFTs normalise. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

Surgery is reserved for failed medical management, large goitre with compression, suspected malignancy, or patient preference; it is not first-line for new Graves in a non-pregnant patient. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

Propylthiouracil is reserved for first trimester of pregnancy, thyroid storm, and thionamide intolerance because of higher hepatotoxicity risk than carbimazole; not first-line outside these indications. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

explanation.summary: In thunderclap headache (sudden severe maximal intensity within 60 seconds), non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset has greater than 99 percent sensitivity for SAH; beyond 6 hours the sensitivity falls and further investigation is needed. Two acceptable pathways: lumbar puncture after 12 hours from onset looking for xanthochromia by spectrophotometry, or CT angiography to identify aneurysm. If LP is positive (xanthochromia) or CTA shows aneurysm, neurosurgical referral for coiling or clipping is required. Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours and BP control are standard once SAH is confirmed.
key_points: CT <6 h of onset: 99+ percent sensitivity for SAH.
CT >6 h: LP at 12 h onset for xanthochromia, or CTA.
Xanthochromia by spectrophotometry, not visual.
Confirmed SAH: nimodipine 60 mg/4h + neurosurgery referral.
explanation.pearls: Traumatic tap is distinguished from SAH by a falling red cell count between bottles 1 and 4 and absence of xanthochromia; collect at least 4 bottles and send the final two for cell count and spectrophotometry.

options.rationale: Serial CT does not exclude SAH if the index scan was already insensitive at this timepoint; LP or CTA is required at this presentation, not delayed reimaging. (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

The 99 percent sensitivity threshold applies to CT within 6 hours of headache onset; her scan was at 9.5 hours and sensitivity falls to around 92 to 95 percent so SAH must still be excluded by lumbar puncture (or CT angiography). (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

Once CT is performed beyond 6 hours from onset and is negative, LP for xanthochromia is required; CSF should be collected at least 12 hours after headache onset to allow bilirubin formation, and analysed by spectrophotometry (not visual inspection alone). (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)
Sumatriptan is contraindicated in undifferentiated thunderclap headache because vasoconstriction worsens RCVS or cerebral ischaemia; SAH must be excluded first. (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

Nimodipine and the diagnosis of RCVS are considered once SAH has been excluded and after vascular imaging; empirical treatment without exclusion of SAH is inappropriate. (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

explanation.summary: Suspected PE in pregnancy is investigated with bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound first when DVT signs are present (positive USS confirms VTE and obviates chest imaging). If USS is negative, next imaging is CXR; if CXR is normal, V/Q scan (lower maternal breast radiation) is preferred over CTPA. CTPA is acceptable if V/Q is unavailable or CXR is abnormal. D-dimer is unreliable in pregnancy because of physiological elevation. Empirical therapeutic LMWH is started if there is high clinical suspicion while imaging is arranged.
key_points: Leg USS first if DVT signs - confirms VTE without radiation.
If USS neg + CXR normal: V/Q scan preferred over CTPA.
D-dimer unreliable - elevated by pregnancy.
Empirical LMWH if high suspicion and delay anticipated.
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic enoxaparin in pregnancy is dosed 1 mg/kg twice daily based on early pregnancy weight; monitor anti-Xa levels in extremes of weight, renal impairment or recurrent VTE on treatment.

options.rationale: CTPA exposes the maternal breast to significant radiation and is reserved for when leg USS is negative and CXR is normal; in pregnancy, leg USS first avoids unnecessary radiation when DVT signs are present. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

V/Q scan is the chest imaging of choice in pregnancy with a normal CXR if leg USS is negative; however leg USS first is preferred when DVT signs are present because positive USS treats both. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy and even with trimester-adjusted cutoffs it has poor diagnostic utility; international guidelines advise against relying on D-dimer to rule out VTE in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

RANZCOG and Thrombosis Australia recommend bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound as the first imaging step in suspected PE in pregnancy when DVT signs are present; positive USS confirms VTE and treats both diagnoses with the same anticoagulation, avoiding radiation. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

Empirical anticoagulation without imaging exposes mother and baby to bleeding risk without diagnostic confirmation; bedside lower-limb USS is rapid and usually available. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a clinical emergency in known or suspected adrenal insufficiency presenting with hypotension, vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock. Management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg over 24 hours (continuous infusion or 50 mg IV/IM every 6 hours), aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline (1 to 2 litres in the first hour), correction of hypoglycaemia, identification and treatment of precipitant (infection commonest), and electrolyte monitoring. Once recovering, transition to oral hydrocortisone at 2 to 3 times maintenance dose and taper over days. Fludrocortisone is resumed once on usual oral dose.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg/24 h.
Aggressive isotonic saline + glucose if hypoglycaemic.
Treat precipitant - usually infection.
No delay for cortisol testing if clinical adrenal crisis.
explanation.pearls: Every patient with adrenal insufficiency should have an emergency hydrocortisone 100 mg IM ampoule at home, a medic-alert ID, and a sick-day rule (double oral steroid for moderate illness, IM stat for vomiting); educate before discharge.

sources.label: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.rationale: Oral dosing fails in vomiting and adrenal crisis; the patient needs immediate parenteral hydrocortisone, not oral dose adjustment. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available intravenously and provides only mineralocorticoid effect; high-dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at the dose used in crisis. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.rationale: Synacthen testing is not performed in acute crisis because treatment cannot be delayed; in established Addison disease, immediate hydrocortisone is given on clinical grounds without further confirmatory testing. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis requires immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus (then 200 mg over 24 hours), aggressive volume resuscitation with isotonic saline, correction of hypoglycaemia, and treatment of any precipitant; mineralocorticoid effect comes from high-dose hydrocortisone so fludrocortisone is not the priority. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.rationale: Oral medication is inappropriate in a vomiting shocked patient and dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid effect; IV hydrocortisone is required immediately. Investigations should not delay treatment. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

explanation.summary: Step-up therapy for adult asthma not controlled on medium-dose ICS-LABA, despite good adherence and technique, is triple therapy with addition of a LAMA (tiotropium 5 mcg daily or once-daily ICS-LABA-LAMA combinations). Biologics are PBS-funded for severe asthma based on phenotype: omalizumab (allergic, IgE-driven), mepolizumab/benralizumab (eosinophilic), dupilumab (eosinophilic or type 2 high). Always reassess adherence, inhaler technique, environmental triggers, smoking, comorbidities (rhinitis, reflux, obesity, OSA, mental health) before escalating.
key_points: Confirm adherence and technique before stepping up.
Step 4-5: ICS-LABA medium dose + LAMA add-on.
Biologics for severe disease, phenotype-driven.
Maintenance oral steroids only after biologics fail.
Treat comorbidities: rhinitis, reflux, OSA, obesity, smoking.
explanation.pearls: Always check for vocal cord dysfunction in adult-onset wheeze responding incompletely to maximal therapy - inspiratory wheeze, sudden onset and offset, and laryngoscopy during attack confirm the diagnosis and reduce unnecessary asthma escalation.

options.rationale: Montelukast adds modest benefit and carries TGA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects; LAMA is preferred third controller. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

Australian asthma guidance recommends LAMA add-on as the preferred step-up when ICS-LABA at medium dose with good adherence and technique fails to control symptoms, before biologics. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)
Biologics are PBS-funded for severe asthma after optimisation of inhaled therapy including LAMA; she has not yet stepped up to triple therapy. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)
Maintenance oral steroids carry significant long-term morbidity and are reserved for severe refractory asthma after biologic options exhausted. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)
Doubling ICS provides only small additional benefit beyond medium dose and increases systemic effects; LAMA add-on is preferred per current guidance. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

explanation.summary: HIV is notifiable in New South Wales by both laboratories and treating doctors under the Public Health Act 2010, and notification goes to the local public health unit. Partner notification is a separate obligation of care: the Australasian Contact Tracing Guidelines set out patient referral, where the person tells partners himself with your coaching, and provider referral, where the sexual health service or a contact tracing officer contacts them without revealing the index patient's identity. Look-back for sexual partners is guided by the likely window of infection. In context, a new HIV diagnosis carries three parallel jobs: linkage to an s100 prescriber for same-week antiretroviral therapy, statutory notification, and partner notification with testing and post-exposure prophylaxis where a recent contact qualifies.
key_points: HIV is notifiable in NSW by the diagnosing doctor as well as the laboratory.
Partner notification may be patient referral or provider referral, and the index patient is not identified.
Support is available from the sexual health service and contact tracing officers.
Recent contacts may still be within the 72 hour window for post-exposure prophylaxis.
explanation.pearls: Notification and partner notification are different duties with different pathways; doing one does not discharge the other.

options.rationale: HIV is a notifiable condition in New South Wales, and the diagnosing doctor notifies the local public health unit while offering the patient support to notify partners, which he may do himself or through the sexual health service. (Source: NSW Public Health Act 2010; Australasian Contact Tracing Guidelines)

Provider referral by a clinician or contact tracing officer is one accepted method, but it is used with the patient's knowledge after discussion, and anonymously as to his identity; acting behind him breaches confidentiality and deters future testing. (Source: Australasian Contact Tracing Guidelines)

Confidentiality governs who may access his identified record; it does not remove the statutory notification duty, which is met with data handled under the Act's privacy provisions. (Source: NSW Public Health Act 2010)

Public health notification is not contingent on his partner notification choices; escalation to the public health unit for a person who will not notify and continues placing others at risk is a separate and later step. (Source: NSW Public Health Act 2010)

Laboratories notify reactive results independently, but the treating doctor's duty and the clinical information the unit needs are not covered by that, and partner notification would be left undone. (Source: NSW Public Health Act 2010)

explanation.summary: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus uses TB-specific antigens that do not cross-react with BCG vaccination, so a positive result in this patient indicates Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Active TB must be excluded by clinical assessment, chest imaging and respiratory samples before latent treatment to avoid generating resistance. Standard latent TB treatment options include isoniazid 9 months with pyridoxine, rifampicin 4 months or weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid 12 doses. TNF-alpha inhibitors substantially increase risk of reactivation, so treatment should start before biologic initiation when possible. Monitor for hepatotoxicity with monthly liver function tests.
key_points: QuantiFERON-Plus does not cross-react with BCG.
Exclude active TB before treating latent TB.
Isoniazid 9 months with pyridoxine is standard latent therapy.
Start latent TB treatment before TNF-alpha inhibitor.
Monitor LFTs and adherence monthly.
explanation.pearls: Rifapentine plus isoniazid weekly for 12 doses (3HP regimen) is now preferred in many jurisdictions for adherence; rifapentine is not currently widely available in Australia but is on the NTAC option list.

options.rationale: QuantiFERON Gold Plus antigens do not cross-react with BCG vaccination so a positive result indicates Mycobacterium tuberculosis exposure. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)
Active TB must be excluded before treating as latent, otherwise monotherapy risks resistance and progression on biologic therapy. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)
Repeating QuantiFERON without exclusion of active disease and treatment delays both immunosuppression and tuberculosis management. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)
Active TB must first be excluded with directed imaging and microbiology; once excluded, latent TB treatment is given before TNF-alpha inhibitor therapy. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)
RIPE four-drug therapy is for active tuberculosis disease; latent TB is treated with isoniazid monotherapy or short rifamycin regimens. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality exceeding 25 percent and rising rapidly with delay. Pain out of proportion to skin findings, systemic toxicity, crepitus, dusky discolouration and haemorrhagic bullae are red flags. Broad spectrum cover with carbapenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin (for toxin suppression in group A streptococcal disease) is started immediately, with surgical debridement within 6 hours as the strongest determinant of survival. The LRINEC score supports but never excludes the diagnosis when clinical features are present. Repeat debridement and ICU admission are usually required.
key_points: Pain out of proportion plus crepitus or bullae - necrotising fasciitis.
Imaging must not delay surgery in clear clinical cases.
Carbapenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin empirically.
Surgical debridement within 6 hours saves lives.
LRINEC supports but does not exclude the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Add clindamycin specifically for ribosomal toxin suppression in group A streptococcal infection; it works even when beta-lactam efficacy is reduced by high bacterial load in the Eagle effect.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection
WSACS Guidelines for the Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

options.rationale: Imaging delays surgical intervention; necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis with definitive treatment in theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy without urgent surgical exploration in suspected necrotising fasciitis significantly increases mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis demands immediate broad spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin for toxin suppression and urgent surgical debridement; imaging must not delay theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: LRINEC supports but does not replace clinical judgement; a low score does not exclude necrotising fasciitis with classic clinical features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: Outpatient management is inappropriate; necrotising fasciitis requires inpatient resuscitation, IV antibiotics and theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

explanation.summary: Septic shock is defined by hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg plus lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluid resuscitation. The hour 1 bundle covers lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within an hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at least 4, and vasopressors if hypotension persists. Source control (urinary obstruction relief, abscess drainage) is essential and should occur within 6-12 hours. Re-measure lactate and reassess perfusion within 2-4 hours.
key_points: Hour 1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors as needed.
Antibiotics within 1 hour - each hour of delay increases mortality.
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at least 4.
Noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor when MAP below 65 after fluids.
Source control within 6-12 hours of recognition.
explanation.pearls: Use balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte) over 0.9 percent sodium chloride because chloride-restrictive strategies show reduced AKI in critically ill patients (SMART and PLUS trials).

options.rationale: Imaging must not delay antibiotic administration; first-dose antibiotic within an hour is the strongest hour 1 priority. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)
Septic shock requires intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics; oral therapy is inadequate and admission requires high-acuity area not a ward. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)

Cultures before antibiotics if achievable without delay, antibiotic within 1 hour and 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension or lactate above 4 are the hour 1 bundle priorities. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)
Antibiotic delay in septic shock dramatically increases mortality with about 8 percent rise for each hour of delay. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)
Vasopressors are added after initial fluid resuscitation if MAP remains below 65 mmHg, not as first-line ahead of fluids. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening hypotensive emergency in patients with primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency, typically triggered by infection, vomiting or surgery. Immediate management is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat, rapid volume replacement with normal saline 1 L in 30 minutes (up to 3 L in first hour), correction of hypoglycaemia with dextrose, then hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours. At 100 mg/day mineralocorticoid activity is sufficient so fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. Patient education on sick day rules and emergency hydrocortisone injection is essential to prevent recurrence.
key_points: Sick day rules: double oral dose for fever or stress.
Crisis = IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus saline plus dextrose.
Maintain hydrocortisone 50 mg q6h while ill.
Fludrocortisone not needed at high hydrocortisone doses.
Every patient needs an emergency steroid card and self-injection kit.
explanation.pearls: If hyperpigmentation in a Caucasian patient or postural hypotension persists after starting hydrocortisone, suspect primary (not secondary) adrenal insufficiency and arrange Synacthen test plus aldosterone and renin once the patient is stable.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate stat 100 mg IV hydrocortisone, rapid volume resuscitation with normal saline, glucose correction and ongoing parenteral steroid replacement. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
Oral steroids are inappropriate in vomiting hypotensive patients; parenteral hydrocortisone is required to reverse adrenal crisis. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
Dexamethasone has minimal mineralocorticoid activity required for volume management and giving it first delays definitive treatment unnecessarily. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
Vasopressors will not correct cortisol-deficient hypotension which is volume and steroid responsive; treat with fluid and hydrocortisone first. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
Fludrocortisone is not available intravenously and is irrelevant in crisis when high-dose hydrocortisone already provides mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis is upper tract infection with fever, loin pain and lower tract symptoms. In Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, non-pregnant non-septic adults are treated with intravenous gentamicin (5 mg/kg once) plus oral trimethoprim or amoxicillin-clavulanate as step-down, with total duration 10-14 days. Severe sepsis, immunocompromise, obstruction or pregnancy require parenteral broad-spectrum cover such as piperacillin-tazobactam. Urine culture before antibiotics directs targeted therapy. Image (ultrasound or CT) if no improvement at 48-72 hours to exclude obstruction or abscess.
key_points: Gentamicin single dose plus oral step-down for non-pregnant pyelo.
Avoid nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin in pyelonephritis.
Use ciprofloxacin only after culture and stewardship review.
Image at 48-72 hours if no improvement to exclude obstruction.
Total duration 10-14 days with directed oral step-down.
explanation.pearls: Single-dose gentamicin 5 mg/kg leverages concentration-dependent killing with a long post-antibiotic effect, allowing safer transition to oral therapy without ongoing aminoglycoside levels monitoring.

sources.label: Australian Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: IV gentamicin single dose followed by directed oral therapy is recommended for non-pregnant pyelonephritis without sepsis features in Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)
Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal concentrations and is inappropriate for pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

Piperacillin-tazobactam is reserved for severe sepsis, complicated pyelonephritis or healthcare-associated infection rather than uncomplicated cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

Ampicillin gentamicin combination is broader than necessary; gentamicin alone or single dose plus oral step-down meets the standard regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

Fluoroquinolones are reserved for second-line after culture due to resistance, toxicity (tendinopathy, dysglycaemia) and antimicrobial stewardship in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome screening uses any two of three first-line tests: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol above 50 nmol/L next morning is abnormal), 24-hour urinary free cortisol (twice to confirm), and late-night salivary cortisol (twice). Two positive tests support the diagnosis. Avoid screening during illness, depression, alcohol use disorder, recent dexamethasone interaction with CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin) which causes false negatives. Once Cushing is confirmed biochemically, plasma ACTH discriminates ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) and imaging follows.
key_points: Two positive tests of 1 mg DST, 24 h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol.
Avoid screening during acute illness, recent OCP, alcohol use.
ACTH after confirmation: dependent (pituitary or ectopic) vs independent (adrenal).
Pituitary MRI only after biochemical confirmation.
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling for ACTH-dependent equivocal cases.
explanation.pearls: Oestrogen-containing OCP raises cortisol-binding globulin and falsely elevates urinary free cortisol; stop OCP for 6 weeks before screening, or use late-night salivary cortisol which is not CBG-affected.

options.rationale: Random ACTH and cortisol are not diagnostic; Cushing screening requires demonstration of failure of cortisol suppression or elevated unbound cortisol. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)
Catecholamine testing screens for phaeochromocytoma, not Cushing syndrome which requires cortisol assessment. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)
Imaging is performed only after biochemical confirmation; pituitary incidentalomas are common and imaging first leads to misdiagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)
Insulin tolerance assesses adrenal sufficiency or growth hormone deficiency, not Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)
Initial Cushing screening requires two positive tests of the three first-line options: 1 mg DST, 24 h UFC, and late night salivary cortisol. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days started within 48 hours of symptom onset reduces duration, complications and need for antibacterial therapy in influenza. Australian guidelines treat high-risk adults including: age 65+, pregnant or postpartum, chronic respiratory/cardiac/renal/liver/neurological disease, diabetes, immunocompromise, BMI above 40, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults, residential aged care. Treat hospital inpatients regardless of duration. Renal dose-adjust oseltamivir below 60 mL/min. Continue vaccination programs as the primary prevention; treatment is adjunctive.
key_points: Treat influenza in high-risk adults within 48 hours of onset.
Oseltamivir 75 mg BD for 5 days, dose adjust for renal function.
Treat inpatients regardless of symptom duration.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults are a treatment-priority group.
Vaccination remains the primary prevention.
explanation.pearls: Single dose oral baloxavir is a polymerase inhibitor alternative; consider if compliance with 5-day BD oseltamivir is a concern, but resistance can emerge during therapy so it is reserved cases.

sources.label: Australian Influenza Surveillance and Treatment Guidance

options.rationale: Oseltamivir within 48 hours of symptom onset reduces complications and is recommended for high-risk adults (chronic disease, immunocompromise, age 65+) in Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)
Symptom onset within 48 hours is the window for antiviral benefit; this patient is 28 hours in and meets criteria for treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)

Antibacterial therapy is reserved for bacterial superinfection (high fever returning, focal consolidation, sputum change) not empirically with isolated influenza. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)
Inhaled steroid escalation and oral prednisolone treat COPD exacerbation, but the diagnosis here is influenza without exacerbation features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)
Remdesivir is an antiviral for COVID-19, not influenza; oseltamivir or zanamivir are first-line for influenza in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism affects up to 10 percent of resistant hypertension and is associated with disproportionate end-organ damage. Screen with morning plasma aldosterone (PAC) and renin (PRA or direct renin concentration) to calculate ARR. Correct hypokalaemia first; spironolactone, eplerenone and amiloride should be stopped for 6 weeks; beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics may need substitution with verapamil SR or doxazosin. ARR cut-offs vary by assay; confirmatory testing (saline suppression, fludrocortisone suppression, oral salt loading) follows positive screen. Adrenal venous sampling subtypes unilateral vs bilateral for surgical planning.
key_points: Screen resistant HTN, spontaneous hypokalaemia, adrenal incidentaloma with ARR.
Correct potassium and substitute interfering medications before testing.
Confirm with saline suppression or other confirmatory test.
AVS to subtype unilateral vs bilateral disease.
Unilateral disease - laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
explanation.pearls: ACE inhibitors and ARBs suppress aldosterone less than they suppress renin in primary aldosteronism, so an inappropriately measurable PAC with suppressed PRA on these drugs still raises suspicion - do not be reassured by perindopril use.

options.rationale: Phaeochromocytoma screening is appropriate for paroxysmal hypertension; this clinical picture with hypokalaemia strongly suggests aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

Renovascular imaging is reasonable in some patterns but does not explain the spontaneous hypokalaemia, which points to primary aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

Empirical mineralocorticoid blockade obscures subsequent diagnostic testing and prevents confirmation, subtyping and consideration of surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

Aldosterone to renin ratio (after potassium replacement and substituting verapamil/doxazosin for interfering medications) is the recommended screening for primary aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)
DST screens Cushing syndrome which does not typically cause spontaneous hypokalaemia and is less likely than primary aldosteronism here. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman is an osteoporotic event regardless of DXA T-score, and is an indication for pharmacological therapy. Alendronate or risedronate are first-line oral options, with zoledronic acid annual IV for poor oral tolerance or compliance, supported by calcium 1000-1300 mg/day and vitamin D 800-2000 IU/day. Dental review and treatment of any active disease before initiation reduces ONJ risk. PBS criteria for funded therapy include T-score at or below minus 2.5, prior minimal trauma fracture, or steroid use. Reassess at 3-5 years; consider drug holiday if low risk and stable.
key_points: Minimal trauma fracture triggers pharmacological therapy regardless of T-score.
Alendronate weekly oral is first-line.
Zoledronic acid IV yearly if oral intolerance.
Pre-treatment dental review reduces ONJ risk.
Calcium 1000-1300 mg and vitamin D 800-2000 IU daily.
explanation.pearls: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously six-monthly is an alternative for renal impairment (eGFR below 35) but stopping abruptly causes rebound vertebral fractures - always transition to a bisphosphonate when ceasing denosumab.

sources.label: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: Pharmacological therapy is indicated for prior minimal trauma fracture or T-score below minus 2.5; calcium and vitamin D alone are inadequate. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip fractures and is second-line behind bisphosphonates or denosumab. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: MHT is not first-line bone therapy after 60 due to cardiovascular and breast risks though it may be considered with symptomatic women. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for very high risk or PBS criteria such as a prior fracture on bisphosphonate; not first-line therapy. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: Alendronate is first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with minimal trauma fracture; dental review reduces ONJ risk and ongoing calcium and vitamin D supports efficacy. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

explanation.summary: HSV-1 encephalitis is the most common sporadic viral encephalitis with mortality above 70 percent untreated, falling to 20-30 percent with prompt aciclovir. Classic features are subacute fever, headache, behavioural change, focal seizures and temporal lobe signs, with MRI brain showing asymmetric temporal lobe T2 hyperintensity. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose; HSV PCR is highly sensitive after 48 hours of symptoms. Empirical aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours IV starts before imaging or LP and continues for 14-21 days. Add bacterial meningitis cover (ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone) if meningism present pending results.
key_points: Empirical aciclovir IV before imaging or LP if encephalitis suspected.
Aciclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for 14-21 days.
MRI temporal lobe T2 hyperintensity is classic.
CSF HSV PCR may be negative in first 48 hours - repeat if clinical suspicion.
Add bacterial cover if any meningism or rash.
explanation.pearls: Maintain renal function with prehydration and dose-adjust aciclovir for renal impairment - crystalline nephropathy is a recognised reversible toxicity, monitor creatinine daily during therapy.

options.rationale: Empirical aciclovir within 6 hours significantly reduces mortality and morbidity in HSV encephalitis; never delay for imaging or LP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)
Empirical aciclovir should not be delayed for LP because diagnostic confirmation takes hours and delay increases morbidity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)
Bacterial meningitis cover alone misses HSV encephalitis; aciclovir must be added immediately to any empirical regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)
Anticonvulsants treat seizure activity but do not address the underlying encephalitis; aciclovir is the time-critical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)
Foscarnet is reserved for aciclovir-resistant HSV in immunocompromised patients; aciclovir is first-line empirical therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)

explanation.summary: Adult bacterial meningitis requires immediate empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour of suspicion. The Australian standard regimen is ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h plus benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV q4h for pneumococcus, meningococcus and Listeria cover, with adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h for 4 days given just before or with first antibiotic dose to improve outcomes especially in pneumococcal disease. Add vancomycin if penicillin-resistant pneumococcus is a concern, ampicillin in immunocompromised or above 50 for Listeria. CT before LP if focal neurology, seizures, GCS below 14, immunocompromise or papilloedema. Notify public health for meningococcal disease.
key_points: First-dose IV antibiotic within 1 hour of suspicion.
Ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin empirically in Australia.
Dexamethasone with or just before first dose - reduces hearing loss and mortality.
CT before LP only if focal signs, seizures, GCS below 14, immunocompromise.
Notify public health and give meningococcal prophylaxis to close contacts.
explanation.pearls: Add ampicillin 2 g q4h to cover Listeria in patients over 50, pregnant women, or immunocompromised - cephalosporins have no activity against Listeria and missing this cover increases mortality.

options.rationale: Adjunctive dexamethasone improves outcomes (reduced hearing loss and mortality) in pneumococcal meningitis and is given empirically in Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)
Antibiotics must not be delayed for imaging or LP in suspected meningitis; first-dose within 1 hour is the primary goal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)
Suspected bacterial meningitis requires intravenous antibiotics and inpatient management; oral therapy is inadequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)

Vancomycin monotherapy does not adequately cover meningococcus or Listeria; combination with a third-generation cephalosporin is needed in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)

Empirical regimen for adult bacterial meningitis is ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin with dexamethasone given just before or with the first dose of antibiotic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)

explanation.summary: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) presents in patients over 50 with new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, transient or permanent visual loss, and constitutional symptoms. ESR and CRP are typically elevated. Treatment must begin immediately on clinical suspicion to prevent irreversible vision loss: oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily (1 mg/kg) without visual symptoms; IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days when visual loss is present. Temporal artery biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard and remains positive for up to 2 weeks after starting steroid. Tocilizumab is steroid-sparing in relapse or intolerance. Bone protection and PPI are added with high-dose steroid.
key_points: Treat on clinical suspicion - do not wait for biopsy.
Visual loss requires IV pulse methylprednisolone.
ESR and CRP usually elevated; biopsy is gold standard.
Biopsy yield preserved for up to 2 weeks on steroid.
Bone protection and PPI with high-dose steroid.
explanation.pearls: The halo sign on temporal artery ultrasound (hypoechoic ring around the vessel wall) has high specificity for GCA and is a non-invasive alternative for diagnostic confirmation when biopsy is delayed.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice Giant Cell Arteritis

options.rationale: GCA with amaurosis fugax requires immediate high-dose oral or IV steroid to prevent permanent vision loss; biopsy follows within 1 to 2 weeks. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)
Delaying steroids risks irreversible visual loss; treat first, biopsy after - histology remains diagnostic for up to 2 weeks. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)
Aspirin alone does not treat the underlying vasculitis and waiting for imaging delays sight-saving steroid. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)
Suspected GCA with amaurosis fugax is a sight-threatening emergency; analgesia alone is inadequate. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)
15 mg is a polymyalgia rheumatica dose; GCA needs 40 to 60 mg daily (or 1 g pulsed methylprednisolone with visual loss) to suppress vasculitis. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)

explanation.summary: Cellulitis is a dermal and subcutaneous infection commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. Non-purulent cellulitis (no abscess) is treated with oral cefalexin or dicloxacillin for 5 days in non-severe disease. Severe cellulitis with systemic features, rapid spread, immunocompromise, or facial location warrants IV flucloxacillin. MRSA cover (doxycycline or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is added for known MRSA colonisation, recent residential aged care, recent IV drug use or recurrent infections. Demarcate the leading edge to monitor response and elevate the limb. Failure to improve at 48 hours warrants reassessment for abscess, necrotising fasciitis, or unusual pathogen.
key_points: Cefalexin 500 mg QID for 5 days is first-line.
IV flucloxacillin for severe disease or sepsis.
Add MRSA cover for known risk factors.
Demarcate margin and elevate the limb.
Reassess at 48 hours if no improvement.
explanation.pearls: Bilateral lower limb erythema is rarely cellulitis - consider venous stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis or contact dermatitis since cellulitis is almost always unilateral.

sources.label: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: Cefalexin is first-line for non-severe cellulitis in Australia, covering Streptococcus pyogenes and methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is broader than required for typical limb cellulitis and not first-line; reserved for animal or human bite or polymicrobial wounds. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: Doxycycline is added when MRSA is suspected, not used as monotherapy because of inadequate streptococcal cover. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: IV therapy is reserved for severe cellulitis, sepsis or oral failure; non-severe cellulitis is managed with oral cefalexin or dicloxacillin. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.rationale: Penicillin alone misses Staphylococcus aureus which can also cause non-purulent cellulitis; cefalexin or dicloxacillin is preferred. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

explanation.summary: Untreated Graves disease in pregnancy increases miscarriage, preterm birth, pre-eclampsia, congenital malformations and thyroid storm. Distinguish from transient gestational thyrotoxicosis, which is beta-hCG mediated, peaks at 10 to 12 weeks, occurs without TRAb and resolves by 20 weeks. First-line therapy in Graves in pregnancy is propylthiouracil 50 to 150 mg TDS in the first trimester (carbimazole linked to embryopathy in weeks 6 to 10), switching to carbimazole 5 to 15 mg daily from the second trimester (PTU has higher hepatotoxicity risk). Aim for free T4 at the upper limit of normal. Monitor TRAb in late pregnancy as high levels predict neonatal hyperthyroidism. Beta-blockers add symptom control.
key_points: PTU first trimester, switch to carbimazole second trimester.
Aim for free T4 at upper limit of normal.
Radioactive iodine absolutely contraindicated.
Distinguish Graves from transient gestational thyrotoxicosis.
Monitor TRAb in third trimester for neonatal risk.
explanation.pearls: TSH receptor antibody titre over 3 times the upper limit of normal in the third trimester predicts neonatal Graves disease and warrants paediatric endocrinology handover before delivery.

sources.label: ATA Guidelines on Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Carbimazole is teratogenic in the first trimester (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia); switch to propylthiouracil until end of first trimester. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester because carbimazole has a teratogenic window then; switch to carbimazole after 12 to 14 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
Symptomatic Graves disease with positive TSH receptor antibodies is not transient gestational thyrotoxicosis; treatment is required. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy as it crosses the placenta and ablates the fetal thyroid. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)
Beta blockers control symptoms but do not treat the underlying hyperthyroidism, which carries fetal and maternal risk if untreated. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) presents with the core triad of fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. Supportive features include REM sleep behaviour disorder, severe neuroleptic sensitivity, and reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake on DaTscan. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) improve cognition and reduce hallucinations and are first-line. Antipsychotics provoke severe sensitivity reactions (parkinsonism, autonomic instability, cognitive worsening, NMS-like crisis, mortality) in up to half of patients; even quetiapine carries risk. Manage behavioural disturbance with delirium screen, environmental measures, sleep hygiene, melatonin and cholinesterase optimisation first. When antipsychotic is unavoidable, very low-dose quetiapine is the least bad option.
key_points: Core DLB: fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism.
REM sleep behaviour disorder is supportive.
Cholinesterase inhibitor first-line for cognition and hallucinations.
Avoid antipsychotics - severe sensitivity in up to 50%.
Screen for delirium and reversible triggers.
explanation.pearls: Reduced striatal uptake on dopamine transporter (DaT) imaging differentiates DLB from Alzheimer disease with high specificity and supports DLB diagnosis when clinical features are equivocal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.rationale: Antipsychotics, including atypicals such as olanzapine, cause severe sensitivity reactions in Lewy body dementia and are generally avoided. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.rationale: Donepezil should continue - it improves cognition and reduces hallucinations in DLB; stopping it would worsen the clinical picture. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics like haloperidol are particularly dangerous in DLB, causing severe parkinsonism, cognitive worsening and increased mortality. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.rationale: Non-pharmacological approaches with delirium screen and cholinesterase inhibitor optimisation are first-line; antipsychotics carry up to 50% severe sensitivity reaction rate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.rationale: Levodopa is reserved for disabling motor symptoms and used cautiously because it worsens hallucinations and is not first-line in DLB. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

explanation.summary: Duration of anticoagulation for VTE depends on whether the event was provoked, unprovoked or cancer-associated. Provoked VTE with a major transient risk factor (surgery, immobilisation, trauma, pregnancy) is treated for 3 months. Unprovoked VTE is treated for at least 3 to 6 months with consideration of extended therapy if bleeding risk is acceptable; rivaroxaban 10 mg or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily are validated extended secondary prevention options. Cancer-associated VTE is treated with a DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban) or LMWH for at least 6 months and continued while cancer is active. Routine thrombophilia screening does not change management in most cases.
key_points: Provoked VTE: 3 months of anticoagulation.
Unprovoked VTE: at least 3 to 6 months, consider extended.
Cancer-associated VTE: DOAC or LMWH while cancer active.
Routine thrombophilia screening rarely changes management.
Extended low-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban for select unprovoked cases.
explanation.pearls: The HERDOO2 rule identifies low-risk women with unprovoked VTE (under 50, no hyperpigmentation/oedema/redness, D-dimer under 250) who can safely stop anticoagulation at 3 months; men have no validated equivalent.

sources.label: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.rationale: Aspirin gives only modest VTE recurrence reduction; routine prescription is not standard after provoked DVT once anticoagulation is complete. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.rationale: Residual venous thrombus alone does not mandate indefinite anticoagulation in surgically provoked DVT; the provoking factor has resolved. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.rationale: Extended low-dose secondary prevention is for unprovoked VTE with acceptable bleeding risk, not surgically provoked events with no recurrent risk factor. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.rationale: Thrombophilia screening is not indicated for provoked VTE because it does not change duration of anticoagulation in this scenario. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.rationale: Provoked DVT with a major transient risk factor (recent surgery) is treated for 3 months; longer therapy does not reduce recurrence risk meaningfully and increases bleeding. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection presents with sudden severe ripping chest, back or interscapular pain; pulse deficits, blood pressure differential greater than 20 mmHg between arms, new aortic regurgitation, mediastinal widening and end-organ ischaemia are key supportive features. Initial management is impulse control - lower heart rate to under 60 with IV beta-blockade (esmolol or labetalol) THEN reduce systolic BP to 100 to 120 with vasodilator if still elevated; this minimises shear stress on the dissection flap. CT aortogram is the imaging gold standard; TOE is the bedside alternative. Stanford type A (ascending aorta) requires emergent cardiothoracic surgery; type B (descending only) is managed medically unless complicated.
key_points: Rate first then BP with IV beta-blockade.
CT aortogram is the diagnostic gold standard.
Type A = emergent surgery; Type B = medical unless complicated.
Antiplatelet, anticoagulant, thrombolysis contraindicated.
Pulse deficit and BP differential support diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: The pain-pulse-pressure triad of severe chest pain, BP differential greater than 20 mmHg, and pulse deficit identifies dissection earlier than imaging and should mandate empirical impulse control while CT is arranged.

options.rationale: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is contraindicated in suspected aortic dissection; the clinical picture points to dissection, not NSTEMI. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)
TTE has poor sensitivity for type B dissection and may delay definitive CT or TOE; contrast CT aortogram is the standard. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)
Thrombolysis is catastrophic in aortic dissection causing fatal rupture or extension; ECG does not show STEMI. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)
Vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic wall stress; beta-blockade must precede or accompany vasodilator. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)
Type A or B aortic dissection is treated with impulse control (heart rate then BP) and urgent CT aortogram with cardiothoracic surgical involvement. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)

explanation.summary: STEMI reperfusion strategy depends on time from symptom onset and door-to-balloon delay. Primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Otherwise, fibrinolysis with tenecteplase is given within 30 minutes of arrival, combined with aspirin, clopidogrel (preferred over prasugrel and ticagrelor pre-fibrinolysis) and enoxaparin, then transfer for early angiography within 3 to 24 hours. Contraindications to fibrinolysis include recent intracranial bleed, ischaemic stroke within 3 months, severe hypertension and active internal bleeding.
key_points: PCI is preferred if achievable within 120 minutes; otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 minutes.
Adjuncts post-fibrinolysis: aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin.
Pharmaco-invasive transfer for angiography is undertaken within 3 to 24 hours.
explanation.pearls: When predicted door-to-balloon exceeds 120 minutes, give intravenous tenecteplase within 30 minutes of arrival plus clopidogrel 300 mg and enoxaparin, then transfer for early angiography.

options.rationale: Beta-blockers in STEMI are timed after reperfusion and not before; waiting for troponin delays time-critical therapy. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI)

Delaying reperfusion to 150 minutes when fibrinolysis can be given within 30 minutes loses myocardium; fibrinolysis is preferred when PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI)
Antiplatelet therapy alone does not deliver reperfusion in STEMI; either PCI or fibrinolysis is required. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI)
Ticagrelor is an adjunct after the reperfusion decision and does not substitute for fibrinolysis or PCI. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI)

When PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact, fibrinolysis with tenecteplase plus adjunctive clopidogrel and enoxaparin followed by pharmaco-invasive transfer is the recommended Australian pathway. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI; eTG: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Severity stratification of acute pancreatitis uses the revised Atlanta classification: mild (no organ failure), moderately severe (transient organ failure or local complications) and severe (persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours). Modified Marshall scoring identifies cardiovascular, respiratory and renal dysfunction. Severe disease has 20 to 50% mortality and demands HDU or ICU level care, early enteral nutrition and CT imaging only after 72 hours unless complications are suspected. Prophylactic antibiotics are not supported.
key_points: Persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours defines severe acute pancreatitis.
Modified Marshall score grades respiratory, cardiovascular and renal dysfunction.
Avoid prophylactic antibiotics; reserve CT for after 72 hours.
explanation.pearls: Severe acute pancreatitis is defined by persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours; PaO2 under 60 mmHg, urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/hour or systolic BP under 90 mmHg trigger HDU transfer.

options.rationale: Ranson criteria are designed for prognostic scoring not real-time triage and delay critical care decisions; clinical and physiological assessment must guide escalation now. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis)

Prophylactic antibiotics do not reduce mortality or infected necrosis in acute pancreatitis and are not recommended; antibiotics are reserved for documented infection. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis)
Repeat lipase has no prognostic value and ward-level care is inadequate for a patient meeting organ failure criteria. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis)
ERCP in acute pancreatitis is reserved for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; this presentation is alcohol-related and ERCP is not indicated. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis)

Persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours defines severe acute pancreatitis; tachypnoea with PaO2 under 60 mmHg, oliguria and tachycardia in this patient represent at least respiratory and cardiovascular dysfunction warranting HDU-level care. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis; ANZICS guidance)

explanation.summary: Symptomatic carotid stenosis between 70% and 99% benefits substantially from carotid endarterectomy, with the largest absolute risk reduction when surgery occurs within 14 days of the index event. Number needed to treat to prevent one stroke at 5 years is approximately 6 when surgery happens within 2 weeks but rises sharply with delay. Best medical therapy with aspirin, statin and blood pressure control continues alongside surgery. Carotid artery stenting is an alternative when endarterectomy is contraindicated.
key_points: Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70 to 99% should be operated within 14 days.
Number needed to treat is approximately 6 within 2 weeks and rises with delay.
Continue antiplatelet, statin and BP control alongside surgery.
explanation.pearls: TIA with ipsilateral 70 to 99% carotid stenosis - book carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks; the absolute risk reduction halves if surgery is delayed beyond 4 weeks.

options.rationale: Long-term DAPT has not been shown to substitute for revascularisation in symptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis and increases bleeding risk. (Source: NSF Stroke)

Surgical revascularisation is superior to medical management alone for symptomatic 70 to 99% stenosis; medical-only management is reserved for asymptomatic or surgically high-risk patients. (Source: NSF Stroke)

Symptomatic carotid stenosis between 70% and 99% benefits most from carotid endarterectomy within 14 days of the index event; benefit declines markedly beyond 4 weeks. (Source: NSF Stroke; eTG: Cardiovascular)
Delaying surgery beyond 14 days reduces the absolute risk reduction in stroke; the highest recurrence risk falls in the first 2 weeks. (Source: NSF Stroke)

Carotid endarterectomy remains the standard for symptomatic stenosis in patients over 70 with suitable anatomy; stenting is reserved for surgically high-risk patients or unfavourable anatomy. (Source: NSF Stroke)

explanation.summary: The four pillars of HFrEF therapy are ACE inhibitors or ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors. Modern practice favours rapid sequential introduction of all four pillars at low dose rather than full up-titration of each before adding the next. SGLT2 inhibitors have minimal blood pressure effect and are favoured in low-BP patients. ARNI introduction usually requires SBP above 100 mmHg and a 36-hour ACE inhibitor washout before the first sacubitril-valsartan dose.
key_points: Sequential low-dose introduction of all four HFrEF pillars beats slow uptitration of each.
SGLT2 inhibitors are BP-neutral and effective down to eGFR 20 mL/min.
ARNI introduction generally needs SBP above 100 mmHg and 36-hour ACE inhibitor washout.
explanation.pearls: In low-BP HFrEF the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin or dapagliflozin can be added without dose changes to other pillars and offers mortality benefit within weeks.

options.rationale: Up-titration of ramipril risks hypotension in a patient with SBP 98 mmHg; further BP-neutral pillars should be added before pushing the ACE inhibitor. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure)

Sacubitril-valsartan introduces additional blood pressure-lowering effect and is uncertain in this borderline normotensive patient until SGLT2 inhibitor is established; transition usually requires SBP above 100 mmHg. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure)

MRA addition is appropriate but with current eGFR 46 and potassium 4.6 mmol/L it requires close electrolyte monitoring; SGLT2 inhibition has a more favourable risk profile here as the immediate addition. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure)

SGLT2 inhibitors provide mortality benefit in HFrEF independent of diabetes status, are tolerated down to eGFR 20 mL/min and do not lower blood pressure significantly when added to background therapy; this is the next step in low-BP HFrEF optimisation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure; AMH)
Ivabradine requires sinus rhythm with heart rate above 75 bpm despite maximal beta-blocker therapy; this patient is not yet on a beta-blocker. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure)

explanation.summary: In advanced HIV with CD4 under 100 cells/microL, serum cryptococcal antigen screening identifies subclinical infection. A positive result requires lumbar puncture to exclude cryptococcal meningitis. If meningitis is present, induction antifungal therapy combines intravenous liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine for 2 weeks, followed by consolidation with fluconazole and maintenance. ART is delayed by 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal initiation to reduce cryptococcal IRIS risk.
key_points: Serum CrAg-positive HIV patients with CD4 under 100 cells/microL need LP regardless of symptoms.
Defer ART by 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal start to reduce cryptococcal IRIS risk.
Liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine is the induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis.
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic serum CrAg-positive with CD4 under 100 cells/microL needs LP first; if meningitis is confirmed delay ART by 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal induction.

options.rationale: Untreated cryptococcal infection in advanced HIV progresses to disseminated disease and meningitis; intervention cannot wait. (Source: ASHM: HIV)
Starting ART without first excluding cryptococcal meningitis risks fatal cryptococcal IRIS within weeks of immune reconstitution. (Source: ASHM: HIV)
Oral fluconazole alone is inadequate for cryptococcal meningitis induction therapy if disease is present; LP must be performed to know which regimen is required. (Source: ASHM: HIV)

Asymptomatic serum CrAg positivity in advanced HIV requires lumbar puncture to identify subclinical meningitis, which would mandate induction antifungal therapy with delayed ART start to mitigate IRIS. (Source: ASHM: HIV; BHIVA guidance)
Itraconazole is not the recommended cryptococcal prophylaxis or treatment agent and does not replace evaluation for CNS involvement. (Source: ASHM: HIV)

explanation.summary: Status epilepticus is defined as a seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery between. First-line therapy is benzodiazepine: lorazepam 4 mg IV or midazolam 10 mg IM as a single repeatable dose. After two adequate doses without termination, second-line antiseizure medication is given. Australian and ESETT trial data support levetiracetam, sodium valproate or phenytoin with similar efficacy; levetiracetam is preferred in pregnancy, lactation and young women of childbearing potential.
key_points: Two benzodiazepine doses are first-line; a third is not recommended.
Second-line: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, sodium valproate 40 mg/kg or phenytoin 20 mg/kg.
Levetiracetam is preferred in women of childbearing potential.
explanation.pearls: After two failed benzodiazepine doses in status epilepticus, intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg over 10 minutes is the preferred second-line in women of childbearing potential.

options.rationale: After two adequate doses of benzodiazepine in established status epilepticus, intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg is the preferred second-line option with rapid onset, broad efficacy and no drug interactions. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus; eTG: Neurology)

Phenytoin remains an alternative but ESETT-equivalent trial data show levetiracetam achieves seizure cessation at similar rates with fewer cardiovascular side effects in young adults. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus)

Anaesthesia is third-line therapy after a failed second-line antiseizure medication; jumping to anaesthesia denies the chance of terminating with a non-anaesthetic agent. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus)
Sodium valproate is acceptable but is generally avoided in women of childbearing potential due to teratogenicity; levetiracetam is preferred in this group. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus)

After two adequate benzodiazepine doses the failure rate of a third dose is high and respiratory depression accumulates; the standard next step is second-line antiseizure medication. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus)

explanation.summary: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury risk rises with reduced eGFR, diabetes, heart failure, hypovolaemia and use of nephrotoxic drugs. The most consistently effective preventive strategy is intravenous isotonic crystalloid hydration before and after contrast administration. Metformin is held for 48 hours when eGFR is under 45 mL/min because of the risk of metformin-associated lactic acidosis if AKI develops. Iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast at the smallest necessary volume reduces risk further. N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate are not routinely recommended.
key_points: Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% pre- and post-procedure is the primary intervention.
Hold metformin for 48 hours when eGFR is under 45 mL/min.
N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate are no longer recommended.
