explanation.pearls: For eGFR 30 to 45 mL/min undergoing iodinated contrast, intravenous saline at 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and post-procedure with 48-hour metformin pause is the preventive standard.

options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate has not been shown to be superior to sodium chloride 0.9% and is no longer routinely recommended for contrast-associated AKI prevention. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)
Permanent metformin cessation is unnecessary and oral N-acetylcysteine has been shown to have no benefit in preventing contrast-associated AKI. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)
Diuretics increase intravascular volume depletion and metformin should be withheld when eGFR is under 45 mL/min to avoid lactic acidosis if AKI develops. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)

Patients with eGFR under 45 mL/min undergoing iodinated contrast warrant volume expansion with isotonic saline, minimum contrast volume and temporary metformin withdrawal to prevent lactic acidosis from procedural AKI. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)
Diuretic-induced volume depletion worsens contrast nephropathy risk and is contraindicated as prophylaxis. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative preparation aims to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia and post-resection hypotension. Alpha-blockade is started 10 to 14 days before surgery with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin titrated against orthostatic blood pressure. Once adequate alpha-blockade is achieved, a beta-blocker can be added to control reflex tachycardia. Sodium and water loading expands intravascular volume to prevent post-resection hypotension. Intraoperative adjuncts include magnesium sulfate, sodium nitroprusside and short-acting beta-blockers.
key_points: Alpha-blockade precedes beta-blockade by at least 7 days.
Phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin titrated against orthostatic BP.
Sodium loading expands intravascular volume for post-resection BP support.
explanation.pearls: Start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily 10 to 14 days before phaeochromocytoma resection and only add a beta-blocker once alpha-blockade is established; reverse sequence risks fatal unopposed alpha-mediated crisis.

options.rationale: The Endocrine Society Australia-aligned regimen starts alpha-blockade 10 to 14 days before surgery, adds a beta-blocker only after adequate alpha-blockade to avoid unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis, and uses sodium loading to expand intravascular volume before tumour resection. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia; eTG: Endocrinology)
Starting beta-blockade before adequate alpha-blockade leaves unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Calcium channel blockers are second-line additions when alpha-blockade alone is insufficient; they are not preferred monotherapy because they do not blunt catecholamine surge during tumour manipulation. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)
Unprepared phaeochromocytoma surgery carries 25 to 50% perioperative mortality from cardiovascular collapse and is contraindicated. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)
Magnesium is a useful intraoperative adjunct but is not the recommended preoperative blockade regimen. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: In non-valvular atrial fibrillation with CKD stage 3, apixaban is the preferred DOAC because of its lower dependence on renal clearance compared with dabigatran or rivaroxaban. Apixaban dose reduction criteria are any two of age 80 or more, weight 60 kg or less, or creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. Aspirin alone is not recommended for stroke prevention. Warfarin remains a reasonable option, particularly in valvular AF, but DOACs are preferred when monitoring is difficult.
key_points: Apixaban first-line in CKD stage 3 non-valvular AF.
Dose reduce if two of age 80, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 or more.
Aspirin alone is not appropriate stroke prevention in AF.
explanation.pearls: Recheck the apixaban dose-reduction criteria at each annual review; weight loss in older patients tips many into the 2.5 mg twice daily dose.

options.rationale: Dabigatran is 80% renally cleared and is not preferred when eGFR is below 50; doses below 30 mL/min are contraindicated. (Source: NHFA)

Warfarin remains an option (and the only option in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis), but DOACs are preferred when not contraindicated, particularly when reliable INR monitoring is difficult. (Source: NHFA)
Aspirin alone is no longer recommended for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF because it offers little stroke benefit at significant bleeding risk. (Source: NHFA)

Apixaban is preferred in CKD G3b because it has the lowest renal clearance of the available DOACs in AU; dose-reduction criteria (any two of age over 80, weight under 60 kg, creatinine over 133 micromol/L) drive the 2.5 mg twice daily dose. (Source: NHFA AF guideline 2023)
Documented paroxysmal AF on ECG with a CHA2DS2-VA score above 1 already meets criteria for anticoagulation; no time-in-AF threshold is required. (Source: NHFA)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is sustained BP elevation with acute target organ damage (encephalopathy, acute LV failure, dissection, eclampsia, retinopathy, AKI). It is managed with IV titratable agents (labetalol, hydralazine, GTN, clevidipine) in a monitored setting, with a controlled 20 to 25 percent reduction in MAP in the first hour to avoid watershed ischaemia. Hypertensive urgency without acute target organ damage is managed with reintroduction or up-titration of oral therapy in primary care or short-stay observation.
key_points: Reduce MAP 20-25% in the first hour, then more gradually.
Use IV titratable agents in a monitored bed.
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated due to rapid swings.
explanation.pearls: In aortic dissection or pre-eclampsia the BP target is tighter and faster (systolic under 120 within minutes); for encephalopathy aim only for a 20-25% MAP reduction in the first hour.

options.rationale: A hypertensive emergency with acute target organ damage cannot be managed as an outpatient; it requires monitored IV therapy. (Source: NHFA)

In hypertensive emergency with acute target-organ damage (encephalopathy, retinopathy, AKI), the standard is a controlled fall in MAP of 20 to 25% over the first hour using IV titratable agents in a monitored setting; abrupt larger reductions risk watershed ischaemia. (Source: Heart Foundation hypertension guideline 2024)
Documented hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage warrants immediate treatment without further ambulatory monitoring. (Source: NHFA)
Oral combination therapy with hydralazine and clonidine is less controllable than IV titratable agents in a hypertensive emergency and can cause unpredictable BP swings. (Source: NHFA)
Rapid uncontrolled drops, particularly with sublingual nifedipine, are associated with watershed cerebral and renal infarction and are not recommended. (Source: NHFA)

explanation.summary: ABCD2 score predicts early stroke risk after TIA using age, blood pressure, clinical features, duration and diabetes. Scores of 4 or more, or any TIA with atrial fibrillation, warrant urgent same-day assessment in Australia. Aspirin 300 mg loading then 100 mg daily plus carotid imaging within 24 hours reduces early stroke. Dual antiplatelet with aspirin and clopidogrel for 21 days further reduces recurrence after minor stroke and high-risk TIA. Statin and BP control complete secondary prevention.
key_points: ABCD2 4 or more is high-risk for early stroke recurrence.
Load with aspirin 300 mg then 100 mg daily.
Image carotids and brain within 24 hours.
Use DAPT for 21 days after high-risk TIA or minor stroke.
explanation.pearls: About 5 percent of high-risk TIA patients have an ischaemic stroke within 48 hours; an effective rapid-access TIA clinic combined with same-day antiplatelet loading reduces this risk by approximately 80 percent.

options.rationale: ABCD2 score 6 is high-risk for stroke within 48 hours; admit and complete carotid imaging and antiplatelet loading the same day to reduce early recurrence. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)
ABCD2 6 places this patient in the highest-risk group; outpatient management delays urgent revascularisation if a critical stenosis is present. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)
DOACs are reserved for cardioembolic TIA with atrial fibrillation; he is in sinus rhythm and antiplatelet therapy is appropriate. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)
Antiplatelet should not be delayed to wait for MRI; loading dose of aspirin reduces early recurrence and can be given before further imaging. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)
Delaying assessment and antiplatelet therapy by a week in a high-risk TIA misses the window for preventing early stroke recurrence. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

explanation.summary: For atrial fibrillation of definite onset under 48 hours, cardioversion can proceed after at least one therapeutic DOAC dose. For uncertain or longer-duration AF, either three weeks of effective anticoagulation or transoesophageal echo exclusion of thrombus is required first. Anticoagulation continues for at least four weeks after cardioversion regardless of CHA2DS2-VA score. Long-term anticoagulation depends on CHA2DS2-VA score; 2 or more warrants ongoing DOAC therapy in non-valvular AF.
key_points: Cardiovert under 48 h after a single DOAC dose.
Use TOE if onset uncertain or anticoagulation incomplete.
Continue anticoagulation 4 weeks after cardioversion.
CHA2DS2-VA 2 or more triggers long-term DOAC.
explanation.pearls: About 5 percent of patients have post-cardioversion stunning and silent thromboembolism even after successful restoration of sinus rhythm; four weeks of post-cardioversion anticoagulation reduces this to under 1 percent in non-valvular AF.

options.rationale: Onset under 48 hours allows early cardioversion after pre-procedural anticoagulation; full 3 week pretreatment is for established or uncertain onset AF. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

AF onset under 48 hours allows early cardioversion after at least one DOAC dose, with at least 4 weeks of anticoagulation afterwards and long-term anticoagulation given high CHA2DS2-VA. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)
Transthoracic echo cannot exclude left atrial appendage thrombus; TOE is required if cardioversion is needed without prior anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)
Heparin bridging is unnecessary with effective DOAC therapy; modern Australian practice favours single DOAC dose then cardioversion within 48 hour window. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)
Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF; CHA2DS2-VA 4 needs full anticoagulation with a DOAC or warfarin. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle requires lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor for ongoing hypotension to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg. Noradrenaline is first-line and can be initiated through a large-bore peripheral cannula while central venous access is arranged. Vasopressin is added when the noradrenaline dose exceeds 0.25 to 0.5 micrograms/kg/min. Hydrocortisone 200 mg per day is added for refractory shock.
key_points: Start vasopressor if MAP under 65 after 30 mL/kg fluid.
Noradrenaline is the first-line agent in septic shock.
Vasopressin is added at noradrenaline 0.25 mcg/kg/min.
Hydrocortisone is reserved for refractory shock.
explanation.pearls: Each hour of antibiotic delay in septic shock increases mortality by approximately 7 percent; in Australian EDs the eMR sepsis pathway aims for antibiotic administration within 60 minutes of triage triggered by qSOFA or screening tool.

options.rationale: Fluid above 30 mL/kg without response is unlikely to correct vasodilatory hypotension and increases pulmonary oedema risk; start vasopressor now. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

Septic shock with MAP under 65 after 30 mL/kg fluid requires vasopressor; noradrenaline is first-line and can be initiated peripherally while central access is being secured. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Adrenaline boluses are reserved for cardiac arrest; adrenaline infusion is second line in septic shock when noradrenaline plus vasopressin are insufficient. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Dopamine is no longer recommended first line in septic shock due to arrhythmia risk; noradrenaline is preferred. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Hydrocortisone is added when noradrenaline doses exceed 0.25 micrograms/kg/min, not as a substitute for vasopressor; treatment of hypotension comes first. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection presents with tearing chest or back pain, differential pulses or BP, and mediastinal widening. CT angiography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is the standard imaging. Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and requires urgent cardiothoracic surgery. Type B is medically managed unless complicated. Initial pharmacotherapy targets HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg using intravenous esmolol or labetalol first, then nitroprusside or glyceryl trinitrate for ongoing blood pressure control. Analgesia with morphine is administered alongside.
key_points: Image with CT angiography of the aorta urgently.
Beta blocker before vasodilator to prevent reflex tachycardia.
Type A dissection needs urgent cardiothoracic surgery.
Avoid anticoagulation until dissection is excluded.
explanation.pearls: Initial Type A dissection mortality is around 1 percent per hour for the first 48 hours; phone the on-call cardiothoracic surgeon before the CT report is finalised if the patient is haemodynamically unstable or pulse deficits are progressive.

options.rationale: TTE has limited sensitivity for descending dissection; CT angiography is the standard first-line investigation with rapid availability. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)
Heparin is contraindicated until dissection is excluded because it can cause catastrophic haemorrhage from the false lumen; image first. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)
Vasodilator without prior rate control causes reflex tachycardia, increasing shear stress and dissection propagation; beta blocker is initiated first. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

CT angiogram aorta is the first-line investigation in suspected dissection; rate control with esmolol before vasodilator nitroprusside prevents reflex tachycardia and propagation. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)
Differential blood pressure with sudden tearing pain and a widened mediastinum is dissection until proven otherwise; discharge would be catastrophic. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

explanation.summary: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity and reverses anticoagulant effect within minutes. Indications include life-threatening or uncontrolled major bleeding and emergency surgery in patients on dabigatran. Dose is 5 g intravenously as two 2.5 g boluses. Andexanet alfa is the equivalent for apixaban and rivaroxaban, with PCC 25 to 50 IU/kg as alternative when unavailable. Local pharmacy stock and approval pathways should be confirmed in advance for major centres.
key_points: Idarucizumab 5 g IV in two boluses reverses dabigatran fast.
Andexanet alfa or PCC reverses Xa inhibitors.
Vitamin K and FFP do not reverse DOACs.
Confirm pharmacy stock and pathway in advance.
explanation.pearls: About 10 percent of patients re-anticoagulate within 12 to 24 hours after idarucizumab if intrinsic clearance is delayed by renal impairment; recheck thrombin time at 12 and 24 hours and consider a second dose if bleeding recurs.

options.rationale: PCC is the agent of choice for warfarin or factor Xa inhibitor reversal; dabigatran requires the specific reversal antibody idarucizumab as first-line. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)
Idarucizumab is the specific monoclonal antibody fragment reversing dabigatran and is indicated for life-threatening bleeding in patients on dabigatran in Australia. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)
Vitamin K and FFP are for warfarin reversal; they do not reverse the direct thrombin inhibition by dabigatran in significant time. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)
Tranexamic acid does not reverse dabigatran and is not standard therapy for spontaneous ICH; idarucizumab is required for dabigatran reversal. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)
Dialysis removes dabigatran but takes hours; idarucizumab acts within minutes and is the first-line intervention in active major bleeding. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)

explanation.summary: Giant cell arteritis is a medical emergency because of risk of permanent vision loss from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Immediate high-dose corticosteroid 1 mg/kg orally is recommended on clinical suspicion before biopsy. Visual symptoms warrant intravenous methylprednisolone 500 to 1000 mg daily for 3 days. Temporal artery biopsy remains diagnostic for around two weeks after starting steroid. Tocilizumab is steroid-sparing for relapsing or refractory disease. Bone protection, gastric prophylaxis and infection screening accompany prolonged glucocorticoid therapy.
key_points: Start prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally on clinical suspicion.
Use IV methylprednisolone if visual symptoms are present.
Biopsy remains positive for about 2 weeks after starting steroid.
Tocilizumab is the steroid-sparing agent for relapsing disease.
explanation.pearls: Once one eye is affected by anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy in GCA, the contralateral eye becomes involved within 1 to 2 weeks in about 25 to 50 percent of untreated cases; immediate steroid plus ophthalmology review is mandatory.

options.rationale: Australian guidance recommends immediate high-dose corticosteroid in suspected GCA to prevent visual loss; biopsy within 2 weeks remains diagnostic despite early steroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)
Delay in starting steroid risks permanent visual loss; biopsy remains positive for around 2 weeks after corticosteroid commencement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)
Pulsed IV steroid is reserved for visual loss or visual symptoms; oral high-dose prednisolone is appropriate in uncomplicated suspected GCA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)
NSAIDs do not prevent ischaemic complications of GCA and steroid therapy is mandatory; delay is dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)
Low-dose steroid is insufficient for GCA; ultrasound is adjunctive and does not replace high-dose corticosteroid plus biopsy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma crisis is managed by establishing alpha adrenergic blockade first to prevent unopposed alpha vasoconstriction. Phentolamine intravenously is the agent of choice during a crisis, with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin orally during preparation for surgery. Beta blockade with propranolol or metoprolol is added only after alpha blockade is established, to control reflex tachycardia. Adequate sodium loading and volume repletion are required because chronic catecholamine excess contracts the intravascular volume. Definitive treatment is surgical resection after 7 to 14 days of pre-operative blockade.
key_points: Always block alpha receptors before beta in phaeochromocytoma.
Phentolamine IV is the acute alpha blocker of choice.
Adequate sodium loading precedes surgery.
Definitive treatment is laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
explanation.pearls: Aim for postural blood pressure below 120/80 sitting and not below 90/45 standing on alpha blockade, with mild nasal congestion as a clinical marker of adequate blockade before surgery is planned by the multidisciplinary team.

options.rationale: Beta blockade before alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma causes unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis; this sequence is contraindicated. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)
Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia in catecholamine excess and is not first line; alpha blockade is the priority. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)
Labetalol has predominant beta blockade and weak alpha blockade and is not adequate alpha blockade for phaeochromocytoma crisis. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)

Acute phaeochromocytoma crisis is managed with alpha blockade first using IV phentolamine; beta blockade is added once alpha block is established to prevent unopposed alpha effects. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)
Magnesium can be adjunctive in phaeochromocytoma crisis but does not replace alpha blockade which is the cornerstone of management. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)

explanation.summary: Rhabdomyolysis can cause AKI through myoglobin precipitation, ischaemia and oxidative injury, especially with hypovolaemia. Australian and KDIGO guidance recommends early aggressive isotonic crystalloid to keep urine output around 200 to 300 mL/h. Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is treated with calcium gluconate first for membrane stabilisation, then insulin dextrose, salbutamol and sodium bicarbonate to shift potassium intracellularly. Renal replacement therapy is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, uraemic complications or volume overload. Compartment syndrome should be reassessed serially.
key_points: Calcium gluconate stabilises membranes immediately.
Aim for urine output 200 to 300 mL/h with isotonic fluid.
Avoid loop diuretics and mannitol routinely.
Dialysis is reserved for refractory complications.
explanation.pearls: Compartment syndrome can develop with high CK and tense tender muscles even after initial neurovascular exam is normal; serial compartment pressure measurement and early fasciotomy consultation with orthopaedics prevents irreversible muscle and nerve damage.

options.rationale: Insulin and dextrose lower potassium but ECG changes also require immediate membrane stabilisation with calcium before serum potassium-lowering measures. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)
Loop diuretics do not provide protective renal benefit in rhabdomyolysis; volume resuscitation is the priority and furosemide may worsen the situation if hypovolaemic. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)
Myoglobin is not effectively cleared by dialysis; dialysis is reserved for severe AKI with classical indications. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)
Mannitol does not improve renal outcomes in rhabdomyolysis and can worsen AKI if hypovolaemic; isotonic crystalloid is preferred. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)

ECG changes with K 6.4 require immediate calcium gluconate for membrane stabilisation, plus aggressive isotonic crystalloid to maintain urine output above 200 mL/h in rhabdomyolysis. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)

explanation.summary: Therapeutic Guidelines recommend intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours for native-valve MSSA infective endocarditis for at least 4 weeks, with longer courses for prosthetic valve or complicated disease. Empirical therapy in suspected IE before cultures should cover Staphylococcus aureus (flucloxacillin) and, in prosthetic valve disease or MRSA-prevalent settings, MRSA (vancomycin). All patients need transoesophageal echocardiography for embolic and abscess assessment, daily clinical review, and surgical evaluation for complications.
key_points: Flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly is preferred for native-valve MSSA.
Vancomycin is reserved for MRSA or beta-lactam allergy.
Add gentamicin only as advised for synergy in selected scenarios.
TOE is required to assess complications.
explanation.pearls: Right-sided endocarditis in injecting drug users with uncomplicated MSSA disease, no metastatic abscess, normal renal function and no embolic complications can sometimes be treated with shortened intravenous courses or step-down oral therapy under infectious diseases supervision; never make this decision without specialist input.

options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for MRSA or beta-lactam allergy; flucloxacillin has superior outcomes for MSSA infective endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

MSSA infective endocarditis on a native valve is treated with intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours for at least 4 weeks; right-sided uncomplicated disease may be eligible for shorter courses with specialist input. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Amoxicillin and gentamicin target enterococcal or streptococcal endocarditis; this regimen under-treats Staphylococcus aureus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Ceftriaxone has weaker MSSA activity than flucloxacillin and is not recommended as preferred therapy in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Oral antibiotics are insufficient for native-valve endocarditis; intravenous therapy is required with inpatient initiation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 elements include measuring lactate, drawing blood cultures, administering broad-spectrum antibiotics, giving 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and starting vasopressors if hypotension persists. Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor with a MAP target of at least 65 mmHg. Vasopressin and hydrocortisone are added in vasopressor-refractory disease. Source control and re-evaluation drive the next phase of care.
key_points: Lactate above 4 and persistent hypotension after 30 mL/kg meet shock criteria.
Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor.
MAP target is at least 65 mmHg.
Add vasopressin and hydrocortisone in refractory shock.
explanation.pearls: In Australian practice, peripheral noradrenaline through a well-placed proximal large bore cannula is safe for at least the first few hours while a central line is being arranged; do not delay vasopressor initiation waiting for a central access in deteriorating septic shock.

options.rationale: Persistent hypotension and lactate above 4 after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid (achieved at this weight) means further large boluses risk pulmonary oedema; vasopressors should be started now. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Dopamine is associated with more arrhythmia and worse outcomes than noradrenaline and is no longer recommended as a first-line vasopressor in septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

Hydrocortisone is reserved for vasopressor-refractory septic shock; it does not substitute for vasopressor initiation when hypotension persists after fluid resuscitation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

Fluid-refractory hypotension with lactate above 4 meets septic shock criteria; noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor in Australian and international guidelines, targeting MAP at least 65. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Antibiotic therapy must continue without interruption once initiated; deferring doses increases mortality in septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

explanation.summary: Empirical therapy for adult bacterial meningitis in Australia is ceftriaxone for pneumococcal and meningococcal cover, with the addition of benzylpenicillin for Listeria in patients over 50, immunocompromised or pregnant. Adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 hours is given with or before the first antibiotic dose for suspected pneumococcal disease to reduce neurological sequelae. Lumbar puncture, blood cultures and CT brain in selected cases guide ongoing therapy.
key_points: Ceftriaxone covers pneumococcus and meningococcus.
Add benzylpenicillin in patients over 50 or immunocompromised for Listeria.
Dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly reduces sequelae in pneumococcal disease.
Do not delay antibiotics for imaging or Gram stain.
explanation.pearls: Indications to do CT before lumbar puncture include focal neurology, GCS under 10, recent seizure or significant immunosuppression; if any are present, draw blood cultures, give empirical antibiotics and dexamethasone immediately, then arrange CT, and proceed to lumbar puncture once safe.

options.rationale: In patients over 50 or immunocompromised, Listeria cover with benzylpenicillin is required alongside ceftriaxone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Amoxicillin and gentamicin under-treat the typical pneumococcal and meningococcal organisms; cephalosporin cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Adult patients over 50 or immunocompromised need ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly for pneumococcus and meningococcus, benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly for Listeria, and dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Vancomycin alone does not cover Listeria and is reserved for adjunctive cover of penicillin-resistant pneumococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Delaying therapy in bacterial meningitis worsens mortality and neurological outcome; empirical therapy precedes Gram stain results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents with non-specific viral symptoms including fever, lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis and maculopapular rash within 2 to 4 weeks of exposure. The fourth-generation combined antigen and antibody test detects infection from about 2 weeks. When the fourth-generation test is negative but clinical suspicion is high during the window period, HIV RNA viral load PCR detects infection from about 10 days. Early diagnosis allows partner notification, prevention of transmission and prompt initiation of treatment.
key_points: Fourth-generation Ag/Ab detects from 2 weeks post-exposure.
HIV RNA PCR detects from 10 days; useful in window period.
Treat partners and notify with patient agreement.
Refer for specialist initiation of antiretrovirals.
explanation.pearls: In the same consultation, take the opportunity to discuss post-exposure prophylaxis for any other recent unprotected encounters and pre-exposure prophylaxis once acute infection is excluded; many MSM at risk are not yet aware of PrEP availability through Medicare in Australia.

options.rationale: Repeat antibody testing alone delays the diagnosis during the window period when transmission risk to partners is high. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

Acute HIV viral load PCR detects infection from around 10 days post-exposure and is the appropriate next test when fourth-generation Ag/Ab is negative but clinical suspicion is high. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)
CD4 count assesses prognosis in established infection rather than diagnosing acute seroconversion; it is not useful in the window period. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)
Antiretrovirals require a confirmed diagnosis and specialist consultation; empirical commencement is not appropriate primary care practice. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)
Symptoms strongly suggest acute seroconversion; reassurance and delayed review risks ongoing transmission and disease progression. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency. Pain out of proportion, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus and dusky erythema are key clinical clues. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, Hb, sodium, creatinine, glucose) supports clinical suspicion but should never delay surgery. Empirical antibiotics combine broad Gram-negative and anaerobic cover with toxin suppression by clindamycin and MRSA cover by vancomycin. Survival is inversely related to time from presentation to operating theatre.
key_points: Pain out of proportion and crepitus are key clinical clues.
LRINEC supports but does not replace clinical suspicion.
Surgical debridement is time-critical for survival.
Empirical cover: pip-taz plus clindamycin plus vancomycin.
explanation.pearls: Group A streptococcal necrotising fasciitis often presents with hyperacute onset and disproportionate pain before visible skin changes; if the pain story is dramatic and the leg looks deceptively mild, lean towards calling the surgeons early rather than waiting for the rash to declare itself.

sources.label: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

options.rationale: Oral therapy and outpatient review are dangerously inadequate; the clinical picture is necrotising soft tissue infection with high mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Antibiotic monotherapy without surgical debridement does not control source in necrotising fasciitis; mortality climbs steeply for every hour of delay to surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)
Skin biopsy delays definitive source control; diagnosis of necrotising fasciitis is clinical and surgical, supported by laboratory clues such as LRINEC. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

MRI delays surgery and adds no value when clinical and laboratory features already strongly indicate necrotising infection; cross-sectional imaging is selectively used. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Time-critical surgical debridement plus broad empirical antibiotic cover (piperacillin-tazobactam for Gram-negatives and anaerobes, clindamycin for toxin suppression, vancomycin for MRSA) is the Australian standard for necrotising soft tissue infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Parkinson disease pharmacotherapy choice balances symptomatic benefit against motor and non-motor complications. In patients over 65 with clear functional impairment, levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor is first-line because it produces the largest symptomatic benefit with lower risk of hallucinations and impulse control disorders than dopamine agonists. Younger patients with mild disease may start a dopamine agonist or MAO-B inhibitor to defer motor fluctuations and dyskinesia. Multidisciplinary care and falls prevention complement pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Levodopa is preferred first-line in patients over 65.
Dopamine agonists risk hallucinations and impulse problems in older patients.
Younger patients may use agonists or MAO-B inhibitors to delay levodopa.
Multidisciplinary care supports long-term function.
explanation.pearls: Sudden withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy can precipitate a parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome that resembles neuroleptic malignant syndrome; always continue or replace dopaminergic therapy during admissions, even when patients cannot swallow, using rotigotine patch or apomorphine if needed.

options.rationale: MAO-B inhibitors give only modest symptomatic benefit and are inadequate when handwriting and daily activities are clearly affected in older patients. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)
Dopamine agonists in patients over 65 risk hallucinations, daytime sleepiness, impulse control disorders and oedema and are not preferred first-line at this age. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)
Amantadine offers only modest benefit and is not standard first-line monotherapy in early Parkinson disease with functional impairment. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)

Levodopa with carbidopa or benserazide is first-line in patients over 65 with functional impairment; it produces the largest symptomatic benefit with lower hallucination risk than dopamine agonists in this age group. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)

Deep brain stimulation is reserved for selected patients with established motor fluctuations or refractory tremor after years of pharmacotherapy; it is not first-line treatment. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Proximal deep venous thrombosis in a haemodynamically stable patient with adequate renal function is managed as an outpatient with a direct oral anticoagulant. Apixaban or rivaroxaban with the loading-dose regimen are first-line in Australia; warfarin remains used in antiphospholipid syndrome, mechanical heart valves and severe renal impairment. Total duration is at least 3 months for provoked DVT and indefinite for unprovoked or cancer-associated thrombosis. Compression stockings reduce post-thrombotic syndrome risk.
key_points: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily is the loading and treatment regimen
Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily is an equivalent direct oral anticoagulant
Provoked DVT is treated for at least 3 months; unprovoked DVT typically indefinite
Warfarin is preferred in antiphospholipid syndrome and severe renal impairment
IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation
explanation.pearls: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated in mechanical heart valves and antiphospholipid syndrome with triple positivity because of inferior outcomes in trials versus warfarin.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Inpatient unfractionated heparin and warfarin bridging is reserved for selected populations such as those with severe renal impairment or antiphospholipid syndrome; first-line outpatient management uses a direct oral anticoagulant. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Outpatient apixaban with the 10 mg twice daily lead-in for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily for at least 3 months, is the Australian first-line treatment for provoked proximal DVT in a patient with normal renal function and no contraindications. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Catheter-directed thrombolysis is reserved for limb-threatening phlegmasia cerulea dolens; routine thrombolysis is not used for typical proximal DVT. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Inferior vena cava filters are reserved for patients with contraindications to anticoagulation; placing one without justification is not standard care. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Surveillance without anticoagulation is appropriate only for selected isolated distal DVT, not for confirmed proximal DVT, which carries a high pulmonary embolism risk. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Acute exacerbations of COPD are treated with short-acting bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids and selective antibiotics. The COPD-X Plan recommends oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days; tapering is unnecessary and does not improve outcomes. Antibiotics are added when at least two of the Anthonisen criteria are met or when ventilatory support is required. Controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 88 to 92% prevents hypercapnic acidosis in CO2 retainers.
key_points: Oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days without taper is the recommended course
Antibiotics if 2 of 3 Anthonisen criteria are met: dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence
Controlled oxygen to SpO2 88 to 92% avoids worsening hypercapnia
Non-invasive ventilation is indicated for pH below 7.35 with pCO2 above 45 mmHg
Smoking cessation and pulmonary rehabilitation reduce future exacerbations
explanation.pearls: Eosinophil count above 0.3 x10^9/L during exacerbation predicts greater response to corticosteroids and is increasingly used to guide steroid use in COPD.

options.rationale: A single hydrocortisone dose alone is insufficient; an oral prednisolone course is required to consolidate the anti-inflammatory effect on the airways. (Source: COPD-X Plan)
Australian guidelines recommend a 5-day course of oral prednisolone for COPD exacerbations; longer courses do not improve outcomes and increase adverse effects. (Source: COPD-X Plan)
Continuous maintenance prednisolone is not recommended for COPD because of the side-effect burden; exacerbations are treated with short courses. (Source: COPD-X Plan)
Exacerbations with hypoxia and accessory muscle use require systemic corticosteroids; inhaled steroid alone does not address the acute airway inflammation. (Source: COPD-X Plan)

Oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days without taper is the Australian COPD-X recommendation; antibiotics are indicated when at least two of the Anthonisen criteria (increased dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) are met. (Source: COPD-X Plan)

explanation.summary: Metformin remains the first-line pharmacotherapy for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes in Australia, alongside lifestyle modification. It is weight neutral, has no hypoglycaemia risk and reduces cardiovascular events in observational data. Renal function should be monitored: dose reduction is required when eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and metformin is contraindicated below 30. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists are added when cardiovascular, renal or weight indications exist.
key_points: Metformin is first-line at HbA1c above 6.5% with eGFR above 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2
Dose reduce at eGFR 30 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and avoid below eGFR 30
SGLT2 inhibitors are added with cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease
GLP-1 receptor agonists are added with obesity, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or for weight loss
Sulfonylureas remain useful third-line but cause weight gain and hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: Hold metformin for 48 hours around iodinated contrast administration if the eGFR is below 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 to reduce lactic acidosis risk from contrast-induced renal impairment.

sources.label: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.rationale: Basal insulin is reserved for severe hyperglycaemia, symptomatic disease or failure of oral therapy; first-line for new type 2 diabetes is metformin. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.rationale: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are typically added to metformin or used first-line with confirmed cardiovascular or renal indications; they are not standard initial monotherapy. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.rationale: An HbA1c of 7.8% at diagnosis warrants concurrent metformin initiation alongside lifestyle measures; lifestyle alone takes too long to achieve target. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.rationale: Metformin is first-line for new type 2 diabetes in Australia with renal function above eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2; gradual titration reduces gastrointestinal side effects and HbA1c review at 3 months guides escalation. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.rationale: Sulfonylureas are second-line because they cause weight gain and hypoglycaemia; metformin is preferred first-line for new type 2 diabetes. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

explanation.summary: New-onset atrial fibrillation in a stable patient is managed with rate control and stroke risk assessment using CHA2DS2-VA. Beta-blockers are first-line rate-control agents in patients without heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or asthma. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are second-line; digoxin is reserved for heart failure or as add-on. A CHA2DS2-VA score of at least 2 in men or at least 3 in women warrants long-term oral anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant.
key_points: Beta-blockers are first-line rate control in stable atrial fibrillation with preserved ejection fraction
CHA2DS2-VA at least 2 in men or at least 3 in women warrants anticoagulation
Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred over warfarin except in mechanical valves or antiphospholipid syndrome
Cardioversion within 48 hours still requires anticoagulation if stroke risk factors are present
Amiodarone is reserved for rhythm control in structural heart disease or refractory cases
explanation.pearls: The CHA2DS2-VA score replaced CHA2DS2-VASc in Australian practice in 2024, removing sex as a stroke risk variable; both men and women are evaluated on the remaining clinical risk factors.

options.rationale: Digoxin is reserved as second-line rate control or for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; beta-blockers are first-line in stable patients with preserved ejection fraction. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

A beta-blocker is the first-line rate-control agent for atrial fibrillation in a stable patient without heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or asthma; concurrent direct oral anticoagulation is started because his CHA2DS2-VA score is 2. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

Even within a 48-hour window, anticoagulation is recommended at the time of cardioversion in patients with an elevated CHA2DS2-VA score and ongoing thereafter. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

Amiodarone is reserved for symptomatic rhythm control in patients failing other rhythm-control agents or with structural heart disease; it is not first-line for stable rate control. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are second-line and avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; beta-blockers are preferred first-line in Australia. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is diagnosed by sputum microbiological testing after appropriate airborne infection control. Three early-morning sputum specimens are submitted for acid-fast smear, Xpert MTB/RIF nucleic acid amplification and mycobacterial culture. Xpert provides a rapid result with rifampicin resistance information within hours and is now standard first-line testing in Australia. Treatment with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol is started once microbiological diagnosis is confirmed, ideally with directly observed therapy.
key_points: Airborne isolation in a single negative-pressure room precedes sampling and treatment
Three sputum specimens are submitted for smear, Xpert MTB/RIF and culture
Xpert MTB/RIF provides rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistance within hours
Tuberculin skin testing and interferon gamma release assays detect latent infection, not active disease
HIV testing is recommended in all newly diagnosed cases of tuberculosis
explanation.pearls: All new diagnoses of active tuberculosis in Australia are notifiable to the relevant state or territory public health authority within 24 hours of suspicion, even before culture confirmation.

options.rationale: Empirical treatment before sampling compromises microbiological diagnosis and drug susceptibility testing; airborne isolation and rapid sampling are required first. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

Tuberculin skin testing assesses latent infection and may be negative in active disease; it does not establish active tuberculosis diagnosis or guide treatment. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

Interferon gamma release assays detect latent infection and are not diagnostic of active pulmonary tuberculosis; sputum testing for nucleic acid amplification and culture is required. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

Australian guidance requires airborne isolation, three sputum specimens for smear, Xpert MTB/RIF nucleic acid amplification testing and culture; Xpert results within hours allow rapid initiation of treatment with rifampicin resistance information. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

Bronchoscopy is reserved for sputum-scarce or sputum-negative cases; sputum sampling is the first-line investigation and avoids unnecessary aerosolisation. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

explanation.summary: Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism is defined by haemodynamic compromise including persistent hypotension or shock. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin and resuscitation reduces mortality. Submassive (intermediate-risk) pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain and raised troponin is managed with anticoagulation and close monitoring, with rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs. Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed thrombolysis is reserved for contraindications to systemic thrombolysis or thrombolysis failure.
key_points: Massive PE with hypotension or shock warrants systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg
Intermediate-risk PE is anticoagulation with monitoring; rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs
Low-risk PE may be treated as outpatient with direct oral anticoagulants
Right ventricular dilation and septal bowing are echocardiographic markers of high risk
Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy is reserved for thrombolysis failure or contraindication
explanation.pearls: Half-dose alteplase 50 mg has been used in catheter-directed thrombolysis trials for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism with reduced bleeding rates, although mortality benefit remains unproven.

options.rationale: Therapeutic enoxaparin alone is appropriate for haemodynamically stable patients; massive pulmonary embolism with shock requires reperfusion therapy in addition to anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)
Inferior vena cava filters are considered when anticoagulation is contraindicated; they do not address the existing pulmonary embolism causing shock. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism with shock requires systemic thrombolysis with alteplase plus heparin and vasopressor support; this regimen reduces mortality in haemodynamically unstable patients. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

Oral apixaban and outpatient management are appropriate for low-risk pulmonary embolism; massive pulmonary embolism with shock requires inpatient reperfusion therapy. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

Surgical embolectomy is reserved for thrombolysis failure or contraindication and centres with cardiothoracic capability; systemic thrombolysis is first-line if no absolute contraindication. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening complication of adrenal insufficiency precipitated by intercurrent illness, vomiting or missed steroid doses. Diagnosis is clinical and treatment must not be delayed for laboratory confirmation. Immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, aggressive crystalloid resuscitation with dextrose to correct hypoglycaemia, and treatment of the precipitant are time-critical. Patients with known adrenal insufficiency should carry a steroid emergency card and have a hydrocortisone autoinjector or intramuscular hydrocortisone available at home.
key_points: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis; do not delay treatment for cortisol levels
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg six-hourly or 200 mg over 24 hours infusion
Aggressive crystalloid resuscitation with dextrose 5% corrects volume, sodium and hypoglycaemia
Identify and treat precipitants: infection, surgery, vomiting, missed steroid doses
Hydrocortisone at this dose provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity, so fludrocortisone is paused
explanation.pearls: Sick-day rules for patients on long-term steroids include doubling the oral dose for fever above 38 °C and tripling for fever above 39 °C, with intramuscular hydrocortisone for vomiting or unable to take oral medications.

options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity; hydrocortisone is the agent of choice because it provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effect at high dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Oral hydrocortisone is inappropriate when the patient is vomiting and in shock; intravenous administration is required, and triple oral dosing is reserved for milder intercurrent illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Hypertonic saline and fluid restriction are inappropriate in adrenal crisis with hypovolaemic shock; aggressive isotonic fluid replacement and intravenous hydrocortisone are required first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis; treatment must not be delayed for laboratory results because mortality rises rapidly with delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis treated with stat intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, aggressive crystalloid resuscitation with dextrose, and treatment of any precipitant such as infection; do not delay for laboratory results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: SIADH is a euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia diagnosed by low plasma osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine (above 100 mOsm/kg), urine sodium above 30 mmol/L and normal adrenal and thyroid function. Pneumonia, central nervous system disease and many drugs are common precipitants. First-line treatment is fluid restriction to 800 to 1000 mL per day; tolvaptan is reserved for refractory or chronic cases. Correction must not exceed 10 mmol/L in 24 hours and 18 mmol/L in 48 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SIADH criteria: euvolaemia, plasma osmolality below 275, urine osmolality above 100, urine sodium above 30
Free water restriction to 800 to 1000 mL per day is first-line therapy
Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms: seizures, coma or severe confusion
Correction limit is 10 mmol/L in 24 hours and 18 mmol/L in 48 hours
Tolvaptan is used in chronic or refractory SIADH under specialist supervision
explanation.pearls: Overcorrection of chronic hyponatraemia at more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks central pontine myelinolysis with locked-in syndrome; if overcorrection occurs, dextrose 5% and desmopressin re-lower the sodium safely.

options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or coma; this patient has mild confusion only and free water restriction is the first-line measure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Intravenous isotonic saline in SIADH worsens hyponatraemia because the sodium is excreted while water is retained; free water restriction is the correct approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Plasma osmolality of 256 mOsm/kg confirms true hyponatraemia; pseudohyponatraemia from severe hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia is excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, urine osmolality above 100, low plasma osmolality, euvolaemia and pneumonia as precipitant confirm SIADH; free water restriction is first-line, and reviewing precipitants is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist used in chronic or refractory SIADH; it is not first-line and risks overcorrection if used without specialist supervision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: ST-elevation myocardial infarction within 12 hours of onset requires immediate reperfusion. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention is the preferred strategy where it can be delivered within 90 minutes of first medical contact, or 120 minutes from first medical contact if patient transfer is required. Fibrinolysis is used when PCI cannot be delivered within these windows, followed by routine angiography 3 to 24 hours later (pharmacoinvasive strategy). Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation are commenced before angiography.
key_points: Primary PCI preferred if door-to-balloon within 90 minutes onsite
Fibrinolysis with tenecteplase if PCI not available within 120 minutes from first contact
Pharmacoinvasive strategy: angiography 3 to 24 hours after successful fibrinolysis
Dual antiplatelet loading and anticoagulation before angiography
Cardiogenic shock or mechanical complications mandate immediate angiography regardless of timing
explanation.pearls: Failed fibrinolysis (under 50% ST resolution at 90 minutes) mandates rescue PCI as soon as possible, distinct from the routine pharmacoinvasive angiography window.

options.rationale: Fibrinolysis is reserved for STEMI presenting where primary PCI is not available within 90 minutes from first medical contact; here PCI is onsite and is preferred. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)

Delaying revascularisation in a STEMI by 24 hours loses myocardium; reperfusion must be immediate, preferably by primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)

Anterior STEMI within 12 hours of onset at a PCI-capable hospital requires immediate primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact with dual antiplatelet loading and anticoagulation. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)
STEMI is an ECG diagnosis and immediate reperfusion is not delayed for troponin or CT confirmation; CT coronary angiography has no role in acute STEMI. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)
Conservative management without reperfusion in STEMI within the window of opportunity results in avoidable myocardial loss and worse outcomes. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP triages community-acquired pneumonia severity and disposition: scores of 0 to 2 are low risk and suitable for outpatient management. High-dose oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days is first line in Australia. Doxycycline is added or substituted if atypical pathogens are suspected (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila). Moxifloxacin is reserved for beta-lactam allergy or severe disease. SMART-COP 3 to 4 prompts hospital admission, often with intravenous ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline or azithromycin; SMART-COP 5 or more prompts ICU consideration.
key_points: SMART-COP 0 to 2: outpatient oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days
Doxycycline added if atypical pathogens suspected (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila)
Moxifloxacin reserved for severe penicillin allergy or severe disease
SMART-COP 3 to 4 triggers admission for intravenous therapy
Review at 48 hours and escalate if no improvement
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP allocates 2 points each for systolic BP under 90, oxygen saturation under 90% (or under 94% if under 50 years), and pH under 7.35, while age threshold lowers SpO2 cut-off and other variables get 1 point each.

options.rationale: Azithromycin monotherapy is inadequate empirical cover for typical Streptococcus pneumoniae because of high macrolide resistance rates in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cefalexin has poor pneumococcal coverage compared with amoxicillin and is not the recommended first-line agent for community-acquired pneumonia in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Respiratory fluoroquinolones are reserved for severe pneumonia, beta-lactam allergy or proven resistant organisms; routine outpatient use drives resistance and adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

High-dose oral amoxicillin is the first-line agent for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia (SMART-COP 0 to 2) in Australia, with 5 day duration; doxycycline is the macrolide-equivalent alternative for atypical cover when needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for moderate severity, aspiration risk or specific resistant pathogens; it is not first line for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Initial management of new atrial fibrillation prioritises stroke risk assessment and rate control. Stroke risk by CHA2DS2-VA: a score of 2 or more in men or women warrants oral anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban or dabigatran) unless contraindicated, with warfarin reserved for moderate to severe mitral stenosis or mechanical valves. Rate control with a beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is first line; rhythm control with cardioversion, flecainide, sotalol or amiodarone is considered when symptoms persist despite rate control, and catheter ablation is an option in symptomatic recurrent disease.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 or more triggers oral anticoagulation
DOACs first line for non-valvular AF; warfarin for mechanical valves and severe mitral stenosis
Aspirin has no role in atrial fibrillation stroke prevention
Metoprolol or atenolol first line for rate control
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
explanation.pearls: Apixaban dose is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80 years or older, body weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher.

options.rationale: Cardioversion without preceding 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or transoesophageal echocardiogram exclusion of left atrial thrombus risks embolic stroke; aspirin is not adequate for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)
Amiodarone is reserved for specialist-initiated rhythm control because of significant adverse effects, and aspirin is inadequate stroke prevention with CHA2DS2-VA 4. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)
Digoxin is second line for rate control because it controls only resting rate poorly during activity, and aspirin is inadequate anticoagulation for CHA2DS2-VA 4. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

Apixaban is first-line anticoagulation in non-valvular atrial fibrillation with CHA2DS2-VA at least 2, and metoprolol is the standard rate-control agent; rhythm control via specialist review remains an option. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)
Catheter ablation is reserved for symptomatic rhythm control after failure of antiarrhythmic therapy and never replaces stroke-prevention anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Moderate adult asthma is graded by ability to speak in phrases, heart rate under 120, oxygen saturation 92 to 94% on air and peak expiratory flow 50 to 75% of personal best or predicted. First-line treatment is salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer (or 5 mg nebulised) every 20 minutes for an hour, with oxygen targeted to 93 to 95% and oral prednisolone 50 mg within the first hour. Ipratropium bromide is added in severe exacerbations. Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes is reserved for severe or life-threatening exacerbations not responding to first-line therapy.
key_points: Salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer (or 5 mg nebulised) every 20 minutes for 1 hour
Oral prednisolone 50 mg early; intravenous hydrocortisone only if unable to swallow
Oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95%, not 100%
Ipratropium added for severe exacerbations
Intravenous magnesium 2 g for severe disease unresponsive to first-line therapy
explanation.pearls: Oxygen target in acute asthma is 93 to 95% saturation because higher saturations risk worsening V/Q mismatch and hypercapnia, mirroring the COPD principle.

options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or near-fatal asthma; routine antibiotics are not indicated without features of bacterial infection. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

Discharge after only 30 minutes with a peak flow of 200 L/min and ongoing distress is unsafe; bronchodilator response must be assessed at one hour and oral corticosteroids initiated. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

Intravenous corticosteroid offers no advantage over oral in an alert cooperative patient and aminophylline is reserved for severe disease unresponsive to first-line therapy. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

Moderate asthma exacerbation is managed with repeated salbutamol via spacer or nebuliser every 20 minutes for an hour, early oral prednisolone 50 mg and oxygen targeted to 93 to 95%; reassessment at one hour decides disposition. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

Heliox and intravenous magnesium are reserved for severe or life-threatening asthma after failure of first-line therapy; high-dose magnesium of 10 g is not the standard adult dose. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves, broad QRS, sine wave) is a cardiac emergency. Management proceeds in three stages: cardiac membrane stabilisation with intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% (or calcium chloride 10 mL of 10% if central access), potassium shift into cells with insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% dextrose plus nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg, and potassium elimination via dialysis, furosemide if urine output preserved, or oral resin slowly. Identify and reverse contributors: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim, NSAIDs, missed dialysis.
key_points: Calcium gluconate first for ECG changes; effect within 3 minutes, lasts about 30 minutes
Insulin-dextrose and nebulised salbutamol shift potassium intracellularly over 15 to 30 minutes
Dialysis is definitive for advanced CKD or severe refractory hyperkalaemia
Stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim and NSAIDs
Repeat ECG and potassium at 30 minutes after intervention
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim and ACE inhibitor combination in advanced CKD is a common precipitant of severe hyperkalaemia through epithelial sodium channel block plus aldosterone suppression.

options.rationale: Resonium is intravenously inappropriate (oral or rectal) and acts slowly over hours; it does not address the immediate cardiac membrane risk from a potassium of 7.4 with ECG changes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Loop diuretic is slow and unlikely to be effective in advanced kidney disease, and oral salbutamol is not used; nebulised salbutamol is one of the membrane and shift agents. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guidelines)

ECG changes with severe hyperkalaemia mandate immediate intravenous calcium for cardiac membrane stabilisation before shift therapy; relying on insulin-dextrose alone delays myocardial protection. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guidelines)

Drug therapy for hyperkalaemia is faster than mechanical pacing and resolves the underlying cause; intubation is not required if the patient is alert and ventilating. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guidelines)

Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes requires immediate calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then potassium-shifting therapy with insulin-dextrose and salbutamol, and dialysis for definitive removal in this patient with advanced kidney disease. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, reduced conscious state, vomiting from cerebral oedema) is a neurological emergency. Management is 3% sodium chloride 150 mL intravenous bolus over 10 minutes, repeated up to three times until symptoms resolve, aiming for a 4 to 6 mmol/L rise in the first hour. Total correction must not exceed 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, or 18 mmol/L in 48 hours, to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. Subsequent management addresses underlying cause: SIADH from drugs, malignancy, central nervous system or pulmonary disease; volume depletion with isotonic saline; or hypervolaemia with diuresis.
key_points: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia mandates 3% saline 150 mL boluses
Target rise 4 to 6 mmol/L in first hour to resolve symptoms
Cap correction at 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, 18 mmol/L in 48 hours
Recheck sodium every 2 hours during active correction
Identify cause: drugs, SIADH triggers, volume status
explanation.pearls: If correction exceeds 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, give 5% dextrose 6 mL/kg over 1 to 2 hours to relower sodium and prevent osmotic demyelination.

options.rationale: Isotonic saline alone does not correct seizing severe hyponatraemia and may even worsen sodium in SIADH; hypertonic saline is required for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)
Oral measures act too slowly for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure; hypertonic saline is required to raise sodium acutely. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)
Demeclocycline is occasionally used in chronic SIADH for outpatients and has no role in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with seizure. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)
Tolvaptan can cause uncontrolled rapid correction and is contraindicated in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; hypertonic saline is preferred. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)

Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure requires immediate hypertonic saline boluses targeting a 4 to 6 mmol/L rise in the first hour, capped at 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis is characterised by acidaemia, raised paCO2 above the chronic baseline and an elevated bicarbonate reflecting prior renal compensation. In COPD exacerbation with pH under 7.35 and paCO2 over 45 despite controlled oxygen and bronchodilator therapy, non-invasive bilevel ventilation is the standard of care because it reduces intubation, mortality and hospital length of stay. Oxygen is titrated to a target saturation of 88 to 92% to avoid worsening hypercapnia from loss of hypoxic drive and reversal of pulmonary vasoconstriction.
key_points: Elevated HCO3 plus acidaemia signals acute on chronic respiratory acidosis
NIV indicated for pH under 7.35 and paCO2 over 45 despite optimal medical therapy
Oxygen target 88 to 92% in COPD to avoid hypercapnia
Bronchodilators, prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally for 5 days and antibiotic if 2 of 3 Anthonisen criteria
Failure of NIV with worsening pH or conscious state prompts invasive ventilation
explanation.pearls: Bilevel non-invasive ventilation typically starts at IPAP 12 and EPAP 5 with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 88 to 92%, with arterial blood gas reassessed at 1 hour.

options.rationale: The bicarbonate is elevated at 32 indicating metabolic compensation present, not acute respiratory acidosis alone; the picture fits acute on chronic respiratory acidosis. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)

If the picture were fully compensated chronic respiratory acidosis the pH would be near normal; pH 7.28 with paCO2 70 indicates acute decompensation on top of chronic retention. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)
Metabolic alkalosis would raise pH, not lower it; the low pH and very high paCO2 indicate respiratory acidosis as the primary disturbance. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)
Stopping oxygen risks fatal hypoxia; the pattern reflects acute on chronic ventilatory failure requiring non-invasive ventilation, with oxygen titrated to 88 to 92%. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)

Elevated bicarbonate indicates chronic CO2 retention with renal compensation, while the acidaemia and very high paCO2 indicate acute decompensation; non-invasive ventilation is indicated and oxygen targeted to 88 to 92% prevents worsening hypercapnia. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (typically over 180/120) with evidence of acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, retinopathy, acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection or eclampsia). It requires immediate admission to a monitored bed and titrated intravenous antihypertensive therapy. The pressure should be lowered by 20 to 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours; faster reduction risks watershed cerebral, renal or coronary infarction. Specific scenarios alter agent choice: labetalol or esmolol with sodium nitroprusside for aortic dissection, GTN for pulmonary oedema, magnesium for eclampsia.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency requires end-organ damage, not just BP above 180/120
Lower mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25% in the first hour, no faster
Then aim for 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours
Intravenous GTN or labetalol in a monitored bed
Sublingual nifedipine and captopril are contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Aortic dissection requires aggressive beta-blockade with labetalol or esmolol first to reduce shear stress before vasodilator therapy, with target systolic 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate under 60.

options.rationale: Sublingual captopril produces rapid uncontrolled drops in pressure and the target of under 140/90 in the first hour risks cerebral hypoperfusion; admission with parenteral therapy is required. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled drops in blood pressure with risk of stroke and myocardial ischaemia and is no longer recommended in any hypertensive presentation. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

Furosemide and oral therapy do not provide the controlled, titrable reduction needed for hypertensive emergency; intravenous infusion of a short-acting agent in a monitored bed is preferred. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

End-organ damage (acute kidney injury, retinopathy) makes this a hypertensive emergency requiring inpatient parenteral therapy, not titration of oral medications at home. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage is treated with a titrated intravenous infusion (GTN or labetalol) in a monitored bed, with mean arterial pressure reduced by 20 to 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours, to avoid hypoperfusion. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Hard signs include pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, soft tissue gas and rapid progression. LRINEC score combines CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; 6 or above is high-risk and 8 or above strongly suggestive. Management is urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for streptococcal toxin suppression. Imaging must never delay theatre.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus and gas are necrotising fasciitis red flags
LRINEC 6 or above is high-risk; 8 or above strongly suggests necrotising fasciitis
Urgent surgical debridement is the definitive treatment
Empirical antibiotics include broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin for toxin suppression
Imaging supports but does not delay surgical exploration
explanation.pearls: The finger test (insertion of a gloved finger through a small skin incision under local anaesthetic) yields easy dissection through subcutaneous tissue without bleeding when necrotising fasciitis is present; a positive bedside finger test is diagnostic and prompts immediate theatre.

sources.label: ANZ Surgical Site Infection Prevention Guidelines

options.rationale: MRI is supportive but should never delay surgical exploration in suspected necrotising fasciitis; antibiotics are started empirically without waiting for imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Ward-based monotherapy for presumed cellulitis misses necrotising fasciitis features; delay to debridement increases mortality from around 25% to over 50% beyond 24 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, soft tissue gas and LRINEC 6 or above strongly indicate necrotising fasciitis requiring emergency surgical debridement; broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression are commenced concurrently. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: ANZ Surgical Site Infection Prevention Guidelines

options.rationale: Severe sepsis with hypotension, lactate 4.1 and LRINEC 9 cannot be managed at home; oral cefalexin is inadequate for either severe cellulitis or necrotising fasciitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
IVIG is adjunctive in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome but does not replace surgical debridement or empirical antibiotics; delay to theatre is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Australian empirical therapy for adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours, started within 30 minutes of consideration. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or just before the first antibiotic dose reduces death and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal disease. CT before LP is reserved for focal neurology, papilloedema, immunocompromise or recent seizure. Listeria cover with benzylpenicillin is included for over-50, pregnant or immunocompromised patients.
key_points: Empirical ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin within 30 minutes of consideration
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or just before first antibiotic dose for pneumococcal benefit
CT before LP for focal neurology, papilloedema, immunocompromise or recent seizure
Listeria cover with benzylpenicillin for over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised
Continue dexamethasone for 4 days only if CSF or blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone reduces unfavourable outcomes only in pneumococcal meningitis and should be stopped at 48 hours if CSF or blood cultures grow another organism or are negative; continuing in non-pneumococcal cases offers no benefit and risks hyperglycaemia.

sources.label: ASID Adult Bacterial Meningitis Position Statement

options.rationale: Although CT before LP is reserved for specific risk factors, antibiotics should still precede LP when LP is delayed for any reason; sequence matters because of the urgency of antibiotic timing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Empirical antibiotics must not be delayed beyond 30 minutes for any reason in suspected bacterial meningitis; mortality rises with each hour of delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin is added when penicillin or cephalosporin resistance is suspected (e.g. recent foreign travel, recent antibiotic use); empirical first-line in Australia is ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin without vancomycin in the absence of those risks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Empirical ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, meningococcus and Listeria for over-50 or vulnerable; dexamethasone given with or just before the first antibiotic dose reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: ASID Adult Bacterial Meningitis Position Statement

options.rationale: Aciclovir is added when encephalitis is also suspected; this woman has classic meningitis features. Dexamethasone is given with the first antibiotic dose for suspected bacterial meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal in supratherapeutic INR follows Australian Red Cross Lifeblood guidance based on INR and bleeding status. INR over 9 without bleeding: stop warfarin and give oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg. INR 4.5 to 9 without bleeding: stop or reduce warfarin and recheck. Major bleeding or emergency surgery: Prothrombinex-VF (PCC) 25 to 50 units/kg plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg. FFP is reserved for when PCC is unavailable. Trimethoprim, sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole and amiodarone potentiate warfarin and frequently cause supratherapeutic INRs.
key_points: INR over 9 without bleeding: stop warfarin and oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg
