INR 4.5 to 9 without bleeding: stop or reduce warfarin and recheck
Major bleeding: Prothrombinex-VF plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg
FFP only when Prothrombinex-VF is unavailable
Trimethoprim, metronidazole and amiodarone are common warfarin potentiators
explanation.pearls: Oral vitamin K is preferred over intravenous in non-emergency reversal because IV doses over 5 mg often cause warfarin resistance for 1 to 2 weeks, complicating re-anticoagulation in a patient who still needs stroke prevention.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.rationale: INR over 9 without bleeding is managed with warfarin cessation and oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg; this corrects INR within 24 hours without overcorrection that complicates rewarfarinisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.rationale: INR over 9 carries a high bleeding risk in the next 48 hours; withholding warfarin alone is insufficient and vitamin K is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K is reserved for major bleeding or emergency surgery; in asymptomatic INR over 9 this overcorrects and risks rebound prothrombotic state. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.rationale: FFP is no longer first-line for warfarin reversal in Australia due to volume load and slow correction; vitamin K alone is sufficient for asymptomatic supratherapeutic INR. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.rationale: Continuing warfarin with INR over 9 risks major haemorrhage; routine 7-day review delays correction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis based on respiratory distress, hypotension, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance. ANZCOR recommends immediate needle thoracostomy in the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line in adults (replacing the older 2nd ICS midclavicular site, which fails in around a third of adults due to chest wall thickness). Definitive treatment is intercostal catheter insertion. Imaging must not delay decompression.
key_points: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis
Adult needle thoracostomy site is 5th ICS anterior axillary line per ANZCOR
Imaging must not delay decompression
Definitive treatment is intercostal catheter
Positive pressure ventilation before decompression worsens tension physiology
explanation.pearls: Up to a third of adult needle decompressions at the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line fail because of chest wall thickness exceeding 5 cm; the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line is now the ANZCOR-preferred adult site.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.rationale: Imaging confirmation delays life-saving decompression in tension pneumothorax; the diagnosis is clinical and immediate needle thoracostomy is required. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax with hypotension, tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds is a clinical emergency; immediate needle decompression at the 5th ICS anterior axillary line (preferred over 2nd ICS midclavicular in adults) followed by formal intercostal catheter is the Australian standard. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.rationale: Positive pressure ventilation in tension pneumothorax worsens the situation by forcing more air into the pleural space; decompression is required first. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.rationale: While fluids and oxygen are supportive, they do not address the mechanical obstruction; echocardiography delays decompression and the clinical signs strongly favour pneumothorax over tamponade. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.rationale: Intubation and high tidal volume ventilation accelerate tension physiology; adrenaline does not address the underlying mechanical problem. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome screening uses any two of three first-line tests: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or late-night salivary cortisol. Two abnormal results trigger specialist confirmation and source localisation. Pituitary MRI follows biochemical evidence of ACTH-dependent disease. Steroidogenesis inhibitors are reserved for confirmed disease under endocrine supervision. Pseudo-Cushing states (depression, alcohol, severe obesity) must be excluded.
key_points: Use any 2 of: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol
Two abnormal results trigger specialist confirmation and source workup
Pituitary MRI follows biochemical evidence of ACTH-dependent disease
Pseudo-Cushing must be excluded: depression, alcohol, severe obesity, late pregnancy
ACTH measurement differentiates ACTH-dependent (pituitary, ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) disease
explanation.pearls: Pregnancy, severe obesity, chronic alcohol use and depression cause pseudo-Cushing with elevated cortisol and incomplete suppression on the 1 mg dexamethasone test; the late-night salivary cortisol is the most specific screening test in obesity because it reflects loss of diurnal variation.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.rationale: Random cortisol has poor sensitivity and specificity for Cushing syndrome screening due to diurnal variation and physiological stress effects; structured testing is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.rationale: High-dose dexamethasone testing distinguishes pituitary from ectopic source after hypercortisolism is confirmed; it is not the first-step screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.rationale: Endocrine Society and Australian guidance recommend any 2 of 1 mg overnight dexamethasone, 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol as initial screening for Cushing syndrome; abnormal results trigger endocrinology referral for confirmation and source identification. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.rationale: Pituitary MRI is performed after biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism and ACTH-dependent disease; first-line imaging without biochemistry leads to incidental finding misinterpretation. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.rationale: Steroidogenesis inhibitors are commenced only after diagnosis confirmation and under endocrinology supervision; empirical use without diagnosis is not safe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy presents with polyuria, dehydration, confusion, constipation and short QT interval. Management is staged: aggressive isotonic crystalloid 3 to 6 litres in the first 24 hours to restore renal calcium excretion, then intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg once euvolaemic. Denosumab is preferred when eGFR is under 35 mL/min/1.73m2. Calcitonin is an adjunct for rapid 12 to 48 hour reduction. Loop diuretics are used only for fluid overload, not as primary calciuresis.
key_points: Restore intravascular volume with isotonic crystalloid 3 to 6 litres in 24 hours first
Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV once euvolaemic is the standard antiresorptive
Denosumab preferred when eGFR under 35 mL/min/1.73m2
Calcitonin is adjunctive for the first 48 hours with tachyphylaxis
Loop diuretics are not first-line; reserved for fluid overload during rehydration
explanation.pearls: Zoledronic acid maximal calcium-lowering effect occurs at day 4 to 7, so calcitonin or denosumab is required as bridging therapy in patients with corrected calcium over 3.5 mmol/L or symptomatic neurological involvement requiring faster reduction.

options.rationale: Calcitonin is adjunctive for rapid initial decrease but tachyphylaxis develops in 48 to 72 hours; volume resuscitation is the foundation of treatment, not contraindicated by orthostatic hypotension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Cinacalcet is reserved for parathyroid carcinoma and primary hyperparathyroidism, not hypercalcaemia of malignancy where PTH is suppressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Australian first-line management is aggressive crystalloid rehydration restoring renal calcium excretion, followed by intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg once euvolaemic; zoledronic acid takes 2 to 4 days to peak effect but provides sustained reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Routine loop diuretic use without volume overload is no longer recommended for hypercalcaemia management and risks worsening dehydration; bisphosphonate is the standard once euvolaemic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Denosumab is preferred over zoledronic acid in renal impairment (eGFR under 35 mL/min/1.73m2) but volume resuscitation remains the first step in symptomatic hypercalcaemia. (Source: eviQ Hypercalcaemia of Malignancy Protocol)

explanation.summary: Severe influenza pneumonia in vulnerable adults requires combined antibiotic and antiviral therapy. Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily is standard for eGFR over 30 mL/min/1.73m2; the dose is reduced to 30 mg daily for eGFR 10 to 30. Empirical antibiotic cover with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (or doxycycline) addresses bacterial co-infection. Corticosteroids are reserved for specific indications and not routine. Annual influenza vaccination is the foundation of prevention and is funded for at-risk groups in Australia.
key_points: Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily is standard for eGFR over 30 mL/min/1.73m2
Reduce oseltamivir to 30 mg daily for eGFR 10 to 30
Severe CAP with influenza needs both antibiotic and antiviral cover
Corticosteroids are not routine in influenza pneumonia
Annual influenza vaccination is funded for at-risk groups under the National Immunisation Program
explanation.pearls: Bacterial co-infection in severe influenza is dominated by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus; staphylococcal cover with vancomycin is added when there is cavitation, severe sepsis, or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus risk factors.

options.rationale: Although these antibiotics cover typical and atypical organisms, the oseltamivir dose 30 mg BD is too low for an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73m2; standard dose is 75 mg twice daily until eGFR falls below 30. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Awaiting PCR delays antiviral therapy; oseltamivir is most effective started within 48 hours and should be given empirically to high-risk patients during an outbreak. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Intravenous oseltamivir is not available in Australian inpatient formularies; oral oseltamivir at appropriate dose is used. Benzylpenicillin alone misses atypicals which are important in severe community-acquired pneumonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Severe CAP plus suspected influenza during an outbreak warrants combined empirical antibiotic and antiviral therapy; oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily is standard for eGFR 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73m2, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin covers typical and atypical bacterial co-infection, and ICU is indicated for SMART-COP at least 3. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Routine corticosteroid use in influenza pneumonia is associated with worse outcomes outside specific indications; antiviral therapy is required for influenza and should not be withheld. (Source: ASID Influenza Antiviral Use Statement)

explanation.summary: The hour-1 sepsis bundle requires lactate measurement, blood culture before antibiotics, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid within 3 hours for hypotension or lactate over 4, and vasopressor titration to a MAP target of 65 mmHg if hypotension persists. Source control is identified and addressed urgently. Australian empirical cover for urosepsis is typically amoxicillin plus gentamicin or piperacillin-tazobactam. Vasopressors are not commenced before adequate fluid resuscitation.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors as indicated
30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours in hypotension or lactate over 4
Vasopressors target MAP 65 mmHg if hypotension persists
Source control identified and addressed within 6-12 hours
Urosepsis empirical: amoxicillin plus gentamicin or piperacillin-tazobactam
explanation.pearls: In catheter-associated urosepsis remove or change the catheter as part of source control; antibiotics alone without source control are associated with higher mortality and persistent bacteraemia.

options.rationale: Septic shock with hypotension and lactate over 2 requires immediate IV antibiotics, IV crystalloid resuscitation and source control in hospital, not oral antibiotics at home. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Management)
Blood cultures should be obtained before antibiotics where this does not delay therapy beyond 45 minutes; pre-antibiotic cultures retain higher yield. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Empirical antibiotics must be given within 1 hour of recognition of septic shock; waiting for culture results increases mortality. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

The hour-1 sepsis bundle includes lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours and vasopressor initiation if MAP remains under 65 after fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Vasopressors are added after a 30 mL/kg crystalloid trial in fluid-responsive sepsis; source control work-up should not be deferred to the next day in pyelonephritis with sepsis. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Management)

explanation.summary: Suspected PE workup uses the Wells score to estimate pre-test probability. Low-moderate probability patients have D-dimer testing using age-adjusted cut-offs in those over 50 (age x 10 ng/mL). High probability patients proceed directly to imaging without D-dimer. CTPA is the imaging modality of choice. VQ scan is reserved for renal impairment, pregnancy or contrast allergy. Therapeutic anticoagulation follows confirmation of diagnosis or pending imaging if high probability and no contraindication.
key_points: Wells score stratifies low, moderate, high probability
Age-adjusted D-dimer (over 50): age x 10 ng/mL
High pre-test probability: image directly without D-dimer
CTPA is first-line imaging; VQ scan if contraindication
Confirmed PE: anticoagulate (apixaban or rivaroxaban) 3-6 months
explanation.pearls: Age-adjusted D-dimer reduces unnecessary CTPA scans by approximately 12% in older adults with no decrease in sensitivity; the cut-off applies only in low-moderate Wells probability and only in patients aged over 50.

options.rationale: Wells PE score should be calculated first and confirmatory imaging obtained for moderate or high probability before commencing anticoagulation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
Chest radiograph and ECG are insensitive for PE and should not be used to exclude the diagnosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Pulmonary Embolism)
Repeating D-dimer adds no diagnostic value; the decision is to image or apply age-adjusted threshold (already exceeded here). (Source: BMJ Best Practice Pulmonary Embolism)

The Wells score arithmetic shown is incorrect; recent surgery scores 1.5 only if within 4 weeks AND immobilisation criteria are otherwise weighted; more importantly, high pre-test probability bypasses D-dimer and proceeds directly to imaging. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Pulmonary Embolism)

Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off for over-50s is age x 10 ng/mL; 72 x 10 = 720, which equals the D-dimer here so age-adjusted threshold is met and CTPA is indicated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Pulmonary Embolism)

explanation.summary: KDIGO defines AKI by absolute creatinine rise of 26.5 micromol/L within 48 hours, 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours. Stage 1 is 1.5 to 1.9 times baseline, stage 2 is 2 to 2.9 times, stage 3 is 3 times or RRT requirement. Management starts with identifying the cause (pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal), withholding nephrotoxins, fluid resuscitation if hypovolaemic, and treating the precipitant. RRT indications are AEIOU.
key_points: KDIGO stage 1: 1.5-1.9x baseline; stage 2: 2-2.9x; stage 3: 3x or RRT
Pre-renal AKI: withhold nephrotoxins, isotonic crystalloid, treat precipitant
Investigate cause: pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal
Ultrasound if obstruction suspected
RRT indications (AEIOU): acidosis, electrolytes, ingestion, overload, uraemia
explanation.pearls: Fractional excretion of sodium under 1% supports pre-renal aetiology in oliguric AKI not on diuretics; if patient is on diuretics use fractional excretion of urea instead (under 35% suggests pre-renal pattern).

options.rationale: ACE inhibitors should be withheld in acute kidney injury related to volume depletion; furosemide does not convert oliguric to non-oliguric AKI in this setting and may worsen hypovolaemia. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)
Empirical steroids are not indicated for AKI from pre-renal causes; ramipril should be withheld during acute volume depletion. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

KDIGO indications for renal replacement (AEIOU: acidosis, electrolyte, ingestion, overload, uraemia) are not met here; stage 2 AKI alone without indications is treated with fluid resuscitation and removal of nephrotoxins. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

N-acetylcysteine is not recommended for AKI prevention or treatment in current guidelines; while ultrasound is appropriate, the key intervention is fluid resuscitation. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

Pre-renal AKI from sepsis and reduced intake (creatinine 2-3 times baseline = KDIGO stage 2) is managed with withholding nephrotoxins, prompt isotonic crystalloid resuscitation, treating the precipitant and monitoring fluid responsiveness. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

explanation.summary: SIADH is diagnosed when there is euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine (over 100 mOsm/kg), urine sodium over 30 mmol/L, normal thyroid and adrenal function and no diuretic. First-line management is fluid restriction to 800 to 1000 mL per day plus treatment of the underlying cause. Correction is limited to under 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Tolvaptan and hypertonic saline are reserved for refractory or severe symptomatic cases.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia, low serum osmolality, urine osmolality over 100, urine sodium over 30
Exclude thyroid and adrenal insufficiency and diuretic use
First-line: fluid restriction 800-1000 mL/day plus treat the cause
Correct sodium under 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid ODS
Hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia only
explanation.pearls: Small-cell lung cancer is the commonest paraneoplastic cause of SIADH in adults; sodium correction over 10-12 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination, presenting 2-6 days later with quadriparesis, dysarthria and locked-in syndrome.

options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma, severe vomiting); mild symptoms with chronic onset are managed with fluid restriction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and elevated urine sodium with no diuretic, normal thyroid and cortisol meets SIADH criteria; fluid restriction is first-line with correction limited to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

Isotonic saline in SIADH can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia as the sodium is excreted while the free water is retained; demeclocycline is third-line and rarely used. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

Tolvaptan is reserved for fluid-restriction failure and requires inpatient initiation with cautious titration due to over-rapid correction risk; it is not first-line. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)
Free fluid in SIADH worsens dilution; salt tablets without fluid restriction are inadequate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

explanation.summary: Severe acute pancreatitis is identified by validated scores (Modified Glasgow 3 or more, APACHE II over 8) at 48 hours, organ failure or CRP over 150. Management is HDU/ICU care, aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation to maintain urine output, multimodal analgesia, early enteral nutrition (within 24-72 hours) and contrast CT at 72-96 hours to assess for necrosis. Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated. ERCP is reserved for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. Necrosectomy is delayed.
key_points: Severity scores: Modified Glasgow 3+, APACHE II over 8, BISAP over 3, CRP over 150
Severe pancreatitis: HDU/ICU, aggressive crystalloid, analgesia
Enteral nutrition preferred and early
CT at 72-96 hours to assess for necrosis
ERCP only for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction
explanation.pearls: Modified Glasgow uses mnemonic PANCREAS: PaO2 under 60, Age over 55, Neutrophils WCC over 15, Calcium under 2, Renal urea over 16, Enzymes LDH over 600 ALT over 200, Albumin under 32, Sugar glucose over 10; 3 or more positive at 48 hours indicates severe disease.

options.rationale: Modified Glasgow score 4 (PaO2 under 60, urea over 16 not present here so 1 fewer; consider 3 with PaO2 + albumin + calcium + glucose) plus CRP 220 indicates severe acute pancreatitis requiring HDU/ICU care with aggressive IV resuscitation, not oral hydration. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)
Enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral; prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated unless infected necrosis or cholangitis is suspected. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

Severe acute pancreatitis (Modified Glasgow with PaO2, calcium, albumin, glucose abnormalities and CRP over 150 in this index admission) mandates HDU level care, aggressive fluid resuscitation, analgesia and delayed CT (72-96 hours) to assess for necrosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

ERCP is reserved for acute pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; alcohol-related pancreatitis without biliary obstruction does not benefit. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

Surgery in necrotising pancreatitis is delayed to at least 4 weeks where possible and is reserved for infected necrosis; immediate laparotomy is harmful early in the disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

explanation.summary: Native-valve infective endocarditis empirical cover targets streptococci, staphylococci and enterococci. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin until cultures are available. Vancomycin replaces flucloxacillin if MRSA is suspected. The modified Duke criteria classify cases as definite, possible or rejected. Transoesophageal echocardiography is performed when transthoracic is inconclusive or to assess for abscess. Surgical indications include heart failure, abscess, large vegetation, fungal aetiology and persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate therapy.
key_points: Empirical native valve: benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin
Replace flucloxacillin with vancomycin if MRSA
Three separate blood culture sets before antibiotics
TOE for inconclusive TTE or to assess abscess
Surgical indications: heart failure, abscess, large vegetation, fungal, persistent bacteraemia
explanation.pearls: Modified Duke criteria definite endocarditis requires 2 major, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria; major criteria are typical organism in 2 cultures or persistent bacteraemia plus echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement or new valvular regurgitation.

options.rationale: Empirical native valve endocarditis cover requires combination therapy targeting Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci and enterococci; monotherapy ceftriaxone is inadequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Australian native-valve empirical regimen uses benzylpenicillin (not flucloxacillin) for streptococci, plus flucloxacillin OR vancomycin (not both) for staphylococci, plus gentamicin; this option triples antibiotic cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
A single dose of vancomycin upfront is not appropriate; vancomycin replaces flucloxacillin if MRSA suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Therapeutic Guidelines empirical native valve endocarditis cover is benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin for streptococci, staphylococci and enterococci until culture-directed therapy is possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Meropenem is not a standard empirical regimen for endocarditis; combination therapy with the specific cover above is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate intravenous hydrocortisone, intravenous fluid resuscitation, glucose correction and treatment of the precipitant. Standard initial dosing is 100 mg intravenous hydrocortisone followed by 50 mg every 6 hours or a continuous infusion. Hydrocortisone has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity at these doses, so additional fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. Patients with known adrenal insufficiency should be educated to triple oral hydrocortisone during minor illness and use intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg if vomiting.
key_points: Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 50 mg q6h
IV 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation 1 L in first hour
Correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose
No need for fludrocortisone acutely at IV hydrocortisone doses
Triple oral dose for minor illness; IM hydrocortisone 100 mg if vomiting
explanation.pearls: Issue every patient with adrenal insufficiency an emergency injection kit (intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg) for vomiting illness or accident; their MedicAlert bracelet and steroid emergency card alert paramedics and ED clinicians to give parenteral steroid before transfer.

options.rationale: Adrenaline is not the primary treatment of adrenal crisis; intravenous hydrocortisone with fluid resuscitation is first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Vomiting prevents oral absorption; she is in established adrenal crisis with hypotension and hypoglycaemia requiring intravenous therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Established adrenal crisis is treated with immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, intravenous fluid resuscitation with normal saline, glucose correction and ongoing hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours pending stabilisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Diagnosis is already established; hydrocortisone is preferred over dexamethasone for its mineralocorticoid activity. Synacthen testing is unnecessary in a known case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Intravenous fludrocortisone is not available; high-dose intravenous hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity in adrenal crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Duration of anticoagulation in VTE depends on whether the event was provoked by a transient major risk factor (3 months typically), provoked by a persistent risk factor (continue while factor present), or unprovoked (consider extended therapy after 6 months). Aspirin reduces recurrence less than anticoagulants and is reserved for those declining anticoagulation. Routine thrombophilia screening after a single VTE rarely changes management. Reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban is an option for extended therapy after unprovoked VTE.
key_points: Provoked by transient factor: 3 months anticoagulation
Provoked by persistent factor: continue while factor present
Unprovoked: consider extended after 6 months
Reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban for extended therapy in unprovoked
Thrombophilia screening rarely alters management after single VTE
explanation.pearls: HERDOO2 and DASH scores can identify a subset of women with unprovoked VTE who can stop anticoagulation safely at 6 to 12 months; men with unprovoked VTE have a higher recurrence rate and benefit from extended therapy.

options.rationale: DVT provoked by a transient major risk factor (recent long-haul flight) without other risk factors typically requires only 3 months of anticoagulation; longer treatment does not improve outcomes once the provoking factor has resolved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
Indefinite anticoagulation is for unprovoked or recurrent VTE; provoked DVT with resolved transient factor does not require indefinite anticoagulation. (Source: BMJ Best Practice DVT)
Reduced-dose extended therapy applies to unprovoked VTE after 6 months of initial full-dose treatment; flight-associated DVT is provoked. (Source: BMJ Best Practice DVT)

Routine thrombophilia screening rarely changes management and is not recommended after a single provoked VTE; identification of low-risk thrombophilias does not extend anticoagulation. (Source: HSANZ Thrombophilia Guidelines)

Aspirin reduces recurrent VTE risk less effectively than DOAC or warfarin and is reserved for those who decline ongoing anticoagulation; it is not the standard step after a provoked DVT. (Source: BMJ Best Practice DVT)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects obese women of reproductive age. Modified Dandy criteria: symptoms/signs of raised ICP (headache, papilloedema, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, CN VI palsy), no localising features beyond CN VI, normal CSF composition, opening pressure over 250 mmCSF (over 280 if BMI over 30), no other identifiable cause on neuroimaging including venography. Treatment: weight loss (5 to 10%) is the most effective long-term measure. Acetazolamide first-line pharmacotherapy, topiramate second-line. Surgical options for fulminant or progressive visual loss: optic nerve sheath fenestration, lumboperitoneal or ventriculoperitoneal shunt, or venous sinus stenting where stenosis is documented.
key_points: IIH demographic: obese women of reproductive age
Modified Dandy: symptoms ICP + papilloedema + normal CSF + OP over 250 (280 if BMI over 30)
Imaging must include venography to exclude CVST
First-line: weight loss + acetazolamide; second-line topiramate
Visual loss: ONSF, shunt, or sinus stenting (if stenosis)
explanation.pearls: Visual loss in IIH occurs through papilloedema-induced optic atrophy, not directly from raised ICP; ophthalmology co-management with formal visual fields every 1-3 months in untreated/severe cases drives treatment escalation before permanent loss.

sources.label: RANZCO: Papilloedema and raised intracranial pressure
BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.rationale: After secondary causes are excluded by neuroimaging (including venography), LP with opening pressure over 250 mmCSF (over 280 in BMI over 30) and normal CSF composition confirms IIH (modified Dandy criteria). (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.rationale: Treatment should follow diagnostic confirmation by LP (Dandy criteria); empirical treatment before confirmation risks missing alternative causes such as hidden venous sinus pathology. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.rationale: She has already had MRI brain WITH venography - this has been done. The next step is LP with opening pressure. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.rationale: Surgical interventions are reserved for fulminant IIH or progressive visual loss despite medical therapy; diagnostic workup including LP is required first. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.rationale: Routine paraneoplastic and autoimmune workup is not part of initial IIH evaluation; the clinical and imaging features are typical for IIH and do not suggest paraneoplastic. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

explanation.summary: Acute exacerbation of COPD with respiratory acidosis (pH under 7.35, pCO2 over 45 mmHg) despite controlled oxygen and maximal medical therapy is the indication for non-invasive ventilation (bilevel positive airway pressure). Target oxygen saturation 88 to 92 percent using a Venturi mask. Bronchodilators (salbutamol plus ipratropium nebulised), systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 30 to 40 mg daily for 5 days), and antibiotics for infective exacerbations (amoxicillin or doxycycline first-line per Australian guidelines) are concurrent. Reassess ABG at 1 hour - failure of NIV (worsening acidosis, persistent pH under 7.25 at 2 hours, hypoxia, agitation) triggers escalation to intubation.
key_points: AECOPD with pH under 7.35 and pCO2 over 45 = NIV
Controlled O2 88-92% via Venturi mask
Salbutamol + ipratropium nebulised, plus oral prednisolone 5 days
Antibiotics if infective features (amoxicillin or doxycycline)
Reassess ABG at 1 hour, escalate if no improvement at 2 hours
explanation.pearls: Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in chronic CO2 retention is multifactorial: reversal of hypoxic vasoconstriction worsening V/Q mismatch is the main mechanism (not solely loss of hypoxic drive).

options.rationale: NIV is first-line for AECOPD with hypercapnic acidosis even with mild drowsiness due to hypercapnia (it often improves with NIV); intubation is reserved for failure of NIV or absolute contraindication. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

High-flow O2 in COPD type 2 failure worsens hypercapnia and acidosis; controlled O2 (target 88-92%) is the rule, and BiPAP is required for the respiratory acidosis. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

Type 2 respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis (pH under 7.35, pCO2 over 45) despite controlled oxygen and bronchodilator therapy is the trigger for BiPAP in AECOPD per Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory and TSANZ. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

Aminophylline is no longer routinely recommended in AECOPD and magnesium has limited evidence; neither replaces NIV for type 2 respiratory failure with acidosis. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)
Antibiotics and bronchodilators are needed but do not address the type 2 respiratory failure with acidosis, which requires NIV. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

explanation.summary: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema is classified by perfusion and congestion. Hypertensive wet-and-warm (this patient) is treated with sitting upright, NIV (CPAP or BiPAP), IV nitrate infusion titrated to BP (starting 5 to 10 mcg/min), and IV loop diuretic (furosemide 1 to 2 times the home oral daily dose IV). Underlying triggers (ischaemia, AF, infection, non-adherence, NSAIDs, salt load) are sought and managed. Chronic disease-modifying therapy (ACE inhibitor or ARB or sacubitril-valsartan, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) is continued unless contraindicated by hypotension or shock. Cardiogenic shock (wet-and-cold) needs inotrope or mechanical support.
key_points: Wet-and-warm hypertensive APO: NIV + IV nitrate + IV furosemide
Wet-and-cold cardiogenic shock: inotropes (dobutamine), possible mechanical support
Avoid IV fluids unless RV-dominant or normotensive dry-and-cold
Continue chronic GDMT unless hypotensive
Find and treat the trigger
explanation.pearls: IV nitrate is contraindicated if SBP under 100 mmHg, severe aortic stenosis with low gradient, or recent PDE5 inhibitor use - these are the three traps to avoid before reaching for the GTN infusion.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018
Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Acute heart failure

options.rationale: He is hypertensive and warm-perfused so not in cardiogenic shock; vasopressors and adrenaline are contraindicated in this hypertensive APO subtype. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

options.rationale: Acute IV beta blocker worsens cardiogenic shock and pulmonary oedema; chronic beta blocker may be continued but not up-titrated in acute decompensation. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

options.rationale: IV fluids worsen pulmonary oedema; morphine increases mortality in APO per current evidence and is no longer routinely recommended. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

options.rationale: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with hypertension and SpO2 under 90 on air is managed with NIV, IV nitrate for preload and afterload reduction and IV loop diuretic per CSANZ heart failure guideline and Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

options.rationale: Chronic ACE inhibitor and beta blocker are continued unless hypotensive or in shock; oral diuretic alone in acute APO is inadequate and IV route is required. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T, prolonged PR, wide QRS, sine wave) is a life-threatening emergency. Management priorities are membrane stabilisation, intracellular shift, removal and prevention. First-line: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (or 5 mL of 10% calcium chloride via central line) over 2 to 5 minutes - effect within minutes, lasts 30 to 60 minutes, repeat as needed. Shift: 10 units short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV over 10 minutes plus nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg. Removal: loop diuretic if making urine, oral or rectal cation exchange resin (resonium or patiromer), urgent haemodialysis for refractory or severe disease. Stop ACE inhibitor, MRA, K supplements, NSAIDs. Manage cause (AKI, rhabdomyolysis, adrenal insufficiency).
key_points: ECG changes + K over 6.5 = immediate IV calcium
Calcium stabilises membrane in minutes
Insulin-dextrose 10 U with 50 mL 50% dextrose for shift
Salbutamol nebs adjunct shift
Definitive removal: resonium, diuretic, dialysis
explanation.pearls: Calcium chloride 5 mL of 10% has 3 times the elemental calcium of calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% but requires central venous access due to vesicant risk - gluconate is the safer peripheral option.

options.rationale: Dialysis is appropriate for refractory or severe hyperkalaemia but is preceded by IV calcium and insulin-dextrose for immediate cardioprotection while access is being arranged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

Resonium has slow onset (hours) and no role in immediate cardioprotection; with ECG changes and K above 6.5, IV calcium and insulin-dextrose are first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)
Furosemide may help if there is preserved diuresis but is not first-line cardioprotection; with ECG changes IV calcium is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

Bicarbonate is an adjunct in significant acidosis and is slower than insulin-dextrose for shifting; not first-line monotherapy in this scenario. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

ECG changes with K above 6.5 mmol/L require immediate calcium gluconate for cardiac stabilisation, followed by insulin-dextrose shift therapy and ongoing nebulised salbutamol and definitive potassium removal per Therapeutic Guidelines and KHA-CARI. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection (NSTI) is a surgical emergency with mortality 20 to 40 percent. Recognise by pain disproportionate to appearance, rapid progression, dusky or violaceous discolouration, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia of overlying skin and systemic toxicity. LRINEC score at or above 6 raises suspicion (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose), at or above 8 is high probability. Diabetes, immunosuppression and IV drug use are risk factors. Management is urgent surgical debridement (the cornerstone), broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-positives (including MRSA), Gram-negatives and anaerobes (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin per Australian guidelines), aggressive ICU-level resuscitation, and consideration of IVIG for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.
key_points: Pain disproportionate to appearance + bullae + crepitus + toxicity = NSTI
LRINEC score helps risk-stratify but never delays surgery
Urgent surgical debridement is the cornerstone
Empirical: meropenem + clindamycin (toxin suppression) + vancomycin
ICU support, IVIG for documented strep TSS
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added not for its antibacterial spectrum but to suppress streptococcal exotoxin production (Eagle effect) - it is included in regimens regardless of the primary antibiotic choice.

sources.label: Surgical Infection Society guideline: Skin and soft tissue infection

options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis demands urgent (not elective) surgical debridement and broader antibiotic cover; flucloxacillin alone misses Gram-negatives, anaerobes and streptococcal toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

LRINEC at or above 8 with clinical features (pain disproportionate, dusky discolouration, bullae, crepitus, toxicity) is necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise; broad-spectrum cover (carbapenem + clindamycin for toxin suppression + vanco for MRSA) and urgent surgical debridement save life. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

Imaging may help but never delays surgical debridement in suspected nec fasc; the diagnosis is clinical and surgical findings are confirmatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

Topical management is inappropriate for necrotising fasciitis; this strategy will result in rapid progression and death without surgical debridement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

IVIG may be adjunctive in severe group A streptococcal toxic shock but is not monotherapy and does not replace surgery and broad-spectrum antibiotics. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

explanation.summary: Sepsis hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at or above 4 mmol/L, and start vasopressors if hypotensive during or after fluid to maintain MAP at or above 65 mmHg. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor (peripheral acceptable up to 0.2 mcg/kg/min as a bridge to central). Vasopressin 0.03 U/min is added if noradrenaline above 0.25 mcg/kg/min. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day is added when MAP is inadequate despite noradrenaline plus vasopressin. Source control (drain, debride, decompress) is sought urgently. Reassess lactate at 2 hours and clinical response.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluid, vasopressors
30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4
Noradrenaline first-line; vasopressin add-on, adrenaline rescue
Hydrocortisone for refractory shock on dual vasopressor
Source control is critical
explanation.pearls: Peripheral noradrenaline infusion is safe up to 0.2 mcg/kg/min via a proximal antecubital vein for short periods (under 6 hours) - this avoids delaying haemodynamic support while central access is being secured.

options.rationale: After 30 mL/kg of fluid with persistent shock, vasopressors are started; further crystalloid risks fluid overload and pulmonary oedema. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Septic shock with persistent hypotension after 30 mL/kg fluid is the indication for early vasopressor (noradrenaline first-line) with MAP target of at least 65 mmHg, ICU referral and source control investigation (urinary tract imaging) per the Surviving Sepsis bundle and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Noradrenaline is first-line per Surviving Sepsis and ANZICS; adrenaline is added if MAP is inadequate on noradrenaline plus vasopressin. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) is added only when MAP is inadequate despite escalating vasopressors; it is not first-line nor monotherapy for septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Antibiotic choice should be optimised but vasopressors cannot be delayed; double Gram-negative cover is not routinely required in community-acquired urinary sepsis. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection presents with sudden severe tearing chest or back pain, pulse differential, new aortic regurgitation murmur, neurological signs (carotid involvement), syncope or limb ischaemia. Type A involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency (mortality 1 to 2 percent per hour without surgery). Type B (descending only) is managed medically unless complicated. Initial management is rate-and-pressure control with intravenous beta blocker (esmolol or labetalol) targeting HR 60 to 80 and SBP 100 to 120, then vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside or GTN) added if BP target not met. Opioid analgesia, large-bore IV access, group and crossmatch and urgent CT angiogram of the whole aorta with cardiothoracic surgical consultation are the immediate steps.
key_points: Sudden tearing chest/back pain + pulse differential + AR murmur
CT angiogram of aorta (CTA) is the imaging of choice
Beta blocker FIRST to reduce shear stress, then vasodilator if needed
Target HR 60-80, SBP 100-120
Type A: surgical emergency. Type B: usually medical
explanation.pearls: A normal D-dimer has high negative predictive value (above 95 percent) for aortic dissection in low-pretest probability patients - a useful rule-out tool when CT angiogram is delayed, but never used to rule out in high-risk presentations.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.rationale: Angiography risks instrument-induced dissection extension; CTA aorta is the imaging of choice when dissection is suspected. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.rationale: DAPT in aortic dissection causes catastrophic bleeding on aortic repair; the dissection picture (tearing pain, pulse differential, widened mediastinum, AR murmur) trumps the marginal troponin. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.rationale: Vasodilator without prior beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia which increases wall shear stress and propagates dissection; beta blocker is given first. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.rationale: PE does not cause pulse differential or AR murmur and anticoagulation is catastrophic in undiagnosed dissection; CTA aorta not CTPA is the correct first imaging. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.rationale: Suspected type A aortic dissection mandates immediate beta blockade (rate then BP) to reduce shear stress, opioid analgesia, urgent CT angiography of the aorta and cardiothoracic surgical involvement per Heart Foundation and Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis presents with hypotension unresponsive to fluids, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and a known or suspected adrenal insufficiency precipitated by intercurrent illness, surgery, missed steroid doses or trauma. It is a clinical diagnosis - treat immediately and confirm later. Management is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as a bolus, then 200 mg over 24 hours (50 mg every 6 hours or continuous infusion), aggressive isotonic crystalloid resuscitation, dextrose for hypoglycaemia and treatment of the precipitant. Fludrocortisone is unnecessary at hydrocortisone doses above 50 mg/day because the gluco at high dose provides mineralocorticoid activity. Sick-day rules (double oral dose for febrile illness, IM hydrocortisone for vomiting), patient-held steroid emergency card and emergency IM hydrocortisone kit are core education points.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg STAT then 200 mg over 24 hours
IV 0.9% saline aggressive resuscitation
IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Treat precipitant
Sick-day rules + IM emergency kit + steroid emergency card are lifesaving for prevention
explanation.pearls: A morning cortisol drawn during crisis that is over 550 nmol/L effectively excludes adrenal insufficiency; a value under 100 nmol/L while critically unwell is diagnostic for crisis and treatment cannot wait for short Synacthen testing.

sources.label: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis: rapid IV hydrocortisone 100 mg + IV saline + dextrose for hypoglycaemia, continue hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours (50 mg q6h or infusion), source-control of precipitant, per Australasian Endocrine Society and Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available IV and is not first-line in crisis; high-dose IV hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and at-dose mineralocorticoid effect. ACTH testing has no place during a crisis. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.rationale: Dexamethasone can be used if diagnosis is uncertain and stimulation testing is planned, but in established Addison's hydrocortisone is preferred for its combined gluco- and mineralocorticoid actions and immediate efficacy. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.rationale: Vasopressor without urgent hydrocortisone replacement will fail because vascular tone is corticosteroid-dependent; immediate IV hydrocortisone with fluid resuscitation is first-line. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia of adrenal crisis resolves with IV hydrocortisone and saline; oral hydrocortisone will not be absorbed in shock with vomiting and is not an acceptable substitute. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

explanation.summary: After 3 months of treatment-dose anticoagulation for an unprovoked PE, decision-making centres on the recurrence-versus-bleeding balance. Unprovoked PE carries around 10% recurrence in year 1 and 30 to 40% at 5 years off therapy. For low-bleed-risk patients, indefinite anticoagulation is preferred; the AMPLIFY-EXT and EINSTEIN-CHOICE trials support reduced-dose extended therapy (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily) as non-inferior for recurrence with a halved bleeding rate. Aspirin is markedly inferior. Annual reassessment of bleeding risk and renal function guides ongoing therapy.
key_points: Unprovoked PE recurrence: ~10% year 1, ~30 to 40% at 5 years off anticoagulation
Extended therapy: rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, non-inferior to full-dose with lower bleeding
Provoked PE with reversible risk factor: 3 months total anticoagulation usually sufficient
Annual review: bleeding risk, renal function, ongoing recurrence-risk vs bleeding balance
explanation.pearls: After an unprovoked PE in a low-bleed-risk patient, the default plan is indefinite anticoagulation at extended-reduced dose - aspirin is a fallback only when the patient declines DOAC, not an equivalent option.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.rationale: DOACs are first-line and at least as effective as warfarin for VTE secondary prevention without monitoring; switching to warfarin in a stable patient introduces inconvenience and bleeding risk without benefit. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.rationale: Unprovoked PE has a high recurrence risk (around 10% in year 1, 30 to 40% at 5 years off therapy); current Australian guidance favours indefinite anticoagulation in low-bleed-risk patients, with reduced-dose rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) or apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) for extended therapy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.rationale: Ceasing anticoagulation at 3 months after an unprovoked PE leaves the patient with an unacceptably high recurrence rate; routine surveillance D-dimer does not replace ongoing pharmacological prophylaxis in this context. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.rationale: Aspirin provides only modest VTE recurrence reduction and is markedly inferior to extended-dose DOAC; it is not a satisfactory substitute when extended anticoagulation is otherwise appropriate. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.rationale: Extended-dose reduction (rivaroxaban 10 mg or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily) is non-inferior for recurrence and lowers bleeding risk; routine surveillance CTPA at 12 months is not standard in an asymptomatic patient with normal saturations and exercise tolerance. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

explanation.summary: Early seropositive rheumatoid arthritis should be treated with a conventional synthetic DMARD within a window of opportunity, ideally within 3 months of symptom onset, to prevent erosive joint damage. Methotrexate (oral or subcutaneous) is first-line, started at 10 to 15 mg weekly and uptitrated to 20 to 25 mg weekly over 4 to 8 weeks, with weekly folic acid 5 mg on a non-methotrexate day. Short prednisolone bridging (15 to 20 mg with taper over 8 to 12 weeks) controls symptoms while methotrexate takes effect. Pre-treatment workup includes HBV, HCV, HIV and latent TB serology. Biologics are reserved for inadequate response under PBS criteria.
key_points: Methotrexate first-line; start 10 to 15 mg weekly, uptitrate to 20 to 25 mg over 4 to 8 weeks
Weekly folic acid 5 mg on a non-methotrexate day reduces mucositis, hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal side effects
Short prednisolone bridge while methotrexate takes effect (8 to 12 weeks then taper off)
Pre-treatment screen: HBV, HCV, HIV, latent TB, varicella immunity, baseline LFTs and FBC
explanation.pearls: If oral methotrexate is not achieving remission at maximum tolerated dose, switch to subcutaneous methotrexate before adding biologics - subcutaneous has higher bioavailability and rescues a meaningful proportion of inadequate oral responders.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.rationale: Long-term steroid monotherapy in RA causes significant morbidity (diabetes, osteoporosis, infections) without preventing joint damage; steroid is used only as a short bridge while DMARD takes effect. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.rationale: Early DMARD initiation within a window of opportunity (under 3 months from symptom onset) improves long-term outcomes; NSAID monotherapy fails to prevent joint damage in seropositive disease. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.rationale: Biologic DMARDs are reserved for inadequate response to conventional DMARD therapy after at least 6 months (typically methotrexate plus another csDMARD) under PBS criteria; not first-line. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.rationale: Triple therapy from outset is not first-line in Australia; methotrexate monotherapy with bridging steroid and rapid uptitration with intensified treatment if remission is not achieved at 3 months is preferred. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.rationale: Methotrexate is first-line DMARD for early seropositive rheumatoid arthritis; rapid uptitration with weekly folate and short-term oral steroid bridging is standard practice with frequent disease activity reassessment. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

explanation.summary: In T2DM with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure or albuminuric chronic kidney disease, the second-line agent in Australia is an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin or ertugliflozin) independent of glycaemic control because of demonstrated cardiorenal benefit. GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, dulaglutide) are also appropriate, especially with obesity or atherosclerotic disease without heart failure. Sulfonylureas and DPP-4 inhibitors lack cardiorenal benefit. SGLT2 inhibitors are contraindicated with frequent genital infections, eGFR below threshold (varies by agent), and require sick-day rules and ketone monitoring counselling.
key_points: T2DM with CVD, HF or albuminuric CKD: SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA as second-line, independent of glycaemic control
SGLT2 inhibitor pre-treatment: counsel on sick-day rules, genital infection risk, euglycaemic DKA, foot care
GLP-1 RA: prefer if obese or atherosclerotic disease without HF; injectable except oral semaglutide
Sulfonylureas: lower cost but hypoglycaemia and weight gain; no cardiorenal benefit
explanation.pearls: For T2DM with CVD or albuminuric CKD, the second drug after metformin is not the cheapest agent that lowers HbA1c - it is the SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist that will prevent his next cardiac event and slow his CKD progression.

sources.label: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.rationale: Insulin is generally considered after failure of oral combination therapy or when symptomatic hyperglycaemia or glucotoxicity is present; at an HbA1c of 8.5% on metformin alone the cardiorenal benefits of SGLT2 inhibition take precedence. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.rationale: Sulfonylureas are not first-choice second-line in a patient with established cardiovascular disease and albuminuric CKD because they provide no cardiorenal benefit and carry hypoglycaemia and weight gain risks. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.rationale: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral and well tolerated but provide no cardiovascular or renal protective benefit, making them inferior to SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with established CVD or albuminuric CKD. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.rationale: Increasing metformin above 2 g daily yields little additional glucose-lowering and more gastrointestinal effects; he needs a second agent now and his clinical profile favours an SGLT2 inhibitor with cardiorenal benefits. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors are first-line second-agent in T2DM with established cardiovascular disease or albuminuric chronic kidney disease in Australian guidance because of demonstrated cardiovascular and renal benefits independent of glycaemic effects. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

explanation.summary: Latent TB infection in a recent household contact of smear-positive disease has approximately 10% lifetime risk of progression to active disease, with greatest risk in the first 2 years. Australian regimens for LTBI include isoniazid for 6 to 9 months with pyridoxine, or shorter rifamycin-containing regimens (rifampicin 4 months, or weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 12 doses where available). Active TB must be excluded clinically and radiologically before LTBI treatment begins. HIV testing and baseline LFTs are required; treatment is managed by state TB services with monthly clinical and biochemical review.
key_points: LTBI diagnosis: QFT-Plus or T-spot positive, asymptomatic, normal CXR, no microbiological evidence of active TB
Treatment options: isoniazid 6 to 9 months, rifampicin 4 months, isoniazid-rifapentine weekly for 12 doses
Pre-treatment: HIV serology, LFTs, FBC; pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy
Risk of progression: ~10% lifetime, highest in first 2 years and in HIV co-infection
explanation.pearls: Always pair isoniazid with pyridoxine 25 mg daily in adults - peripheral neuropathy is the dose-limiting side effect, and the relative cost of pyridoxine is so low that omitting it is never the right call.

sources.label: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.rationale: Recent household contact of smear-positive TB confers around a 10% lifetime risk of progression (highest in the first 2 years), which clearly outweighs the side-effect burden of isoniazid in a young woman without liver disease. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.rationale: QFT-Plus has excellent specificity (around 99%) and a positive result in a household contact of smear-positive disease is acted upon directly; repeat testing delays appropriate prevention of disease progression. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.rationale: Quadruple RIPE therapy is for active TB; she has no symptoms, normal CXR and no microbiological evidence of active disease, so latent TB treatment is the correct intervention. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.rationale: Invasive sampling is not indicated in an asymptomatic contact with a clear chest x-ray; latent TB treatment can begin once symptoms, x-ray and clinical examination exclude active disease. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.rationale: She has latent TB infection (QFT-Plus positive, asymptomatic, normal CXR) as a household contact of smear-positive pulmonary TB; Australian guidance recommends isoniazid plus pyridoxine for 6 to 9 months under specialist TB service supervision after active TB exclusion. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents with a mononucleosis-like syndrome (fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash, oral ulcers) typically 2 to 4 weeks after exposure. The 4th-generation Ag/Ab combination assay detects p24 antigen and is reactive earlier than antibody-only assays; however, the Western blot may be indeterminate in early infection before antibody bands have fully developed. HIV-1 RNA viral load is the appropriate confirmatory test (very high viral loads, often above 10^6 copies/mL in acute infection). ART is started promptly regardless of CD4 count: this reduces reservoir size, lowers set-point viral load and prevents transmission, and is referred to a sexual health or infectious diseases physician.
key_points: Acute HIV: 4th-gen Ag/Ab positive plus Western blot often indeterminate before bands develop
Confirmatory test: HIV-1 RNA viral load (typically very high in acute infection)
ART started promptly regardless of CD4 count; reduces reservoir, set-point, transmission
PEP window 72 hours post-exposure only; partner notification and contact tracing essential
explanation.pearls: An indeterminate Western blot after a reactive 4th-generation HIV assay in someone with a mononucleosis-like illness is acute seroconversion until proven otherwise - request HIV RNA the same day and start the referral to sexual health, do not wait 4 weeks to repeat serology.

sources.label: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.rationale: Post-exposure prophylaxis must start within 72 hours of exposure; at 18 days post-exposure with reactive screening this is no longer PEP but established acute infection requiring HIV RNA confirmation and ART initiation. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.rationale: In suspected acute seroconversion with a reactive 4th-generation Ag/Ab assay and indeterminate Western blot (typical of early seroconversion before band development), HIV RNA viral load is the appropriate confirmatory test; ART is started promptly. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.rationale: CD4 count does not confirm HIV diagnosis; modern ART is started regardless of CD4 count to maximise immunological recovery, suppress viral reservoir and reduce onward transmission. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.rationale: Delaying diagnosis and ART forfeits the substantial benefit of early treatment in acute infection (reduced reservoir, lower set-point, reduced transmission); HIV RNA viral load resolves diagnostic uncertainty today. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.rationale: Delaying confirmation in suspected acute seroconversion forfeits the substantial individual and public health benefit of early ART; HIV RNA viral load provides definitive same-day confirmation in this scenario. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

explanation.summary: Indications for elective AAA repair are: diameter at or above 5.5 cm in men (5.0 cm in women), rapid expansion above 1 cm per year (or above 0.5 cm in 6 months), and symptomatic disease at any size. EVAR is preferred over open repair where anatomy permits (suitable proximal neck length, angulation, iliac access), lower perioperative mortality but higher reintervention rate over time; open repair is more durable in younger fit patients. Medical management focuses on smoking cessation, BP control (avoid statin and antihypertensive omission), and lipid lowering to reduce expansion rate.
key_points: Elective repair threshold: 5.5 cm in men, 5.0 cm in women, or rapid expansion above 1 cm per year
EVAR vs open: EVAR lower 30-day mortality, higher long-term reintervention; open more durable
Suitability for EVAR depends on proximal neck length above 15 to 20 mm, angle, iliac access
Medical therapy: smoking cessation, BP control, statin, no role for routine beta-blocker for expansion
explanation.pearls: Rapid expansion above 1 cm in a year independently triggers repair even below 5.5 cm - growth rate is as important as absolute size, so always document interval growth on serial imaging rather than just the current diameter.

sources.label: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.rationale: The Australian and international threshold for elective repair in men is 5.5 cm, not 6 cm; rapid expansion of 0.8 cm over 12 months is an independent indication for intervention. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.rationale: At 5.6 cm with rapid expansion the annual rupture risk substantially exceeds operative mortality; deferral with intensified medical therapy is not appropriate. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.rationale: EVAR is preferred in patients with suitable anatomy due to lower perioperative mortality; open repair is reserved for unsuitable anatomy, younger patients with long life expectancy, or failed EVAR. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.rationale: Surgical repair is indicated at 5.5 cm or greater in men, rapid expansion above 1 cm per year, or symptoms; he meets size, growth and morphology criteria, and EVAR is appropriate where anatomy permits and cardiac fitness allows. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.rationale: Asymptomatic AAA above 5.5 cm without leakage is electively repaired within weeks, not as an emergency; emergency repair is for symptomatic, leaking or ruptured aneurysms. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

explanation.summary: Pre-operative preparation for phaeochromocytoma resection requires 10 to 14 days of alpha-adrenergic blockade (phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated, or doxazosin 2 mg daily titrated) with salt and fluid loading to restore intravascular volume. A beta blocker is added only after adequate alpha blockade to control reflex tachycardia, never before. Adequacy markers: sitting BP under 130/80, standing systolic above 90, nasal congestion, mild postural drop. Post-resection hypotension is managed with fluids and vasopressors. Genetic testing is offered to all (at least 30% have a hereditary cause) and contralateral adrenal preservation is considered in hereditary syndromes.
key_points: Alpha blockade 10 to 14 days pre-op: phenoxybenzamine (irreversible) or doxazosin (selective alpha-1)
Beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade; never first because of unopposed alpha vasoconstriction risk
Salt and fluid loading during alpha blockade to refill the contracted intravascular volume
Genetic testing for all (at least 30% hereditary): SDHB/C/D, RET, VHL, NF1, MAX, TMEM127
explanation.pearls: The single most preventable peri-operative phaeochromocytoma death is starting a beta blocker before alpha blockade - if a surgical team books a phaeochromocytoma case for next week and the patient is on no antihypertensives, your first prescription is phenoxybenzamine, never metoprolol or labetalol.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.rationale: Pre-operative non-selective alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine for 10 to 14 days, with salt and fluid loading, followed by addition of a beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade is the recognised sequence; starting a beta blocker before alpha blockade risks unopposed alpha effects and hypertensive crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.rationale: Starting a beta blocker before alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma can precipitate hypertensive crisis through unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction; the established sequence is alpha first, then beta. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.rationale: Labetalol has relatively weak alpha-blocking activity and its mixed profile can precipitate unopposed beta effects; phenoxybenzamine (or doxazosin in some centres) followed by a separate beta blocker is preferred. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.rationale: Operating on an unblockaded phaeochromocytoma carries very high perioperative mortality from intraoperative hypertensive crisis and post-resection hypotension; 10 to 14 days of alpha blockade is mandatory. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.rationale: Calcium channel blockade does not adequately blunt the catecholamine surge of surgical manipulation; alpha blockade for 10 to 14 days with salt and fluid loading is the standard pre-operative preparation. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis with systemic features or inability to tolerate oral therapy requires IV antibiotics and admission. Australian first-line empiric therapy is gentamicin (covering most gram-negative uropathogens with renal concentration and synergy) plus ampicillin (for enterococcal cover). De-escalation is guided by culture sensitivity within 48-72 hours. Nitrofurantoin and oral fosfomycin do not penetrate the upper tract and are not used for pyelonephritis.
key_points: Severe pyelonephritis: IV gentamicin + IV ampicillin first-line in Australia
Nitrofurantoin: lower-tract UTI only, not pyelonephritis
Ciprofloxacin: not empiric first-line due to resistance and adverse effect profile
explanation.pearls: If gentamicin contraindicated (significant renal impairment, ototoxicity risk), substitute IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily; consider ESBL coverage if recent healthcare exposure or known carriage.

sources.label: eTG Complete: Urinary tract infections in adults

options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate when the patient cannot tolerate oral intake due to vomiting and has systemic features, and trimethoprim is no longer a recommended empiric choice for pyelonephritis given resistance rates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

Australian first-line empiric therapy for acute pyelonephritis requiring admission is IV gentamicin plus IV ampicillin, providing cover for E. coli and enterococci with synergy and renal concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

Fluoroquinolones are not first-line empiric pyelonephritis therapy in Australia due to resistance and adverse effect concerns, and oral therapy is unsuitable when the patient is vomiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

Piperacillin-tazobactam is reserved for severe sepsis, healthcare-associated infection or known resistant pathogens; first-line for community pyelonephritis is gentamicin plus ampicillin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue or serum concentrations to treat upper urinary tract infection and is contraindicated for pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis supported by pain out of proportion, rapid spread, dusky skin, bullae, crepitus and systemic toxicity. LRINEC at or above 6 indicates intermediate risk and at or above 8 high risk, but no score excludes the diagnosis. Management is immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics including a protein-synthesis inhibitor (clindamycin or linezolid) for toxin suppression, plus urgent surgical fascial exploration and debridement. Imaging should not delay theatre.
key_points: Necrotising fasciitis: surgical emergency; do not wait for imaging
Antibiotics: pip-tazo + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
LRINEC >=6 intermediate, >=8 high risk; clinical features still trump score
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin (or linezolid) is added specifically to inhibit toxin production from group A streptococci and Clostridium species; continue until clinical improvement and de-escalation guided by intra-operative cultures.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection
Stevens et al IDSA SSTI Guidelines
