key_points: ABCD2 above 4 or minor stroke NIHSS up to 3 indicates DAPT for 21 days
Add high-intensity statin and aggressive BP control
Urgent stroke clinic review and AF screening within 24-48 hours
explanation.pearls: Prolonged cardiac monitoring (Holter or implantable loop recorder) is indicated when initial ECG is normal and a cardioembolic source remains a concern after standard workup.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention

options.rationale: Aspirin alone is inadequate for high-risk TIA in the first 3 weeks; dual antiplatelet therapy reduces early recurrent stroke per CHANCE and POINT trials. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: Anticoagulation is for cardioembolic stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation or other indications; there is no AF demonstrated and warfarin is not indicated for non-cardioembolic TIA. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention

options.rationale: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 above 4 or minor stroke with NIHSS up to 3) is treated with aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days then aspirin alone, high-intensity statin, BP control and urgent stroke clinic review within 24-48 hours. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: Thrombolysis is reserved for established ischaemic stroke within the eligibility window, not for TIA with resolved symptoms. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: DOACs are not indicated for non-cardioembolic TIA; investigation for AF is appropriate but empirical anticoagulation is not. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention

explanation.summary: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura presents with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, renal injury and fever; ADAMTS13 activity is very low. Urgent therapeutic plasma exchange and high-dose corticosteroids must be initiated within hours of suspicion. Caplacizumab and rituximab are added in immune TTP. Platelet transfusion is avoided unless life-threatening bleeding.
key_points: TTP pentad: MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurological, renal, fever
Initiate plasma exchange within hours of suspicion, do not wait for ADAMTS13
Platelet transfusion is avoided unless life-threatening bleeding
explanation.pearls: Differentiate TTP from atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (complement-mediated, treated with eculizumab) and from DIC (abnormal coagulation, low fibrinogen, treat the cause).

options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP unless life-threatening bleeding, due to risk of worsening microvascular thrombosis; antibiotics do not address the underlying ADAMTS13 deficiency. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura guideline)

Microangiopathic haemolysis with neurological signs and renal injury and very low platelets fits TTP not ITP; IVIG would delay definitive plasma exchange. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura guideline)

AKI in TTP is part of the microangiopathic process and is treated by plasma exchange; haemodialysis is reserved for refractory metabolic indications. (Source: ANZSBT: Therapeutic apheresis indications)

Suspected TTP requires urgent initiation of therapeutic plasma exchange (within hours), high-dose corticosteroids, and addition of caplacizumab and rituximab in acquired disease while awaiting ADAMTS13 results; outcome depends on minimising delay. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura guideline)
Anticoagulation is not indicated in TTP and would worsen bleeding with thrombocytopenia; plasma exchange and steroids are first-line. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura guideline)

explanation.summary: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days has become first-line for non-severe Clostridioides difficile infection in Australia, displacing metronidazole on the strength of higher cure and reduced recurrence. Fidaxomicin is an alternative, particularly when recurrence risk is high. Severe disease, ileus, megacolon or sepsis prompts admission, oral plus rectal vancomycin and surgical review. Antimotility agents are avoided. FMT is reserved for multiple recurrences.
key_points: Oral vancomycin 125 mg QID for 10 days is first-line in non-severe CDI
Loperamide is contraindicated because of toxic megacolon risk
FMT is reserved for multiply recurrent disease after standard antibiotic failure
explanation.pearls: Stop the inciting antibiotic whenever possible at CDI diagnosis; this alone resolves around a quarter of mild cases before oral vancomycin has finished a 10-day course.

sources.label: ACSQHC: Clostridioides difficile clinical care standard

options.rationale: IV metronidazole achieves poor colonic concentrations in CDI; current AU and international guidance favours oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin even for non-severe disease. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)
Antimotility agents are contraindicated in CDI because of toxic megacolon risk; treatment should not be delayed in a PCR-positive symptomatic case. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)
Rifaximin is used as a tapered chaser for recurrent CDI in some protocols, not as primary therapy for a first episode. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)
FMT is reserved for multiply recurrent CDI after standard antibiotic regimens have failed; it is not first-line for an initial episode. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days is the AU first-line regimen for non-severe CDI; metronidazole is no longer preferred. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)

explanation.summary: Stable atrial flutter with preserved LVEF is rate-controlled with a beta blocker (or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker if beta blockade is not tolerated). Digoxin is reserved for sedentary patients or as an add-on. Adenosine has a diagnostic role by transiently unmasking flutter waves but does not convert. Anticoagulation follows CHA2DS2-VA assessment; this man with a score of 3 warrants long-term oral anticoagulation.
key_points: Beta blockers are first-line rate control in flutter with preserved LVEF
Adenosine is diagnostic, not therapeutic, in flutter
CHA2DS2-VA >= 2 prompts oral anticoagulation in Australian guidance
explanation.pearls: A regularly conducted narrow-complex tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise; vagal manoeuvres or adenosine will reveal the sawtooth pattern.

options.rationale: Beta blockade is first-line rate control in atrial flutter with preserved LVEF and no heart failure; CHA2DS2-VA above 2 requires anticoagulation review. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)
Adenosine transiently unmasks flutter waves but does not convert flutter; it is diagnostic, not therapeutic, in this rhythm. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

Amiodarone is reserved for rhythm control in selected patients, often with heart failure; it is not first-line rate control for stable preserved-EF flutter. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

Elective cardioversion in stable patients with arrhythmia under 48 hours can be considered but is not the routine first step; rate control with anticoagulation review is the AU pathway. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

Digoxin monotherapy provides poor rate control during exertion and is reserved for patients with sedentary lifestyle or as add-on; not first-line in this man. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

explanation.summary: Mild gallstone pancreatitis is managed with goal-directed intravenous crystalloid (Hartmann's preferred), parenteral analgesia, early oral or enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours, and same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence. Prophylactic antibiotics do not improve outcomes. Urgent ERCP is reserved for cholangitis or persisting common bile duct obstruction. Severity assessment can be made with bedside scores supplemented by lactate and urea trends.
key_points: Same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy is recommended for mild gallstone pancreatitis
Early enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours improves outcomes versus prolonged NBM
Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated in mild pancreatitis without infection
explanation.pearls: Same-admission cholecystectomy after mild gallstone pancreatitis reduces 30-day readmission for recurrent biliary events by around 75 percent compared with delayed surgery.

options.rationale: Urgent ERCP is reserved for gallstone pancreatitis with ascending cholangitis or persisting obstruction; without those features there is no early ERCP benefit. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)

Prolonged NBM and TPN are no longer preferred; early enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours improves outcomes; routine early CT is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or deterioration. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)
Acute pancreatitis requires admission for IV fluids and analgesia; discharge from ED with active disease is inappropriate. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)
Prophylactic antibiotics do not improve outcomes in mild pancreatitis and are reserved for proven infection or infected necrosis. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)
AU and GESA guidance recommend goal-directed fluids, early feeding and same-admission cholecystectomy for mild gallstone pancreatitis. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)

explanation.summary: Mild diabetic foot infection (cellulitis under 2 cm wide, no systemic features) is treated with oral narrow-spectrum antistaphylococcal antibiotics. Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days is AU first-line; cefalexin substitutes in non-severe penicillin allergy. Concurrent off-loading, sharp debridement, dressings and glycaemic optimisation are essential. Pseudomonas cover is not required in mild infection. Probe-to-bone or exposed bone prompts MRI and osteomyelitis pathway.
key_points: Flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 7 days is AU first-line for mild diabetic foot infection
Off-loading and debridement are as important as antibiotics in foot infection
Probe-to-bone or positive bone exposure triggers osteomyelitis workup with MRI
explanation.pearls: Probe-to-bone positivity in a diabetic foot ulcer has a positive predictive value above 80 percent for underlying osteomyelitis and prompts MRI rather than plain film alone.

options.rationale: Mild diabetic foot infection in a non-allergic patient is treated with narrow-spectrum oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics; flucloxacillin is AU first-line. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)
Mild diabetic foot infection without systemic features does not require IV broad-spectrum therapy or admission. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)
Surrounding cellulitis indicates a need for systemic, not topical, antibiotics in diabetic foot infection. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)
Anaerobic monotherapy misses the dominant Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species in mild infections. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)
Mild infections require around 7 days of treatment; prolonged dual therapy is reserved for osteomyelitis or moderate-severe infection. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection management centres on reducing aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt). Intravenous beta blockade (esmolol or labetalol) is started first, targeting heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 120 mmHg, with a vasodilator added if BP control is inadequate. Uncomplicated type B dissection is medically managed; complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain) is treated with TEVAR. Type A dissection requires urgent cardiothoracic surgery.
key_points: Target heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 120 mmHg with IV beta blockade first
Vasodilators are added second after beta blockade to avoid reflex tachycardia and shear stress
Uncomplicated type B dissection is medically managed; complicated type B prompts TEVAR
explanation.pearls: Always start a beta blocker before any vasodilator in aortic dissection because pure vasodilator therapy causes reflex tachycardia and increased dP/dt, worsening shear stress on the dissection flap.

options.rationale: Vasodilators alone can reflex-increase shear stress (dP/dt); rate control with a beta blocker must precede or accompany them. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)
Fluid loading is inappropriate in hypertensive dissection and oral beta blockade is too slow for acute shear stress reduction. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)
Uncomplicated type B dissection is initially medical; surgery or TEVAR is reserved for malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)
Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because of haemorrhage and false lumen extension risk. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)
Acute aortic dissection management targets shear stress reduction with IV beta blockade first, BP under 120 systolic, vasodilator added second if needed. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)

explanation.summary: Acute severe ulcerative colitis (Truelove-Witts criteria) is treated by admission, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six hourly, VTE prophylaxis (despite bleeding), CDI exclusion, and daily clinical reassessment. Day 3 Travis criteria (stool frequency above 8 or CRP above 45 mg/L with 3 to 8 stools) predict steroid failure and trigger rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin and surgical review. Colectomy is reserved for refractory or complicated disease.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six hourly is first-line in acute severe UC
Day 3 Travis criteria identify steroid non-responders for rescue therapy
VTE prophylaxis is essential despite bloody stools because of pro-thrombotic flare state
explanation.pearls: Day 3 of IV steroids: more than 8 stools per day or CRP above 45 with 3 to 8 stools predicts steroid failure and triggers infliximab or ciclosporin rescue and surgical co-review.

options.rationale: Truelove-Witts severe UC is treated with IV corticosteroids and VTE prophylaxis; CDI testing rules out the major mimic. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)
Oral aminosalicylates and budesonide are inadequate for severe acute UC; IV steroids are required. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)
Empirical antibiotics are not first-line in acute severe UC without infection; they delay definitive immunosuppression. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)
Biologics are second-line after failure or contraindication to IV corticosteroids in acute severe UC; adalimumab is not first-choice rescue. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)
Colectomy is for failure of medical rescue, toxic megacolon, perforation or massive haemorrhage; not an immediate first response. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological features (subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns) requires intramuscular hydroxocobalamin loading followed by lifelong maintenance every 3 months in pernicious anaemia. Oral high-dose cyanocobalamin is acceptable in dietary deficiency without neurological involvement. Folate must never precede B12 replacement in macrocytic anaemia because of precipitation risk. Metformin and PPIs are common contributors. Anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies support pernicious anaemia.
key_points: IM hydroxocobalamin loading is preferred in B12 deficiency with neurological features
Never give folate before B12 in macrocytic anaemia because of SCDC precipitation risk
Metformin and PPIs are common contributors to B12 deficiency
explanation.pearls: Hydroxocobalamin 1000 micrograms intramuscular every 2 to 3 days for 2 weeks then 3-monthly for life is the AU regimen for pernicious anaemia with neurological involvement.

options.rationale: Pernicious anaemia with neurological involvement is treated with IM hydroxocobalamin loading then 3-monthly maintenance for life. (Source: AMH: hydroxocobalamin)
Oral high-dose B12 is acceptable in dietary deficiency without neurological features; AU practice prefers IM loading for neurological involvement. (Source: AMH: hydroxocobalamin)
Giving folate alone can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. (Source: AMH: folic acid)
Hb 102 with stable cardiorespiratory status does not warrant transfusion; correction of the deficiency restores haematopoiesis. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)
Metformin causes B12 deficiency, not macrocytic anaemia from its withdrawal; iron addresses microcytic, not macrocytic anaemia. (Source: AMH: metformin and B12)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy requires aggressive intravenous saline rehydration (3 to 4 litres over 24 hours), correction of magnesium and potassium, and a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid 4 mg IV) once renal function permits. Calcitonin (4 IU/kg 12-hourly) gives faster but short-lived calcium lowering as a bridge in symptomatic patients. Denosumab is used when bisphosphonates fail or in renal failure. Loop diuretics are added only after volume repletion in normal renal function.
key_points: Saline rehydration precedes any pharmacological calcium-lowering therapy
Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV gives sustained calcium lowering within 48 hours
Calcitonin acts within hours but with tachyphylaxis within 48 hours
explanation.pearls: Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV lowers calcium across 48 to 96 hours with effects lasting around 4 weeks; calcitonin 4 IU/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours bridges that delay but loses effect within 48 hours.

options.rationale: Loop diuretics are added only after adequate volume repletion in normal renal function; using them first worsens dehydration and hypercalcaemia. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)

Volume repletion with saline is the first-line move; IV zoledronic acid provides sustained calcium lowering once renal function is restored; calcitonin offers a rapid bridging effect. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)
Dialysis is reserved for severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with renal failure not responsive to fluids and pharmacology; not first-line. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)
Denosumab is used when bisphosphonates fail or are contraindicated by renal failure; it is not first-line monotherapy in initial hypercalcaemia. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)
Cinacalcet is used in parathyroid carcinoma and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, not as first-line for hypercalcaemia of malignancy. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)

explanation.summary: Hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated and does not respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or corticosteroids. Acute attacks (especially laryngeal) are treated with C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor), alongside airway preparedness. Long-term prophylaxis options include attenuated androgens (danazol), tranexamic acid, lanadelumab, and prophylactic C1-INH. C4 is a useful screening test in steady state.
key_points: HAE does not respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or corticosteroids
Acute therapy is C1-INH concentrate or icatibant alongside airway preparedness
Danazol is long-term prophylaxis, not acute attack therapy
explanation.pearls: A persistently low C4 between attacks is the most useful screening test for hereditary angioedema and prompts confirmatory C1 esterase inhibitor antigenic and functional assays.

options.rationale: Adrenaline targets histamine-mediated anaphylaxis; bradykinin-mediated HAE does not respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or corticosteroids. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)
Corticosteroids, antihistamines and beta agonists do not work in bradykinin-mediated HAE; targeted C1-INH replacement or bradykinin pathway inhibition is required. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)
HAE laryngeal attacks require C1-INH concentrate or icatibant as first-line; ASCIA recommends airway-ready monitoring. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)
Danazol is long-term prophylaxis in HAE, not acute attack therapy; onset is far too slow for laryngeal involvement. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)
Airway management plans must be in place, but specific HAE therapy is not delayed; C1-INH or icatibant is given concurrently with airway preparation. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma crisis is managed with alpha blockade first (intravenous phentolamine in crisis, oral phenoxybenzamine for at least 7 to 14 days preoperatively), followed by beta blockade for tachycardia once alpha blockade is established. Beta blockade alone causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and worsens hypertension. Adequate salt and fluid loading is required during alpha blockade. Surgery is planned after biochemical and haemodynamic optimisation.
key_points: Alpha blockade precedes beta blockade by 7 to 14 days preoperatively in phaeochromocytoma
Beta blockade before alpha blockade causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction
Salt and fluid loading during alpha blockade supports intraoperative haemodynamics
explanation.pearls: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated upward over 7 to 14 days is the standard AU preoperative regimen, with adequate salt and fluid intake to limit postoperative hypotension.

options.rationale: Beta blockade before adequate alpha blockade causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and worsens crisis; avoid until alpha-blocked. (Source: AMH: phenoxybenzamine; eTG Endocrinology: phaeochromocytoma)
Short-acting sublingual nifedipine causes rapid swings and reflex tachycardia and is not preferred; alpha blockade is the targeted therapy. (Source: AMH: nifedipine)
Magnesium is an adjunct in severe phaeochromocytoma crisis but is not first-line monotherapy; alpha blockade is the pillar. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: phaeochromocytoma)

Phaeochromocytoma management requires alpha blockade first; beta blockade is added only after alpha blockade is established to avoid unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: phaeochromocytoma)
Adrenalectomy without 7 to 14 days of alpha blockade and 2 to 3 days of beta blockade is associated with severe intraoperative crisis and mortality. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: phaeochromocytoma)

explanation.summary: Empirical therapy for suspected infective endocarditis in an IVDU covers Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA with vancomycin, with gentamicin added for synergy and gram-negative cover until cultures return. Three sets of cultures from separate venepunctures precede antibiotics where time allows. Transthoracic echo identifies right-sided vegetations; transoesophageal echo is indicated if TTE is non-diagnostic or left-sided IE is suspected. Surgical referral applies to large vegetations, heart failure or refractory sepsis.
key_points: IVDU-associated right-sided IE is most commonly Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA
Empiric IV vancomycin plus gentamicin covers MRSA and provides synergy until cultures return
Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites precede antibiotics where the clinical state allows
explanation.pearls: Septic pulmonary emboli with a tricuspid vegetation in an IVDU points to Staphylococcus aureus; start vancomycin with gentamicin once cultures are drawn.

options.rationale: AU empiric therapy for suspected IE in an IVDU covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with vancomycin and adds gentamicin for synergy until cultures and susceptibilities return. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)
Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not reliably cover MRSA, the dominant pathogen in IVDU-associated right-sided IE. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)
Delaying antibiotics in a febrile patient with vegetations and septic emboli risks progression; empirical cover is started after cultures are drawn. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)
Oral therapy is inadequate for the induction phase of IE; intravenous therapy in hospital is required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)
Benzylpenicillin alone misses MRSA and Staphylococcus aureus, the leading IVDU IE pathogens. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)

explanation.summary: High-risk occupational HIV exposure (deep hollow-needle injury from a viraemic source) mandates three-drug PEP started as soon as possible, ideally within hours and within 72 hours, for 28 days. The Australian first-line regimen is tenofovir disoproxil plus emtricitabine with dolutegravir or raltegravir. Baseline HIV serology is taken in parallel and repeated at 6 weeks, 3 months and (if indicated) 6 months. Hepatitis B and C status of source and worker are also documented.
key_points: Three-drug PEP within 72 hours, ideally within hours, of high-risk HIV exposure
First-line AU regimen: tenofovir disoproxil with emtricitabine plus dolutegravir for 28 days
Follow-up HIV serology at 6 weeks and 3 months, with earlier symptomatic testing if seroconversion is suspected
explanation.pearls: PEP started within 4 hours and continued for 28 days reduces the risk of HIV seroconversion after needlestick by around 80 percent; tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir is the AU preferred regimen.

sources.label: Australian Society for Infectious Diseases occupational exposure statement

options.rationale: PEP efficacy declines steeply beyond 24 hours; starting prophylaxis cannot wait for baseline serology when the source is high-risk. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)
High-risk occupational exposure to a high viral load source mandates three-drug PEP started as soon as possible, ideally within hours, for 28 days. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)
Single-dose monotherapy is not endorsed PEP; three-drug regimens for 28 days are the standard. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)
Worker baseline serology is essential but does not delay PEP initiation in a high-risk exposure. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)
Hepatitis B immunity does not protect against HIV; PEP is required for a needlestick from a viraemic HIV source. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic QFT-positive new migrants without radiological or microbiological active disease are offered preventive treatment for latent TB infection. AU options are 9 months of isoniazid with pyridoxine or 4 months of rifampicin; the rifampicin regimen has comparable efficacy with fewer hepatotoxicity events. Monthly clinical and LFT review during treatment is standard. Active TB must be excluded before preventive monotherapy.
key_points: Latent TB preventive therapy is offered after excluding active disease with symptoms screen and CXR
9 months isoniazid with pyridoxine or 4 months rifampicin are both accepted AU regimens
Monthly LFTs and symptom review screen for hepatotoxicity during preventive therapy
explanation.pearls: 4 months of daily rifampicin gives equivalent protection to 9 months of isoniazid in latent TB with lower rates of hepatotoxicity and better completion.

sources.label: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection
Communicable Diseases Network Australia: tuberculosis guideline

options.rationale: RIPE is for active TB; there is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of active disease here. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

options.rationale: Untreated latent TB has a 5 to 10 percent lifetime reactivation risk; recent migrants from high-prevalence settings benefit from preventive therapy. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

options.rationale: Latent TB preventive therapy with isoniazid for 9 months or rifampicin for 4 months reduces reactivation risk by 60 to 90 percent; AU programs accept either, with LFT monitoring. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

options.rationale: Sputum AFB is for suspected active TB; without symptoms or CXR changes there is no indication. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

options.rationale: QFT-Plus does not require routine repeat for confirmation in an asymptomatic positive result with consistent risk factors. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

explanation.summary: The AU sepsis pathway and Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle for septic shock include lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics, empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg, and vasopressor escalation to target a MAP of at least 65. Source imaging and source control follow. Hydrocortisone is reserved for vasopressor-refractory shock. Empiric agents for urosepsis include gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam.
key_points: Sepsis hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors to MAP 65
Empiric urosepsis: gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam pending culture sensitivities
Hydrocortisone reserved for vasopressor-refractory shock
explanation.pearls: Lactate above 4 mmol/L with hypotension defines septic shock; 30 mL/kg crystalloid plus broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour reduces mortality.

options.rationale: 30 mL/kg crystalloid in the first hour is recommended for septic shock; a 250 mL ceiling under-resuscitates. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)
Antibiotics are given within 1 hour for septic shock; cultures are obtained before antibiotics where possible without delay. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)
Vasopressor support is escalated alongside or after initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid, not before any fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)

The AU sepsis pathway delivers a balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg, empiric IV antibiotics within 1 hour after cultures, and lactate trending; gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam covers the likely organism for urosepsis pending sensitivities. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)
Hydrocortisone is reserved for vasopressor-refractory shock; bicarbonate is not routine in sepsis with pH above 7.15. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)

explanation.summary: Suspected bacterial meningitis is treated empirically without delay. In adults under 50 with no immunocompromise the AU regimen is IV ceftriaxone 2 g with IV dexamethasone 10 mg given before or with the first dose. Add benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover when over 50, immunocompromised or pregnant. CT brain is reserved for focal neurology, seizures or impaired conscious level; otherwise LP follows immediately after the first antibiotic dose.
key_points: Empiric IV ceftriaxone 2 g plus IV dexamethasone 10 mg given immediately after blood cultures
Add benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover if over 50, immunocompromised or pregnant
Pre-LP CT is reserved for focal neurology, seizures or impaired conscious level
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV given with or immediately before the first dose of ceftriaxone reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis when started before antibiotics.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: meningococcal disease

options.rationale: Antibiotics and dexamethasone are not delayed for LP results; doses are given as soon as cultures are drawn. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)
Dexamethasone 10 mg given immediately before or with the first dose reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)
Bacterial meningitis empirical therapy is given immediately for any suspicion; HSV cover is added when encephalitic features are present. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)
Imaging beyond non-contrast CT is unnecessary before LP and antibiotics in alert patients with no focal neurology. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)
Empirical dexamethasone 10 mg given before or with the first dose of ceftriaxone reduces neurological sequelae; LP follows immediately. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)

explanation.summary: Frail older adults in aged care with confirmed influenza receive oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, started as soon as possible after symptom onset. Treatment remains worthwhile beyond 48 hours in severe or high-risk disease. Renal dose adjustment applies at eGFR below 30. Amantadine is obsolete due to resistance. Outbreak control includes droplet precautions, cohort isolation and post-exposure prophylaxis for residents and staff per CDNA guidance.
key_points: Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is first-line for high-risk influenza A
Renal dose adjustment of oseltamivir applies at eGFR below 30
Amantadine is no longer used due to resistance
explanation.pearls: Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days started within 48 hours of symptoms reduces complications and length of illness in high-risk adults including frail aged-care residents.

sources.label: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units

options.rationale: AU CDNA recommends neuraminidase inhibitor therapy for high-risk individuals such as frail aged-care residents within 48 hours of symptom onset; 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is standard at eGFR above 30. (Source: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units)
source_refs: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units

options.rationale: Standard adult dose is 75 mg twice daily for 5 days; routine doubling is not recommended for non-immunocompromised hosts. (Source: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cellulitis is typically driven by beta-haemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. First-line empirical therapy in non-allergic adults is oral di/flucloxacillin 500 mg six-hourly for 5 days; cefalexin substitutes for non-severe penicillin allergy. IV therapy and broader cover are reserved for sepsis, severe local features or rapid spread. MRSA cover is added only for known colonisation, recurrent disease or high-risk exposures. Limb elevation, marking of erythema and 48-hour clinical review identify treatment failure early.
key_points: Di/flucloxacillin is first-line for non-severe cellulitis in non-allergic adults
Cefalexin substitutes for non-severe penicillin allergy
Vancomycin or clindamycin is added only for severe disease or known MRSA risk
explanation.pearls: 5 days of di/flucloxacillin 500 mg six-hourly resolves most uncomplicated lower-limb cellulitis; mark the leading edge and review at 48 hours for failure to improve.

options.rationale: Cefalexin is an acceptable substitute for non-severe penicillin allergy but is not first-line over di/flucloxacillin in non-allergic patients. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)

Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus drive uncomplicated cellulitis; di/flucloxacillin covers both and is the AU first-line in non-allergic adults with non-severe disease. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)
Empirical MRSA cover is reserved for known colonisation, severe sepsis, recurrent disease or high-risk exposures, none of which apply here. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)
Topical therapy alone is inadequate for cellulitis; systemic therapy is required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)
Doxycycline misses many group A streptococcal isolates and is not first-line monotherapy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant adult woman is treated empirically with trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally six-hourly for 5 days. Cefalexin and amoxicillin-clavulanate are alternatives. Fluoroquinolones are reserved for resistant or complicated infections. Pre-treatment midstream urine for culture is not required for sporadic uncomplicated episodes but is sent in recurrent or complicated cases.
key_points: Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days is the AU first-line for uncomplicated cystitis
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg six-hourly for 5 days is an equivalent first-line alternative
Fluoroquinolones are reserved for resistant or complicated UTI
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days resolves most uncomplicated lower UTI in non-pregnant women; switch to nitrofurantoin in late pregnancy or trimethoprim-resistant isolates.

options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for resistant or complicated infections in Australia; not first-line for uncomplicated lower UTI. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)
Fosfomycin is a second-line AU option used where first-line agents are unsuitable; not the routine first choice. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)

Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days is the AU first-line empirical therapy for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant adults; nitrofurantoin for 5 days is an alternative. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)
IV therapy is reserved for pyelonephritis, sepsis or oral failure; not first-line for uncomplicated cystitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)
Amoxicillin has high E. coli resistance rates in Australia; trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin are preferred and 14 days is excessive. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)

explanation.summary: Post-menopausal osteoporosis with incident vertebral fracture meets criteria for antifracture pharmacotherapy. Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) are AU first-line with weekly dosing on PBS, paired with calcium and vitamin D repletion. Dental review precedes initiation given osteonecrosis risk. Denosumab and teriparatide are subsequent options when bisphosphonates fail or are contraindicated. Hormone therapy is not first-line in older post-menopausal women.
key_points: Vertebral fracture with T-score under -2.5 is an indication for antiresorptive therapy
Oral alendronate or risedronate is AU first-line with calcium and vitamin D repletion
Pre-treatment dental review reduces osteonecrosis risk
explanation.pearls: Alendronate 70 mg weekly reduces vertebral fracture risk by about 45 percent in established osteoporosis; couple with daily calcium 1300 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU when intake is low.

sources.label: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.rationale: An incident vertebral fracture with T-score under -2.5 mandates antiresorptive therapy; supplements alone are insufficient. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.rationale: Denosumab is an option but discontinuation without bisphosphonate cover triggers rebound fractures; first-line is usually an oral bisphosphonate. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.rationale: Menopausal hormone therapy is not first-line for established osteoporosis in older women given cardiovascular and thromboembolic risks. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.rationale: Oral bisphosphonates are AU first-line for post-menopausal osteoporosis with vertebral fracture; calcium and vitamin D repletion plus dental review and upright dosing maximise effectiveness and safety. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe disease or bisphosphonate failure under PBS criteria; not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)

explanation.summary: Provoked DVT in a non-cancer patient is treated for 3 months with a direct oral anticoagulant. Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily is the AU regimen; rivaroxaban with a 21-day loading then 20 mg daily is an alternative. Lifelong therapy is reserved for unprovoked or recurrent disease, malignancy or thrombophilia. Counselling on recurrence symptoms and travel prevention closes the encounter.
key_points: Provoked proximal DVT is treated for 3 months with a DOAC at standard dosing
Lifelong therapy is reserved for unprovoked, recurrent, cancer-associated or thrombophilia VTE
IVC filter is reserved for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation
explanation.pearls: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for 3 months is the standard AU regimen for provoked proximal DVT in a non-cancer adult.

options.rationale: Lifelong therapy is reserved for unprovoked or recurrent VTE, malignancy or significant thrombophilia, none of which apply. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)
A 6-week course is insufficient for a proximal DVT; standard duration is at least 3 months. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)
Cross-over to warfarin is not standard; provoked first DVT does not warrant indefinite therapy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)

Anticoagulation is the cornerstone; IVC filters are reserved for active major bleeding or absolute contraindications to anticoagulation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)

Provoked proximal DVT in a non-cancer patient is treated for 3 months with a DOAC at standard dosing; the apixaban induction-maintenance schedule is the AU regimen. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)

explanation.summary: HHS presents with marked hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis. Initial management is cautious volume resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid, gradual correction of osmolality (sodium fall 4 to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours), low-rate insulin (0.05 units/kg/hour) started after fluid response, and potassium replacement when below 5.0 with adequate urine output. Source control of any precipitant (such as UTI) is essential. Cerebral oedema and central pontine myelinolysis are the feared correction-rate complications.
key_points: HHS: fluid first with isotonic crystalloid, then low-rate insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour
Limit corrected sodium fall to 4 to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours
Treat the precipitating infection or omission of insulin
explanation.pearls: Capping the fall in corrected sodium at 8 mmol/L per 24 hours and using insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour after fluid response prevents the cerebral oedema and pontine myelinolysis that follow over-aggressive HHS correction.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society inpatient hyperglycaemia statement

options.rationale: HHS requires cautious volume resuscitation first; insulin starts after fluid response and at lower rates than DKA, with sodium fall capped at 4 to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid pontine myelinolysis or cerebral oedema. (Source: JBDS-IP guideline for HHS adapted for AU practice; ADIPS resources)
Rapid hypotonic correction and early insulin bolus risk rapid osmolar shifts, cerebral oedema and hypokalaemia. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS guideline)
HHS is more dehydrated than acidotic; fluid first, low-dose insulin after fluid response, not DKA-style. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS guideline)
Hypertonic saline is not used in HHS; it would worsen the hyperosmolar state. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS guideline)
Acidaemia is mild and not driven by ketoacidosis; bicarbonate is not indicated and high-rate insulin risks rapid osmolar shift. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS guideline)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency. Pain out of proportion, crepitus, dusky skin, bullae and cutaneous anaesthesia raise suspicion; LRINEC above 6 supports it. Management is simultaneous resuscitation, blood cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin or alternatives per eTG), and urgent surgical debridement within hours. Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after debridement. Delay to theatre is the dominant driver of mortality.
key_points: LRINEC above 6 with clinical features mandates immediate surgical consult
Empiric IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin covers the polymicrobial picture
Surgical debridement is the definitive treatment and is the strongest predictor of survival
explanation.pearls: Debridement within 6 hours of presentation is the single biggest determinant of survival in necrotising soft tissue infection; clindamycin adds toxin suppression to broad-spectrum cover.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

options.rationale: This is necrotising fasciitis with septic shock; oral therapy at home is unsafe. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection requires emergent broad-spectrum antibiotics including a toxin-inhibitor (clindamycin) and MRSA cover, with surgical debridement within hours as the definitive treatment. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)

options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after antibiotics and debridement, not a substitute. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

options.rationale: Waiting for confirmatory imaging in a clinical necrotising soft tissue infection delays life-saving surgery; monotherapy under-covers the polymicrobial picture. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

options.rationale: Single-dose therapy and discharge are unsafe in septic shock from necrotising fasciitis; emergency surgery is required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)

explanation.summary: A positive aldosterone-to-renin ratio screens for primary aldosteronism but is not diagnostic. Confirmation requires withdrawal of interfering agents (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, betablockers, ACE inhibitors as feasible) and a suppression test (saline, fludrocortisone, oral sodium loading, or captopril). Adrenal CT identifies macroadenomas but is insufficient for lateralisation; adrenal vein sampling localises the source for surgical candidates. Unilateral disease is treated with laparoscopic adrenalectomy; bilateral hyperplasia with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.
key_points: Confirm primary aldosteronism with a suppression test before any treatment decisions
Adrenal vein sampling is required before adrenalectomy because imaging misses small functioning adenomas
Bilateral hyperplasia is treated medically with spironolactone or eplerenone
explanation.pearls: After a positive ARR, perform a saline suppression test (2 L of 0.9 percent saline over 4 hours): failure of aldosterone to fall below 140 pmol/L confirms autonomous secretion.

options.rationale: Stopping all antihypertensives without confirmatory testing delays diagnosis and is unsafe at this BP. (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline: case detection, diagnosis, and treatment of primary aldosteronism)
A screening ARR is not diagnostic; confirmatory suppression and subtyping with adrenal vein sampling are required before surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society guideline: primary aldosteronism)

The Endocrine Society pathway after a positive screening ARR is medication washout, confirmatory suppression testing, then adrenal imaging and vein sampling to identify a unilateral surgical lesion. (Source: Endocrine Society guideline: primary aldosteronism)
Empirical mineralocorticoid blockade may treat the BP but misses unilateral disease amenable to surgical cure and forfeits the diagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society guideline: primary aldosteronism)
Metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma; here aldosteronism is suggested by the ARR and hypokalaemia. (Source: Endocrine Society guideline: primary aldosteronism)

explanation.summary: Pituitary apoplexy is haemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma presenting with thunderclap headache, visual or cranial nerve compromise and acute hypopituitarism. Hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia and a low random cortisol indicate secondary adrenal insufficiency. Immediate management is high-dose IV hydrocortisone, fluid resuscitation and urgent neurosurgical referral for transsphenoidal decompression when there is visual or cranial nerve compromise. Subsequent replacement covers thyroid, gonadal and posterior pituitary axes as required.
key_points: Acute apoplexy is a neurosurgical and endocrine emergency
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours treats secondary adrenal insufficiency
Transsphenoidal decompression is indicated for visual or cranial nerve compromise
explanation.pearls: A low random cortisol below 100 nmol/L with hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia in a patient with a pituitary mass mandates IV hydrocortisone 100 mg before any other intervention.

sources.label: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline
Endocrine Society guideline: hormonal replacement in hypopituitarism

options.rationale: Antihypertensives in a hypotensive patient with acute hypopituitarism worsen hypoperfusion; immediate corticosteroid replacement is the priority. (Source: Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance: pituitary apoplexy)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

options.rationale: Acute apoplexy with neuro-ophthalmic compromise and adrenal insufficiency is an inpatient emergency, not an outpatient pathway. (Source: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

options.rationale: Stress-dose hydrocortisone is required for adrenal insufficiency; dexamethasone alone misses the mineralocorticoid context and curbs further endocrine workup. (Source: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

options.rationale: Acute pituitary apoplexy with hypotension, hyponatraemia and a low random cortisol mandates immediate hydrocortisone replacement; visual field or cranial nerve compromise prompts urgent transsphenoidal decompression. (Source: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

explanation.summary: Seropositive RA with high disease activity warrants early DMARD initiation within the window of opportunity. Methotrexate 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid is the AU first-line anchor drug, paired with bridging glucocorticoids and a treat-to-target plan. Screening before initiation includes LFTs, eGFR, hepatitis B and C, tuberculosis (QFT-Plus) and pneumococcal vaccination. Step-up to combination conventional synthetic DMARDs or biologic therapy follows failure to reach remission at 3 to 6 months.
key_points: Methotrexate is the AU anchor DMARD for seropositive RA
Early initiation within 3 months of symptom onset preserves joint function
Step-up to combination or biologic therapy when remission is not achieved at 3 to 6 months
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate started at 10 mg weekly with folic acid and titrated to 20 to 25 mg weekly over 6 to 8 weeks reaches remission in around 30 percent of seropositive RA as monotherapy.

options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy does not modify joint damage and incurs cumulative toxicity; a conventional synthetic DMARD is mandatory. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association rheumatoid arthritis position statement)
NSAIDs treat symptoms only; they do not prevent erosive progression in seropositive RA. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association RA statement)
Window-of-opportunity data favour DMARD start within 3 months of symptom onset; deferral worsens long-term outcomes. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association RA statement)

Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy is inadequate for seropositive high-activity RA; it features in combination regimens but not as monotherapy here. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association RA statement)

Methotrexate is the AU anchor DMARD for seropositive RA, started after screening (CXR, hepatitis, eGFR, LFTs), with a short bridging glucocorticoid and a treat-to-target plan stepping to combination or biologic therapy if remission is not achieved. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association RA statement)

explanation.summary: Suspected giant cell arteritis with any visual feature is treated with high-dose corticosteroids before biopsy: oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily for uncomplicated GCA, IV methylprednisolone pulse for vision loss. Temporal artery biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks remains diagnostic; biopsy yield is preserved on early treatment. Aspirin 100 mg daily reduces ischaemic events, while calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates and a PPI cover steroid harms. Tocilizumab is a steroid-sparing add-on for relapsers.
key_points: Start high-dose corticosteroids immediately on clinical suspicion; do not wait for biopsy
Aspirin 100 mg daily reduces ischaemic events in GCA
Biopsy yield is preserved for 1 to 2 weeks after starting steroids
explanation.pearls: Visual symptoms in suspected GCA prompt IV methylprednisolone 500 to 1000 mg daily for 3 days; otherwise oral prednisolone 60 mg daily, with biopsy within 14 days.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: rheumatology - giant cell arteritis

options.rationale: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms is started immediately on high-dose corticosteroids; biopsy yield is preserved for 1 to 2 weeks. Aspirin reduces ischaemic events; bone and PPI cover address steroid harms. (Source: BSR guideline on GCA management; eviQ general rheumatology)
Delaying steroids risks permanent visual loss; biopsy yield is preserved for up to 2 weeks of treatment. (Source: BSR GCA guideline)
GCA is systemic; topical therapy does not address arteritis. (Source: BSR GCA guideline)
NSAID monotherapy will not control vasculitis and exposes the patient to preventable visual loss. (Source: BSR GCA guideline)
Tocilizumab is a steroid-sparing add-on in relapsing or steroid-toxic GCA; not monotherapy at first presentation. (Source: BSR GCA guideline)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is bulbar or respiratory failure on a background of myasthenia gravis. Bedside markers include FVC under 1 L (or under 15 mL/kg), single-breath count under 20 and rising pCO2. Management is ICU admission for ventilatory support (NIV trialled cautiously, intubation when paradoxical breathing or rising pCO2 develops), treatment of triggers (infection, drugs such as aminoglycosides), and rapid immunomodulation with IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days or plasma exchange. Steroid up-titration is initiated under cover of immunomodulation given the risk of transient worsening.
key_points: FVC under 1 L or single-breath count under 20 signals impending respiratory failure
IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days or plasma exchange is the rescue therapy of choice
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides and magnesium can precipitate or worsen crisis
explanation.pearls: Single-breath count under 20 or FVC below 15 mL/kg in known myasthenia signals impending respiratory failure; mobilise IVIG or plasma exchange and prepare the airway team.

sources.label: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

options.rationale: Increasing pyridostigmine in crisis risks cholinergic crisis and does not address respiratory failure; admission is mandatory. (Source: Australian Myasthenic Association clinician resources; eTG Neurology)
source_refs: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

options.rationale: Myasthenic crisis with FVC under 1 L and hypercapnia requires ICU-level airway support, treatment of precipitants, and rapid immunomodulation with IVIG or plasma exchange. (Source: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management)
source_refs: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

options.rationale: Edrophonium is no longer routine in known seropositive disease and does not address respiratory failure. (Source: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management)
source_refs: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

options.rationale: Slow steroid titration cannot rescue acute crisis; early steroid up-titration also risks transient worsening. (Source: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management)

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen ventilatory drive and risk respiratory arrest in neuromuscular failure. (Source: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management)

explanation.summary: Clinically isolated syndrome with MRI findings that satisfy dissemination in space and time meets McDonald 2017 criteria for relapsing-remitting MS. Acute optic neuritis is treated with high-dose methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3 to 5 days; recovery is typically excellent. Early initiation of a disease-modifying therapy (such as fingolimod, ocrelizumab, natalizumab or platform injectable agents per PBS criteria) reduces relapse rate, MRI activity and long-term disability accrual. AQP4 and MOG antibodies are checked to exclude NMOSD and MOGAD.
key_points: McDonald 2017 allows MS diagnosis after a first attack when dissemination in space and time are present on MRI
Treat acute optic neuritis with methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3 to 5 days
Initiate DMT promptly to reduce long-term disability accrual
explanation.pearls: A first demyelinating attack with periventricular and juxtacortical lesions and concurrent gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI satisfies dissemination in space and time under McDonald 2017.

options.rationale: Active disease meeting McDonald criteria warrants prompt DMT initiation; delay accrues disability. (Source: MS International Federation; MSAANZ DMT consensus)
Plasma exchange is reserved for severe steroid-refractory attacks; it is not first-line acute or maintenance therapy for typical optic neuritis. (Source: MSAANZ DMT consensus)

Dissemination in space and time on the first MRI satisfies McDonald 2017 criteria and supports diagnosing relapsing-remitting MS, with acute high-dose steroids and prompt DMT to reduce relapse and disability accrual. (Source: McDonald 2017 criteria; MSAANZ DMT consensus)
DMT initiation reduces relapse rate, MRI activity and long-term disability; discharge without DMT misses the window of opportunity. (Source: MSAANZ DMT consensus)
Modern McDonald 2017 criteria allow diagnosis after the first attack when imaging shows dissemination in space and time; waiting harms outcomes. (Source: McDonald 2017 criteria)

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome is a new pulmonary infiltrate with respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease. Mortality in adults is around 5 to 10 percent. Management is oxygen to maintain saturation above 95 percent, judicious crystalloid (avoiding overload), opioid analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering typical and atypical organisms (eg ceftriaxone plus azithromycin), bronchodilators if reactive airways, incentive spirometry, and simple top-up transfusion or exchange transfusion for severe disease. Haematology and ICU involvement is essential. Triggers (infection, hypoventilation, fat embolism, atelectasis) are sought and addressed.
key_points: Acute chest syndrome: new infiltrate plus respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease
Broad-spectrum antibiotics cover typical and atypical pathogens
Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe disease (hypoxia, falling Hb, multi-lobar involvement)
explanation.pearls: Adult acute chest syndrome mortality drops with early ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, incentive spirometry every hour while awake, and exchange transfusion when SpO2 falls below 90 percent on supplemental oxygen.

sources.label: HSANZ sickle cell disease position statement

options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is a key salvage therapy in severe acute chest syndrome; it is not contraindicated. (Source: BSH guidelines for the management of sickle cell disease; HSANZ paediatric and adult statements)
Acute chest syndrome demands antibiotic cover, oxygen and consideration of transfusion regardless of hydroxycarbamide status. (Source: BSH sickle cell disease guideline)
Non-invasive ventilation is an adjunct; antibiotics, opioid analgesia and transfusion are core therapy. (Source: BSH sickle cell disease guideline)

Acute chest syndrome is managed with oxygen, judicious fluids, opioid analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering typical and atypical pathogens, incentive spirometry, and simple top-up transfusion (or exchange transfusion for severe disease), with haematology and ICU involvement. (Source: BSH sickle cell disease guideline)
Hydroxycarbamide is long-term prevention; it does not rescue acute chest syndrome. (Source: BSH sickle cell disease guideline)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulant-associated intracranial haemorrhage requires emergent reversal with the agent specific to the anticoagulant. For factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban), andexanet alfa is the targeted reversal agent where available; otherwise 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg is the alternative. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran. Concurrent BP control to 140 systolic, neurosurgical referral for haematoma evacuation candidates, and reversal of antiplatelet therapy with platelet transfusion (selective, in operative cases) complete the package.
key_points: Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban; 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg is the alternative
Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran
BP target under 140 systolic and neurosurgical referral are concurrent priorities
explanation.pearls: In apixaban-associated ICH, andexanet alfa 400 to 800 mg IV bolus followed by infusion (or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg when andexanet unavailable), with BP lowered to under 140 systolic, halves haematoma expansion compared with no specific reversal.

options.rationale: FFP does not reverse direct factor Xa inhibitors; specific reversal is required. (Source: THANZ position statement on anticoagulant reversal; AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline)
Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not DOACs; not the agent of choice here. (Source: THANZ anticoagulant reversal statement)
TXA is not a substitute for specific reversal in DOAC ICH; outcome trials show minimal effect on functional outcome. (Source: THANZ anticoagulant reversal statement; TICH-2)
Active intracerebral bleeding within an apixaban dosing interval requires immediate reversal, not observation. (Source: THANZ anticoagulant reversal statement)

Specific factor Xa reversal with andexanet alfa, or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg when andexanet is unavailable, is the AU pathway for DOAC ICH, alongside BP control under 140 systolic and neurosurgical referral. (Source: THANZ anticoagulant reversal statement; AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline)

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax management has shifted to a symptom-led approach: stable patients with minimal symptoms may be observed, while symptomatic patients with large pneumothoraces are increasingly managed with ambulatory pneumothorax devices or needle aspiration rather than admission with a chest drain. Tension pneumothorax (haemodynamic compromise, tracheal deviation) is decompressed immediately by needle thoracostomy followed by chest drain. Secondary pneumothorax (underlying lung disease) usually warrants admission and chest drain. Recurrence prevention with VATS and pleurodesis is considered for recurrent disease, persistent air leak over 5 days, bilateral disease, or high-risk occupations (pilots, divers).
key_points: Symptom-led approach replaces strict size cut-offs for primary spontaneous pneumothorax
Ambulatory pneumothorax devices are an option for stable symptomatic primary disease
Surgical pleurodesis is reserved for recurrence, persistent air leak, bilateral disease, or high-risk occupation
explanation.pearls: Needle thoracostomy is reserved for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise; in clinical practice it is replaced by finger thoracostomy in many AU prehospital settings.

options.rationale: Observation alone for a large primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a symptomatic patient is no longer routine first-line; ambulatory drain or aspiration is preferred. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)
Current British Thoracic Society 2023 guidance supports ambulatory management of large primary spontaneous pneumothorax in selected stable patients. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)
Needle thoracocentesis is reserved for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)

Large bore chest drains are reserved for secondary pneumothorax or trauma; primary spontaneous pneumothorax is managed with smaller drains or ambulatory devices. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)
Surgical pleurodesis is for recurrent, bilateral, persistent air leak, or high-risk occupation pneumothorax, not first presentation. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance recommends sizing pneumothorax by interpleural distance at the hilum or apex. Rim less than 2 cm and asymptomatic suits conservative observation. Rim of 2 cm or more or symptomatic warrants intercostal catheter, often a small bore 8 to 14 French catheter. Needle aspiration is an alternative but with lower success in larger rims. Tension pneumothorax with tracheal deviation, haemodynamic compromise, or hypoxia requires immediate needle decompression and chest drain placement.
key_points: Rim less than 2 cm and asymptomatic: observe with oxygen
Rim of 2 cm or more or symptomatic: insert intercostal catheter
Tension pneumothorax: immediate needle decompression then drain
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation is the single most important secondary prevention measure after primary spontaneous pneumothorax; the risk of recurrence is halved.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.rationale: A primary spontaneous pneumothorax with rim of 2 cm or more or symptomatic at rest warrants intercostal catheter drainage in Australian practice. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.rationale: Needle aspiration is an option for small primary pneumothoraces but is less effective than intercostal catheter for rims of 2 cm or more with significant symptoms. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.rationale: Conservative observation alone is for small asymptomatic primary pneumothoraces with rim less than 2 cm and reliable follow-up. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.rationale: Definitive surgery is reserved for second ipsilateral pneumothorax, persistent air leak, contralateral history, or occupational indication. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.rationale: Needle decompression is reserved for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise or tracheal deviation, neither of which is present. (Source: ANZCOR: Adult Advanced Life Support)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated non-purulent cellulitis is most commonly caused by Streptococcus species and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Australian first-line therapy is oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days in patients without severity criteria, allergy, or risk factors for community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Marking the erythema edge and reviewing at 48 hours guides response. Intravenous therapy is reserved for severe infection, sepsis criteria, or failure of oral therapy.
key_points: Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days is first-line for uncomplicated cellulitis
Mark the erythema edge and review at 48 hours
Vancomycin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are reserved for specific risk factors
explanation.pearls: Recurrent leg cellulitis often reflects tinea pedis as the portal of entry; treat the fungal foot infection to prevent further episodes.

options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is broader spectrum and not first-line for uncomplicated cellulitis without diabetic foot ulcer or animal bite. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is reserved for suspected community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with purulent infection, not non-purulent cellulitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)
Empirical vancomycin is reserved for severe infection, suspected methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, or beta-lactam allergy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)
Clindamycin is an alternative in penicillin allergy; it is not first-line in patients tolerant of beta-lactams. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)

Flucloxacillin oral 500 mg four times daily covers Streptococcus and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus for uncomplicated non-purulent cellulitis; recent Australian guidance supports 5 days for clinically improving cases. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is a common cause of resistant hypertension, particularly with spontaneous hypokalaemia. Screening uses the aldosterone-renin ratio after potassium repletion and washout of interfering medications. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, eplerenone, and amiloride must be stopped 4 weeks beforehand. Beta-blockers reduce renin and increase the ratio falsely. ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and dihydropyridines may be continued with caution. Sampling is done in the morning after 2 hours upright.
key_points: Replete potassium before sampling
Stop mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for 4 weeks before testing
Verapamil, prazosin, hydralazine, and moxonidine do not interfere with screening
explanation.pearls: Confirmatory testing with saline loading or fludrocortisone suppression follows a positive screen; do not commit to surgery on a screen alone.

options.rationale: Some antihypertensives substantially alter the aldosterone-renin ratio and must be adjusted before testing. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)
Beta-blockers also suppress renin and increase the aldosterone-renin ratio, generating false positives. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists must be stopped 4 weeks before sampling; potassium must be replete; non-interfering agents like prazosin, hydralazine, moxonidine, and verapamil can manage hypertension during testing. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)
Sampling is done after 2 hours of upright posture in the morning, not in the supine position at midnight. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)
Sodium restriction alters the renin-aldosterone axis and is not part of routine screening preparation. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency requiring immediate intravenous hydrocortisone and aggressive fluid resuscitation. Standard dosing is hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours. Hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid effect at these doses, so fludrocortisone is not required acutely. Glucose monitoring and treatment of hypoglycaemia are essential. Investigation for and treatment of precipitating infection occurs simultaneously.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous followed by 200 mg over 24 hours in adrenal crisis
Fluid resuscitate with sodium chloride 0.9% and treat hypoglycaemia
Identify and treat precipitating illness in parallel
explanation.pearls: All patients with adrenal insufficiency should have hydrocortisone for self-injection at home and stress-dose instructions; an Australian endocrine emergency wristband or card aids identification.

options.rationale: Persistent vomiting precludes oral absorption; parenteral hydrocortisone is required without delay in adrenal crisis. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

Adrenal crisis requires immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by infusion or repeated doses to total 200 mg over 24 hours, plus aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

Hydrocortisone is preferred because it provides mineralocorticoid as well as glucocorticoid coverage; dexamethasone is used only when retaining diagnostic capacity matters. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at 100 mg or more daily. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

Empirical steroids are given immediately in suspected adrenal crisis without waiting for cortisol level results; antibiotics are added if sepsis is suspected. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Preoperative blockade in phaeochromocytoma must be alpha first, beta second, to prevent unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. Phenoxybenzamine is the most common alpha blocker; doxazosin is an alternative when phenoxybenzamine causes troublesome side effects. A high-sodium diet and increased fluid intake expand intravascular volume. Beta blockade is added only after adequate alpha blockade if reflex tachycardia develops. Surgery is generally performed at 10 to 14 days when targets are met.
key_points: Alpha first, beta second for phaeochromocytoma preoperative blockade
Phenoxybenzamine is the standard alpha blocker; doxazosin is an alternative
High-sodium diet and volume expansion are essential adjuncts
explanation.pearls: Labetalol is contraindicated as monotherapy in phaeochromocytoma because the relative beta blockade overshadows the alpha component and can precipitate crisis.

options.rationale: Beta blockade before alpha blockade unopposes alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and can precipitate hypertensive crisis. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)
Calcium channel blockade alone is inadequate preoperative blockade; alpha blockade is mandatory. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)
Preoperative blockade for 10 to 14 days reduces intraoperative haemodynamic instability and is mandatory. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

Australian and international practice is alpha blockade first, typically phenoxybenzamine, with high-salt diet to expand volume; beta blockade added only if reflex tachycardia, then adrenalectomy at 10 to 14 days. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)
Labetalol has greater beta than alpha activity and can produce paradoxical hypertension in phaeochromocytoma. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

explanation.summary: Massive or high-risk pulmonary embolism is defined by sustained hypotension and is a class I indication for systemic thrombolysis. Standard dosing is alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours followed by unfractionated heparin once activated partial thromboplastin time is approaching normal. Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy is reserved for those with absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis. Intermediate-high risk pulmonary embolism with normotension but right ventricular strain may benefit from selective rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs.
key_points: Massive pulmonary embolism with hypotension warrants systemic thrombolysis
Alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours then heparin is standard dosing
Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy is reserved for thrombolysis contraindications
explanation.pearls: Even after thrombolysis many patients have persistent right ventricular strain; follow-up echocardiography at 3 to 6 months screens for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: Massive pulmonary embolism with sustained hypotension is a class I indication for systemic thrombolysis, typically alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours, followed by anticoagulation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: Therapeutic anticoagulation alone is inadequate for haemodynamically unstable massive pulmonary embolism; reperfusion is required. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: Inferior vena cava filters are reserved for those with contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent emboli despite therapy. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation does not address the haemodynamic obstruction; delay in reperfusion increases mortality. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: Catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy is considered for those with absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis; delay of 7 days is unacceptable in massive pulmonary embolism. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

explanation.summary: A positive probe-to-bone in a chronic diabetic foot ulcer with raised inflammatory markers and cortical erosion on x-ray is highly predictive of osteomyelitis. Optimal management combines admission for multidisciplinary input including orthopaedic, infectious diseases, vascular, podiatry, and diabetes care. Bone biopsy with histology and culture guides 6 weeks of intravenous followed by oral culture-directed antibiotic therapy. Surgical resection of infected bone is considered when medical therapy fails, when there is extensive necrosis, or when sepsis threatens limb viability.
key_points: Probe-to-bone plus cortical erosion strongly predicts diabetic foot osteomyelitis
Bone biopsy with culture guides 6-week antibiotic therapy
Multidisciplinary care reduces amputation rates
