explanation.pearls: Vascular assessment with ankle-brachial index and toe pressures is essential before antibiotic-only management because ischaemia mandates revascularisation.

sources.label: Diabetes Feet Australia: Diabetic Foot Guidelines

options.rationale: Outpatient cefalexin is inadequate for suspected osteomyelitis; bone-penetrating broader regimens are required after appropriate sampling. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)
Delay of 8 weeks in suspected osteomyelitis risks progression and amputation; admission and timely sampling are warranted. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)
Metronidazole alone does not cover Staphylococcus aureus or aerobic streptococci, which are the dominant pathogens in diabetic foot osteomyelitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)
Surgical resection of infected bone is selective; amputation is reserved for failed medical therapy, extensive necrosis, or limb-threatening sepsis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)

Positive probe-to-bone with cortical erosion is highly predictive of osteomyelitis; targeted bone biopsy guides 6 weeks of culture-directed antibiotic therapy with surgical input as needed. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency in patients with primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency, precipitated by infection, surgery, trauma, missed steroid doses, vomiting or stress. Features include hypotension, shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (primary AI only), hypoglycaemia and altered mental state. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat (continuing 200 mg/24 h infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours), IV isotonic saline resuscitation (1 L in first hour), glucose correction, and empirical treatment of the precipitant. Educate patients on sick-day rules: double oral dose for fevers/minor illness, IM hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef) injection for vomiting.
key_points: Adrenal crisis = hypotension + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia.
Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat.
IV crystalloid 1 L in first hour, then maintenance.
Treat precipitant (sepsis): empirical antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines.
Patient education: double oral dose for minor illness; IM hydrocortisone for vomiting.
explanation.pearls: Patients on regular prednisolone 5 mg or higher for 4 weeks or longer have functional secondary adrenal insufficiency and need stress-dose hydrocortisone for major surgery or sepsis even if their primary disease (eg PMR, asthma) seems quiescent.

options.rationale: Oral dosing is inadequate when vomiting and shocked; IV hydrocortisone is required. (Source: ESE 2020)

Adrenal crisis (hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia) on top of sepsis requires immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, IV fluid resuscitation, glucose correction and antibiotics per sepsis pathway. (Source: ESE adrenal crisis 2020; eTG)
Diagnosis is already established by medic-alert bracelet and clinical picture; do not delay hydrocortisone for biochemical testing in established Addison's. (Source: ESE 2020)
Vasopressors are ineffective without glucocorticoid replacement in established adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone must come first. (Source: ESE 2020)
Delay for imaging in shocked adrenal crisis worsens outcome; treat empirically and image after stabilisation. (Source: ESE 2020)

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) treatment is offered to those at risk of progression: recent contacts of infectious cases, immunosuppression including anti-TNF therapy, HIV, dialysis, organ transplant, silicosis, and migrants from high-prevalence countries. Acceptable Australian regimens include isoniazid 6 months, isoniazid plus rifampicin 3 months, and rifampicin 4 months. Anti-TNF agents increase reactivation risk 4 to 8-fold; LTBI treatment should begin at least 4 weeks before biologic therapy. Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid peripheral neuropathy.
key_points: Recommended LTBI regimens: 6H, 3HR, or 4R as per NTAC
Anti-TNF therapy increases TB reactivation 4 to 8-fold
LTBI treatment should start at least 4 weeks before biologic therapy
Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy
explanation.pearls: Isoniazid hepatotoxicity rises markedly above age 35 and with alcohol intake - baseline ALT and monthly LFT monitoring during treatment catches early hepatitis and most resolves with prompt drug cessation.

sources.label: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.rationale: He has no respiratory symptoms and a normal chest X-ray, so sputum sampling is not required. Active TB workup is reserved for symptomatic or radiographically suspicious cases. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.rationale: Anti-TNF therapy in the presence of untreated latent TB carries a 4 to 8-fold increase in reactivation, often as extrapulmonary or miliary disease. Treatment of latent TB must precede or run alongside biologic therapy. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.rationale: RIPE is the regimen for active tuberculosis, not latent infection. Treating latent infection as if it were active causes unnecessary toxicity. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.rationale: BCG vaccination does not treat existing latent infection and is contraindicated in immunosuppressed adults due to disseminated BCG risk. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.rationale: Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine for 6 months is a recommended Australian regimen for latent tuberculosis. Treatment should start at least 4 weeks before commencing anti-TNF therapy to reduce the risk of reactivation. Pyridoxine prevents peripheral neuropathy. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

explanation.summary: VTE anticoagulation duration depends on whether the event was provoked or unprovoked and on bleeding risk. Provoked VTE (surgery, trauma, immobilisation) is treated for 3 months. Unprovoked proximal DVT or PE warrants extended (indefinite) anticoagulation in low-bleeding-risk patients because recurrence is around 10% in year one without therapy. Reduced-dose DOACs (apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) are as effective and safer than full dose for the extended phase. Annual reassessment of bleeding risk is essential.
key_points: Provoked VTE: 3 months of anticoagulation
Unprovoked proximal VTE: extended therapy if low bleeding risk
Reduced-dose DOAC (apixaban 2.5 mg BID, rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) for extended phase
Annual bleeding-risk reassessment is the cornerstone of extended therapy
explanation.pearls: After the first 6 months of full-dose anticoagulation for unprovoked VTE, reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) lowers recurrence by approximately 80% compared with placebo with major bleeding rates similar to no anticoagulation.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for VTE in patients without contraindications because they offer similar efficacy with lower intracranial bleeding rates and avoid INR monitoring. Switching for cost alone is not recommended. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Stopping anticoagulation after 3 months for unprovoked proximal DVT leaves a recurrence risk of around 10% in the first year, with case fatality of recurrent VTE around 5%. Extended therapy is recommended in low-bleeding-risk patients. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Aspirin reduces VTE recurrence by only around 30% compared with around 80% reduction from a DOAC, with similar bleeding rates at the low-dose DOAC extended dose. DOAC is preferred. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Both AMPLIFY-EXT and EINSTEIN-CHOICE showed that reduced-dose DOACs are as effective and safer for extended-phase therapy after the initial 6 months. Full-dose is reserved for higher-risk profiles. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: After an unprovoked proximal DVT, indefinite anticoagulation is recommended for low bleeding-risk patients because annual recurrence after stopping is around 10% in year one and 5% per year thereafter. Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is the evidence-supported extended-phase dose with similar efficacy and lower bleeding than full-intensity therapy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle for adults with septic shock includes obtaining lactate and blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor support if MAP remains below 65 mmHg after fluid resuscitation. Empirical antibiotic choice follows source: urinary tract sepsis with shock is commonly treated with piperacillin-tazobactam in Australia, narrowed when cultures return. Source control (drainage, surgical intervention) is pursued in parallel for abscess, biliary sepsis, or other surgical foci.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour of septic shock recognition
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for shock or lactate > 4 mmol/L
Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor target MAP > 65 mmHg
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if vasopressor-dependent shock persists
explanation.pearls: Each hour of delay in appropriate antibiotic administration after recognition of septic shock increases in-hospital mortality by approximately 4 to 8% - early administration is among the highest-yield interventions in sepsis care.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network
ANZICS Clinical Trials Group - ANZICS Sepsis Resources

options.rationale: 1 L is well below the recommended 30 mL/kg initial volume for septic shock and inadequate for this 80 kg patient. The Surviving Sepsis bundle calls for 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours, ideally front-loaded in the first hour. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

options.rationale: Each hour of delayed antibiotic administration in septic shock increases mortality by 4 to 8%. Cultures are obtained but treatment is not delayed. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

options.rationale: Septic shock with hypotension and lactate over 2 mmol/L mandates broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour and 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid resuscitation. Piperacillin-tazobactam covers community urinary sepsis with shock per Australian sepsis pathways. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

options.rationale: Noradrenaline is added when fluid resuscitation has failed to restore MAP above 65 mmHg. Starting vasopressors before fluid in this patient bypasses the proven mortality-reducing fluid bolus. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added only when fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support have failed to maintain MAP above 65 mmHg. It is not a first-hour intervention before fluids and antibiotics. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax most commonly affects tall, thin, young men and is managed by size and symptoms. Interpleural distance under 2 cm at the hilum with minimal symptoms is observed. Larger or symptomatic primary pneumothoraces are treated by needle aspiration first, with small-bore intercostal catheter for failure. Tension physiology mandates immediate needle decompression. After a first primary pneumothorax, recurrence rate is approximately 30% within 1 year; VATS pleurodesis or bullectomy is offered after a second event or for persistent air leak.
key_points: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax under 2 cm: observation only
Larger or symptomatic: needle aspiration first-line
Persistent air leak or recurrence: small-bore intercostal catheter then VATS
Recurrence after first event around 30% within 1 year
explanation.pearls: Tall thin young males who smoke have a 7 to 10-fold higher risk of recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax, and smoking cessation is the single most important secondary prevention measure even after surgical pleurodesis.

options.rationale: VATS pleurodesis is reserved for recurrent pneumothorax, persistent air leak, or first occurrence in high-risk occupations. It is not first-line for a stable primary pneumothorax at first presentation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

Large-bore intercostal catheters cause more pain and longer hospital stays than aspiration or small-bore drains in primary pneumothorax, and are not first-line in a stable patient. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

Conservative management is acceptable for small primary pneumothorax (under 2 cm) with minimal symptoms but is not first choice for a 3 cm moderately symptomatic pneumothorax. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

British Thoracic Society and Australian guidance support needle aspiration as first-line for a symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax with interpleural distance more than 2 cm at the hilum. Aspiration succeeds in around 60% of cases and avoids intercostal catheter insertion. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

A symptomatic moderate primary pneumothorax requires active management before discharge. Home discharge without aspiration or drainage risks progression and tension physiology. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis is classified by valve type and timing. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (less than 12 months from surgery) is dominated by Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and enterococci, with high methicillin resistance. Empirical therapy is vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin, narrowed when cultures return. Modified Duke criteria require 2 major, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor for definite IE. Three blood culture sets are drawn from separate sites before antibiotics. Transoesophageal echo has higher sensitivity than transthoracic for prosthetic valve vegetations.
key_points: Early PVE (under 12 months): vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin empirical
Late PVE (over 12 months): treated similarly to native valve disease
Three blood culture sets from separate sites before antibiotics
TOE > TTE sensitivity for prosthetic valve vegetations
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin is added in prosthetic valve endocarditis specifically because of its biofilm penetration; it is not used in native valve disease and has potent CYP3A4 induction with major drug-interaction implications.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand - Endocarditis
ESC Guidelines for the Management of Endocarditis

options.rationale: Ceftriaxone alone is inadequate for prosthetic valve endocarditis and misses staphylococcal organisms. It is appropriate for native valve streptococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin alone cover oral streptococci but miss staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis, which is the dominant pathogen group within 12 months of surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

Flucloxacillin monotherapy fails to cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and biofilm-associated organisms typical of early prosthetic valve infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

Prosthetic valve endocarditis within 12 months of surgery is treated empirically with vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin to cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci including coagulase-negative species, which dominate this window. Rifampicin penetrates biofilm on prosthetic material. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

Once endocarditis is clinically suspected with new murmur and persistent fever after sending three culture sets, empirical antibiotics are commenced immediately because delay increases embolic and mortality risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (commonly above 180/120) with acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, retinopathy, pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, myocardial ischaemia, aortic dissection). Lowering blood pressure too rapidly causes watershed cerebral and coronary infarction. Targets are approximately 25% reduction in MAP within the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours, except in aortic dissection (systolic under 120 mmHg within 20 minutes) and ischaemic stroke (carefully titrated). IV nitrates, labetalol, and clevidipine are common Australian choices.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency: severe BP plus acute end-organ damage
Target: 25% MAP reduction in first hour, then 160/100 by 2 to 6 hours
Aortic dissection: systolic under 120 mmHg within 20 minutes
Pulmonary oedema: IV nitrate plus loop diuretic; avoid pure beta-blockade
explanation.pearls: Excessive rapid BP lowering in hypertensive emergency causes watershed cerebral infarction because chronic hypertension shifts the cerebral autoregulation curve - aiming for 25% MAP reduction in the first hour respects this rightward shift.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines
ESC Guidelines for the Management of Arterial Hypertension

options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema is treated with an intravenous nitrate (GTN) infusion plus loop diuretic, with target reduction in MAP of approximately 25% within the first hour and to 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours to avoid hypoperfusion. GTN reduces both preload and afterload. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

options.rationale: Oral short-acting nifedipine causes uncontrolled hypotension and rebound stroke or myocardial ischaemia. It is not appropriate for hypertensive emergency. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

options.rationale: Pure beta-blockade in pulmonary oedema worsens cardiac decompensation and the rapid normalisation target risks cerebral and coronary hypoperfusion. Beta-blockade is reserved for selected scenarios like aortic dissection alongside a vasodilator. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

options.rationale: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia (problematic in possible coronary ischaemia) and is unpredictable for titration. It is not first-line in hypertensive emergency outside pregnancy. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

options.rationale: Sublingual or oral captopril is unpredictable and risks precipitous hypotension and AKI in a patient with rising creatinine. ACE inhibition has no role in acute IV management of hypertensive emergency. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma crisis arises from massive catecholamine release, often during anaesthesia, surgical manipulation, or interventional procedures in an undiagnosed or inadequately blocked patient. The cardinal management rule is alpha-blockade first, then beta-blockade for tachycardia. Acute IV options include phentolamine (non-selective alpha), sodium nitroprusside, and nicardipine. Volume resuscitation addresses contracted intravascular volume. Once stabilised, oral phenoxybenzamine is used for 10 to 14 days of preoperative blockade before definitive surgical removal. Plasma free metanephrines are the diagnostic test of choice.
key_points: Phaeochromocytoma crisis: alpha-blockade first, beta-blockade only after alpha is established
Acute IV options: phentolamine, nitroprusside, nicardipine
Plasma free metanephrines have the highest sensitivity for diagnosis
Preoperative oral phenoxybenzamine for 10 to 14 days plus volume loading before surgery
explanation.pearls: Unopposed beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma can precipitate fatal hypertensive crisis within minutes because removing beta-mediated vasodilation unleashes catecholamine alpha-vasoconstriction - the order of blockade is non-negotiable.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.rationale: Unopposed beta-blockade in suspected phaeochromocytoma crisis precipitates catastrophic alpha-mediated hypertension because circulating catecholamines lose their beta-vasodilatory counter. Phentolamine (non-selective alpha-blocker) is first-line for the acute crisis; sodium nitroprusside is an alternative. Beta-blockade is added only after alpha-blockade is established to control reflex tachycardia. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.rationale: Unopposed beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma crisis is contraindicated because removal of beta-mediated vasodilation unmasks unopposed alpha-vasoconstriction, causing severe hypertensive crisis and possible cardiogenic shock. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.rationale: Labetalol has a 7:1 beta-to-alpha ratio when given intravenously and is functionally a beta-predominant agent in phaeochromocytoma, risking the same paradoxical hypertension as pure beta-blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.rationale: The tachycardia is catecholamine-driven and amiodarone is not the appropriate agent. Treatment must address the catecholamine excess via alpha-blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.rationale: Magnesium is an adjunct but not a primary agent for phaeochromocytoma crisis. Phentolamine or nitroprusside provides specific alpha-mediated vasodilation matched to the pathophysiology. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

explanation.summary: DVT workup uses the Wells score to stratify pretest probability. Low probability (under 2) allows D-dimer rule-out. Likely DVT (2 or more) directs straight to compression ultrasound. Therapeutic guidance favours apixaban or rivaroxaban for proximal DVT without cancer or severe renal impairment. Provoked DVT (long-haul flight, surgery, immobilisation) is treated for 3 months; unprovoked DVT requires extended duration consideration.
key_points: Wells score guides whether to use D-dimer or imaging first
Compression duplex ultrasound is first-line imaging
Apixaban or rivaroxaban first-line for non-cancer DVT; 3 months for provoked
explanation.pearls: Cancer-associated thrombosis: LMWH or DOAC (apixaban, edoxaban) both acceptable per ASH 2021; rivaroxaban has higher bleeding risk in GI cancers.

options.rationale: MR venography is reserved for specific cases (pelvic veins, IVC); not first-line for typical leg DVT. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)
D-dimer rules out only with low pretest probability; with Wells 3 or more, proceed to imaging directly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)
Compression ultrasound is first-line; CT venography is not standard initial imaging for DVT. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)

Anticoagulation may be commenced empirically if imaging is delayed but diagnosis must still be confirmed promptly; deferring confirmation 7 to 10 days is inappropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)

Wells score 3 or more (likely DVT) directs straight to compression ultrasound rather than D-dimer; her score totals 3 (calf swelling, pitting oedema unilateral, recent immobilisation). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is defined by acute onset (minutes to hours) with respiratory or cardiovascular compromise plus skin or mucosal involvement, or hypotension after known allergen exposure. IM adrenaline (1:1000) 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg in adults into anterolateral thigh is first-line. Repeat every 5 minutes as needed. Lay patient flat (head up if breathing difficulty), IV fluids for hypotension, salbutamol for persistent wheeze, corticosteroids as adjunct. Observe at least 4 hours.
key_points: IM adrenaline first-line; do not delay for IV access
Lay patient flat; sitting up increases mortality risk in hypotension
Observe 4 hours minimum; biphasic reaction in up to 20%
explanation.pearls: ASCIA action plan emphasises supine positioning; sitting up or standing during anaphylaxis is associated with empty ventricle syndrome and sudden death.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids have slow onset and are adjunctive; they do not replace adrenaline as the time-critical intervention. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg into anterolateral thigh is first-line for anaphylaxis; delay increases biphasic and fatal reaction risk. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Antihistamines treat urticaria but not airway or cardiovascular compromise; adrenaline must come first. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
Salbutamol may help bronchospasm but does not address upper airway swelling or hypotension; adrenaline IM is first. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)
IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after multiple IM doses; IM is first-line due to safer pharmacokinetics. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute intracerebral haemorrhage with systolic BP over 180 mmHg is managed by smooth controlled BP lowering targeting systolic 140 within 1 hour per INTERACT2. Labetalol is first-line in Australia; alternatives include glyceryl trinitrate or hydralazine. Avoid sublingual nifedipine and nitroprusside. Reverse anticoagulation, neurosurgical consult, and care in stroke unit improve outcomes. Ischaemic stroke uses different targets (permissive unless thrombolysis or over 220/120).
key_points: ICH systolic target 140 within 1 hour per INTERACT2
Ischaemic stroke: permissive hypertension unless over 220/120 or pre-thrombolysis (under 185/110)
Avoid sublingual nifedipine and nitroprusside in acute stroke
explanation.pearls: INTERACT2 showed intensive BP lowering (target 140 systolic) in ICH did not reduce mortality but improved functional outcomes; ATACH-II did not replicate this benefit, but Australian Living Guidelines retain the 140 target.

options.rationale: Nitroprusside risks cyanide accumulation and can raise ICP; aggressive lowering to 100 risks hypoperfusion. Target is 140 systolic. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)
Sublingual or oral immediate-release nifedipine causes unpredictable rapid BP drop and is contraindicated in acute stroke. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)
Oral perindopril has slow onset and cannot control hypertensive emergency; IV agents are needed. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)

Intracerebral haemorrhage with systolic over 180 is treated with IV labetalol targeting systolic 140 within 1 hour per INTERACT2 and AHA guidance; smooth controlled lowering reduces haematoma growth. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)
Permissive hypertension applies to ischaemic stroke (not for thrombolysis) and not to ICH; ICH benefits from intensive BP lowering. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion (Fiebig stages I to V) presents with mononucleosis-like illness 2 to 4 weeks after exposure: fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, sore throat, myalgia. Fourth-generation antigen/antibody combination tests detect from around 2 weeks; HIV RNA detects from around 10 days. In symptomatic patients with prior negative serology, HIV RNA is the test of choice. Early diagnosis allows ART initiation, reduces transmission risk, and supports partner notification.
key_points: Fourth-generation HIV test window 2 to 4 weeks; HIV RNA from 10 days
Acute seroconversion presents as mononucleosis-like illness 2 to 4 weeks post-exposure
Early ART initiation reduces transmission and preserves CD4
explanation.pearls: Australian U=U (undetectable equals untransmittable) messaging changed HIV care; early ART and treatment-as-prevention are central to ASHM guidance. Discuss PrEP for partners at notification.

options.rationale: Window period for fourth-generation tests is up to 4 weeks; in symptomatic likely acute HIV, HIV RNA detects earlier and confirms diagnosis with repeat serology. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)
Three-month delay misses time-sensitive acute HIV diagnosis and partner notification opportunities; HIV RNA is indicated now. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)
Although HSV is possible, the rash distribution and unprotected sex history with mononucleosis-like illness mandates HIV RNA testing first. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)
Rapid Strep was negative and the pattern fits acute HIV; antibiotics will not address the diagnosis. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)
EBV is in the differential but should not be tested in isolation given the high-risk exposure and need to exclude acute HIV. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Latent TB infection screening with QFT-Plus is offered to people from high-incidence countries, healthcare workers, immunocompromised, and contacts of active TB. Treatment is recommended in those with reactivation risk factors and reasonable expected adherence. First-line regimens are 3HR (3 months rifampicin + isoniazid), 3HP (3 months weekly rifapentine + isoniazid), or 4R (4 months rifampicin); 6H or 9H remain acceptable alternatives. Active TB must be excluded before LTBI therapy.
key_points: Exclude active TB with symptom screen and CXR before treating LTBI
Short rifamycin-containing regimens have better completion than 9H
5 to 10% lifetime reactivation risk in immunocompetent LTBI
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin interacts with combined oral contraceptive pills (reduces efficacy); counsel about alternative contraception during and for 28 days after rifamycin course.

options.rationale: QFT-Plus is reliable; repeat testing is not standard. Treatment should follow a single confirmed positive in appropriate clinical context. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)
9H is acceptable but no longer first-line; shorter rifamycin-containing regimens have better completion and similar efficacy. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)
Untreated LTBI has 5 to 10% lifetime risk of reactivation; deferral is not justified in a young healthy person planning healthcare work. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)

Short-course regimens (3HR daily or 3HP weekly) are equivalent to 6 to 9 months isoniazid with fewer hepatotoxicity events and better completion; first-line in current TB guidance. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)
Asymptomatic with normal chest X-ray in non-immunocompromised does not require CT; this delays treatment. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Atypical parkinsonian syndromes include progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and corticobasal syndrome. Red flags suggesting atypical disease include early postural instability and falls (PSP), vertical gaze palsy (PSP), prominent autonomic failure (MSA), cerebellar signs (MSA-C), pyramidal signs, apraxia and alien limb (CBS), and poor levodopa response. MRI features (hummingbird sign in PSP, hot cross bun in MSA-C) support diagnosis. Survival is shorter than idiopathic PD.
key_points: Early falls + vertical gaze palsy + axial rigidity + poor levodopa = PSP
Autonomic failure + cerebellar signs + parkinsonism = MSA
Asymmetric apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss = CBS
explanation.pearls: Hummingbird sign on midsagittal MRI (midbrain atrophy with preserved pons) is highly specific for PSP; MRI parkinsonism index combines midbrain and pons measurements for improved diagnostic accuracy.

options.rationale: Gradual onset shuffling gait without other red flags is typical of idiopathic PD. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)
These features support idiopathic Parkinson disease rather than an atypical syndrome. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)

Progressive supranuclear palsy is identified by vertical (especially downward) supranuclear gaze palsy, early postural instability with backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity, and poor levodopa response. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)
Late dyskinesias and bilateral involvement are typical PD progression rather than atypical features. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)
Hyposmia and RBD are pre-motor features of idiopathic PD, not red flags for atypical syndromes. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)

explanation.summary: GBS is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy classically post-Campylobacter or post-viral. CSF shows cytoalbuminologic dissociation (raised protein with normal cell count). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg total (usually 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) or plasma exchange; both equivalent and steroids do not help. Respiratory monitoring with serial FVC and NIF is critical; FVC under 20 mL/kg or rapidly falling triggers ICU and intubation consideration.
key_points: CSF cytoalbuminologic dissociation: high protein with normal cells
IVIG or plasma exchange equivalent; steroids ineffective
FVC under 20 mL/kg, NIF less negative than minus 30, rapid decline trigger ICU
explanation.pearls: Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS) predicts ventilation risk by combining days since onset, facial or bulbar weakness, and MRC sum score; useful for triage decisions.

options.rationale: Steroids are not effective in GBS (multiple trials) and are not recommended; IVIG or plasma exchange are first-line. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)

Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with cytoalbuminologic dissociation needs IVIG or plasma exchange and respiratory monitoring; FVC under 20 mL/kg or under 60% predicted is an intubation trigger. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)
GBS progresses rapidly and respiratory failure can develop within hours; admission is mandatory not optional. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)
Post-Campylobacter or Zika GBS does not need antibiotics; the immune-mediated neuropathy is treated by IVIG or PLEX. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)
Rapid progression and FVC 78% predicted with ascending weakness requires admission and immunomodulation. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma crisis requires alpha-blockade before beta-blockade. Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated up over 10 to 14 days is the standard preoperative agent (alternatives doxazosin or prazosin). After alpha-blockade is established, beta-blockade can be added if tachycardia persists (atenolol or metoprolol). Volume expansion with liberal salt intake is essential. Acute crisis management uses phentolamine boluses or infusion. Adrenalectomy follows 10 to 14 days of full blockade.
key_points: Alpha-blockade strictly precedes beta-blockade (10 to 14 days)
Phenoxybenzamine is the standard alpha-blocker; doxazosin or prazosin alternatives
Volume expansion is essential before surgery to prevent post-resection hypotension
explanation.pearls: Genetic counselling and testing for hereditary syndromes (SDHx, VHL, RET, NF1) is recommended in all phaeochromocytoma patients regardless of age; 30 to 40% have an identifiable germline mutation.

options.rationale: Amiodarone does not address catecholamine excess; alpha-blockade is the foundational treatment. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

Beta-blockade without prior alpha-blockade causes unopposed alpha stimulation and fatal hypertensive crisis; this is a classic catastrophic error. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)
Surgery without alpha-blockade has very high mortality; 10 to 14 days of alpha-blockade with volume repletion is mandatory before resection. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

Nitroprusside controls BP acutely but does not block the underlying catecholamine receptor activation, leaving arrhythmia risk; structured alpha then beta-blockade is standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

Alpha-blockade must precede beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma to avoid unopposed alpha stimulation and fatal hypertensive crisis; phenoxybenzamine is the standard agent for 10 to 14 days preoperatively. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian sepsis pathway (ANZICS, Sepsis Australia) and Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >=4, and start vasopressors if hypotension persists during or after resuscitation to maintain MAP >=65. Source control should be pursued within 6 to 12 hours when feasible. For suspected urosepsis with septic shock, empirical antibiotic typically piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin per local antibiogram. Reassessment at 3 to 6 hours guides further fluid or vasopressor titration. Lactate clearance is a useful marker of response.
key_points: Hour-1: lactate, cultures, broad-spectrum abx, 30 mL/kg crystalloid
Vasopressors if MAP <65 after fluid (target MAP >=65)
Source control within 6-12 hours when feasible
Hydrocortisone for vasopressor-refractory shock only
Lactate clearance is a marker of response
explanation.pearls: Each hour delay in appropriate antibiotic for septic shock increases in-hospital mortality by approximately 7%, which is the basis for the hour-1 bundle.

options.rationale: Central access and CVP monitoring should not delay initial fluid bolus and antibiotic; goal-directed CVP targets are no longer mandated by Surviving Sepsis. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Antibiotics should not be delayed for imaging; broad-spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour for septic shock is the priority. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)
Noradrenaline is added after initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid if MAP <65 persists; starting vasopressor without fluid is not the first step. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)

Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle and ANZICS recommend lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >=4 within the first hour. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Hydrocortisone is considered if vasopressor-refractory shock after adequate fluid; it is not the first step in the hour-1 bundle. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)

explanation.summary: Australian empirical therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults is IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly, with dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly given before or with the first antibiotic dose to reduce neurological sequelae from pneumococcal meningitis. For patients >=50, immunosuppressed, alcohol misuse, or pregnant, add benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly or amoxicillin 2 g 4-hourly for Listeria cover. Vancomycin is added when highly resistant pneumococcus is suspected (e.g. travel to high-resistance regions). Lumbar puncture should follow empirical antibiotic if delay is anticipated >30 minutes or if there are red flags for CT first (GCS <11, new focal neurology, seizures, papilloedema, immunocompromised). Public health notification and contact prophylaxis as required.
key_points: Empirical: ceftriaxone 2 g 12h + dexamethasone 10 mg 6h
Add Listeria cover if age >=50, immunosuppression, alcohol misuse, pregnant
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic dose - mortality and sequelae benefit
CT before LP if GCS <11, focal signs, seizures, papilloedema, immunocompromised
Public health notification + contact prophylaxis for meningococcal disease
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly for 4 days reduces severe hearing loss by about 50% in pneumococcal meningitis if given with or before the first antibiotic dose; the benefit is lost if delayed.

options.rationale: Listeria cover (benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin) is added for age >=50 OR immunosuppression OR pregnancy; at 56 with no risk factors this is borderline but the dexamethasone is the critical first dose addition. The cleanest answer per eTG covers pneumococcus + meningococcus, with the Listeria addition for age >=50 specifically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Benzylpenicillin alone does not cover ceftriaxone-sensitive but penicillin-resistant pneumococcus; ceftriaxone is the empirical choice in Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin is added if highly penicillin-resistant pneumococcus is suspected (overseas exposure) but is not standard empirical in Australia where resistance rates are low. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Meropenem is reserved for ceftriaxone allergy or specific resistance patterns; ceftriaxone is first-line empirical in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

eTG and ANZICS recommend IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12 hourly for empirical bacterial meningitis in adults, with dexamethasone 10 mg 6 hourly before or with first dose to reduce neurological sequelae from pneumococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Australian eTG recommends oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 BD for 14 days for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in haemodynamically stable patients tolerating oral intake. Admission is indicated for sepsis, persistent vomiting, pregnancy, urological abnormality, immunocompromise, age >65 with comorbidities, or social factors limiting safe discharge. Inpatient empirical therapy is gentamicin 4-5 mg/kg IV plus ampicillin or amoxicillin, or alternatively ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, with oral switch when stable. Imaging (CT KUB or renal tract ultrasound) is indicated for recurrence, persistent fever after 48 hours, suspected obstruction or abscess. Recurrent pyelonephritis warrants urology referral.
key_points: eTG outpatient: ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD x 7d OR trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole x 14d
Admit for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, urological abnormality, immunocompromise
Inpatient empirical: gentamicin + amoxicillin, or ceftriaxone
Image if persistent fever >48 hours, recurrence, or suspected obstruction
Avoid cefalexin and nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis
explanation.pearls: Fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli rates have risen to about 15% in Australian community urine isolates, so clinical review at 48 to 72 hours to confirm response is essential.

options.rationale: eTG recommends oral ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in haemodynamically stable patients who can tolerate oral fluids; admission is not mandatory when there is no sepsis or complicating feature. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Cefalexin is not recommended first-line for pyelonephritis in Australian eTG because of high E. coli resistance and poor renal tissue concentrations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

She does not meet admission criteria (no sepsis, no vomiting, tolerating oral, no complicating factors); admission is unnecessary and IV monotherapy gentamicin then oral switch is not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Pip-tazo is unnecessarily broad for community-acquired uncomplicated pyelonephritis without urological history, instrumentation, or sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Nitrofurantoin achieves urinary but not renal tissue concentrations and is unsuitable for pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency where mortality is determined more by time to debridement than by antibiotic choice. Classic features are pain out of proportion to visible inflammation, rapidly advancing erythema, tense induration, dusky or blistered skin, crepitus (late), and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, Cr, glucose) supports diagnosis but does not exclude it; clinical features take precedence. Empirical antibiotics combine broad-spectrum (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) plus MRSA cover (vancomycin) plus toxin suppression (clindamycin or linezolid). Surgical exploration with debridement of all necrotic tissue is mandatory and may be repeated daily. Mortality is approximately 25% even with prompt treatment, rising to >50% if delayed beyond 24 hours.
key_points: Pain out of proportion is the key clinical sign
LRINEC score supports but does NOT exclude diagnosis
Triple antibiotic: pip-tazo + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
Surgical debridement is the definitive treatment; do not delay for imaging
Mortality ~25%; rises >50% if delayed >24 hours
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin in necrotising fasciitis suppresses streptococcal exotoxin synthesis, providing mortality benefit independent of bactericidal activity; it is added even when penicillin is in the regimen.

options.rationale: Flucloxacillin alone treats simple cellulitis but is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis where polymicrobial cover and surgical debridement are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Pain out of proportion, tense induration with dusky discolouration, sepsis physiology and high LRINEC components (CRP 320, WCC 22, Cr 142, Na 132, glucose 14) point to necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical debridement plus piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin + clindamycin (for toxin suppression) is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZICS Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)
Imaging should not delay surgical exploration when clinical suspicion is high; MRI may help in uncertain cases but is not required before debridement here. (Source: ANZICS NSTI)

LRINEC is supportive but not sufficient to drive management; clinical features (pain out of proportion, dusky skin, sepsis) trump LRINEC and indicate immediate surgical referral. (Source: ANZICS NSTI)
Medical admission without surgical involvement is inappropriate; necrotising fasciitis mortality rises sharply with each hour delay to debridement. (Source: ANZICS NSTI)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative preparation requires alpha-adrenergic blockade for 7 to 14 days to control hypertension and restore intravascular volume. Phenoxybenzamine (non-selective irreversible) or doxazosin (selective alpha-1) are first-line. Beta blockers are added only after alpha blockade is established, to control reflex tachycardia and tachyarrhythmias; starting beta blocker first causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction with risk of fatal hypertensive crisis. High-sodium diet (5 g/day) and oral fluids are recommended to restore volume depleted by catecholamine excess. BP target preoperatively is 130/80 mmHg seated and >90 mmHg systolic standing. Genetic testing (RET, VHL, SDH, NF1, MAX) is indicated for all phaeochromocytomas as 40% are hereditary. Surgical resection is curative in non-metastatic disease.
key_points: Alpha blockade FIRST (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 7-14 days
Beta blocker only AFTER alpha blockade established
High-sodium diet + fluid for volume expansion preoperatively
BP target 130/80 seated, >90 systolic standing
Genetic testing in all phaeochromocytomas (40% hereditary)
explanation.pearls: Phenoxybenzamine is started at 10 mg twice daily and titrated up by 10 to 20 mg every 2 to 3 days until target BP and mild orthostatic symptoms are achieved, indicating adequate blockade.

options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are adjunctive in phaeochromocytoma but do not replace alpha blockade; salt restriction is contraindicated as volume expansion is needed pre-surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

Starting beta blocker before alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and can precipitate severe hypertensive crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

Australian endocrinology practice and international guidelines: alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine for 7 to 14 days preoperatively to control hypertension and prevent intraoperative crisis; beta blocker is added ONLY after alpha blockade is established, to prevent unopposed alpha vasoconstriction. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline; eTG Endocrinology)

Labetalol has predominantly beta over alpha blockade (ratio 7:1 oral) and is not adequate alpha blockade for phaeochromocytoma; phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin is preferred. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

Diagnosis is confirmed phaeochromocytoma by elevated metanephrines; spironolactone is for primary aldosteronism and does not address catecholamine excess. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

explanation.summary: The McDonald 2024 criteria diagnose MS based on dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT). DIS requires >=1 T2 lesion in >=2 of 4 typical CNS regions (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord). DIT can be met by a second clinical attack OR new T2 or enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI OR simultaneous presence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same scan OR CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (which substitute for DIT). Following confirmation, early initiation of disease-modifying therapy (DMT) is recommended. Australian MBS-funded options include glatiramer acetate, interferon beta, fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide for moderate activity, and natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine for high activity. JC virus serology should be checked before natalizumab.
key_points: McDonald 2024: DIS = T2 lesion in >=2 of 4 CNS regions
DIT = second attack, new MRI lesion, OR simultaneous Gd-enhancing + non-enhancing, OR CSF OCBs
CSF-specific OCBs substitute for DIT after single attack with DIS
Early DMT initiation reduces relapse rate and disability accumulation
JCV serology required before starting natalizumab
explanation.pearls: Ocrelizumab (anti-CD20) is the first DMT approved by TGA for primary progressive MS and is given as IV infusion every 6 months following an initial divided loading dose.

options.rationale: McDonald 2024 allows diagnosis after a single clinical attack with appropriate paraclinical evidence (DIS on MRI + CSF OCB or simultaneous enhancing/non-enhancing lesions). (Source: McDonald 2024)
She has only one clinical attack (optic neuritis); dissemination in time requires either a second clinical attack or paraclinical evidence. (Source: McDonald 2024)

While the simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing pattern does meet DIT, the more direct criterion fulfilled here under McDonald 2024 is the CSF-specific oligoclonal bands acting as DIT substitute alongside DIS. Both are acceptable but the OCB pathway is the cleanest for clinical decision-making. (Source: McDonald 2024)

McDonald 2024 criteria allow a single attack (here optic neuritis) plus DIS demonstrated on MRI plus CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time, confirming MS. (Source: McDonald 2024)
Evoked potentials are no longer required under McDonald 2024 if MRI and CSF criteria are met. (Source: McDonald 2024)

explanation.summary: Distinguishing shock subtypes at the bedside requires integration of clinical signs, haemodynamic profile and bedside imaging. Cardiogenic shock typically has cold peripheries, low cardiac index, raised PCWP and low mixed venous saturation. Septic shock typically has warm peripheries, normal or high cardiac index after initial fluid, low SVR, and normal or elevated mixed venous saturation. Hypovolaemic shock has cold peripheries, low cardiac index, low PCWP, low ScvO2. Mixed shock is increasingly recognised in critically ill patients with multiple insults. Empirical hospital-acquired pneumonia therapy in Australia is typically piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin if MRSA risk, with anti-pseudomonal cover for HAP onset >=5 days. Reassessment of shock subtype after initial intervention with serial echo, lactate, and central venous oximetry is essential.
key_points: Septic shock: warm, high CI after fluid, low SVR, normal/high ScvO2
Cardiogenic: cold, low CI, raised PCWP, low ScvO2
Hypovolaemic: cold, low CI, low PCWP, low ScvO2
HAP empirical (Australian): pip-tazo +/- vancomycin if MRSA risk
Reassess shock subtype after initial intervention
explanation.pearls: Mixed venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) >70% with hypotension and lactate elevation is classic for distributive shock; ScvO2 <60% favours cardiogenic or hypovolaemic patterns.

options.rationale: Stable troponin and stable echo make reinfarction unlikely; fever and infiltrates point to sepsis. (Source: NHFA STEMI Guideline)
Echo shows stable LV function and no mechanical complication; warm peripheries with elevated ScvO2 are not typical of cardiogenic shock. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)
No evidence of bleeding; fever, purulent sputum and infiltrates point to infective rather than hypovolaemic cause. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)
Bilateral consolidation with purulent sputum and fever fit infective rather than embolic pattern; PE typically shows oligaemic lung fields. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Warm peripheries despite hypotension, fever, new infiltrates, purulent sputum, raised lactate and elevated mixed venous saturation (76% suggests distributive component) point to septic shock from HAP rather than cardiogenic deterioration; treat as septic shock with IV crystalloid and empirical antipseudomonal cover. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: NHFA/CSANZ AF guideline: CHA2DS2-VA (Victorian replacement of CHA2DS2-VASc, no sex category) >=2 in men or women is an indication for oral anticoagulation. DOACs are first-line over warfarin for non-valvular AF. Apixaban 5 mg BD (or 2.5 mg BD if 2 of: age >=80, weight <=60 kg, Cr >=133 micromol/L), rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (15 mg if CrCl 15 to 50), dabigatran 150 mg BD (110 mg BD if age >=75 or bleeding risk; contraindicated CrCl <30), edoxaban 60 mg daily (30 mg if CrCl 15 to 50). Warfarin remains preferred for mechanical valves, moderate to severe mitral stenosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, end-stage renal disease. Aspirin should be ceased on starting DOAC unless concurrent recent ACS within 12 months. HAS-BLED guides bleeding risk discussion but is rarely a reason to withhold anticoagulation when stroke risk is high. Annual review of renal function (more often if CKD), weight, age, and bleeding events.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA >=2: anticoagulate (DOAC first-line)
Apixaban dose reduction needs 2 of 3: age >=80, weight <=60, Cr >=133
Dabigatran contraindicated CrCl <30; rivaroxaban/edoxaban reduce at CrCl 15-50
Aspirin offers no stroke benefit in AF and should be ceased on DOAC
Warfarin reserved for mechanical valves, moderate-severe MS, APS
explanation.pearls: Apixaban demonstrated lower major bleeding (especially intracranial haemorrhage) than warfarin in ARISTOTLE, including in patients with CKD and the elderly, making it the preferred DOAC in renal impairment down to CrCl 25 mL/min.

options.rationale: Aspirin is not effective stroke prevention in AF and is no longer recommended; CHA2DS2-VA 5 with high stroke risk mandates anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

DOACs are NOT contraindicated at CrCl 38; apixaban and rivaroxaban have approved dosing down to CrCl 15 to 30 with dose reduction; warfarin is acceptable but not preferred. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)
Adding aspirin to oral anticoagulation in AF (without recent ACS or PCI) increases major bleeding without reducing stroke; aspirin should be ceased on starting DOAC. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

Apixaban 5 mg BD is correct here: dose reduction requires 2 of 3 criteria (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, Cr >=133); she meets 0 to 1 (Cr 132 borderline; age 78 <80; weight 62 >60). Aspirin must be ceased to avoid net bleeding harm; apixaban has best bleeding profile among DOACs especially in CKD and elderly. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline; AMH)

Dabigatran requires dose reduction (110 mg BD) for age >=75 and is renally cleared (80%); contraindicated below CrCl 30 and risky between 30 and 50; apixaban is safer in CKD. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP stratifies CAP severity in Australia: Systolic BP <90 (2), Multilobar infiltrate (1), Albumin <35 (1), Respiratory rate >=25 (under 50 = 1, over 50 = 2), Tachycardia >=125 (1), Confusion new (1), Oxygen low (under 50 yo SpO2 <94 or PaO2 <70 = 2; over 50 yo SpO2 <90 or PaO2 <60 = 2), pH <7.35 (2). Score 0 to 2 mild (community oral); 3 to 4 moderate (admit, IV antibiotic); >=5 severe (ICU consideration). Mild CAP empirical: amoxicillin 1 g TDS oral for 5 days. Moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly + oral doxycycline 100 mg BD (or oral azithromycin); switch to oral when stable. Severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily + IV azithromycin 500 mg daily +/- oseltamivir in influenza season; ICU consultation. Mycoplasma and Chlamydia coverage with doxycycline or macrolide when atypical features (younger patient, dry cough, extrapulmonary manifestations). Follow-up CXR at 6 weeks to confirm resolution and exclude underlying malignancy especially in smokers over 50.
key_points: SMART-COP: severity stratification (0-2 mild, 3-4 mod, >=5 severe)
Mild oral: amoxicillin 1 g TDS x 5 days
Moderate: IV benzylpenicillin + oral doxycycline
Severe: IV ceftriaxone + IV azithromycin + ICU consult
Repeat CXR at 6 weeks especially in smokers >50
explanation.pearls: Australian eTG shortened first-line amoxicillin duration from 7 to 5 days for mild CAP based on the OAR (Outpatient Antibiotic Reduction) and ANTIC pneumonia trials showing non-inferior outcomes and reduced selection pressure.

options.rationale: Mild CAP (SMART-COP 0 to 2) managed in community: amoxicillin 1 g TDS for 5 days is Australian first-line per eTG; reserve doxycycline for atypical concern or amoxicillin allergy; combination therapy is for moderate to severe CAP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; eTG)
Augmentin + doxycycline is moderate-severity CAP regimen; SMART-COP 0 mild CAP does not need this; broader spectrum is unnecessary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
IV admission is reserved for moderate to severe CAP (SMART-COP >=3) or social/medical factors preventing oral therapy; not indicated here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Macrolide monotherapy is not Australian first-line for CAP due to increasing pneumococcal resistance; reserved for atypical-only presentations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Respiratory fluoroquinolone is reserved for severe penicillin allergy or specific atypical or resistant infections; routine first-line is amoxicillin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Australian osteoporosis treatment indications: T-score <=-2.5 at any site, or prior minimal trauma vertebral or hip fracture (regardless of T-score), or T-score -1.5 to -2.5 with FRAX 10-year hip fracture risk >=3% or major osteoporotic risk >=20%. First-line oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly) - 50% reduction in vertebral fractures and 40% reduction in hip fractures. Pre-treatment: dental check (BRONJ prevention), correct vitamin D and calcium, exclude secondary causes (multiple myeloma, hyperthyroidism, coeliac, hyperparathyroidism, Cushing). Contraindications: eGFR <35, oesophageal disease (oral), recent or planned invasive dental work (relative). Alternatives: IV zoledronic acid annually (oral intolerance), denosumab 60 mg SC 6-monthly (CKD-compatible but rebound vertebral fracture risk on cessation), teriparatide (severe), romosozumab (very severe), raloxifene (third-line). DXA review at 2 to 3 years. Drug holiday after 5 years oral or 3 years IV in low-risk patients; continue indefinitely if high risk.
key_points: Treat: T <=-2.5, OR prior fragility fracture, OR T -1.5 to -2.5 + high FRAX
First-line: oral alendronate or risedronate (50% vertebral, 40% hip fracture reduction)
Pre-treat: dental check, vitamin D, exclude secondary causes
Contraindications oral: eGFR <35, oesophageal disease
Drug holiday consideration at 5 years oral or 3 years IV
explanation.pearls: Denosumab cessation carries a 10-fold rebound vertebral fracture risk within 12 months if not transitioned to a bisphosphonate, making it a less reversible choice than oral alendronate for patients who may discontinue therapy.

options.rationale: IV zoledronic acid is reserved for oral bisphosphonate intolerance, upper GI contraindication, or adherence concerns; oral alendronate is first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

Denosumab is an acceptable alternative but is reserved as second-line for intolerance or contraindication to bisphosphonates per PBS criteria; oral alendronate is preferred first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)
Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis (T-score <-3.0 with multiple vertebral fractures) under specialist supervision; not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)
Raloxifene is third-line, reduces vertebral but not hip fractures, and carries VTE risk; not first-line in 68-year-old with hip T-score -2.5. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) is Australian first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with prior fragility fracture or T-score <=-2.5; PBS criteria met; no contraindications; eGFR 64 (>35 required for bisphosphonates). (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline; AMH)

explanation.summary: Australian acute asthma severity: mild-moderate (PEF >50%, full sentences, normal mental state, RR <25, HR <110); severe (PEF 33 to 50%, phrases not sentences, RR >=25, HR >=110); life-threatening (silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis, hypotension, altered consciousness, PEF <33%, normal or raised PaCO2). Treatment: oxygen titrated to SpO2 93-95%; salbutamol nebulised 5 mg (or via spacer if mild-moderate); ipratropium 500 mcg nebulised added for severe; systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 50 mg or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if vomiting); reassess at 15 to 30 minutes. Step up to IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes if poor response. ICU consult for life-threatening features, rising PaCO2, or fatigue. Avoid sedatives. Salbutamol can cause lactic acidosis and hypokalaemia; check VBG and K. Discharge criteria: PEF >70%, sustained off bronchodilator for 4 hours; 5-day oral prednisolone 50 mg daily; written asthma action plan; ICS commencement or step-up if not already; GP/respiratory follow-up.
key_points: Severe: PEF 33-50%, phrases, RR>=25, HR>=110
First-line severe: nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium + steroid + targeted O2
Target SpO2 93-95% (avoid hyperoxia worsening V/Q)
IV magnesium 2 g if poor response at 30-60 minutes
Discharge: 5d prednisolone, written action plan, ICS step-up
explanation.pearls: Salbutamol-induced lactic acidosis and hypokalaemia are dose-dependent and common after continuous nebulisation; check VBG and replace potassium when K <3.5 to avoid arrhythmia, while continuing therapy.

options.rationale: Severe asthma (PEF 33 to 50%, RR >=25, HR >=110, unable to speak in full sentences) requires combined nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, targeted oxygen (SpO2 93-95 to avoid hyperoxia worsening V/Q), and early systemic steroid (oral prednisolone equivalent to IV); reassess at 15 to 30 minutes. (Source: Asthma Australia; National Asthma Council)

FiO2 1.0 risks hypercapnic worsening in severe asthma; target SpO2 is 93 to 95%; spacer salbutamol alone undertreats severe exacerbation without ipratropium or systemic steroid. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)
IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, not asthma exacerbation; reserved for asthma with anaphylactic features or impending arrest. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)
She is severe but not life-threatening (no silent chest, no exhaustion, normal CO2); medical therapy trial is appropriate before intubation. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)
IV magnesium is added if no response to first-line nebulised therapy + steroid at 30 to 60 minutes; not initial treatment. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is classified by Stanford: type A (involves ascending aorta) - surgical emergency; type B (descending only, distal to left subclavian) - medical management unless complicated. DeBakey I (asc + arch + desc), II (asc only), III (desc only). Medical therapy targets reduction of dP/dt (rate of pressure change) by lowering BP AND heart rate simultaneously - shear stress propagates dissection. Australian first-line: IV labetalol (combined alpha-beta) infusion titrated to HR <60 and SBP 100 to 120; alternatives are IV esmolol (very short half-life) plus IV nitroprusside or GTN. Rate control MUST precede vasodilator (pure vasodilator alone increases dP/dt via reflex tachycardia). Type A: emergency cardiothoracic surgery (mortality 1 to 2% per hour untreated). Complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or BP, rapid expansion): TEVAR (thoracic endovascular aortic repair) at vascular surgery centre. Uncomplicated type B: ICU/HDU medical therapy with serial imaging; lifelong intensive BP control after discharge.
key_points: Stanford A (asc): surgery emergency; B (desc): medical if uncomplicated
Reduce dP/dt: target HR <60 + SBP 100-120
IV labetalol first-line (combined alpha-beta)
Rate control MUST precede vasodilator
TEVAR for complicated B: malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain
explanation.pearls: Untreated type A aortic dissection has a mortality of approximately 1 to 2% per hour in the first 24 to 48 hours, which is why CT aortogram must be expedited and cardiothoracic surgery contacted before transfer rather than after.

options.rationale: Acute aortic dissection requires rapid BP control AND heart rate control (rate-pressure product reduction); IV labetalol (combined alpha and beta blockade) is Australian first-line, targeting HR <60 and SBP 100 to 120 (lowest tolerating end-organ perfusion); arterial line for continuous monitoring; rate control must precede vasodilator therapy. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection; ESC Aortic)
Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia which increases dP/dt and propagates dissection; pure vasodilator without rate control is contraindicated as initial therapy. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)
Nitroprusside is potent vasodilator but causes reflex tachycardia; if used, must be combined with beta blocker first; not standalone first-line. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

Type B dissection without malperfusion or rupture is managed medically initially (Best Medical Therapy); endovascular repair reserved for complications; medical BP control still first priority. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)
Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled hypotension and reflex tachycardia and is contraindicated; smooth controlled IV titration is required. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency = severe BP elevation (typically SBP >180 or DBP >120) with acute target organ damage: hypertensive encephalopathy, acute stroke (ischaemic or haemorrhagic), pulmonary oedema, acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, AKI, eclampsia, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (malignant hypertension). Hypertensive urgency = same BP without end-organ damage; managed with oral therapy and outpatient review. Emergency target: reduce MAP by no more than 20 to 25% over the first hour, to 160/100 to 110 over next 2 to 6 hours, then to normal over 24 to 48 hours. Exception: aortic dissection requires more aggressive reduction (target SBP 100 to 120 within 20 minutes); ischaemic stroke for thrombolysis target <185/110; haemorrhagic stroke target SBP <140; eclampsia target diastolic 90 to 100. IV agents: labetalol (broadly applicable), nicardipine (dihydropyridine CCB), GTN (LV failure, ACS), nitroprusside (rarely used now, cyanide risk in renal failure), hydralazine (used in eclampsia). Avoid: sublingual nifedipine (no longer recommended), clonidine for rapid lowering. Investigate secondary causes (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism) once stable.
key_points: Emergency: severe BP + target organ damage (CNS, cardiac, renal, MAHA)
First hour: reduce MAP by max 20-25%; over-rapid risks watershed infarction
Then to 160/100-110 over 2-6 hours, normal over 24-48 hours
Aortic dissection exception: SBP 100-120 within 20 min
Sublingual nifedipine contraindicated in modern practice
explanation.pearls: Malignant hypertension is diagnosed by severely elevated BP with papilloedema (grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy) or flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots (grade 3), and untreated 1-year mortality is approximately 80%; aggressive yet controlled BP reduction reduces this to under 10%.

options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled hypotension and reflex tachycardia; contraindicated in hypertensive emergency; IV titration is required. (Source: ESC Hypertension)
Rapid reduction to near-normal risks watershed cerebral infarction in chronically autoregulated patients; 20 to 25% MAP reduction in first hour is the safe target. (Source: ESC Hypertension)
Targeting below 110/70 risks malperfusion of chronically autoregulated brain, kidney, and coronary beds; nitroprusside risks cyanide toxicity in renal impairment. (Source: ESC Hypertension)
Oral therapy is too slow for hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage; IV titrated agent required to gain hour-by-hour control. (Source: ESC Hypertension)

Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage (encephalopathy, malignant hypertension with retinopathy, AKI, MAHA): reduce MAP by 20 to 25% over first hour, then to 160/100 to 110 over next 2 to 6 hours, then to normal over 24 to 48 hours; IV labetalol or nicardipine; faster reduction risks watershed infarction. (Source: ESC Hypertension; AAFP)

explanation.summary: Light criteria define exudative pleural effusion when ANY ONE of: pleural/serum protein ratio >0.5; pleural/serum LDH ratio >0.6; pleural LDH >2/3 upper limit of normal serum LDH. Transudate (failed criteria): heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia. Exudate: malignancy, infection (parapneumonic, empyema, TB), connective tissue disease, pulmonary embolism, chylothorax, pancreatitis. Additional fluid analysis informs cause: pH <7.20 + glucose <2.2 + LDH >1000 = complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage; pH <7.20 alone in malignant effusion suggests entrapment; ADA >40 U/L supports TB; chyle >1.24 mmol/L triglycerides; amylase raised in pancreatitis and oesophageal rupture. For exudate of unclear cause: cytology (3 large samples, sensitivity 40 to 60%), CT chest (assess parenchyma, pleura, mediastinum), then thoracoscopy or image-guided pleural biopsy (sensitivity >90% for mesothelioma and TB). Occupational asbestos exposure mandates mesothelioma workup. Pleurodesis (talc) or indwelling pleural catheter for recurrent malignant effusion. ANSCO guidelines support multidisciplinary referral for confirmed mesothelioma.
key_points: Light criteria: protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, or pleural LDH >2/3 ULN
Transudate: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
Exudate: malignancy, infection, CTD, PE, pancreatitis
Mesothelioma workup: asbestos history + thoracoscopic biopsy
Cytology sensitivity 40-60%; biopsy required for definitive diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Cytology has only 40 to 60% sensitivity for mesothelioma and 60% for adenocarcinoma; thoracoscopic pleural biopsy is the gold standard for both, yielding diagnosis in approximately 95% of cases and allowing simultaneous talc pleurodesis.

options.rationale: Light criteria not met for transudate: pleural/serum protein ratio 0.56 (>0.5) and pleural/serum LDH ratio 1.27 (>0.6); this is exudative. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline)

Pleural/serum protein 0.56 (>0.5) AND LDH ratio 1.27 (>0.6) AND pleural LDH >2/3 ULN serum = exudate (any one criterion is sufficient); shipbuilding occupational asbestos history with pleural thickening and nodularity makes mesothelioma the priority concern; thoracoscopic or image-guided biopsy is the next step (cytology alone misses about 50% of mesothelioma). (Source: BTS Pleural Disease; ATS Mesothelioma)

Pleural pH 7.34 is above the empyema threshold of 7.20; glucose 4.0 also against empyema (typically <2.2); clinical features and CT findings point to malignancy not infection. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline)
No infective history, no fever, normal WCC, glucose and pH within transudate/non-infective range; this is not parapneumonic. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline)
Chylothorax appears milky and triglyceride-rich; straw-coloured fluid excludes this; no history of trauma or thoracic surgery. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women is one of the most common presentations in primary care. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days as first-line empiric therapy. Mid-stream urine should be sent for culture before starting antibiotics but treatment should not be delayed. Complicated UTIs (pregnancy, male sex, structural abnormality, catheter, immunosuppression) require broader empiric cover and longer courses. Fluoroquinolones should be reserved for complicated infections due to antimicrobial stewardship principles.
key_points: Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days is first-line for uncomplicated cystitis in Australia
3-day courses are as effective as longer courses for uncomplicated cystitis in women
Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated UTIs and pyelonephritis
Culture should be sent but empiric treatment should not be delayed in symptomatic cystitis
explanation.pearls: The Australian trimethoprim dose of 300 mg once daily differs from the international standard of 160 mg (as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) or 200 mg twice daily; this higher once-daily dose is specific to Australian guidelines and achieves equivalent urinary concentrations with better adherence.

options.rationale: For uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant woman, trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days is first-line in Australian guidelines. It has excellent urinary concentration, narrow spectrum, and low resistance rates for community E. coli in Australia. Three-day courses are as effective as longer courses for uncomplicated cystitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is broader spectrum than necessary for uncomplicated cystitis and is reserved for complicated UTIs or when first-line agents are contraindicated. Antimicrobial stewardship principles favour the narrowest effective agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fluoroquinolones are not recommended as first-line for uncomplicated cystitis in Australia due to antimicrobial stewardship concerns, broad spectrum, and risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, tendinopathy, and QT prolongation. They are reserved for complicated UTIs or pyelonephritis when oral options are needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Cefalexin is a reasonable alternative if trimethoprim is contraindicated (e.g. in early pregnancy or allergy), but it is second-line for uncomplicated cystitis. It has a broader spectrum and longer course than necessary when trimethoprim is suitable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Nitrofurantoin is an effective alternative for uncomplicated cystitis and is first-line in some international guidelines. In Australian guidelines, trimethoprim remains the preferred first-line agent for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women. Nitrofurantoin is a good second-line choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Osteoporosis is defined by a T-score at or below -2.5 or a fragility fracture regardless of T-score. A low-trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman mandates treatment beyond calcium and vitamin D alone. Alendronate or risedronate are first-line oral bisphosphonates, with proven efficacy in reducing vertebral, non-vertebral, and hip fractures. Secondary causes should be excluded (vitamin D deficiency, thyroid disease, myeloma, coeliac disease). The FRAX tool integrates clinical risk factors to estimate 10-year fracture probability and guides treatment thresholds.
key_points: A fragility fracture with T-score below -2.5 constitutes established osteoporosis requiring pharmacotherapy
Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) are first-line; denosumab is second-line
Bisphosphonates should be taken fasting, upright, with water, and 30 minutes before food
Treatment review is recommended after 5 years of oral bisphosphonate therapy
explanation.pearls: After 5 years of oral bisphosphonate therapy, a drug holiday of 1-2 years may be considered in patients who are no longer high-risk; however, patients with hip T-score below -2.5, previous vertebral fracture, or ongoing corticosteroid use should continue treatment without interruption.

options.rationale: This patient has established osteoporosis (T-score below -2.5 plus fragility fracture) and requires pharmacological treatment beyond supplementation alone.
