Calcium and vitamin D are important adjuncts but are insufficient as sole treatment in established osteoporosis with fracture. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia: Treatment Guidelines)

This patient has established osteoporosis with a fragility fracture, meeting PBS criteria for bisphosphonate therapy. Alendronate is first-line, reducing vertebral fracture risk by 44% and hip fracture risk by 40%. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation ensures adequate substrate for bone formation, and falls prevention addresses the modifiable fracture risk. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia: Treatment Guidelines)

Denosumab is highly effective for osteoporosis but is generally second-line in Australian practice, used when oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated or not tolerated (oesophageal disorders, unable to remain upright). Denosumab requires indefinite treatment as cessation causes rapid bone loss and rebound vertebral fractures. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia: Treatment Guidelines)

Raloxifene reduces vertebral fracture risk but has not demonstrated hip fracture reduction and increases VTE risk. It is not first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a peripheral fracture where bisphosphonates have superior evidence for non-vertebral fracture prevention. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia: Treatment Guidelines)

Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple fractures or very low BMD refractory to bisphosphonates. PBS criteria require two or more fractures with T-score below -3.0 or failure of bisphosphonate therapy. This patient does not meet these criteria. (Source: PBS: Teriparatide Authority Criteria)

explanation.summary: Distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy is the most common pattern of peripheral neuropathy. Diabetes is the leading cause (approximately 30%), followed by alcohol, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, and paraproteinaemia. A borderline macrocytic MCV (98 fL) may indicate early B12 deficiency. The initial workup should be systematic and cost-effective: glucose/HbA1c, B12, folate, TFTs, SPEP, liver function, and renal function identify a cause in approximately 50% of cases. Nerve conduction studies characterise the neuropathy as axonal or demyelinating, guiding further investigation.
key_points: Diabetes and impaired glucose tolerance account for approximately 30% of peripheral neuropathy cases
B12 deficiency can cause neuropathy before overt anaemia develops
Serum protein electrophoresis screens for paraproteinaemic neuropathy which is treatable
Up to 30% of distal sensorimotor neuropathies remain idiopathic after comprehensive workup
explanation.pearls: Impaired glucose tolerance (pre-diabetes) can cause a painful small-fibre neuropathy even before HbA1c reaches the diabetic range; an oral glucose tolerance test should be considered when fasting glucose and HbA1c are normal but clinical suspicion for metabolic neuropathy is high.

options.rationale: NCS/EMG will confirm and characterise the neuropathy but will not identify the underlying cause. An aetiological workup is essential alongside electrophysiology, as most peripheral neuropathies have a treatable or modifiable cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

The symmetrical stocking distribution, absent ankle reflexes, and positive Romberg sign indicate a peripheral neuropathy rather than radiculopathy. Radiculopathy typically causes asymmetric dermatomal symptoms. Lumbar MRI is not the appropriate first investigation for this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

The initial workup for a distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy should screen for the most common treatable causes: diabetes (fasting glucose, HbA1c), B12 deficiency (common with macrocytic MCV), thyroid disease, and paraproteinaemia. These investigations identify the cause in approximately 50% of cases and are cost-effective first-line screening. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Anti-ganglioside antibodies and CSF protein are relevant for inflammatory neuropathies (GBS, CIDP) which present acutely or subacutely with motor-predominant and often proximal weakness. This patient has a chronic sensory-predominant distal neuropathy, making inflammatory causes less likely as a first consideration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Hereditary neuropathies such as CMT typically present in younger patients with pes cavus, hammer toes, and a family history. This patient's late onset at 62 and absence of these features makes hereditary neuropathy unlikely as a first consideration. Common acquired causes should be excluded first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Fibromyalgia is a central sensitisation disorder characterised by widespread pain, fatigue, non-restorative sleep, and cognitive symptoms (fibro fog). Diagnosis is clinical, based on the 2016 revised ACR criteria: widespread pain index and symptom severity scale, with symptoms present for at least 3 months and no better explanation. Normal inflammatory markers and negative autoimmune serology exclude mimicking conditions. Management is multimodal with non-pharmacological strategies as the foundation: patient education, graded aerobic exercise, sleep hygiene, and psychological support. Pharmacological adjuncts include low-dose amitriptyline, duloxetine, or pregabalin.
key_points: Fibromyalgia is a clinical diagnosis made after excluding inflammatory and metabolic mimics
Non-pharmacological management (exercise, education, sleep hygiene) is the foundation of treatment
Opioids are contraindicated in fibromyalgia due to inefficacy and harm
Amitriptyline 10-25 mg nightly, duloxetine, and pregabalin are evidence-based pharmacological adjuncts
explanation.pearls: Graded aerobic exercise at moderate intensity for 30 minutes three times weekly reduces fibromyalgia pain scores by approximately 30% in meta-analyses - an effect size comparable to or exceeding that of any pharmacological intervention.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not effective for fibromyalgia and carry significant side effects. Normal inflammatory markers and negative autoimmune serology argue against an inflammatory condition. A steroid trial may provide transient non-specific improvement but will not address the underlying pain processing disorder. (Source: RACGP: Fibromyalgia Management)

The normal inflammatory markers, negative ANA and RF/anti-CCP, and absence of joint swelling or synovitis make an autoimmune diagnosis very unlikely. Repeating negative serological tests is low-yield and may delay appropriate management of fibromyalgia. (Source: RACGP: Fibromyalgia Management)

Opioids are not recommended for fibromyalgia. They are ineffective for central sensitisation pain and carry risks of dependence, hyperalgesia, and functional decline. All major guidelines strongly recommend against opioid use in fibromyalgia. (Source: RACGP: Fibromyalgia Management)

Fibromyalgia management is multimodal. Non-pharmacological approaches form the foundation: patient education about central sensitisation, graded aerobic exercise (shown to improve pain and function in multiple RCTs), and sleep hygiene. Pharmacotherapy (low-dose amitriptyline, duloxetine, or pregabalin) is adjunctive. This patient meets the 2016 ACR criteria for fibromyalgia with widespread pain, fatigue, and cognitive symptoms. (Source: RACGP: Fibromyalgia Management)

Pregabalin is TGA-approved for fibromyalgia and can be effective for pain, but pharmacotherapy alone without non-pharmacological strategies has limited benefit. Exercise, education, and sleep optimisation should be established first, with pharmacotherapy added if symptoms persist. (Source: RACGP: Fibromyalgia Management)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Bowel Cancer Screening Program invites individuals aged 50-74 to complete an iFOBT every 2 years. A positive result detects haemoglobin in stool above the threshold (usually 20 microg Hb/g faeces). All positive results require colonoscopy regardless of symptoms or haemoglobin level. The diagnostic yield of colonoscopy after positive iFOBT is approximately 4% for cancer and 17% for advanced adenomas. Timely colonoscopy within 30 days maximises the benefit of screening by detecting cancers at earlier, more treatable stages.
key_points: All positive iFOBT results require colonoscopy - do not repeat the iFOBT
Colonoscopy should be performed within 30 days of a positive screening result
Approximately 4% of positive iFOBTs detect colorectal cancer, 17% detect advanced adenomas
The NBCSP targets adults aged 50-74 with biennial iFOBT screening
explanation.pearls: iFOBT detects human haemoglobin specifically (unlike guaiac-based FOBTs) and does not require dietary restriction before testing; however, it may miss proximal right-sided cancers more often than left-sided ones due to haemoglobin degradation during colonic transit.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening

options.rationale: A positive iFOBT should not be repeated as a confirmatory test. The specificity of iFOBT is high, and repeating it may produce a false-negative that inappropriately reassures. All positive iFOBT results require colonoscopy as the next step. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening

options.rationale: CT colonography is an alternative when colonoscopy is contraindicated or technically incomplete, but it cannot take biopsies. A positive screening iFOBT warrants colonoscopy as the gold standard, as any lesion found will likely require biopsy or polypectomy at the same procedure. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening

options.rationale: A normal haemoglobin and absence of symptoms do not negate a positive iFOBT result. Up to 50% of colorectal cancers detected by screening are in asymptomatic patients with normal haemoglobin. The purpose of screening is to detect preclinical disease. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening

options.rationale: Flexible sigmoidoscopy examines only the distal colon and would miss right-sided lesions, which account for approximately 30% of colorectal cancers. A positive iFOBT requires full colonoscopy to examine the entire colon. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening

options.rationale: All positive iFOBT results from the NBCSP require follow-up colonoscopy. Guidelines recommend colonoscopy within 30 days of a positive result to minimise diagnostic delay. Approximately 1 in 25 positive iFOBT results will detect colorectal cancer, and 1 in 6 will find advanced adenomas. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Bowel Cancer Screening

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in any man or postmenopausal woman should be considered secondary to GI blood loss until proven otherwise. The most important diagnosis to exclude is colorectal cancer. GESA guidelines recommend colonoscopy as the first-line investigation, with upper GI endoscopy if colonoscopy is normal. Bidirectional endoscopy (both upper and lower) in a single session is efficient and recommended by many centres. Even if a benign cause such as peptic ulcer disease is found on upper GI endoscopy, colonoscopy should still be performed to exclude a synchronous colorectal lesion.
key_points: Iron deficiency in men and postmenopausal women mandates GI investigation to exclude malignancy
Colonoscopy is the priority investigation followed by upper GI endoscopy if normal
Bidirectional endoscopy in a single session is the most efficient approach
Iron replacement should be commenced concurrently with investigation, not as an alternative
explanation.pearls: Approximately 10-15% of patients investigated for iron deficiency anaemia with bidirectional endoscopy have synchronous upper and lower GI pathology; this is why both investigations are recommended even if a single source is found at one site.

options.rationale: While iron replacement is needed, treating iron deficiency without investigating the cause in a man over 50 risks missing an underlying malignancy. Iron deficiency anaemia in any postmenopausal woman or any man warrants GI investigation before attributing it to dietary insufficiency. (Source: GESA: Iron Deficiency Anaemia)

While upper GI pathology (gastric cancer, peptic ulcer, Cameron lesion) is an important cause of iron deficiency, colonoscopy should be the priority investigation in a man of this age. Colorectal cancer is the most important diagnosis to exclude. Ideally both upper and lower GI investigations are performed. (Source: GESA: Iron Deficiency Anaemia)

CT may identify large masses but has poor sensitivity for mucosal lesions, flat polyps, and early-stage colorectal cancer. It also cannot biopsy lesions. Colonoscopy is the gold standard for evaluating iron deficiency anaemia as it allows direct visualisation and tissue sampling. (Source: GESA: Iron Deficiency Anaemia)

Iron deficiency anaemia in men and postmenopausal women mandates GI investigation to exclude malignancy. Colonoscopy is the priority investigation given the higher prevalence of colorectal cancer. If colonoscopy is normal, upper GI endoscopy should follow to assess for gastric cancer, peptic ulcer disease, and coeliac disease (despite negative serology, as duodenal biopsy is more sensitive). (Source: GESA: Iron Deficiency Anaemia)

Faecal calprotectin is useful for distinguishing inflammatory bowel disease from functional bowel disorders but does not screen for malignancy. In an older man with new iron deficiency, exclusion of colorectal cancer via colonoscopy is the priority regardless of calprotectin result. (Source: GESA: Iron Deficiency Anaemia)

explanation.summary: Australia has the highest incidence of melanoma globally. The ABCDE criteria (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution) guide clinical suspicion. Any suspicious pigmented lesion should undergo excision biopsy with a 2 mm clinical margin, preserving the ability to accurately measure Breslow thickness. The Breslow thickness determines definitive wide excision margins: in situ (5 mm), less than 1 mm (1 cm), 1-2 mm (1-2 cm), and greater than 2 mm (2 cm). Sentinel lymph node biopsy is considered for melanomas with Breslow thickness greater than 0.8 mm.
key_points: Excision biopsy with 2 mm margin is the gold standard initial investigation for suspected melanoma
Breslow thickness is the single most important prognostic factor
Definitive wide excision margins depend on Breslow thickness measured on the initial biopsy
Sentinel lymph node biopsy is considered for melanomas >0.8 mm Breslow thickness
explanation.pearls: Amelanotic melanoma accounts for approximately 5% of all melanomas and presents as a pink or red papule or nodule without significant pigmentation; it is frequently misdiagnosed as basal cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, or dermatofibroma, leading to delayed diagnosis and poorer outcomes.

options.rationale: A pigmented lesion meeting ABCDE criteria (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution) requires excision biopsy for histological assessment. The entire lesion should be excised with a 2 mm clinical margin to allow accurate Breslow thickness measurement, which determines definitive excision margins and staging. Incisional or punch biopsy may underestimate depth. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Guidelines)

Punch biopsy samples only a portion of the lesion and may miss the area of greatest Breslow thickness, potentially understaging the melanoma. Excision biopsy is preferred for pigmented lesions suspicious for melanoma as it allows complete histological assessment including accurate Breslow thickness measurement. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Guidelines)

A lesion with clear ABCDE criteria and documented change over 4 months should not be monitored. Monitoring delays diagnosis and risks progression. The clinical features are sufficiently suspicious to warrant immediate excision biopsy. Short-interval monitoring is appropriate for equivocal lesions, not for those meeting clinical criteria. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Guidelines)

Wide excision margins are determined by Breslow thickness, which can only be measured on the initial excision biopsy specimen. Performing wide excision without histological staging risks either inadequate or excessive margin, and may complicate reconstruction. The two-step approach (excision biopsy then definitive wide excision) is standard. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Guidelines)

While dermatology referral is appropriate, a 4-6 week wait is too long for a clinically suspicious melanoma. In general practice, if the GP is confident in performing excision biopsy, this should be done promptly rather than delaying for specialist review. If referral is needed, it should be urgent within 2 weeks. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) is the most common cause of secondary hypertension, affecting 5-10% of patients with resistant hypertension. The diagnostic pathway involves screening with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR), confirmatory testing (saline infusion test or oral sodium loading), adrenal CT for localisation, and adrenal venous sampling to distinguish unilateral adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia. Medications affecting the RAAS (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, beta-blockers) must be washed out or replaced with non-interfering agents (verapamil, prazosin) before confirmatory testing.
key_points: Screen with ARR in resistant hypertension, spontaneous hypokalaemia, or adrenal incidentaloma
Confirmatory testing (saline infusion or oral sodium loading) is mandatory before lateralisation
Adrenal venous sampling distinguishes unilateral adenoma (surgical) from bilateral hyperplasia (medical)
Spironolactone is first-line medical management for bilateral disease or non-surgical candidates
explanation.pearls: Hypokalaemia is present in only 30-40% of primary hyperaldosteronism cases; normokalaemic presentations are more common and ARR screening should not be restricted to hypokalaemic patients with resistant hypertension.

options.rationale: While adrenal CT is important for localisation, it should follow biochemical confirmation of primary hyperaldosteronism. CT alone cannot reliably distinguish between aldosterone-producing adenoma and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, which require different treatments. Confirmatory testing must precede imaging. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Aldosteronism)

The elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR >70 pmol/L per mIU/L with aldosterone >400 pmol/L) is consistent with primary hyperaldosteronism, but confirmatory testing is required before proceeding to lateralisation studies. The saline infusion test (2 L normal saline IV over 4 hours) is the most commonly used confirmatory test; failure to suppress aldosterone below 140 pmol/L confirms autonomous aldosterone production. Medications affecting the RAAS must be washed out or switched to non-interfering agents. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Aldosteronism)

Adrenal venous sampling is the gold standard for lateralisation of aldosterone excess, distinguishing unilateral adenoma (surgical) from bilateral hyperplasia (medical). However, it is performed after biochemical confirmation, not as the confirmatory test itself. It is an invasive procedure requiring interventional radiology expertise. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Aldosteronism)

24-hour urinary aldosterone after oral sodium loading is an alternative confirmatory test but is less commonly used than the saline infusion test due to patient compliance issues with the sodium-loading protocol. The saline infusion test is preferred in most Australian centres. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Aldosteronism)

While spironolactone is the first-line medical treatment for primary hyperaldosteronism, starting it without confirmatory testing precludes accurate diagnosis. If the patient has a unilateral adenoma, surgical cure with adrenalectomy may be possible and is preferred over lifelong medication. Proper workup should not be bypassed. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Aldosteronism)

explanation.summary: Prolactinomas are the most common functioning pituitary adenoma (40% of all pituitary tumours). They are classified as microprolactinomas (<10 mm) or macroprolactinomas (>=10 mm). Unlike other pituitary adenomas, the first-line treatment is medical: dopamine agonists (cabergoline or bromocriptine) normalise prolactin and shrink tumours in the majority of cases. Cabergoline is preferred due to superior efficacy and tolerability. Surgery is reserved for medical therapy failure or intolerance. Prolactin level generally correlates with tumour size: levels >5000 mIU/L suggest a macroprolactinoma.
key_points: Cabergoline is first-line for all prolactinomas with superior efficacy to bromocriptine
Dopamine agonists achieve tumour shrinkage in 80-90% of macroprolactinomas
Surgery is reserved for medical therapy failure, intolerance, or visual emergency
Prolactin level correlates with tumour size; a macroadenoma with mildly elevated prolactin suggests stalk effect rather than prolactinoma
explanation.pearls: The hook effect can cause falsely low prolactin levels in giant prolactinomas (>40 mm) due to antibody saturation in the immunoassay; if a large pituitary mass has only mildly elevated prolactin, the laboratory should be asked to repeat the assay with serial dilutions to unmask the true (very high) level.

options.rationale: Unlike other pituitary adenomas, prolactinomas are uniquely responsive to medical therapy with dopamine agonists, which achieve tumour shrinkage in 80-90% of cases. Surgery is reserved for medication intolerance, resistance, or visual compromise not responding to medical therapy. (Source: Endocrine Society: Prolactinoma Guidelines)

While bromocriptine is effective, cabergoline is preferred for prolactinomas due to its higher efficacy (normalises prolactin in 85% vs 65% for bromocriptine), better tolerability, and convenient twice-weekly dosing. Bromocriptine requires daily or twice-daily dosing with more frequent GI side effects. (Source: Endocrine Society: Prolactinoma Guidelines)

Cabergoline is the first-line treatment for all prolactinomas regardless of size. It normalises prolactin in approximately 85% of macroprolactinomas and achieves significant tumour shrinkage in 80-90%. Starting at 0.25 mg twice weekly with gradual titration minimises side effects (nausea, postural hypotension). Visual fields and MRI should be monitored during treatment. (Source: Endocrine Society: Prolactinoma Guidelines)

Radiosurgery is a third-line option reserved for prolactinomas resistant to dopamine agonists and not amenable to surgical cure. It carries risks of hypopituitarism and has a delayed onset of action. Medical therapy should be the first approach. (Source: Endocrine Society: Prolactinoma Guidelines)

A 14 mm macroprolactinoma with a prolactin of 8500 mIU/L causing amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea requires treatment. Observation risks tumour growth with potential optic chiasm compression. Untreated hypoestrogenism from hyperprolactinaemia causes bone density loss. (Source: Endocrine Society: Prolactinoma Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Primary hyperparathyroidism is characterised by hypercalcaemia with inappropriately elevated or non-suppressed PTH. The most common cause is a single parathyroid adenoma (85%). Elevated urinary calcium (>5.0 mmol/day) distinguishes primary hyperparathyroidism from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. Surgical indications per the Fourth International Workshop include: age <50, serum calcium >0.25 mmol/L above upper limit, T-score <-2.5 at any site, vertebral fracture, eGFR <60, or urinary calcium >10 mmol/day with stone risk. Parathyroidectomy has a cure rate exceeding 95%.
key_points: Elevated calcium with elevated PTH and elevated urinary calcium confirms primary hyperparathyroidism
Distal radius cortical bone is preferentially lost in hyperparathyroidism
Parathyroidectomy is indicated when any surgical criterion is met
24-hour urinary calcium distinguishes PHPT from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
explanation.pearls: The calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CaCr ratio) below 0.01 suggests familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia rather than primary hyperparathyroidism; a ratio above 0.02 favours PHPT, while 0.01-0.02 is indeterminate and genetic testing for CaSR mutations may be needed.

options.rationale: This patient has biochemically confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism (elevated calcium with inappropriately elevated PTH, elevated urinary calcium excluding FHH). She meets surgical criteria per the Fourth International Workshop: age under 50 years is one criterion, but she also meets criteria via T-score below -2.5 at any site and serum calcium >0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit of normal (2.82 - 2.60 = 0.22, borderline, but the distal radius T-score of -2.7 independently meets surgical criteria). Parathyroidectomy is the only curative treatment. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)

Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic that lowers calcium by inhibiting the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells. It is reserved for patients who meet surgical criteria but are unfit for or decline surgery, or for parathyroid carcinoma. It does not improve bone density or address the underlying adenoma. Surgery is preferred in surgical candidates. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)

Conservative monitoring is appropriate for patients who do not meet surgical criteria. This patient meets criteria (T-score below -2.5) and has significant bone loss at the cortical-predominant distal radius site, which is characteristically affected in hyperparathyroidism. Delaying surgery risks further bone loss and fracture. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)

While bisphosphonates can improve BMD in primary hyperparathyroidism, they do not address the underlying parathyroid adenoma, the hypercalcaemia, or its associated complications. Parathyroidectomy normalises calcium and improves BMD at all sites. Surgery is the preferred approach when criteria are met. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)

Thiazide diuretics are contraindicated in primary hyperparathyroidism as they reduce renal calcium excretion and can worsen hypercalcaemia. They are used in hypercalciuria from other causes but are the opposite of what is needed here. (Source: Endocrine Society: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)

explanation.summary: A clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) is a single clinical episode consistent with demyelination. The 2017 McDonald criteria allow MS diagnosis at CIS if MRI demonstrates dissemination in space (lesions in >=2 of 4 typical locations: periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) and dissemination in time (new lesion on follow-up MRI, simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, OR CSF oligoclonal bands). This patient meets criteria for MS at first presentation, allowing early treatment. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial established IV methylprednisolone as the acute treatment standard.
key_points: 2017 McDonald criteria allow MS diagnosis at first clinical episode with appropriate MRI and CSF findings
CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time
IV methylprednisolone hastens visual recovery in optic neuritis but does not alter long-term visual outcome
Oral prednisolone alone is contraindicated for optic neuritis due to increased relapse risk
explanation.pearls: Relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) persists after optic neuritis recovery even when visual acuity returns to 6/6, because the damaged optic nerve conducts impulses more slowly; this permanent finding can be the only clinical evidence of a previous episode when evaluating dissemination in time.

options.rationale: While she has had only one clinical episode (optic neuritis), the MRI demonstrates dissemination in space (periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial lesions) and CSF oligoclonal bands. Under the 2017 McDonald criteria, this meets the criteria for MS diagnosis, as CSF OCBs can substitute for dissemination in time. Early disease-modifying therapy is recommended to reduce relapse risk and disability accumulation. (Source: MSIF: McDonald Criteria 2017)

Acute optic neuritis with significant visual loss should be treated with IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3-5 days) to hasten visual recovery. Given the MRI findings meeting 2017 McDonald criteria for MS (dissemination in space on MRI plus CSF OCBs substituting for dissemination in time), early disease-modifying therapy should be commenced to reduce relapse risk and prevent disability accumulation. (Source: MSIF: McDonald Criteria 2017)

The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial demonstrated that oral prednisolone alone (without prior IV methylprednisolone) was associated with a higher relapse rate of optic neuritis than placebo. Oral steroids alone are not recommended for acute optic neuritis. IV methylprednisolone is the appropriate acute treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

The 2017 McDonald criteria allow CSF oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time, meaning a second MRI is not required to confirm the diagnosis in this patient. Waiting 6 months delays treatment and increases the risk of further relapses and disability. (Source: MSIF: McDonald Criteria 2017)

Plasma exchange is reserved for severe relapses (particularly myelitis or brainstem attacks) that fail to respond to IV methylprednisolone. It is not first-line for optic neuritis and should only be considered if IV steroids produce no improvement after 5 days. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord is caused by severe B12 deficiency affecting the posterior columns (loss of vibration and proprioception), lateral corticospinal tracts (upper motor neuron signs), and peripheral nerves (absent ankle reflexes). The paradoxical finding of absent ankle reflexes with brisk knee reflexes and extensor plantars reflects combined peripheral neuropathy and myelopathy. Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells) is confirmed by positive intrinsic factor antibodies. Urgent parenteral B12 replacement is essential as neurological damage may become irreversible if treatment is delayed.
key_points: Absent ankle reflexes with extensor plantars indicates combined peripheral neuropathy and myelopathy
Neurological involvement mandates parenteral rather than oral B12 replacement
Folic acid alone can mask haematological markers while neurological damage progresses
Intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific (close to 100%) but only 50-60% sensitive for pernicious anaemia
explanation.pearls: Neurological manifestations of B12 deficiency can occur before anaemia develops or with a normal MCV; up to 28% of patients with B12 deficiency neuropathy have a normal MCV, so a normal blood count does not exclude B12 deficiency as a cause of neurological symptoms.

options.rationale: While high-dose oral B12 can achieve adequate absorption through passive diffusion even without intrinsic factor, neurological involvement (subacute combined degeneration) is an indication for parenteral replacement. Intramuscular injections ensure rapid and reliable repletion, which is critical when neurological damage is progressing. Oral supplementation may be used for maintenance after neurological recovery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

Folic acid supplementation in the context of B12 deficiency can correct the anaemia but does NOT treat or prevent neurological damage, and may even mask the haematological markers of B12 deficiency while neurological deterioration continues. B12 must be replaced first or simultaneously, and folic acid alone is dangerous in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

Subacute combined degeneration with neurological involvement requires urgent parenteral B12 replacement. The standard Australian regimen is IM hydroxocobalamin 1000 microg on alternate days for 2 weeks (to rapidly replete stores and halt neurological progression), then every 3 months indefinitely for pernicious anaemia. Early treatment maximises the chance of neurological recovery, but established damage may be irreversible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

The anaemia is megaloblastic due to B12 deficiency and should respond to B12 replacement. Transfusion is not indicated at Hb 98 g/L without haemodynamic compromise. B12 replacement will stimulate erythropoiesis with a reticulocyte peak at 7-10 days. Iron is not indicated as this is not iron deficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

While MRI may show characteristic posterior and lateral column signal changes in subacute combined degeneration, treatment should not be delayed for imaging. The combination of severely low B12, megaloblastic anaemia, positive intrinsic factor antibodies, and the classic neurological triad (peripheral neuropathy, posterior column dysfunction, and pyramidal signs) is diagnostic. Delaying B12 replacement risks irreversible neurological damage. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: B12 Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis is the most common genetic condition in people of Northern European descent, with C282Y homozygosity present in approximately 1 in 200 Australians. Iron overload causes end-organ damage including liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, and hypogonadism. The diagnostic pathway is: elevated fasting transferrin saturation (>45%), HFE genotyping, then staging (ferritin level, liver fibrosis assessment). Venesection to maintain ferritin below 50-100 microg/L is the standard treatment and prevents further organ damage. The characteristic arthropathy affecting the 2nd and 3rd MCPs with hook-shaped osteophytes is a clinical clue.
key_points: Fasting transferrin saturation >45% on two occasions is the screening threshold for HFE genotyping
C282Y homozygosity confirms hereditary haemochromatosis in 85% of clinically affected Australians
Ferritin >1000 microg/L warrants assessment for hepatic fibrosis (MRI or biopsy)
Venesection targets ferritin below 50-100 microg/L and prevents further end-organ damage
explanation.pearls: The 2nd and 3rd MCP arthropathy of haemochromatosis is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition (pseudogout) triggered by iron-mediated chondrocyte damage; X-ray characteristically shows hook-shaped osteophytes and chondrocalcinosis, and the arthropathy may not improve with venesection as the joint damage is structural.

options.rationale: Liver biopsy was previously the gold standard but has been largely replaced by HFE genotyping for diagnosis and MRI for iron quantification. Biopsy is now reserved for staging fibrosis when ferritin exceeds 1000 microg/L in confirmed haemochromatosis, not as the initial diagnostic test. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis Guidelines)

MRI T2* (FerriScan) is useful for quantifying hepatic iron overload and can detect fibrosis, but it is a staging investigation performed after confirming the genetic diagnosis. The primary diagnostic test for suspected hereditary haemochromatosis is HFE genotyping. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis Guidelines)

Hepcidin testing is primarily a research tool and is not routinely available or recommended in clinical practice for haemochromatosis diagnosis. HFE genotyping is the standard diagnostic approach and is widely available and Medicare-rebated. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis Guidelines)

In a Northern European patient with elevated transferrin saturation (>45%) and elevated ferritin, HFE genotyping is the diagnostic test of choice. C282Y homozygosity confirms hereditary haemochromatosis (type 1) and is found in approximately 85% of clinically affected patients in Australia. Compound heterozygosity (C282Y/H63D) accounts for a smaller proportion. Testing is Medicare-rebated when transferrin saturation exceeds 45%. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis Guidelines)

HCC screening with ultrasound is important in established haemochromatosis with cirrhosis, but it is a surveillance tool rather than a diagnostic investigation. The priority is confirming the diagnosis with HFE genotyping, then assessing for end-organ damage including fibrosis staging and HCC risk. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle includes: measuring lactate, obtaining blood cultures before antibiotics, administering broad-spectrum antibiotics, beginning rapid crystalloid infusion for hypotension or elevated lactate, and applying vasopressors if hypotension persists. For severe community-acquired pneumonia in Australia, the recommended empiric regimen is IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Early recognition and aggressive management within the first hour significantly reduce mortality.
key_points: Blood cultures must be obtained before antibiotics but should not delay antibiotic administration beyond 1 hour
30 mL/kg IV crystalloid is the recommended initial fluid bolus for sepsis-induced hypotension
Lactate above 4 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion and triggers aggressive fluid resuscitation
Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the Australian guideline-recommended empiric regimen for severe CAP
explanation.pearls: Serial lactate measurements (at least every 2-4 hours) guide resuscitation adequacy in sepsis - a lactate clearance of at least 20% in the first 2 hours is associated with improved mortality outcomes.

options.rationale: This patient has sepsis (suspected infection with organ dysfunction) likely secondary to community-acquired pneumonia. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle mandates: (1) blood cultures before antibiotics, (2) broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, (3) IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate 4 mmol/L or above, (4) reassess haemodynamic status and lactate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic)

Flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is an inappropriate antibiotic combination for community-acquired pneumonia. Flucloxacillin covers Staphylococcus aureus but not the typical CAP pathogens. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the Australian guideline-recommended regimen for severe CAP. CT chest is not urgently needed when CXR shows consolidation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic)

This patient has sepsis with hypotension and elevated lactate, requiring aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg) and IV antibiotics. Oral amoxicillin alone is appropriate for mild CAP, not severe sepsis. A 500 mL infusion over 2 hours is grossly inadequate. (Source: ANZICS - Sepsis Management)

Vasopressors should not be commenced before adequate volume resuscitation. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid as the initial resuscitation fluid, with vasopressors added if hypotension persists despite fluid resuscitation. (Source: ANZICS - Sepsis Management)

Piperacillin-tazobactam is broader than necessary for initial empiric treatment of severe CAP in a patient without healthcare-associated risk factors. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin provides appropriate coverage. Urgent bronchoscopy is not indicated and would delay essential resuscitation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: The diagnostic workup for Cushing syndrome follows a stepwise approach: (1) confirm hypercortisolism with at least two concordant first-line screening tests (overnight 1 mg DST, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or late-night salivary cortisol), (2) determine ACTH-dependence with plasma ACTH measurement, (3) localise the source with imaging, and (4) differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH if needed. Exogenous glucocorticoid use must be excluded before testing. The clinical features in this case are highly suggestive of endogenous Cushing syndrome.
key_points: The 1 mg overnight DST is the most widely used first-line screening test for Cushing syndrome
At least two concordant positive screening tests are needed before proceeding to further investigation
Exogenous glucocorticoid use including inhaled, topical, and intra-articular must be excluded before testing
Imaging should only be performed after biochemical confirmation to avoid incidentaloma confusion
explanation.pearls: The 1 mg overnight DST has a false-positive rate of approximately 5% - common causes include depression, alcohol excess, obesity, oral oestrogen therapy (increases cortisol-binding globulin), and shift work disrupting the HPA axis circadian rhythm.

options.rationale: A random morning cortisol has very poor sensitivity and specificity for Cushing syndrome because cortisol has a pulsatile diurnal secretion pattern and can be normal even in Cushing syndrome. It does not assess the loss of normal diurnal variation or suppressibility. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test is one of the recommended first-line screening tests for Cushing syndrome. The patient takes dexamethasone 1 mg at 11 pm and serum cortisol is measured at 8 am the next morning. A cortisol level below 50 nmol/L essentially excludes Cushing syndrome. Abnormal results require confirmation with additional tests. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

Pituitary MRI is used to localise the source of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome AFTER biochemical confirmation. Imaging before biochemical confirmation risks identifying incidental pituitary lesions (present in up to 10% of the population) and leading to inappropriate surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society - Cushing Syndrome Guidelines)

Plasma ACTH measurement is the second step in the diagnostic workup, used to differentiate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome. It is performed after biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism, not as the initial screening test. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is a later step used to distinguish pituitary Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH secretion. It is performed after hypercortisolism is confirmed and ACTH-dependence established, not as an initial screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society - Cushing Syndrome Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The duration of anticoagulation for VTE depends primarily on whether the event was provoked or unprovoked and the patient's bleeding risk. Provoked VTE requires 3 months. Unprovoked proximal DVT carries a high recurrence risk after cessation, and extended therapy is recommended if bleeding risk is acceptable. After the initial treatment period, dose reduction to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily provides effective secondary prevention as demonstrated in the EINSTEIN CHOICE and AMPLIFY-EXT trials.
key_points: Unprovoked proximal DVT carries approximately 10% annual recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation
Extended DOAC therapy at reduced dose is recommended for unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk
Rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or apixaban 2.5 mg BD are the evidence-based reduced doses for extended prevention
Annual reassessment of bleeding risk and patient preference should guide continuation decisions
explanation.pearls: The EINSTEIN CHOICE trial demonstrated that rivaroxaban 10 mg daily reduced VTE recurrence by 70% compared with aspirin, with no significant increase in major bleeding - making reduced-dose DOAC the preferred extended prevention strategy.

sources.label: CHEST Guidelines - Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE

options.rationale: Three months is the minimum duration for proximal DVT, but the decision to extend depends on whether the VTE was provoked or unprovoked, bleeding risk, and patient preference. Unprovoked proximal DVT carries a 10% annual recurrence risk after cessation. Extended therapy is generally recommended if bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Haematology)

DOACs are preferred over warfarin for most patients with VTE due to non-inferior efficacy, lower bleeding risk, and no requirement for INR monitoring. There is no reason to switch this patient from rivaroxaban to warfarin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Haematology)

For unprovoked proximal DVT with low bleeding risk, extended anticoagulation is recommended. After the initial treatment period, DOAC dose reduction for extended secondary prevention is supported by the EINSTEIN CHOICE trial (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily). These reduced doses maintain significant recurrence reduction with a lower bleeding profile. Annual reassessment is essential. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Haematology)

Aspirin provides modest (approximately 30%) reduction in VTE recurrence, significantly inferior to reduced-dose DOAC therapy (approximately 70-80% reduction). Aspirin is considered only when anticoagulation is contraindicated or refused. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Haematology)

While elevated D-dimer after cessation is associated with increased recurrence risk, current Australian practice for unprovoked proximal DVT with low bleeding risk favours extended anticoagulation rather than a stop-and-test strategy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Haematology)

explanation.summary: Adult bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency requiring immediate empiric antibiotics and adjunctive dexamethasone. Dexamethasone commenced before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality by approximately 50% in pneumococcal meningitis. Empiric therapy with ceftriaxone plus vancomycin covers both sensitive and resistant pneumococci. Asplenia is a major risk factor for overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated organisms, with Streptococcus pneumoniae being the most common pathogen.
key_points: Dexamethasone must be given before or with the first dose of antibiotics for pneumococcal meningitis
Empiric ceftriaxone plus vancomycin provides coverage for penicillin-resistant pneumococci
CSF glucose to serum glucose ratio below 0.4 strongly suggests bacterial meningitis
Asplenic patients are at extreme risk of OPSI from encapsulated organisms
explanation.pearls: The survival benefit of adjunctive dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis is only proven for Streptococcus pneumoniae - if cultures identify a different organism, dexamethasone should be discontinued as it may reduce CNS antibiotic penetration without providing benefit.

sources.label: IDSA - Practice Guidelines for Bacterial Meningitis
de Gans J et al. NEJM 2002 - Dexamethasone in Bacterial Meningitis

options.rationale: While ceftriaxone is appropriate, this answer omits adjunctive dexamethasone (which reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis) and vancomycin (needed empirically in a post-splenectomy patient to cover penicillin-resistant pneumococci). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic)

While benzylpenicillin covers penicillin-sensitive pneumococci and dexamethasone is appropriate, penicillin alone does not provide adequate coverage for potentially resistant organisms. In a post-splenectomy patient, the consequences of treatment failure are catastrophic. Empiric therapy should include ceftriaxone plus vancomycin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic)

Meropenem is not first-line empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis. It is reserved for specific situations such as Listeria cover or beta-lactam allergy scenarios. The standard empiric regimen is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic)

The CSF confirms pneumococcal meningitis. Management requires: (1) IV dexamethasone 10 mg given before or with the first dose of antibiotics, which reduces mortality by 50% in pneumococcal meningitis (de Gans trial), (2) IV ceftriaxone as the primary antibiotic, (3) IV vancomycin added empirically for potential penicillin resistance in this asplenic patient, and (4) dexamethasone continued for 4 days. Dexamethasone should be ceased if a non-pneumococcal organism is identified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic)

Ampicillin for Listeria is indicated in patients over 50 or immunocompromised, but the Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci - diagnostic for Streptococcus pneumoniae, not Listeria (Gram-positive rods). Vancomycin to cover potential resistance is more important than Listeria coverage given the confirmed organism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency that occurs when glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency results in cardiovascular collapse. Common precipitants include intercurrent illness, surgery, and medication non-adherence. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat is the cornerstone of treatment, providing both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity at high doses. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation corrects hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia. Prevention through patient education about sick-day rules and provision of emergency injection kits is essential.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity in crisis
Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely as stress-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid effect
Aggressive IV normal saline is critical for hypovolaemia correction
All patients with adrenal insufficiency should have an emergency IM hydrocortisone injection kit at home
explanation.pearls: Patients with Addison disease should be educated on sick day rules: double the oral hydrocortisone dose for febrile illness, triple it for severe illness, and administer IM hydrocortisone 100 mg if unable to take oral medications - then present to the emergency department.

options.rationale: This patient is in acute adrenal crisis with shock, reduced consciousness, and inability to tolerate oral medications. Oral replacement is completely inadequate. Parenteral stress-dose hydrocortisone is required urgently. Doubling the usual oral dose is for minor illness only. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

Hydrocortisone is the preferred glucocorticoid in adrenal crisis because it provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity at stress doses. Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and would not address the aldosterone deficiency component of primary adrenal insufficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

The hydrocortisone dose is suboptimal (100 mg is the standard stress dose, not 50 mg) and commencing vasopressors before adequate volume resuscitation is incorrect. Hypotension in adrenal crisis is primarily due to volume depletion. Volume resuscitation is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

There is no IV formulation of fludrocortisone. IV hydrocortisone at stress doses (100 mg) provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity to address the aldosterone deficiency in the acute setting. Oral fludrocortisone is resumed once the patient can tolerate oral medications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

Adrenal crisis management requires: (1) IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat followed by 50 mg IV 6-8 hourly, (2) aggressive IV 0.9% sodium chloride (typically 1 L in the first hour), (3) IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia, (4) identification and treatment of the precipitating cause (gastroenteritis). Once stabilised, taper to oral hydrocortisone at double the usual dose, resume fludrocortisone, and arrange an emergency injection kit and sick-day education. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Sepsis with organ dysfunction requires activation of the hour-1 bundle. The three immediate priorities are blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 1 hour, and crystalloid resuscitation at 30 mL/kg for hypotension or elevated lactate. Delays in antibiotic administration are associated with increased mortality. Source control should be identified and addressed as soon as feasible.
key_points: Blood cultures before antibiotics but never delay antibiotics beyond 1 hour
30 mL/kg IV crystalloid for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or lactate >=4 mmol/L
Reassess haemodynamics after initial fluid bolus to determine vasopressor need
Lactate clearance is a key marker of resuscitation adequacy
explanation.pearls: Each hour of delay in antibiotic administration in septic shock is associated with approximately 4% increase in mortality per the Kumar 2006 landmark study, reinforcing the non-negotiable 1-hour target.

options.rationale: Delaying treatment for radiological confirmation is inappropriate in a patient meeting sepsis criteria with organ dysfunction. The clinical presentation is sufficient to initiate empiric therapy while investigations proceed concurrently. Imaging should not delay resuscitation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vasopressors are indicated in septic shock refractory to fluid resuscitation. The initial priority is volume resuscitation with 30 mL/kg crystalloid. Starting vasopressors before adequate fluid loading is premature. Prolonged noradrenaline infusion ideally requires central venous access. (Source: ANZICS; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle mandates blood cultures before antibiotics, IV antibiotics within 1 hour, and initiation of 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >=4 mmol/L. Cultures should be drawn first but must not delay antibiotic administration beyond the 1-hour window. This patient has septic shock (hypotension, lactate 4.2, organ dysfunction) requiring immediate parallel resuscitation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Urinary catheterisation for monitoring is reasonable but is not the initial priority. Fluid resuscitation and empiric antibiotics take precedence in the hour-1 bundle. Monitoring interventions should be established concurrently, not sequentially before treatment. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Oral antibiotics are inappropriate in septic shock - IV administration is required for reliable bioavailability in patients with haemodynamic compromise and potential gut hypoperfusion. The volume of fluid (500 mL) is also inadequate; 30 mL/kg is the recommended initial bolus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZICS)

explanation.summary: Fluid-refractory septic shock requires vasopressor initiation targeting a MAP of 65 mmHg or above. Noradrenaline is the universally recommended first-line agent due to its favourable balance of vasoconstrictive and inotropic effects. The VASST and VANISH trials established vasopressin as adjunctive rather than first-line. Ongoing fluid responsiveness should be assessed dynamically rather than by administering fixed additional volumes.
key_points: Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor for septic shock in all major guidelines
Target MAP >=65 mmHg with vasopressor titration
Vasopressin is adjunctive, typically added at noradrenaline 0.25-0.5 mcg/kg/min
Rising lactate despite fluid resuscitation signals inadequate tissue perfusion requiring escalation
explanation.pearls: Noradrenaline can be commenced via peripheral IV access for up to 24 hours if central access is delayed, as supported by the PEPPER trial, though central access should be obtained as soon as practicable.

options.rationale: Adrenaline is a second-line vasopressor in septic shock, reserved for patients failing noradrenaline. It carries higher risk of tachyarrhythmias and may increase lactate through beta-2 stimulation, confounding lactate-guided resuscitation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor for septic shock per the Surviving Sepsis Campaign and ANZICS guidelines. It provides potent alpha-1 vasoconstriction with mild beta-1 inotropic effect. This patient has fluid-refractory septic shock (persistent hypotension after 30 mL/kg) and central access is established, making immediate noradrenaline initiation appropriate. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; ANZICS)

The initial 30 mL/kg fluid bolus has been completed and the patient remains hypotensive with rising lactate, indicating fluid-refractory shock. Excessive fluid beyond 30 mL/kg without reassessment risks pulmonary oedema and worsening organ dysfunction. Vasopressors should be initiated when hypotension persists after adequate initial resuscitation. (Source: ANZICS; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Vasopressin is recommended as an adjunctive agent to noradrenaline, typically added when noradrenaline requirements exceed 0.25-0.5 mcg/kg/min. It is not recommended as the sole first-line vasopressor in septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist that may reduce cardiac output. It is generally avoided in septic shock unless there are specific contraindications to noradrenaline such as significant tachyarrhythmia. It is not appropriate as first-line management. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; ANZICS)

explanation.summary: Migraine prophylaxis is indicated when attacks occur 4 or more days per month or cause significant disability. Australian first-line options include propranolol, amitriptyline, and topiramate. Drug selection must account for comorbidities and contraindications. Recurrent nephrolithiasis is a relative contraindication to topiramate, and reproductive-age considerations weigh against valproate.
key_points: Prophylaxis indicated with >=4 migraine days per month or significant functional impairment
Propranolol is preferred when topiramate is contraindicated and no coexisting depression
Topiramate increases nephrolithiasis risk via carbonic anhydrase inhibition
Valproate requires pregnancy prevention program in women of childbearing potential
explanation.pearls: Propranolol 80-160 mg daily reduces migraine frequency by approximately 50% in responders, with onset of benefit typically at 4-6 weeks; a 3-month trial at therapeutic dose is recommended before deeming it ineffective.

options.rationale: Topiramate is effective for migraine prophylaxis but is associated with nephrolithiasis. In a patient with recurrent calcium oxalate stones, topiramate increases stone risk through carbonic anhydrase inhibition causing metabolic acidosis and hypocitraturia. This makes it a poor choice despite its proven efficacy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; AMH)

Amitriptyline is a reasonable prophylactic option particularly when migraine coexists with tension-type headache, insomnia, or depression. However, in the absence of these comorbidities it is not preferred over propranolol as first-line, given its anticholinergic side-effect burden including sedation, dry mouth, and weight gain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Valproate is effective in migraine prophylaxis but carries significant teratogenic risk in women of childbearing age. Australian guidelines recommend against its use in this population unless no alternative exists and pregnancy prevention measures are in place via the valproate safety program. Its side-effect profile also includes weight gain and tremor. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Propranolol is a first-line migraine prophylactic agent with strong evidence. In this patient, it avoids the nephrolithiasis risk of topiramate, the teratogenic risk of valproate, and the anticholinergic burden of amitriptyline. There are no contraindications such as asthma, bradycardia, or peripheral vascular disease. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend beta-blockers as first-line options for episodic migraine prevention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; AMH)

Pizotifen is a second-line option for migraine prophylaxis in Australia. Its main limitation is significant weight gain due to appetite stimulation. Given that more effective first-line options without this side effect are available, it would not be the preferred initial choice. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Cluster attacks peak within minutes, so an abortive treatment has to act fast: high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask and subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg are the two first-line options, and intranasal zolmitriptan is the alternative when injection is impractical. Oral triptans and simple analgesics are too slow to be useful. Subcutaneous sumatriptan is limited to two doses in 24 hours and is contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension and previous stroke, so the cardiovascular history is checked before it is supplied. In context: patients often have several attacks a day within a bout, which is why an abortive that can be carried and repeated matters practically, and why a preventer is started at the same time rather than relying on abortives alone.
key_points: Subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg and high-flow oxygen are the two first-line abortives
Maximum two subcutaneous doses in 24 hours
Oral triptans and simple analgesia act too slowly for cluster attacks
Screen for ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension and prior stroke before a triptan
explanation.pearls: A complete and reliable response to indometacin points away from cluster headache and towards paroxysmal hemicrania, the short unilateral autonomic headache most easily mistaken for it.

options.rationale: Subcutaneous sumatriptan relieves most cluster attacks within about fifteen minutes and is the portable first-line abortive where oxygen is not available, limited to two doses in 24 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Oral triptans suit migraine, where pain builds over an hour or more. Absorption is too slow for an attack that peaks in ten minutes and resolves within the hour. (Source: AMH: Sumatriptan)

A short corticosteroid course is transitional cover while a preventer is titrated, not an abortive for an individual attack, and it cannot be used for a whole bout. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
A complete response to indometacin defines paroxysmal hemicrania, which gives shorter attacks many times a day. It does not abort cluster attacks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Opioids are reserved for pain without a specific abortive treatment. In cluster headache they act too slowly, risk dependence in a recurrent condition and are explicitly discouraged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: GCA is a medical emergency when visual symptoms are present. Untreated, it risks permanent bilateral blindness from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. High-dose corticosteroids should be commenced immediately on clinical suspicion. Temporal artery biopsy provides histological confirmation but remains diagnostic for up to 2 weeks after treatment initiation. A prior diagnosis of PMR increases the pre-test probability of GCA substantially.
key_points: Commence high-dose prednisolone immediately on clinical suspicion of GCA
Temporal artery biopsy remains positive for up to 2 weeks after starting steroids
Amaurosis fugax is a warning sign of impending permanent vision loss in GCA
PMR and GCA exist on the same disease spectrum with significant overlap
explanation.pearls: Jaw claudication has the highest positive likelihood ratio (LR+ 4.2) of any individual symptom for GCA, and its presence with new headache and raised inflammatory markers in a patient over 50 warrants same-day corticosteroid initiation.

options.rationale: Temporal artery biopsy is important for diagnostic confirmation but must not delay treatment. Biopsy remains positive for up to 2 weeks after commencing corticosteroids. In a patient with visual symptoms suggesting threatened vision loss, treatment must begin immediately. (Source: RACGP; BSR/BHPR Guidelines for GCA)

Prednisolone 15 mg daily is grossly inadequate for GCA, particularly with visual symptoms suggesting impending vision loss. Standard induction dose for GCA without visual loss is 40-60 mg daily; with visual symptoms, IV methylprednisolone is often warranted. This dose would inadequately suppress the arteritic inflammation. (Source: BSR/BHPR Guidelines for GCA; Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Tocilizumab is an evidence-based steroid-sparing agent for GCA used as adjunctive therapy to reduce relapse and cumulative steroid exposure. However, it is not appropriate as initial monotherapy and does not provide the rapid anti-inflammatory effect needed to prevent imminent vision loss. High-dose corticosteroids remain the immediate treatment. (Source: BSR/BHPR Guidelines for GCA)

While imaging modalities including CTA and temporal artery ultrasound can support the diagnosis of GCA, they should not delay treatment initiation. The amaurosis fugax episode indicates threatened vision, and any delay risks permanent bilateral vision loss. Investigations should proceed in parallel with treatment. (Source: RACGP; BSR/BHPR Guidelines for GCA)

High-dose prednisolone (1 mg/kg up to 60 mg daily) must be commenced immediately when GCA is clinically suspected, without waiting for biopsy confirmation. The episode of amaurosis fugax indicates threatened visual loss. Some guidelines recommend IV methylprednisolone for established visual symptoms, but high-dose oral prednisolone is the minimum standard. Biopsy should be arranged within 2 weeks as histological findings remain interpretable. (Source: BSR/BHPR Guidelines for GCA; Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology; RACGP)

explanation.summary: Early Parkinson's disease management in younger patients aims to balance symptom control against long-term motor complication risk. MAO-B inhibitors provide mild symptomatic benefit with a favourable side-effect profile. Levodopa remains the most effective drug but is typically reserved until symptoms are functionally limiting, especially in patients under 60 where motor complications develop earlier. Treatment should be individualised based on symptom severity, age, and patient preference.
key_points: MAO-B inhibitors are appropriate initial monotherapy for mild early PD in younger patients
Levodopa is most effective but associated with earlier motor complications in younger patients
Dopamine agonists carry impulse control disorder risk requiring specific counselling
Treatment escalation to levodopa is indicated when symptoms become functionally limiting
explanation.pearls: Rasagiline 1 mg daily demonstrated a possible disease-modifying effect in the ADAGIO trial (delayed-start design), though this remains debated; its primary role is symptomatic benefit with a clean side-effect profile in early disease.

options.rationale: Levodopa is the most effective symptomatic treatment for Parkinson's disease but is associated with earlier development of motor complications such as dyskinesia and wearing-off, particularly in younger patients. For a 51-year-old with mild symptoms, initiating high-dose levodopa early increases long-term motor complication risk. It is generally reserved for when symptoms become functionally limiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG71)

MAO-B inhibitors such as rasagiline are appropriate initial monotherapy for early Parkinson's disease with mild symptoms, particularly in younger patients. They provide modest symptomatic benefit while potentially delaying the need for levodopa. This aligns with the patient's preference to delay motor complications. Regular follow-up is essential to step up treatment when symptoms become functionally limiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG71)

Anticholinergics such as benzhexol may help tremor but carry significant side effects including cognitive impairment, urinary retention, and constipation. They are generally avoided in patients over 40 due to central nervous system effects and are considered second-line to other agents. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole are a reasonable alternative in younger patients. However, they carry notable risks including impulse control disorders, excessive daytime somnolence, and hallucinations. For mild symptoms where an MAO-B inhibitor provides adequate control, the favourable side-effect profile of rasagiline makes it the preferred initial choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG71)

Amantadine has mild antiparkinsonian effects and is sometimes used as early monotherapy. However, it is less effective than MAO-B inhibitors and dopamine agonists. Its primary role in Parkinson's management is as an adjunct for levodopa-induced dyskinesia in later disease stages. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Lewy body dementia is characterised by fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behaviour disorder. Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line treatment for both cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Antipsychotic hypersensitivity is a cardinal feature, making most antipsychotics dangerous. The preserved medial temporal lobes on MRI help distinguish DLB from Alzheimer's disease, where hippocampal atrophy is typically prominent.
key_points: Rivastigmine is first-line for hallucinations in DLB
Antipsychotic sensitivity is a core feature of DLB causing severe adverse reactions
If antipsychotics are absolutely necessary, quetiapine at ultra-low doses is the least hazardous option
REM sleep behaviour disorder may precede cognitive symptoms by years in DLB
explanation.pearls: Postural hypotension (systolic drop >=20 mmHg) occurs in up to 50% of DLB patients due to autonomic dysfunction and should be assessed before initiating cholinesterase inhibitors, which may exacerbate it via vagotonic effects.

options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol are absolutely contraindicated in Lewy body dementia. Patients with DLB have extreme sensitivity to antipsychotics, which can cause severe parkinsonism, irreversible decline, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and increased mortality. This is a critical safety concern in DLB management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG97)

While olanzapine has lower D2 receptor affinity than haloperidol, it still carries significant risk of severe adverse reactions in DLB. All antipsychotics with significant dopamine receptor blockade should be avoided. Olanzapine also causes metabolic side effects and excessive sedation in this population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG97)

Quetiapine is sometimes cautiously used in DLB when hallucinations are severely distressing because of its lower D2 affinity. However, it is not first-line; cholinesterase inhibitors are the recommended initial approach. Quetiapine still carries risk in DLB and should only be considered if cholinesterase inhibitors fail and the risk-benefit balance favours cautious use. (Source: NICE NG97; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Cholinesterase inhibitors, particularly rivastigmine, are first-line treatment for cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms in DLB, including visual hallucinations. Rivastigmine has the best evidence in DLB and can reduce hallucination frequency and severity without worsening parkinsonism. The cholinergic deficit in DLB is more profound than in Alzheimer's disease, making these agents particularly effective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG97)

Valproate has no role in treating hallucinations associated with Lewy body dementia. It does not address the underlying cholinergic deficit. It carries risks of sedation, ataxia, and hepatotoxicity in older adults and would add to falls risk in a patient with parkinsonism and postural hypotension. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Cancer-associated thrombosis management has evolved from LMWH-only to include DOACs as first-line options in appropriate patients. The key consideration is the site of malignancy - GI and genitourinary cancers carry higher GI bleeding risk with DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban. Apixaban has the most favourable safety data from the Caravaggio trial. Anticoagulation duration is typically a minimum of 6 months and often extended while cancer remains active.
key_points: DOACs are now first-line for cancer-associated VTE in non-GI malignancies
Apixaban has the best safety profile among DOACs for cancer-associated VTE (Caravaggio trial)
GI and genitourinary cancers should receive LMWH due to DOAC-associated GI bleeding risk
Anticoagulation is typically continued while cancer is active or during chemotherapy
explanation.pearls: The Caravaggio trial demonstrated apixaban was non-inferior to dalteparin for cancer-associated VTE recurrence (5.6% vs 7.9%) with no significant difference in major bleeding (3.8% vs 4.0%), making it the preferred DOAC for this indication.

options.rationale: Warfarin is inferior to both LMWH and DOACs for cancer-associated thrombosis. The CLOT trial demonstrated LMWH superiority over warfarin, and subsequent trials have shown DOACs are non-inferior to LMWH with better convenience. Warfarin is also poorly suited to oncology patients due to drug interactions with chemotherapy and variable absorption. (Source: eviQ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

While LMWH was previously the standard for cancer-associated thrombosis based on the CLOT trial, the SELECT-D and Caravaggio trials have established DOACs as a convenient alternative with equivalent efficacy in non-GI cancers. Daily subcutaneous injections for 6 months impose substantial burden on patients already managing chemotherapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; eviQ)

DOACs are now recommended for cancer-associated VTE in patients without GI or genitourinary tract cancers due to equivalent efficacy and improved convenience over LMWH. The Caravaggio trial specifically demonstrated apixaban was non-inferior to dalteparin with no increased GI bleeding in a predominantly non-GI cancer population. For lung cancer without GI involvement, apixaban is the preferred option per Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; eviQ; Caravaggio trial)

Rivaroxaban is an effective DOAC for cancer-associated VTE but showed increased GI bleeding in the SELECT-D trial compared with dalteparin. While both rivaroxaban and apixaban are options in non-GI cancers, apixaban demonstrated a more favourable bleeding profile in the Caravaggio trial. The bleeding signal with rivaroxaban makes apixaban the preferred DOAC. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; SELECT-D trial)

UFH requires hospital admission and continuous monitoring. It offers no advantage over LMWH or DOACs in cancer-associated VTE and is only preferred when there is severe renal impairment, high bleeding risk requiring rapid reversibility, or planned invasive procedures. This patient has preserved renal function and no indication for UFH. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; eviQ)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated Type B aortic dissection is managed medically with anti-impulse therapy targeting heart rate below 60 bpm and systolic BP below 120 mmHg. IV beta-blockers are first-line. Vasodilators without prior beta-blockade are contraindicated due to reflex tachycardia. Surgical or endovascular intervention is reserved for complicated dissections featuring malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, or uncontrolled hypertension.
key_points: IV beta-blocker is first-line for uncomplicated Type B dissection
Target HR <60 bpm and SBP <120 mmHg to reduce aortic wall shear stress
Vasodilators without beta-blockade worsen outcomes through reflex tachycardia
Complicated features triggering intervention include malperfusion, rupture, or refractory symptoms
explanation.pearls: Labetalol combines alpha-1 and beta-adrenergic blockade in a ratio of approximately 1:3, making it particularly suited to aortic dissection as it simultaneously reduces heart rate and afterload without the reflex tachycardia seen with pure vasodilators.

options.rationale: Uncomplicated Type B aortic dissection is managed medically with anti-impulse therapy. Endovascular repair (TEVAR) is reserved for complicated dissections with malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, or uncontrollable hypertension. This patient has no features of a complicated dissection. (Source: CSANZ; BMJ Best Practice: Aortic Dissection)

Sodium nitroprusside reduces afterload but causes reflex tachycardia, which increases aortic wall shear stress and may worsen dissection propagation. It should only be used as an adjunct after adequate heart rate control with a beta-blocker has been achieved. Monotherapy with nitroprusside is contraindicated. (Source: CSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Hydralazine is a direct vasodilator that causes reflex tachycardia, increasing aortic wall stress. Like nitroprusside, it should not be used without prior beta-blockade. The target systolic BP in acute dissection is below 120 mmHg, not 140 mmHg. (Source: CSANZ; BMJ Best Practice: Aortic Dissection)

ACE inhibitors do not provide the rapid heart rate reduction critical in aortic dissection. While pain control with opioids is appropriate, the primary haemodynamic goal is reduction of aortic wall shear stress through heart rate AND blood pressure control, which requires a beta-blocker as the first agent. (Source: CSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Anti-impulse therapy with IV beta-blockade is first-line for uncomplicated Type B aortic dissection. Labetalol (combined alpha and beta blocker) or esmolol are preferred. The target is heart rate below 60 bpm and systolic BP below 120 mmHg to minimise aortic wall shear stress and reduce dissection propagation risk. Pain control with IV opioids is concurrent. (Source: CSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; BMJ Best Practice: Aortic Dissection)

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture with a femoral neck T-score of -2.7 requires antiresorptive therapy, but documented erosive oesophagitis is a contraindication to every oral bisphosphonate, not a reason to try a different tablet. Annual intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg is the standard alternative and needs an eGFR of at least 35 mL/min, corrected vitamin D and calcium before infusion, and warning about the acute phase reaction that follows the first dose in about a third of patients. In context, the choice between an oral and a parenteral antiresorptive in Australia is driven by upper gastrointestinal disease, renal function, adherence and the patient's willingness to attend for an infusion, not by fracture site.
key_points: Erosive oesophagitis contraindicates all oral bisphosphonates.
Zoledronic acid needs an eGFR of at least 35 mL/min.
Replete vitamin D and calcium before an infusion.
Warn about the flu-like acute phase reaction after the first dose.
explanation.pearls: Paracetamol taken before and for two days after the first zoledronic acid infusion substantially reduces the acute phase reaction and makes the second infusion far easier to sell.

sources.label: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline
